Formula: Net obligation of participant i = sum of amounts due to i minus sum of amounts due from i (per instrument/currency); only the residual is settled.
Relationships: Clearinghouse, Novation, Settlement, Settlement cycle, Delivery versus payment
Failure modes: Netting concentrates and redistributes risk into the netting system: its legal enforceability in insolvency is critical (close-out netting rights), and netting reduces gross exposures while leaving the net exposure to the CCP intact.
Misconceptions: Netting does not cancel economic exposure or P&L — positions and market risk remain; only the settlement flows are compressed.
Example: If a bank's futures desk buys 1,000 contracts and sells 950 of the same contract during the day, the clearinghouse settles margin and variation on the net 50-contract position rather than processing 1,950 gross deliveries.
Citation: BIS CPMI, Glossary of payments and market infrastructure terminology — https://www.bis.org/cpmi/publ/d00b.htm (Netting; bilateral netting; multilateral netting)
Citation: CFTC Futures Glossary — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Derivatives Clearing Organization (settlement or netting of obligations))
Status: Reviewed

0062. Novation
Domain: Market foundations
Definition: The legal substitution, upon clearing, of the original contract between buyer and seller with two new contracts in which the central counterparty becomes the buyer to the seller and the seller to the buyer. Novation replaces mutual counterparty exposure among traders with exposure to the clearinghouse.
Intuition: Once your trade clears, the person on the other side legally disappears — your contract is now with the clearinghouse, and so is theirs.
Mechanics: When a trade is accepted for clearing, the clearing organization discharges the original bilateral contract and creates matched contracts with itself as central counterparty; this enables multilateral netting and lets either party exit by offsetting, regardless of the original counterparty's identity.
Relationships: Clearinghouse, Netting, Settlement, Over-the-counter market
Failure modes: Novation centralizes credit risk in the CCP, so its benefit depends entirely on the CCP's risk management; in legal disputes, whether and when novation occurred (trade acceptance timing) can determine who bears a default.
Misconceptions: Novation does not make markets risk-free — it substitutes a single, well-collateralized counterparty for many bilateral ones — and uncleared (bilateral) trades never receive this substitution.
Example: Two CME clearing members execute a Eurodollar futures trade with each other; upon clearing, CME Clearing becomes the seller to the buyer and the buyer to the seller, and the members no longer bear each other's credit risk.
Citation: BIS CPMI, Glossary of payments and market infrastructure terminology — https://www.bis.org/cpmi/publ/d00b.htm (Novation; central counterparty)
Citation: CFTC Futures Glossary — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Derivatives Clearing Organization (substitution through novation); Clearing)
Status: Reviewed

0063. Delivery versus payment
Domain: Market foundations
Definition: A securities settlement mechanism that links the transfer of securities to the transfer of funds so that delivery occurs if and only if payment occurs, eliminating principal risk — the risk of delivering securities without receiving the money, or vice versa.
Intuition: The shares and the cash swap hands atomically: neither side can end up having given away its asset without receiving the other side of the deal.
Mechanics: The settlement system conditions the final transfer of securities on the final transfer of funds within the same process (e.g., DTC book-entry delivery against a simultaneous settlement debit/credit); models range from gross-gross (DvP model 1) to net-net (DvP model 3) in BIS terminology.
Relationships: Settlement, Payment versus payment, Settlement cycle, Clearinghouse, Netting
Failure modes: DvP removes principal risk but not liquidity or replacement-cost risk: a counterparty can still fail to deliver, forcing a buy-in, and gridlock can arise when participants wait for incoming securities to fund outgoing deliveries.
Misconceptions: DvP does not guarantee the trade happens — it guarantees that if one leg settles, the other does too; a failed trade under DvP simply does not settle either leg.
Example: When an investor's share purchase settles T+1 at DTC, the seller's account is credited cash and debited shares in the same settlement pass, so the seller never parts with the stock unpaid.
Citation: BIS CPMI, Glossary of payments and market infrastructure terminology — https://www.bis.org/cpmi/publ/d00b.htm (Delivery versus payment (DvP))
Status: Reviewed

0064. Payment versus payment
Domain: Market foundations
Definition: A foreign exchange settlement mechanism that ensures the final transfer of one currency occurs if and only if the final transfer of the countercurrency occurs, eliminating FX settlement (Herstatt) risk — the loss of the full value of a currency paid without receiving the currency bought.
Intuition: Both currency legs of an FX trade move simultaneously; you can never wire your dollars away and get no euros back because the other bank failed that afternoon.
Mechanics: A PvP system (notably CLS Bank, per BIS analysis of FX settlement risk) holds both sides' payment instructions and releases the two currency transfers together; where PvP is unavailable, legs settle in different payment systems and time zones, exposing the paying party until the counterleg arrives.
Relationships: Delivery versus payment, Settlement, Netting, Over-the-counter market
Failure modes: PvP eliminates principal risk but not liquidity risk (a party may fail to fund its side, unwinding the day's queue) or replacement-cost risk (re-doing the trade at a worse rate); coverage gaps leave non-eligible currencies and counterparties exposed.
Misconceptions: PvP is not automatic in FX — it requires settlement through a PvP mechanism such as CLS, and a large share of global FX turnover historically settled with one leg at risk (the 1974 Bankhaus Herstatt failure being the canonical loss).
Example: A USD/EUR trade settles through CLS: the member's dollar payment and euro receipt are released simultaneously at settlement, so neither bank is exposed for the full principal if the other fails intraday.
Citation: BIS CPMI, Glossary of payments and market infrastructure terminology — https://www.bis.org/cpmi/publ/d00b.htm (Payment versus payment (PvP))
Citation: BIS, Settlement risk in foreign exchange transactions (CPSS, March 1996) — https://www.bis.org/cpmi/publ/d17.pdf (Payment versus payment discussion)
Status: Reviewed

0065. Retail trader
Domain: Participants
Definition: A retail trader is an individual, non-professional market participant who trades for his or her own account, typically in relatively small size, as distinct from an institution trading on behalf of others. In FINRA Rule 2210, a 'retail investor' is defined residually as any person other than an institutional investor.
Intuition: A retail trader is an ordinary person buying and selling stocks, options, or crypto with their own money through a brokerage app, rather than a fund or bank trading client or firm capital.
Mechanics: Retail traders access markets through retail brokers, trading individual accounts with their own capital. Because they trade small, they are price takers whose orders are often internalized or routed to wholesalers; they generally lack direct exchange membership, co-location, and institutional research and execution tools.
Relationships: Institutional investor, Broker, Liquidity taker, Speculator
Failure modes: Retail order flow is systematically less informed on average, and retail traders are disproportionately exposed to overtrading costs, behavioral biases, and complex products (options, leveraged ETFs) whose risks they may underestimate.
Misconceptions: It is wrong to assume retail traders as a group reliably move or predict prices; it is equally wrong that 'the little guy' gets the same execution and information as institutions. 'Retail' is a regulatory/economic category, not a statement about any individual's skill.
Example: A teacher opens a brokerage account and buys 20 shares of an ETF with part of a paycheck, paying no explicit commission but receiving a price that embeds the spread and routing economics of retail order flow.
Citation: FINRA Rule 2210 (Communications with the Public) — https://www.finra.org/rules-guidance/rulebooks/finra-rules/2210 (Rule 2210(a)(6), definition of 'retail investor')
Status: Reviewed

0066. Institutional investor
Domain: Participants
Definition: An institutional investor is an organization that pools or manages large amounts of money and trades securities on behalf of others or of the institution — for example banks, insurance companies, registered investment companies, investment advisers, pension and employee benefit plans, and government entities. FINRA Rule 2210(a)(4) enumerates such persons (including persons described in Rule 4512(c)) as 'institutional investors' for communications purposes.
Intuition: Institutional investors are the 'whales' of the market: pension funds, mutual funds, insurers, and endowments trading in large blocks with professional staff, in contrast to individuals trading their own savings.
Mechanics: Institutions trade through prime brokers and execution brokers, often splitting large parent orders into child orders via algorithms to control market impact. Their size gives them access to block trading, dark pools, and negotiated liquidity, but also means their orders can move prices, so execution strategy and information leakage are central concerns.
Relationships: Retail trader, Prime broker, Execution broker, Custodian, Broker-dealer
Failure modes: Large institutional orders create market impact and information leakage, and crowded institutional positioning can amplify drawdowns when many institutions unwind similar trades. Agency problems arise because institutions trade other people's money.
Misconceptions: Institutional investors are not uniformly 'smart money' with superior returns; much institutional flow is index-tracking or liability-driven. Nor does institutional participation guarantee market stability — herding among institutions can be destabilizing.
Example: A pension fund must invest a $200 million contribution; its trader works the order over several days through an execution algorithm to avoid driving up the price of the stocks it buys.
Citation: FINRA Rule 2210 (Communications with the Public) — https://www.finra.org/rules-guidance/rulebooks/finra-rules/2210 (Rule 2210(a)(4), definition of 'institutional investor')
Status: Reviewed

0067. Broker-dealer
Domain: Participants
Definition: A broker-dealer is a person or firm engaged in the business of both effecting securities transactions for the account of others (broker function) and buying and selling securities for its own account (dealer function). Under Section 15 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, most brokers and dealers must register with the SEC, join a self-regulatory organization such as FINRA, and become members of SIPC.
Intuition: A broker-dealer is the standard licensed securities firm: it can execute your trades as your agent and can also sell you securities out of its own inventory as principal.
Mechanics: The firm registers by filing Form BD through the CRD system operated by FINRA, obtains SEC registration and SRO membership, and must comply with net capital, books-and-records, supervision, suitability, and best-execution rules. Trade confirmations must disclose whether the firm acted as agent or principal and the compensation received.
Relationships: Broker, Dealer, Market maker, Prime broker, Custodian, Futures commission merchant
Failure modes: The dual agency/principal capacity creates conflicts of interest (e.g., selling from inventory, proprietary trading alongside customer flow) that disclosure mitigates but does not eliminate. Broker-dealer failure can transmit stress to clients and markets, as seen in 2008.
Misconceptions: A broker-dealer is not a fiduciary in all dealings by default — the historical standard was suitability/fair dealing, with Regulation Best Interest adding a best-interest obligation for retail recommendations. Registration does not mean the SEC has approved the firm's business or products.
Example: A full-service firm executes a customer's stock purchase as agent for a commission on one trade, and on another trade sells the customer a corporate bond from its own inventory as principal, disclosing its capacity on each confirmation.
Citation: SEC, Division of Trading and Markets, Guide to Broker-Dealer Registration — https://www.sec.gov/divisions/marketreg/bdguide.htm (Parts II-III (registration; Form BD; SRO and SIPC membership))
Status: Reviewed

0068. Liquidity provider
Domain: Participants
Definition: A liquidity provider is a market participant that supplies immediacy to a market by posting resting bids and offers — quotes or limit orders that others can trade against — rather than demanding immediate execution. Market makers are the canonical designated liquidity providers, but any participant resting limit orders in the book acts as a liquidity provider.
Intuition: A liquidity provider is the patient party: it posts a price and waits, letting anyone who needs to trade right now come to it — and earns the spread (or a rebate) for that patience.
Mechanics: The provider submits non-marketable limit orders that rest in the order book, adding displayed depth. When a liquidity taker's order executes against the resting order, the provider typically earns the spread and, on maker-taker venues, a liquidity rebate; in return it bears adverse-selection and inventory risk. Market makers formalize this role with continuous two-sided quoting obligations.
Relationships: Market maker, Liquidity taker, Designated market maker, High-frequency trader, Dealer
Failure modes: Posted liquidity is conditional: providers cancel or widen quotes in volatile or informed-flow environments, so visible book depth can vanish in stress (flash-crash dynamics). Providing liquidity to informed flow produces systematic adverse-selection losses.
Misconceptions: Liquidity provision is not a charitable or risk-free activity, and not all posted quotes represent firm intent — quotes can be flickering or spoofed (the latter illegally). High displayed liquidity does not guarantee executable liquidity in size.
Example: A trader posts a limit order to buy 1,000 shares at $49.98 when the market is $49.98 x $50.02; when a seller's market order arrives, the resting order executes, and the venue pays the passive side a maker rebate of $0.002 per share.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Market Maker)
Citation: SEC Investor.gov, Investing Basics Glossary — https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/glossary (Market Makers; Liquidity (or Marketability))
Status: Reviewed

0069. Liquidity taker
Domain: Participants
Definition: A liquidity taker is a market participant that demands immediacy by submitting marketable orders that execute against resting bids and offers posted by liquidity providers, thereby removing displayed liquidity from the book. The taker pays the bid-ask spread (and, on maker-taker venues, a taker fee) for immediate execution.
Intuition: A liquidity taker is the impatient party: it wants to trade right now, so it hits the bid or lifts the offer that someone else posted, paying the spread for the privilege of immediacy.
Mechanics: The taker submits a market order or a marketable limit order that crosses the spread and executes against resting quotes. Each such trade removes depth from the order book; repeated taking in one direction moves the price. Institutional algorithms manage how aggressively they take liquidity to balance urgency against market impact.
Relationships: Liquidity provider, Market maker, Retail trader, Institutional investor, High-frequency trader
Failure modes: Aggressive taking in thin books produces outsized market impact and slippage, and stop-loss cascades occur when many takers' stop orders convert to market orders simultaneously. Taker costs (spread + fees) compound quickly for high-turnover strategies.
Misconceptions: Taking liquidity is not 'free' even at zero commission — the spread and price impact are real costs embedded in execution price. Being a taker also does not imply being uninformed; informed traders often must take to capitalize on information before it decays.
Example: A portfolio manager needs to exit a position immediately and sends a market order to sell 10,000 shares; the order walks down three levels of resting bids, filling at an average price 8 cents below the pre-order bid.
Citation: SEC Investor.gov, Investing Basics Glossary — https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/glossary (Market Makers; Liquidity (or Marketability); Market Order)
Status: Reviewed

0070. Hedger
Domain: Participants
Definition: A hedger is a market participant who enters into positions in a futures or other derivatives market opposite to positions held in the cash market to minimize the risk of financial loss from an adverse price change, or who buys or sells futures as a temporary substitute for a cash transaction that will occur later. One can hedge either a long cash position (e.g., owning the commodity) or a short cash position (e.g., planning to buy it later).
Intuition: A hedger uses the futures market like insurance: they already have real-world price exposure from their business, and they take an offsetting market position so that a bad price move hurts less.
Mechanics: The hedger identifies an underlying commercial exposure (inventory, future purchases or sales, borrowing costs) and takes a derivatives position whose value moves oppositely, e.g., a farmer sells grain futures against the coming harvest. The residual risk is basis risk — the risk that the cash-futures price relationship changes unexpectedly between establishing and lifting the hedge.
Formula: Basis = cash price - futures price; hedge effectiveness depends on the stability of the basis over the hedge horizon.
Relationships: Speculator, Arbitrageur, Futures commission merchant, Commodity trading advisor
Failure modes: Hedges fail through basis risk, contract mismatch (grade, location, timing), and margin-call liquidity strain when the futures leg loses cash before the offsetting physical gain is realized. Over-hedging or hedging a wrongly estimated exposure can convert a hedge into de facto speculation.
Misconceptions: Hedging is not about making money on the futures position — a perfect hedge transfers price risk, it does not create profit. It is also not true that hedging eliminates all risk; it exchanges outright price risk for (smaller) basis risk.
Example: An airline expects to buy 1 million gallons of jet fuel in three months and buys heating-oil futures as a cross-hedge; if fuel prices rise, the futures gain offsets the higher purchase cost.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Hedger (see also Basis Risk))
Status: Reviewed

0071. Speculator
Domain: Participants
Definition: In commodity futures usage, a speculator is a trader who does not hedge, but who trades with the objective of achieving profits through the successful anticipation of price movements. Speculators voluntarily accept price risk that hedgers seek to shed, thereby supplying liquidity and risk-bearing capacity to the market.
Intuition: A speculator is a risk-taker with a view: they have no crop to sell or fuel to buy — they simply bet on where prices are going, hoping to be paid for bearing the risk.
Mechanics: The speculator takes outright long or short positions (or spreads) based on anticipated price moves, posts margin, and profits or loses as prices move. Regulators monitor speculators through large-trader reporting and speculative position limits that cap the size of positions a non-hedger may hold in many futures markets.
Relationships: Hedger, Arbitrageur, High-frequency trader, Proprietary trader, Liquidity taker
Failure modes: Speculative positioning can be crowded, so forced unwinds amplify trends and crashes; leverage plus adverse moves triggers margin spirals. At the market level, heavy one-way speculative flows can detach prices from fundamentals for extended periods.
Misconceptions: Speculation is not inherently manipulative or socially useless — speculators provide liquidity and assume risk hedgers want to offload. Nor is every short-term trader a speculator in the regulatory sense (e.g., bona fide hedgers are excluded from speculative limits).
Example: A trader with no commercial interest in crude oil buys ten WTI futures contracts expecting OPEC supply cuts to lift prices, posts initial margin, and exits two weeks later for a gain or loss.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Speculator (see also Speculative Position Limit))
Status: Reviewed

0072. Arbitrageur
Domain: Participants
Definition: An arbitrageur is a market participant who engages in arbitrage: the simultaneous purchase and sale of identical or equivalent instruments in two or more markets in order to benefit from a discrepancy in their price relationship. Arbitrage activity links related markets and is the economic force that keeps prices of equivalent claims aligned.
Intuition: An arbitrageur is a price policeman: if the same thing sells for $10 in one market and $10.20 in another, they buy cheap and sell dear at the same time, pocketing the difference and pushing the prices back together.
Mechanics: The arbitrageur monitors equivalent instruments (e.g., a stock and its ADR, an ETF and its basket, spot and futures linked by cost of carry) and, when prices diverge beyond transaction costs, simultaneously buys the cheap leg and sells the rich leg, locking in the convergence. Profit requires the price gap to exceed all frictions: fees, borrow costs, funding, and execution risk.
Formula: Arbitrage profit = (P_rich - P_cheap) - total transaction and carry costs; a trade is viable only when this is positive.
Relationships: Hedger, Speculator, High-frequency trader, Authorized participant, Market maker
Failure modes: Real-world arbitrage faces execution leg risk (one side fills, the other doesn't), borrow unavailability for short legs, funding constraints, and convergence risk — mispricings can widen before they close, forcing losses on marked-to-market positions.
Misconceptions: Arbitrage is rarely the textbook riskless, costless trade; 'risk arbitrage' (e.g., merger arb) explicitly involves deal-completion risk and is closer to speculation. Also, apparent arbitrage opportunities on screens often disappear once all fees and market impact are included.
Example: An ETF trades at a 0.3% discount to the value of its underlying basket; an arbitrageur buys the ETF shares and shorts the basket, then uses the creation/redemption mechanism to close both legs at parity.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Arbitrage)
Status: Reviewed

0073. High-frequency trader
Domain: Participants
Definition: A high-frequency trader is a market participant using automated, algorithmic strategies characterized by very high-speed order generation, submission, and cancellation, extremely short position-holding periods, and infrastructure such as co-location of servers near exchange matching engines to minimize latency. HFT is a category of practice rather than a single statutorily defined registration type.
Intuition: An HFT firm is a sprinter among joggers: computers sitting next to the exchange react to price changes in microseconds, jumping in and out of tiny positions thousands of times a day.
Mechanics: HFT firms co-locate servers at the exchange's data center, consume direct market-data feeds, and run algorithms for market making, statistical arbitrage, and latency-sensitive strategies, typically ending the day flat. The CFTC glossary explicitly ties co-location — placing servers in close physical proximity to the matching engine — to facilitating high-frequency trading.
Relationships: Market maker, Arbitrageur, Proprietary trader, Liquidity provider, Liquidity taker
Failure modes: HFT liquidity is fleeting: algorithms withdraw simultaneously in stress, contributing to flash events (e.g., the May 6, 2010 Flash Crash dynamics). Speed races also create arms-race costs and can make displayed depth unrepresentative of true resting interest.
Misconceptions: HFT is not a single strategy and not all HFT is predatory — much of it is ordinary electronic market making. Nor does speed alone guarantee profit; co-location and technology are costs, and many HFT strategies fail competitively.
Example: An HFT market-making algorithm posts and updates thousands of quotes per second in an equity index future, earns fractions of a tick per round turn, and flattens all positions before the close.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Co-location (defining infrastructure used to facilitate high-frequency trading))
Status: Reviewed

0074. Proprietary trader
Domain: Participants
Definition: A proprietary trader is a person or desk that trades financial instruments as principal for the firm's own account rather than for customers, seeking profit from short-term price movements, resale, or arbitrage. Under the Volcker Rule (12 CFR 248.3), 'proprietary trading' by banking entities — engaging as principal for the trading account — is prohibited, with enumerated exemptions such as market making and hedging.
Intuition: A prop trader bets the house's money, not a client's: the firm keeps all the winnings and absorbs all the losses from the desk's positions.
Mechanics: The trader takes directional or relative-value positions using firm capital, with the desk's positions booked to the firm's trading account. Compensation is tied to desk P&L. For banking entities, the Volcker Rule defines the 'trading account' (short-term resale, short-term price moves, arbitrage profits) and restricts such activity, pushing prop trading into non-bank prop firms.
Relationships: Dealer, Principal trader, High-frequency trader, Speculator, Market maker
Failure modes: Prop desks concentrate tail risk in the firm; large losses (e.g., rogue or crowded positions) can threaten firm capital. Distinguishing prohibited prop trading from permitted market making is a persistent supervisory and compliance challenge.
Misconceptions: Prop trading is not the same as market making, though both trade as principal — the distinction is intent and customer-facing facilitation, which regulators police. 'Prop firm' retail evaluation programs are a separate, largely simulated-capital business model, not classic bank prop desks.
Example: A bank's rates desk buys Treasury futures as principal expecting yields to fall; under the Volcker Rule the bank must be able to show this fits a permitted activity (e.g., bona fide market making) rather than prohibited proprietary trading.
Citation: 12 CFR 248.3 (Volcker Rule) - Prohibition on proprietary trading — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-12/chapter-II/subchapter-A/part-248/subpart-A/section-248.3 (Paragraphs (a)-(b): definition of proprietary trading and trading account)
Citation: SEC, Division of Trading and Markets, Guide to Broker-Dealer Registration — https://www.sec.gov/divisions/marketreg/bdguide.htm (Part II.B (dealer vs. trader distinction))
Status: Reviewed

0075. Commodity trading advisor
Domain: Participants
Definition: A commodity trading advisor (CTA) is a person who, for compensation or profit, directly or indirectly advises others as to the value of or the advisability of trading futures contracts, commodity options, or swaps, or issues analyses or reports concerning them; advising indirectly includes exercising trading authority over a customer's account. CTAs generally must register with the CFTC (CEA Section 1a(12)) and become NFA members.
Intuition: A CTA is a professional futures-market advisor or manager: clients pay them to recommend or run futures trading strategies, similar to how an investment adviser handles securities.
Mechanics: CTAs either publish advice or manage client accounts under power of attorney (managed accounts), charging management and often performance fees. Registration requires proficiency testing, disclosure documents describing strategy, risks, fees, and performance, and ongoing CFTC/NFA compliance; many hedge fund managers are registered as CTAs or CPOs.
Relationships: Futures commission merchant, Introducing broker, Speculator, Hedger, Broker-dealer
Failure modes: CTA performance is strategy-dependent and often trend-following, producing long flat or losing stretches in range-bound markets; disclosed past performance is not predictive. Fraud or inadequate disclosure remains a risk, mitigated by NFA oversight but not eliminated.
Misconceptions: 'CTA' is a regulatory registration category, not proof of a profitable strategy or a quality mark. Also, CTAs need not advise on commodities only — the category covers advice on financial futures, FX, and swaps as well.
Example: A registered CTA manages a $50 million managed-futures program, trading diversified futures trends across energy, rates, and currencies, and charges clients a 2% management fee plus 20% of new profits.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Commodity Trading Advisor (see 7 USC 1a(12)))
Citation: CME Group Education Glossary — https://www.cmegroup.com/education/glossary.html (Commodity Trading Advisor (CTA))
Status: Reviewed

0076. Futures commission merchant
Domain: Participants
Definition: A futures commission merchant (FCM) is an individual, association, partnership, corporation, or trust that solicits or accepts orders for the purchase or sale of any commodity for future delivery on or subject to the rules of an exchange and that accepts payment from or extends credit to those whose orders are accepted. FCMs are the futures-industry analogue of carrying brokers and must register with the CFTC (CEA Section 1a(28)).
Intuition: An FCM is the futures industry's bank-and-broker combined: it takes your futures orders, holds your margin money, and stands between you and the clearing house.
Mechanics: The FCM onboards customers, accepts orders and margin funds, routes trades for execution, and clears them (directly as a clearing member or through one). It must segregate customer funds from firm funds, maintain adjusted net capital, and issue confirmations and statements; introducing brokers without customer-fund handling route their customers to FCMs.
Relationships: Introducing broker, Clearing member, Commodity trading advisor, Broker-dealer, Central counterparty
Failure modes: FCM failure puts customer margin at risk when segregation fails, as in the MF Global (2011) and Peregrine (2012) cases where customer funds were misused. Concentration of clearing among few FCMs creates systemic single points of failure.
Misconceptions: Customer funds at an FCM are not SIPC-insured like securities accounts; protection rests on CFTC segregation rules, not an insurance backstop. An FCM is also not merely an order-taker — its defining feature is holding customer money.
Example: A grain exporter opens a futures account at an FCM, wires $100,000 of margin, and the FCM accepts and clears its hedge orders in corn futures while holding the funds in a segregated customer account.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Futures Commission Merchant (see 7 USC 1a(28)))
Status: Reviewed

0077. Introducing broker
Domain: Participants
Definition: An introducing broker (IB) is a person engaged in soliciting or accepting orders for the purchase or sale of any commodity for future delivery on an exchange who does not accept any money, securities, or property to margin, guarantee, or secure the resulting trades. IBs must register with the CFTC (CEA Section 1a(31)); because they cannot hold customer funds, their customers' accounts are carried by a futures commission merchant.
Intuition: An introducing broker is the storefront without the vault: it finds and services futures customers, but their money and positions are actually held by a larger clearing firm (the FCM).
Mechanics: The IB markets to and services customers, accepts their orders, and passes the orders and accounts to a carrying FCM under a guarantee or independent IB agreement. The IB earns a share of commissions; all margin and customer funds are handled by the FCM. A securities-industry analogue exists for introducing broker-dealers that clear through carrying firms.
Relationships: Futures commission merchant, Commodity trading advisor, Broker, Clearing member
Failure modes: Customers may not realize their assets sit with the FCM, not the IB, so IB marketing failures or misconduct can be misattributed, and the chain complicates accountability. Small IBs can also fail operationally, though customer funds remain at the carrying firm.
Misconceptions: An IB is not a lesser FCM — the legal line is precisely that an IB may not touch customer margin funds. 'IB' in retail marketing can also mean a mere referral affiliate, which is a looser usage than the CFTC registration category.
Example: A two-person agricultural advisory shop registers as an IB, signs up local farmers for hedging accounts, and all orders and margin are carried and cleared through its partner FCM.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Introducing Broker (see 7 USC 1a(31)))
Status: Reviewed

0078. Prime broker
Domain: Participants
Definition: A prime broker is a large broker-dealer or investment bank that provides hedge funds and other institutional clients a bundled package of services: custody of assets, securities lending, margin financing and leverage, centralized clearing and settlement, and consolidated portfolio reporting. The prime brokerage model lets a fund trade through many executing brokers while its positions and collateral are consolidated at the prime broker.
Intuition: A prime broker is a hedge fund's operational headquarters: the fund can trade with dozens of brokers, but all its cash, stock borrowing, financing, and reporting are centralized in one master account.
Mechanics: Executing brokers give up trades to the client's prime broker, which settles them into a master account, holds custody of the assets, extends margin loans against the portfolio, arranges stock borrow for short sales, and produces consolidated risk and P&L reports. Revenue comes from financing and securities-lending spreads plus clearing and other fees; client collateral may be rehypothecated within regulatory limits.
Relationships: Custodian, Execution broker, Institutional investor, Broker-dealer, Dealer
Failure modes: Prime broker failure can trap client assets and financing, as Lehman's 2008 collapse showed when rehypothecated collateral could not be withdrawn. Prime brokers can also abruptly tighten margin and financing in stress, forcing client deleveraging (e.g., the Archegos 2021 unwind hit several prime brokers with large losses).
Misconceptions: Prime brokerage is not a single product or a rating of 'prime' quality — it is a bundle of custody, financing, and settlement services. Clients also do not eliminate counterparty risk by using a famous prime broker, as 2008 demonstrated.
Example: A long/short equity hedge fund executes trades through five different brokers; all trades are given up to its prime broker, which holds the portfolio, lends shares for its shorts, finances its leverage, and delivers one consolidated daily report.
Citation: Wikipedia, 'Prime brokerage' (secondary source) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_brokerage (Lead and services sections)
Status: Reviewed

0079. Custodian
Domain: Participants
Definition: A custodian is a financial institution — typically a bank, registered broker-dealer, or futures commission merchant — that safeguards client funds and securities, holding them in segregated customer accounts. Under the SEC custody rule (17 CFR 275.206(4)-2), investment advisers with custody of client assets must maintain them with a 'qualified custodian' such as a bank, registered broker-dealer, registered FCM, or qualifying foreign financial institution.
Intuition: A custodian is the vault keeper: it physically (or electronically) holds your securities and cash, keeps records of what is yours, and keeps those assets separate from its own.
Mechanics: The custodian holds securities in nominee or street name, settles trades, collects dividends and interest, processes corporate actions, and sends account statements directly to clients at least quarterly. Segregation of client assets from the custodian's proprietary assets is the core protection; advisers with custody face surprise independent verification of those assets.
Relationships: Prime broker, Transfer agent, Broker-dealer, Institutional investor, Central counterparty
Failure modes: Custody breaks down when segregation fails or records are falsified — the Madoff fraud showed the danger of an adviser self-custodying without an independent qualified custodian. Custodian insolvency in weak legal regimes can also entangle client assets despite nominal segregation.
Misconceptions: A custodian does not manage the investments or guarantee their value — it safekeeps and administers assets. Holding assets 'at' a big-name custodian does not validate the strategy or the adviser's honesty if statements are fabricated before reaching the client.
Example: A pension fund's global custodian bank holds its equity and bond portfolio, settles all trades, collects dividends, and issues monthly statements directly to the fund's trustees, independent of the investment manager.
Citation: 17 CFR 275.206(4)-2 - Custody of funds or securities of clients by investment advisers (eCFR) — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/chapter-II/part-275/subpart-A/section-275.206(4)-2 (Paragraph (d)(6), definition of 'qualified custodian')
Status: Reviewed

0080. Central counterparty
Domain: Participants
Definition: A central counterparty (CCP) is a clearing organization that interposes itself between the parties to a trade, becoming the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer, thereby guaranteeing performance and mutualizing counterparty credit risk. In U.S. futures markets a CCP registered with the CFTC is known as a derivatives clearing organization (DCO).
Intuition: A CCP is the market's middleman-of-last-resort: after your trade is done, you no longer rely on the stranger you traded with — you rely on the clearing house, which stands behind every trade.
Mechanics: Through novation, the CCP replaces the original bilateral contract with two contracts against itself. It collects initial and variation margin from clearing members daily, maintains a default fund and other resources, and runs default-management ('waterfall') procedures to absorb a member's failure while continuing to perform on all other trades.
Relationships: Clearing member, Futures commission merchant, Custodian, Broker-dealer
Failure modes: CCPs concentrate risk: a default exceeding margin plus the default fund can force loss mutualization onto surviving members or, in extremis, CCP failure. Procyclical margin increases in stress can drain market-wide liquidity, and CCP risk models can be wrong about tail correlations.
Misconceptions: Central clearing does not eliminate counterparty risk — it transforms and concentrates it in the CCP with a layered default waterfall. Nor is every cleared product equally safe: clearing guarantees performance, not price outcomes.
Example: Two firms trade an interest-rate swap cleared at a CCP; when one member later defaults, the CCP uses the defaulter's margin and default-fund contributions to honor the swap, and the surviving counterparty is unaffected.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Central Counterparty; Clearing Organization; Clearing)
Citation: CME Group Education Glossary — https://www.cmegroup.com/education/glossary.html (Central Counterparty Clearing)
Status: Reviewed

0081. Clearing member
Domain: Participants
Definition: A clearing member is a firm admitted to membership in a clearing organization (CCP) that clears trades directly through it. All trades of non-clearing members must be processed and settled through a clearing member, which is responsible to the CCP for the obligations — margin, settlement, and default contributions — of the trades it clears.
Intuition: A clearing member is the clearing house's guarantor: only these vetted, capitalized firms deal directly with the CCP, and everyone else's trades reach the CCP through them.
Mechanics: Clearing members meet the CCP's financial and operational admission standards, post margin and default-fund contributions, and guarantee the performance of their own and their clients' cleared trades. At futures exchanges, clearing members are often FCMs; customer positions of non-members are carried on a clearing member's books.
Relationships: Central counterparty, Futures commission merchant, Introducing broker, Broker-dealer
Failure modes: A clearing member guarantees client trades, so a client's default can sink the member, and a member's default cascades risk into the CCP's waterfall. Concentration of client clearing in a few large members amplifies systemic exposure.
Misconceptions: Exchange trading membership and clearing membership are distinct — a firm may trade on an exchange without clearing there. End customers of a clearing member are not protected by the CCP directly; their recourse runs through the member and customer-segregation rules.
Example: A small proprietary trading firm is not a clearing member, so it clears its futures trades through an FCM that is a clearing member of the exchange's clearing house and posts margin to the CCP on the firm's behalf.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Clearing Member)
Citation: CME Group Education Glossary — https://www.cmegroup.com/education/glossary.html (Clearing Member; Clearing Firm)
Status: Reviewed

0082. Execution broker
Domain: Participants
Definition: An execution broker is a broker engaged by a client to execute trades in the market, as distinct from the firm that carries, clears, or custodies the account. In prime brokerage and give-up arrangements, the executing broker executes the trade and then 'gives up' the trade at the execution price to the client's designated carrying firm (prime broker or FCM) for clearing and settlement.
Intuition: An execution broker is the hired hand who actually goes into the market and gets the trade done; afterward the trade is handed off to the firm's main broker, which holds and settles the position.
Mechanics: The client routes an order to the execution broker for market access and best execution; once filled, the trade is allocated or given up (e.g., via CME's Allocation Claim System) to the carrying firm, which books, margines, and settles the position. This separation lets institutions use many execution brokers for research, access, or pricing while centralizing positions at one carrying firm.
Relationships: Prime broker, Agency broker, Futures commission merchant, Institutional investor, Broker
Failure modes: Give-up and allocation chains add operational risk: misallocated or unmatched trades, and disputes over execution quality when execution and clearing are split. Reliance on the executing broker for best execution requires monitoring that clients often underperform.
Misconceptions: The executing broker is not the firm that ends up holding the position — confusing execution with carrying/custody misattributes where assets and margin actually sit. 'Execution-only' also implies no advice, but it does not imply best execution is automatic.
Example: A hedge fund directs an order to a regional broker for execution in a stock; the fill is given up to the fund's prime broker, which settles the trade into the fund's master account.
Citation: CME Group Education Glossary — https://www.cmegroup.com/education/glossary.html (Allocation Claim System (executing firms giving up trades to carrying firms))
Citation: SEC, Division of Trading and Markets, Guide to Broker-Dealer Registration — https://www.sec.gov/divisions/marketreg/bdguide.htm (Part V.A.3 (Duty of Best Execution))
Status: Reviewed

0083. Agency broker
Domain: Participants
Definition: An agency broker is a broker that executes customer orders strictly as agent — arranging trades with third parties for a disclosed commission — and never takes the other side of the customer's trade as principal. The agency/principal capacity must be disclosed on customer confirmations under Exchange Act Rule 10b-10.
Intuition: An agency broker is a pure matchmaker: it finds a counterparty for your trade in the market and charges a commission, without ever selling you anything out of its own pocket.
Mechanics: The broker routes the customer's order to an exchange, market maker, or other venue for execution against third-party interest, charging an explicit commission. Because the broker has no inventory position in the trade, it avoids the principal-trade conflicts of markups and trading against the customer, though routing conflicts (payment for order flow) can remain.
Relationships: Broker, Principal trader, Execution broker, Broker-dealer, Dealer
Failure modes: Agency status removes principal conflicts but not routing conflicts: order-routing payments and affiliated-venue routing can still compromise execution quality. Agency-only models are also capacity-constrained in illiquid markets where principal risk-taking is what actually finds liquidity.
Misconceptions: 'Agency' does not guarantee best execution or the absence of all conflicts — it only means no principal capacity in the trade. Customers also often cannot tell from the fill alone whether the firm acted as agent or principal; the confirmation discloses capacity.
Example: An adviser instructs its agency broker to buy 50,000 shares; the broker works the order on exchanges and dark pools against other investors, charges $0.01 per share commission, and buys nothing for its own account.
Citation: SEC, Division of Trading and Markets, Guide to Broker-Dealer Registration — https://www.sec.gov/divisions/marketreg/bdguide.htm (Part II.A-B (broker as agent vs. dealer as principal); Part V.A.4 (capacity disclosure on confirmations))
Status: Reviewed

0084. Principal trader
Domain: Participants
Definition: A principal trader is a firm or desk that trades for its own account and risk, buying from and selling to customers or other dealers out of inventory rather than acting as agent. In a principal trade the customer faces the firm itself as counterparty, and the firm's compensation is embedded in the price as a markup or markdown (or spread) rather than a disclosed commission.
Intuition: A principal trader is the merchant, not the messenger: when you buy from it, you are buying the firm's own merchandise at the firm's price.
Mechanics: The firm fills customer orders from its own inventory, assuming the position risk, and discloses its principal capacity on confirmations. Compensation comes from the difference between the price at which it trades with the customer and the prevailing market (markup/markdown), which regulators police for fairness. Principal trading ranges from dealer market making to directional proprietary trading.
Relationships: Dealer, Proprietary trader, Agency broker, Market maker, Broker-dealer
Failure modes: Principal dealing creates a structural conflict: the firm profits at the customer's expense on each trade, inviting excessive markups or front-running, policed through disclosure and fair-pricing rules. Inventory losses in stress can impair the firm's ability to keep quoting.
Misconceptions: A principal trade is not inherently worse for the customer than an agency trade — in illiquid securities, a dealer's willingness to commit capital may be the only source of immediacy. Nor is a 'riskless principal' trade (offsetting customer order filled from the market) the same as agency execution.
Example: A customer sells 1,000 municipal bonds to a dealer, which buys them into inventory at 98 and resells them the next week at 98.5; the half-point markup, not a commission, is the dealer's compensation.
Citation: SEC, Division of Trading and Markets, Guide to Broker-Dealer Registration — https://www.sec.gov/divisions/marketreg/bdguide.htm (Part II.B (dealer acts as principal); Part V.A.4 (principal capacity and markup disclosure))
Citation: SEC Investor.gov, Investing Basics Glossary — https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/glossary (Markups and Markdowns)
Status: Reviewed

0085. Market data vendor
Domain: Participants
Definition: A market data vendor is a firm that collects quotation and transaction data from exchanges, alternative trading systems, and consolidated feeds, then redistributes it — raw, normalized, or enriched — to traders, brokers, and investors. In the U.S. equity national market system, dissemination of core NMS information is governed by SEC Regulation NMS, whose 2020 Market Data Infrastructure amendments introduced competing consolidators to decentralize consolidation and distribution.
Intuition: A market data vendor is the market's news wire for prices: it gathers every quote and trade from every venue and pipes that stream into trading screens, algorithms, and risk systems.
Mechanics: The vendor licenses data from exchanges and securities information processors (or, under the MDI rule, acts as or buys from competing consolidators and self-aggregators), normalizes symbology and formats, and delivers real-time, delayed, or historical feeds via terminals, APIs, and ticker plants. Latency, completeness, and licensing terms differentiate vendors.
Relationships: Index provider, Broker-dealer, High-frequency trader, Institutional investor
Failure modes: Feed errors, latency differences, or outages at vendors can blind downstream algorithms and distort trading (e.g., the 2013 Nasdaq SIP halt and 2015 consolidated-tape delays). Venues and vendors monetize faster proprietary feeds, creating two-tier data access between those who pay for speed and those on the consolidated feed.
Misconceptions: The free delayed quotes on public websites are not the institutional product — professional trading depends on licensed real-time feeds with strict usage fees. A vendor also does not create prices; it redistributes data generated by trading venues.
Example: A trading firm pays a vendor for a normalized, low-latency feed combining direct data from a dozen equity exchanges, while a retail investor watches 15-minute-delayed quotes from a website that licenses the same underlying data.
Citation: SEC Final Rule: Market Data Infrastructure (Release No. 34-90610) — https://www.sec.gov/rules-regulations/2020/12/market-data-infrastructure (Overview (Regulation NMS consolidation and dissemination of NMS information; competing consolidators))
Status: Reviewed

0086. Index provider
Domain: Participants
Definition: An index provider (benchmark administrator) is the natural or legal person that has control over the provision of a benchmark: it administers the arrangements for determining the index, collects and analyzes the input data, calculates the index value according to a published methodology, and publishes it. Examples include providers of equity, bond, and commodity indices used for benchmarking, index funds, and derivatives settlement.
Intuition: An index provider is the scorekeeper of a market segment: it decides which securities are in the index, how they are weighted, and publishes the number everyone else trades and measures against.
Mechanics: The provider publishes a methodology (universe, eligibility, weighting, rebalancing schedule), applies it to market data to compute index levels, runs periodic reconstitutions and rebalances, and licenses the index to ETF issuers, asset managers, and derivatives exchanges. Because index composition changes force trading by tracking funds, rebalance announcements have real market impact.
Formula: Price-weighted index: I = sum(p_i) / D, where p_i are constituent prices and D is the divisor; market-cap-weighted index: I = (sum(p_i * s_i * f_i) / B) * base value, with s_i shares, f_i free-float factor, B base-period divisor.
Relationships: Market data vendor, Authorized participant, Institutional investor, Custodian
Failure modes: Methodology choices (survivorship in constituent selection, free-float adjustments, corporate-action handling) embed judgment, and index changes can be front-run, moving prices against trackers. Governance failures in benchmarks (e.g., LIBOR manipulation) led to formal benchmark regulation.
Misconceptions: An index is not a neutral law of nature — it is a designed product whose provider makes discretionary methodology choices. Being in a famous index also does not certify an investment's quality, only that it met published rules.
Example: An index provider announces its large-cap index will add a fast-growing company at the quarterly rebalance; tracking funds must buy the stock on the effective date, and arbitrageurs position ahead of that forced demand.
Citation: Regulation (EU) 2016/1011 (EU Benchmarks Regulation) — https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/HTML/?uri=CELEX:32016R1011 (Recital (16) and Article 3(1): definition of 'administrator' and 'provision of a benchmark')
Status: Reviewed

0087. Transfer agent
Domain: Participants
Definition: A transfer agent works for a securities issuer to record changes of ownership, maintain the issuer's security-holder records, cancel and issue certificates, and distribute dividends. Transfer agents are usually banks or trust companies (though an issuer may act as its own) and must register with the SEC, or, if a bank, with a bank regulatory agency.
Intuition: A transfer agent is the issuer's official shareholder bookkeeper: it keeps the master list of who owns the shares and updates it every time shares change hands.
Mechanics: The transfer agent maintains the registered-owner ledger, processes transfers and issuances (including book-entry changes via DTC), handles lost-certificate replacement, and administers dividend payments and shareholder mailings. Mutual fund transfer agents additionally process share purchases and redemptions; the SEC custody rule permits using a mutual fund's transfer agent in lieu of a qualified custodian for fund shares.
Relationships: Custodian, Broker-dealer, Central counterparty, Authorized participant
Failure modes: Transfer-agent record errors or delays can misstate ownership and disrupt settlement, and unregistered or fraudulent transfer agents have featured in microcap fraud (e.g., issuing unauthorized shares). Paper-certificate processes remain slow and error-prone relative to book-entry.
Misconceptions: Most investors in street name never appear on the transfer agent's books — the agent records the broker/depository as registered holder, with the investor as beneficial owner. A transfer agent also does not vouch for the investment merits of the securities it registers.
Example: When an investor holding physical certificates sells them, the transfer agent cancels the old certificate, issues a new one in the buyer's (or nominee's) name, and updates the issuer's shareholder register.
Citation: SEC, Fast Answers: Transfer Agents — https://www.sec.gov/fast-answers/answerstransferagenthtm.html (Entire entry)
Status: Reviewed

0088. Authorized participant
Domain: Participants
Definition: An authorized participant (AP) is a financial institution — typically a large broker-dealer — that enters into a contractual relationship with an exchange-traded fund (ETF) to buy and redeem creation units of ETF shares directly with the fund. APs are the only parties allowed to create or redeem ETF shares in the primary market, usually in large blocks (creation units) and often in kind.
Intuition: An AP is the ETF's wholesale door: ordinary investors trade existing ETF shares with each other, but only APs can exchange a basket of underlying securities for new ETF shares (or vice versa) directly with the fund.
Mechanics: When ETF demand exceeds supply, the AP assembles the fund's designated basket of securities, delivers it to the ETF, and receives a creation unit (commonly tens of thousands of shares) to sell on the exchange; the process reverses for redemptions. This creation/redemption arbitrage is the mechanism that keeps an ETF's market price close to the value of its underlying holdings.
Relationships: Arbitrageur, Market maker, Custodian, Transfer agent, Liquidity provider
Failure modes: If APs step back (balance-sheet constraints, stressed or illiquid underlying markets), creation/redemption weakens and ETF prices can trade at persistent premiums or discounts to net asset value. In-kind baskets can also become hard to source in stressed bond or commodity markets.
Misconceptions: Retail investors cannot create or redeem ETF shares — they trade only in the secondary market. An AP's role is a contractual privilege, not a guarantee that it will always provide liquidity or that the ETF can never deviate from NAV.
Example: An equity ETF trades at a premium to its basket; an AP buys the underlying stocks, delivers them to the fund for a 50,000-share creation unit, and sells the new ETF shares into the market, closing the premium.
Citation: SEC Investor.gov, Investing Basics Glossary — https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/glossary (Authorized Participants; Creation Unit)
Status: Reviewed

0089. Designated market maker
Domain: Participants
Definition: A designated market maker (DMM) is a market-making firm assigned by an exchange to specific securities, with formal obligations — beyond those of an ordinary market maker — to maintain fair and orderly markets in its assigned names, including quoting and participation duties. On the NYSE, DMMs are the successors to floor specialists: specialists were converted into DMMs with a different set of privileges and obligations.
Intuition: A DMM is a stock's officially assigned steward on the exchange: it must be there quoting for its assigned stocks and is expected to lean against disorder, in exchange for informational and trading privileges.
Mechanics: The exchange allocates each listed security to a DMM firm, which must meet quoting-presence and market-quality obligations, facilitate opening and closing auctions, and commit capital when needed to dampen imbalances. In return the DMM receives privileges such as parity in the order book and, historically, unique information about order flow at its post.
Relationships: Market maker, Liquidity provider, Dealer, Authorized participant, High-frequency trader
Failure modes: DMM obligations do not make liquidity unconditional — in extreme stress even DMMs widen quotes, and most modern order flow is electronic, limiting what a single assigned firm can stabilize. The role's human/floor element matters less on fully electronic venues.
Misconceptions: A DMM is not obligated to support a stock's price or prevent declines — its duties concern orderly two-sided markets, not direction. The 'specialist' and 'DMM' labels are often conflated, but the DMM regime replaced the old specialist system with different obligations.
Example: At the NYSE open of an assigned stock, the DMM aggregates overnight imbalance information, publishes imbalance indications, and runs the opening auction, committing its own capital to fill residual imbalances.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Specialist (describing the conversion of NYSE specialists into Designated Market Makers))
Status: Reviewed

0090. Cash market
Domain: Instruments
Definition: The market for the physical or cash commodity (or asset) itself, as contrasted with futures or other derivative contracts on it. It may take the form of an organized central market, a decentralized over-the-counter market, or a local organization serving a small region, and trades settle with prompt delivery and payment through customary market channels.
Intuition: The cash market is where the actual thing changes hands now, not a promise about the future. Its price is the reference point to which futures and forward prices are compared.
Mechanics: Buyer pays seller and delivery occurs within the market's standard settlement period (immediate for spot commodities, T+1/T+2 for most securities). Cash prices are often quoted relative to futures as a basis (e.g., cents over or under a futures month), and cash and futures prices tend to converge as the delivery month approaches.
Relationships: Spot transaction, Futures contract, Forward contract, Commodity, Basis
Failure modes: Cash prices can be thin, local, or grade-specific, so they may not match the standardized grade underlying a futures contract, creating basis risk. Storage, transport, and delivery frictions can also keep cash and futures prices apart longer than convergence arguments suggest.
Misconceptions: That the cash market is a single centralized exchange; for many commodities it is a decentralized web of dealers, elevators, and processors. Also, 'cash' does not mean payment in banknotes — it contrasts with 'futures', not with credit.
Example: A grain elevator buys corn from a farmer at the local cash price quoted as 10 cents under December futures; the farmer delivers physical corn and is paid promptly.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Cash Market; Cash Commodity)
Status: Reviewed

0091. Perpetual futures contract
Domain: Instruments
Definition: A futures-style derivative contract, predominant in cryptoasset markets, that has no expiry or settlement date, so a position can be held indefinitely. Its price is kept anchored to an underlying spot index price through periodic funding payments exchanged between long and short position holders.
Intuition: A perpetual is a futures contract you never have to roll. A funding fee paid by the more crowded side keeps its price tethered to spot.
Mechanics: Positions are leveraged against initial and maintenance margin, marked to a mark price derived from a spot index price, and liquidated if collateral falls below maintenance margin. Funding is paid at fixed intervals (e.g., every 8 hours): when the funding rate is positive, longs pay shorts, and when negative, shorts pay longs; exchanges maintain insurance funds and, as a last resort, auto-deleveraging to absorb bankrupt accounts.
Formula: Funding payment = position notional x funding rate; the funding rate is typically composed of an interest rate component plus a premium index measuring the perp's deviation from the spot index price.
Relationships: Futures contract, Cryptoasset, Margin, Basis
Failure modes: Funding rates can become extremely expensive in one-sided markets, turning a correct directional view into a losing carry trade. In extreme volatility, liquidation engines and insurance funds can be overwhelmed, triggering auto-deleveraging that socializes losses onto profitable traders.
Misconceptions: That having no expiry means there is no cost of carry — funding is a recurring carry cost that substitutes for the futures roll. Also, the contract price can still deviate from spot under stress; the anchor is an incentive, not a guarantee.
Example: A BTCUSDT perpetual trading above its spot index shows a positive funding rate, so every 8 hours long position holders pay shorts a small percentage of their notional, pushing the contract price back toward spot.
Citation: Binance Academy: What Are Perpetual Futures Contracts? — https://academy.binance.com/en/articles/what-are-perpetual-futures-contracts (What is a perpetual futures contract?; What is the funding rate?)
Status: Reviewed

0092. Swap
Domain: Instruments
Definition: A derivative in which two counterparties agree to exchange streams of cash flows over a specified period, computed by applying agreed rates, prices, or formulas to a notional amount. Under the detailed statutory definition in the Commodity Exchange Act (as amended by the Dodd-Frank Act), the term includes interest rate swaps, commodity swaps, currency swaps, equity swaps, and credit default swaps.
Intuition: A swap lets two parties trade one kind of payment obligation for another — for example, exchanging a fixed interest bill for a floating one — without trading the underlying asset itself.
Mechanics: Cash flows are typically netted on each payment date against a notional principal that is usually not exchanged. Swaps are documented under ISDA master agreements; post-Dodd-Frank, many standardized swaps must be centrally cleared through a derivatives clearing organization, executed on swap execution facilities, and reported to swap data repositories.
Formula: Net payment on a payment date = Notional x (rate paid - rate received) x day-count fraction.
Relationships: Interest rate swap, Currency swap, Credit default swap, Total return swap, Variance swap, Forward contract
Failure modes: Uncleared swaps carry bilateral counterparty credit risk over long tenors. Hedged exposures can mismatch the swap's terms (basis risk), and benchmark transitions (e.g., LIBOR cessation) can strand legacy contracts.
Misconceptions: That the notional principal changes hands — in most swaps it never does and exists only to compute payments. Also, swaps are often seen as exotic speculation, but their most common use is routine balance-sheet hedging.
Example: A company with floating-rate debt enters a five-year pay-fixed/receive-floating interest rate swap on $50 million notional, converting its interest expense to a fixed rate.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Swap)
Status: Reviewed

0093. Interest rate swap
Domain: Instruments
Definition: A swap in which the two counterparties agree to exchange interest rate cash flows on a specified notional principal. In the standard plain-vanilla form, one party pays a fixed rate and the other pays a floating rate tied to a reference rate on a series of payment dates; the principal itself is not exchanged.
Intuition: Two parties swap the character of their interest payments — fixed for floating — so each ends up with the rate exposure it wants.
Mechanics: Each leg accrues interest on the same notional using its own rate and day-count convention, and payments are netted on each date. The fixed (swap) rate is set at inception so that the present value of the fixed leg equals the present value of the expected floating leg; thereafter the swap's mark-to-market moves with rates. Standardized IRS are now largely centrally cleared.
Formula: Fixed leg payment = N x R_fixed x alpha; floating leg payment = N x R_float x alpha, where N is notional and alpha the day-count fraction. At inception, the swap rate sets PV(fixed leg) = PV(floating leg).
Relationships: Swap, Forward rate agreement, Interest rate future, Currency swap
Failure modes: Benchmark reform (LIBOR to SOFR and other risk-free rates) changed floating-leg economics for legacy contracts. Rising rates create large negative mark-to-market for fixed-rate payers, generating collateral calls on cleared or margined swaps.
Misconceptions: That counterparties exchange principal — they do not; the notional only scales interest payments. Also, a swap does not create new borrowing; it transforms the rate exposure of existing obligations.
Example: On $100 million of 5-year notional, Party A pays 4% fixed semiannually and receives compounded SOFR; if SOFR averages 4.6% over a period, A receives the net 0.6% on the notional for that period.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Interest Rate Swap)
Status: Reviewed

0094. Currency swap
Domain: Instruments
Definition: A swap that involves the exchange of one currency for another on a specified schedule. Counterparties typically exchange principal amounts in two currencies at inception, exchange interest payments in each currency during the life of the contract, and re-exchange the principals at maturity at the pre-agreed rate.
Intuition: Each party borrows in the currency where it has an advantage, then swaps the proceeds and the interest obligations, so each ends up servicing debt in the currency it actually needs.
Mechanics: Principals are exchanged at the spot rate at inception and re-exchanged at the same (or a contracted) rate at maturity, while periodic interest flows — fixed or floating — in the two currencies are paid in between. This structure hedges both interest rate and exchange rate exposure over the contract's life.
Relationships: Swap, Interest rate swap, Currency pair, Forward contract, FX future
Failure modes: Because principals are re-exchanged at a fixed rate, a large exchange-rate move creates substantial mark-to-market exposure to the counterparty over long tenors. Cross-currency basis can also move against hedgers, making synthetic funding more expensive than direct funding.
Misconceptions: That a currency swap is the same as an FX swap (a spot purchase plus an offsetting forward); a currency swap exchanges ongoing interest payments as well as principal. Also, unlike an interest rate swap, principal typically is exchanged here.
Example: A U.S. firm swaps $100 million for euros with a European firm at inception, pays euro interest and receives dollar interest for seven years, then re-exchanges the same principal amounts at maturity.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Currency Swap)
Status: Reviewed

0095. Total return swap
Domain: Instruments
Definition: A swap in which one party (the total return payer) transfers the full economic performance of a reference asset — its income plus any price appreciation or depreciation — to the other party, which in return pays a financing rate (a reference rate plus a spread) on the notional. It transfers the asset's returns without transferring ownership and is classed among the common credit derivatives.
Intuition: A total return swap lets you collect everything a stock, bond, or index pays and earns — as if you owned it — while posting only a fraction of its value as margin and paying a financing charge.
Mechanics: On each payment date the payer passes through coupons or dividends plus the mark-to-market change in the reference asset; if the asset fell, the receiver pays the loss. The receiver thus holds leveraged synthetic exposure, while the payer (often a dealer that owns or hedges the asset) sheds its price risk.
Formula: Total return payment = income received on the reference asset + (P_end - P_start) x notional quantity; financing leg = notional x (reference rate + spread) x day-count fraction.
Relationships: Swap, Credit default swap, Synthetic asset, Contract for difference
Failure modes: The receiver bears the full downside of the reference asset plus counterparty risk, and the embedded leverage is largely invisible on the balance sheet — the 2021 Archegos collapse was built on equity total return swaps. Financing spreads can also widen or financing be withdrawn in stress.
Misconceptions: That receiving total return confers shareholder rights — it transfers economics only, not voting or ownership. Also, dealers are not betting against the client by default; they typically hedge the reference asset.
Example: A fund receives the total return on $50 million notional of an equity basket and pays SOFR plus 60 basis points quarterly; a 4% rise in the basket over a quarter nets it roughly $2 million minus financing.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Credit Derivative (lists total return swaps among common credit derivatives))
Status: Reviewed

0096. Credit default swap
Domain: Instruments
Definition: A bilateral over-the-counter credit derivative in which the protection seller agrees to make a payment to the protection buyer in the event of a specified credit event (such as a default or bankruptcy) of a reference entity, in exchange for a fixed payment or series of fixed payments. It is the most common type of credit derivative.
Intuition: A CDS works like default insurance on a borrower: you pay a periodic premium, and if the borrower suffers a credit event, you are compensated for the loss in value of its debt.
Mechanics: The buyer pays a periodic spread on the notional until maturity or a credit event. After a credit event is determined by the ISDA determinations committee, the contract settles either physically (the buyer delivers defaulted debt and receives par) or in cash at an auction-determined recovery value (the seller pays par minus recovery).
Formula: Premium leg approximately N x spread x day-count fraction per period; protection leg approximately N x (1 - recovery rate) on a credit event.
Relationships: Swap, Total return swap, Corporate bond, Government bond
Failure modes: The CDS-bond basis can diverge, so hedges are imperfect. Concentrated seller exposure can transmit losses across the system (AIG in 2008), and disputes over what constitutes a credit event can delay or reduce payouts.
Misconceptions: That the buyer must own the reference entity's bonds — 'naked' CDS positions are permitted, so open CDS notional can exceed the debt outstanding. Also, a CDS is not legally an insurance contract and carries no insurable-interest requirement.
Example: An investor buys 5-year CDS protection on $10 million of XYZ Corp at a 200 basis point spread, paying about $200,000 per year; if XYZ defaults and the auction recovery is 40%, the seller pays roughly $6 million.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Credit Default Swap)
Status: Reviewed

0097. Contract for difference
Domain: Instruments
Definition: A leveraged over-the-counter derivative between a client and a provider in which the parties exchange the difference between the opening and closing price of an underlying asset — a share, index, currency, or commodity — without either party owning the underlying. The FCA classifies CFDs as complex, high-risk products that carry a considerable risk of substantial losses.
Intuition: A CFD is a cash-settled bet on a price move: you gain or lose the full change in the asset's price while posting only a fraction of its value as margin.
Mechanics: A position is opened with initial margin; profit or loss equals the price change times position size, and long positions pay daily financing on the full notional. Regulators such as the FCA restrict retail leverage (between 30:1 and 2:1 depending on the underlying), mandate margin close-out, and provide negative balance protection for retail clients.
Formula: PnL (long) = (P_close - P_open) x quantity, minus financing and any commissions.
Relationships: Total return swap, Margin, Futures contract, Forward contract
Failure modes: High leverage means small adverse moves can wipe out the deposit quickly; a large majority of retail CFD accounts lose money. The client also bears provider counterparty risk, and overnight financing charges erode positions held for long periods.
Misconceptions: That a CFD confers ownership or voting rights in the underlying — it is purely a price-difference contract. Also, stop-losses do not guarantee an exit price in gapping markets.
Example: Buying 1,000 share CFDs at GBP 10.00 with 20% margin requires GBP 2,000; if the price rises to GBP 10.50, the gain is GBP 500 minus financing — a 25% return on margin from a 5% price move, with symmetric downside.
Citation: UK Financial Conduct Authority, press release: FCA warns investors in CFDs risk losing out on protections — https://www.fca.org.uk/news/press-releases/fca-warns-investors-cfds-risk-losing-out-protections (Notes to editors: definition and risk characterization of CFDs)
Status: Reviewed

0098. Exchange-traded fund
Domain: Instruments
Definition: An exchange-traded investment product that must register with the SEC as an open-end investment company (or sometimes as a unit investment trust). It pools investor money into a portfolio of assets and its shares trade on a national securities exchange throughout the day at market prices, like a stock.
Intuition: An ETF packages a whole portfolio into a single share you can buy or sell any time the market is open, combining mutual-fund-style pooling with stock-style trading.
Mechanics: Large broker-dealers called authorized participants create and redeem ETF shares in large blocks (creation units, typically 50,000 shares or more), usually in exchange for baskets of the underlying securities in-kind. This creation/redemption arbitrage keeps the ETF's market price close to its net asset value.
Relationships: Mutual fund, Closed-end fund, Exchange-traded note, Market index
Failure modes: In stressed markets the ETF's price can trade at a premium or discount to NAV, and the liquidity of the underlying assets may be much thinner than the ETF's own trading liquidity suggests. Tracking error, fees, and, for leveraged or inverse ETFs, daily-reset compounding can produce returns far from the index multiple investors expect.
Misconceptions: That all ETFs are cheap, passive index trackers — the wrapper also wraps leveraged, inverse, actively managed, and single-commodity products with very different risks. Also, ETF shares are not redeemed for cash by ordinary investors; they are sold on the exchange.
Example: An investor buys 100 shares of an S&P 500 ETF on an exchange at 10:30 a.m. at the prevailing market price, gaining diversified index exposure in one intraday trade.
Citation: SEC Investor.gov Glossary — https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/glossary (Exchange-Traded Fund (ETF); Authorized Participants; Creation Unit)
Status: Reviewed

0099. Exchange-traded note
Domain: Instruments
