Formula: Call intrinsic value = max(S - K, 0); put intrinsic value = max(K - S, 0), where S = underlying price and K = strike price.
Relationships: Intrinsic value, Option premium, Option exercise, Moneyness, Expiration date
Failure modes: Comparing options across different strikes as if the premium alone measures cheapness ignores that the strike determines both payoff and probability of finishing in-the-money.
Misconceptions: The strike is not a price target or forecast — it is a contractual term chosen from listed series, and an at-the-money option is not 'fairly priced' by definition.
Example: A holder of an OICX July 60 call can buy the underlying stock at $60 per share until expiration; if the stock trades at $68, the call has $8 of intrinsic value.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Exercise Price (Strike Price))
Citation: The Options Industry Council (OIC), FAQ: Basics — https://www.optionseducation.org/referencelibrary/faq/basics (What is the strike price?)
Status: Reviewed

0140. Expiration date
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: The date on which an option contract automatically expires and ceases to exist; it is the last day on which the option may be exercised (and for American-style options, the end of the exercise window).
Intuition: An option is a wasting asset with a printed shelf life: after the expiration date the contract is gone, worth whatever final settlement paid — usually zero for out-of-the-money options.
Mechanics: At expiration, in-the-money options are typically exercised 'by exception' above small thresholds (OCC uses $0.01 for equity options) unless contrary instructions are given, while out-of-the-money options expire worthless. Time value decays toward zero as expiration approaches, and for standard monthly U.S. equity options expiration falls on the third Friday of the expiration month.
Relationships: Last trading day, Option exercise, Time value, American-style option, European-style option
Failure modes: Traders who treat expiration day like any other trading day face pin risk (underlying closing near the strike), after-hours price moves that flip moneyness after the close, and automatic-exercise outcomes they did not intend.
Misconceptions: Expiration date is not always the last trading day: for many European-style index options the last trading day is the Thursday before expiration Friday, and the exercise style is set in each product's specifications.
Example: A standard U.S. equity option expiring in July ceases to exist after the third Friday of July; a holder who does not sell or exercise it by then keeps only any automatic-exercise value.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Expiration Date; Automatic Exercise)
Citation: The Options Industry Council (OIC), FAQ: Options Exercise — https://www.optionseducation.org/referencelibrary/faq/options-exercise (Exercise by exception; last trading day)
Status: Reviewed

0141. Maturity date
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: The specified date on which the principal (face value) of a debt instrument such as a bond is scheduled to be repaid to the investor; for futures, 'maturity' refers to the period within which the contract can be settled by delivery.
Intuition: The maturity date is the loan's end date: it is when the borrower's promise to hand back the principal comes due.
Mechanics: A bond pays coupons on a regular schedule until maturity, when the final coupon plus the face value are paid. Time to maturity shortens as time passes, and together with the coupon rate it drives interest-rate sensitivity: longer maturities generally carry greater interest rate risk.
Relationships: Par value, Coupon rate, Yield to maturity, Duration, Delivery month
Failure modes: Selling before maturity exposes the holder to whatever price the market dictates, so 'getting your principal back' holds only if the bond is held to maturity and the issuer does not default; callable bonds can be retired before the stated maturity.
Misconceptions: Maturity date is not the same as duration: a coupon bond's duration is always shorter than its maturity (only a zero-coupon bond's duration equals its maturity), because some cash arrives earlier as coupons.
Example: A 10-year Treasury note issued in 2026 pays interest every six months and repays its face value on its 2036 maturity date; if sold in 2030, the investor receives the then-market price instead of par.
Citation: Investor.gov (SEC Office of Investor Education and Advocacy): Bonds — https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/investment-products/bonds-or-fixed-income-products/bonds (What are bonds?)
Citation: Hillier et al., Fundamentals of Corporate Finance, Chapter 6: Bond Valuation (McGraw-Hill sample chapter) — https://highered.mheducation.com/sites/dl/free/0077149777/1013655/Sample_Chapter.pdf (6.1 Bond Features and Prices (maturity definition))
Status: Reviewed

0142. Option premium
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: The price the buyer of an option pays (and the writer receives) for the rights granted by the contract; it is the market price of the option itself, composed of intrinsic value plus time value.
Intuition: The premium is what you pay for the right-but-not-the-obligation: it is the cost of insurance or of a leveraged bet, paid up front and never refundable.
Mechanics: Premiums are determined by supply and demand in the options market and are driven mainly by the underlying price, strike, time to expiration, implied volatility, and secondarily by dividends and interest rates. Quoted per share (or per unit), the dollar premium equals the quote times the contract multiplier (typically 100 for U.S. equity options).
Formula: Premium = intrinsic value + time value; dollar premium per contract = quoted premium x contract multiplier.
Relationships: Intrinsic value, Extrinsic value, Time value, Strike price, Implied volatility, Contract multiplier
Failure modes: Treating a low premium as 'cheap' ignores implied volatility and moneyness: a $0.10 far out-of-the-money option can be overpriced relative to its probability-weighted payoff.
Misconceptions: The option writer does not 'return' the premium at expiration — the writer keeps it regardless of outcome; and for the buyer, the premium is a sunk cost that must be subtracted from any exercise or resale proceeds to compute net profit.
Example: Buying one equity call quoted at $2.50 costs $250 (2.50 x 100 shares); if the option is later sold for $4.00, the net profit before commissions is $150.
Citation: The Options Industry Council (OIC): What is an Option? — https://www.optionseducation.org/optionsoverview/what-is-an-option (At a Premium; The Value of Options)
Citation: The Options Industry Council (OIC): Options Pricing — https://www.optionseducation.org/optionsoverview/options-pricing (Major Factors Influencing Options Premium)
Status: Reviewed

0143. Intrinsic value
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: The value an option would have if exercised immediately: the amount by which the underlying price exceeds the strike for a call, or by which the strike exceeds the underlying price for a put; only in-the-money options have intrinsic value.
Intuition: Intrinsic value is the cash you could capture right now by exercising and trading out of the underlying — everything above that in the premium is hope, not substance.
Mechanics: For a call with underlying price S and strike K, intrinsic value = max(S - K, 0); for a put, max(K - S, 0). It sets a lower bound on an American-style option's premium, since selling the option for less than intrinsic value would invite immediate-exercise arbitrage.
Formula: Call: IV = max(S - K, 0); Put: IV = max(K - S, 0), where S = current underlying price and K = strike price.
Relationships: Extrinsic value, Time value, Option premium, Strike price, Moneyness
Failure modes: For deep-in-the-money or hard-to-borrow underlyings, quoted premiums can briefly deviate from intrinsic value when the underlying's price is stale or early exercise is optimal, so 'intrinsic value' computed from a stale quote misleads.
Misconceptions: Intrinsic value is not the same as profit: an in-the-money option still loses money for its buyer if the premium paid exceeds the intrinsic value realized.
Example: With the underlying stock at $32.80, a $32.50-strike call has $0.30 of intrinsic value; if its premium is $1.10, the remaining $0.80 is time value.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Intrinsic Value)
Citation: The Options Industry Council (OIC): Options Pricing — https://www.optionseducation.org/optionsoverview/options-pricing (Intrinsic Value (Calls/Puts))
Status: Reviewed

0144. Extrinsic value
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: The portion of an option's premium in excess of its intrinsic value, reflecting the market's payment for the possibility that the option gains value before expiration; in standard usage it is synonymous with time value, though it embeds volatility, carry, and dividend effects as well as time.
Intuition: Extrinsic value is the 'maybe' premium: the extra amount buyers pay over immediate-exercise value for the chance the underlying moves favorably before expiry.
Mechanics: Extrinsic value = premium - intrinsic value. It is largest for at-the-money options with long time to expiration and high implied volatility, and it erodes toward zero as expiration approaches (time decay) or as the option moves deep in- or out-of-the-money.
Formula: Extrinsic value = option premium - intrinsic value.
Relationships: Time value, Intrinsic value, Option premium, Implied volatility, Theta
Failure modes: Because extrinsic value decays nonlinearly (fastest near expiration and near the money), hedged strategies built on a constant-decay assumption misestimate carry; volatility collapses can erase extrinsic value even when the underlying is unchanged.
Misconceptions: Extrinsic value is often equated purely with time; in fact implied volatility, interest rates, and dividends also inflate or deflate it, which is why the term is preferred when discussing non-time influences.
Example: A $32.50-strike call trading at $1.10 with the stock at $32.80 carries $0.80 of extrinsic value ($1.10 premium minus $0.30 intrinsic), which an early exerciser forfeits.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Extrinsic Value (see Time Value); Time Value)
Citation: The Options Industry Council (OIC): Options Pricing — https://www.optionseducation.org/optionsoverview/options-pricing (Time Value; Major Factors Influencing Options Premium)
Status: Reviewed

0145. Time value
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: That portion of an option's premium that exceeds its intrinsic value; it reflects the probability that the option will move (further) into the money before expiration, so the longer the time remaining, the greater the time value, all else equal.
Intuition: Time value is the price of possibility: with more days left, there is more chance for the underlying to move in your favor, and the market charges for that chance.
Mechanics: Time value = premium - intrinsic value. It decays as expiration approaches (theta decay), with decay accelerating in the final weeks and being most pronounced for at-the-money options; higher implied volatility raises it, and it reaches zero at expiration.
Formula: Time value = option premium - intrinsic value.
Relationships: Extrinsic value, Intrinsic value, Option premium, Theta, Expiration date, Implied volatility
Failure modes: Long-option positions lose time value every day even when the underlying is flat, so a correct directional view can still lose money if the move comes too slowly; decay is nonlinear, so linear extrapolation of daily decay underestimates late-life erosion.
Misconceptions: Time value does not measure how much time is left in a literal sense — two options with identical time to expiry can have very different time values because volatility and moneyness differ.
Example: A two-week $32.50 call on a $32.80 stock priced at $1.10 has $0.80 of time value; at expiration, if the stock is still $32.80, the premium collapses to roughly its $0.30 intrinsic value.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Time Value)
Citation: The Options Industry Council (OIC): Options Pricing — https://www.optionseducation.org/optionsoverview/options-pricing (Time Value)
Status: Reviewed

0146. American-style option
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: An option that the holder may exercise at any time on or before the expiration date; all standardized U.S. exchange-traded equity options use American-style exercise.
Intuition: An American option is a standing offer: any day before expiry, the holder can invoke the strike and take or deliver the underlying.
Mechanics: Early exercise is a right, not an obligation, and exercising early forfeits any remaining time value, so holders usually sell rather than exercise; early exercise of a call becomes rational mainly to capture an impending dividend, and of a deep in-the-money put to receive strike proceeds sooner. Because the writer can be assigned at any time, short American options carry early-assignment risk.
Relationships: European-style option, Bermudan option, Option exercise, Option assignment, Time value
Failure modes: Writers who ignore dividend dates or deep-in-the-money scenarios can be assigned early at inopportune times, e.g., losing stock plus dividend entitlements or facing unexpected margin and stock-delivery obligations.
Misconceptions: The label has nothing to do with geography or where the option trades — it names the exercise style; and early exercise is rarely optimal for the holder despite being always available, because it discards time value.
Example: A holder of an American-style OICX July 60 call can instruct their broker to buy 100 shares at $60 on any trading day up to the July expiration, whereas a writer of that call can be assigned on any such day.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (American Option)
Citation: The Options Industry Council (OIC), FAQ: Options Exercise — https://www.optionseducation.org/referencelibrary/faq/options-exercise (American-style exercise; early exercise and dividends)
Status: Reviewed

0147. European-style option
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: An option that may be exercised only on its expiration date; most (but not all) U.S. index options use European-style exercise.
Intuition: A European option is a single-day right: you can trade the contract any time, but you can invoke the strike only on expiration day itself.
Mechanics: The holder can always close the position by selling the option in the market before expiration; only exercise is restricted to the expiry date (and the last trading day is typically the day before expiration for index options). With no early-exercise possibility, European options are simpler to price (e.g., Black-Scholes applies directly) and writers face no early-assignment risk.
Relationships: American-style option, Bermudan option, Option exercise, Expiration date, Black-Scholes model, Cash settlement
Failure modes: Holders needing to monetize before expiry must sell into the market, so wide bid-ask spreads or halted trading can trap value; confusing a European index option's last trading day with its expiration date can leave a position held unintentionally through settlement.
Misconceptions: European-style does not mean the position is locked until expiry — closing trades are always possible; nor does the name imply the option trades in Europe.
Example: A European-style index call can only be exercised at expiration, and its last trading day is usually the Thursday before expiration Friday; a holder wanting out on Tuesday simply sells the option on the exchange.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (European Option)
Citation: The Options Industry Council (OIC), FAQ: Options Exercise — https://www.optionseducation.org/referencelibrary/faq/options-exercise (European-style exercise; index option last trading day)
Status: Reviewed

0148. Bermudan option
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: An exotic option that can be exercised only on a specified set of predetermined dates during its life, an exercise style intermediate between American (any time) and European (at expiry only).
Intuition: A Bermudan option opens the exercise window on a schedule — say, the first business day of each month — rather than every day (American) or just once at the end (European).
Mechanics: The contract lists the permissible exercise dates in advance. Its value sits between that of the equivalent European and American options, and pricing typically requires numerical methods (trees or simulation) that check optimal exercise at each permitted date.
Relationships: American-style option, European-style option, Exotic option, Option exercise
Failure modes: Missing an exercise window is irreversible until the next scheduled date, so holders carry gap risk between windows; pricing models that ignore the discrete exercise schedule misvalue the option relative to both limiting styles.
Misconceptions: Bermudan options are not a blend or average of American and European contracts — they are a distinct exercise schedule, and the name (like the other styles) has no geographic meaning.
Example: A Bermudan swaption might allow the holder to enter the underlying interest rate swap only on the swap's quarterly coupon dates during a five-year window.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Bermudan Option)
Status: Reviewed

0149. Option exercise
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: The act by which the holder of an option invokes the contractual right to buy (call) or sell (put) the underlying at the strike price, converting the option position into a transaction or position in the underlying.
Intuition: Exercising is cashing in the ticket: instead of selling the option, you use it to force the trade at the strike.
Mechanics: The holder gives irrevocable exercise instructions to their broker, which routes them to the clearing organization (OCC for U.S. securities options) before exercise cut-off times; settlement then proceeds as a purchase or sale of the underlying (physical) or a cash payment. At expiration, OCC's 'exercise by exception' automatically exercises options in-the-money by at least $0.01 unless contrary instructions are submitted. Exercising early forfeits remaining time value, so holders often prefer selling the option.
Relationships: Option assignment, Strike price, American-style option, European-style option, Intrinsic value, Expiration date
Failure modes: Exercise requires the cash or stock to complete the underlying transaction; holders without it may be restricted by their broker. Failing to submit explicit instructions around thresholds or after-hours price moves can produce unintended exercises or lapses of in-the-money value.
Misconceptions: Exercise is not the usual way to realize an option's value — most long options are closed by sale (historically roughly 70% of contracts are closed out and only a small share are exercised), because selling preserves time value that exercise destroys.
Example: Exercising an OICX 60 call means buying 100 shares at $60 each; if the stock is $68 and the call trades at $8.50, selling the call realizes $8.50 while exercise-plus-sale realizes only the $8 intrinsic value.
Citation: The Options Industry Council (OIC), FAQ: Options Exercise — https://www.optionseducation.org/referencelibrary/faq/options-exercise (How do I exercise?; Exercise by exception)
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Automatic Exercise; Exercise Price (Strike Price))
Status: Reviewed

0150. Option assignment
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: The designation by the clearing organization of an option writer who must fulfill the contract — selling the underlying at the strike (assigned call) or buying it at the strike (assigned put) — when a holder exercises.
Intuition: Assignment is the other side of exercise: when a holder invokes the ticket, a writer is tapped on the shoulder and must honor the deal.
Mechanics: When exercise notices reach the clearing organization, OCC assigns them randomly to clearing members carrying short positions in that series; members in turn allocate assignments to their customers (by random selection or first-in-first-out). Writers of American-style options can be assigned any trading day, with likelihood rising for in-the-money options near ex-dividend dates (calls) or deep in-the-money (puts).
Relationships: Option exercise, American-style option, Option writer, Strike price, Covered call
Failure modes: Writers can be assigned overnight and discover the resulting stock position only the next morning, leaving them exposed to opening gaps; assignment near ex-dividend dates can also force delivery of stock plus dividend obligations.
Misconceptions: Assignment is not directed at a specific writer by the exercising holder — it is allocated by the clearing organization, so no short writer can predict or prevent being selected; also, closing the short (buy to close) eliminates assignment risk only if done before assignment.
Example: An investor short an OICX 60 call wakes to find the call was exercised: they must sell 100 shares at $60 regardless of the current $68 market price, an immediate $8-per-share adverse fill versus the market.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Assignment)
Citation: The Options Industry Council (OIC), FAQ: Options Exercise — https://www.optionseducation.org/referencelibrary/faq/options-exercise (Assignment allocation; dividends and early assignment)
Status: Reviewed

0151. Physical settlement
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: A provision in a futures or other derivative contract requiring delivery of the actual underlying commodity or asset (or a delivery instrument such as a warehouse receipt) to satisfy the contract at maturity.
Intuition: With physical settlement, holding the contract to the end means real goods or securities change hands — not just a check for the price difference.
Mechanics: After the last trading day, remaining shorts tender delivery notices through the clearing organization, and remaining longs must accept delivery and pay the invoice price (e.g., for bond futures, invoice price = contract size x futures settlement price x conversion factor + accrued interest). Delivery occurs at exchange-approved facilities during the delivery period.
Relationships: Cash settlement, Delivery notice, Warehouse receipt, Delivery month, First notice day, Final settlement price
Failure modes: Traders who fail to close longs before first notice day can be obligated to take (and pay for) full physical delivery, including storage, transport, and financing; squeezes on deliverable supply can distort prices near expiry.
Misconceptions: Most futures positions never reach delivery — they are offset beforehand — but physical settlement is not merely theoretical: the deliverability of the contract is what ties the futures price to the cash market at expiry (convergence).
Example: A refiner holding CME WTI crude futures through expiry receives delivery notices for 1,000-barrel lots at the Cushing, Oklahoma delivery point and pays the invoice price per contract.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Physical Delivery; Delivery; Conversion Factors (invoice price))
Status: Reviewed

0152. Cash settlement
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: A method of settling futures, options, and other derivatives whereby the seller pays the buyer the cash value of the underlying, or a cash amount based on the level of an index or price, according to a procedure specified in the contract, instead of delivering the asset itself.
Intuition: Cash settlement settles the score in money only: at expiry the contract simply pays out the difference, so no barrels, shares, or bonds ever move.
Mechanics: At maturity, positions are valued against the final settlement price computed by the exchange's specified procedure (e.g., a special opening quotation of an index), and the clearing organization credits or debits the difference. Cash settlement is standard where the underlying is not practically deliverable, such as equity indexes.
Relationships: Physical settlement, Final settlement price, Daily settlement price, Underlying asset
Failure modes: The settlement procedure itself becomes the point of fragility: if the reference price is derived from a short window or a manipulable market, the final settlement value can be distorted, and hedges calibrated to continuous prices can slip.
Misconceptions: Cash-settled does not mean 'synthetic' or less connected to the underlying — arbitrage against the cash market still enforces convergence to the settlement value; nor does it mean daily P&L differs, since all futures are marked to market daily regardless of final settlement style.
Example: At expiration, an E-mini S&P 500 futures position is settled in cash against the special opening quotation of the S&P 500 index; no shares of the 500 companies are delivered.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Cash Settlement)
Status: Reviewed

0153. Final settlement price
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: The price at which a cash-settled futures (or option) contract is settled at maturity, determined pursuant to a procedure specified by the exchange.
Intuition: The final settlement price is the official last mark of a contract's life — the single number that decides the terminal cash flows for everyone still holding it.
Mechanics: The exchange's contract rules define exactly how it is computed: common procedures include a special opening quotation based on constituent opening prices (equity index futures) or a volume-weighted average over a defined window. The clearing organization settles all remaining open positions against this price, and it need not equal the last traded price of the contract.
Relationships: Cash settlement, Daily settlement price, Last trading day, Expiration date
Failure modes: Because the final settlement price follows its own procedure, it can deviate sharply from the contract's last traded price (e.g., an opening-rotation quotation after an overnight event), producing unexpected P&L for positions marked against the close.
Misconceptions: It is not simply the closing price of the futures contract on the last trading day; each product's rulebook defines a distinct calculation, and the two can differ materially.
Example: Quarterly S&P 500 index options settle against the special opening quotation (SOQ) of the index on expiration morning, so a trader holding through expiry is exposed to opening prices of the 500 constituents, not the prior close.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Final Settlement Price)
Status: Reviewed

0154. Daily settlement price
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: The official daily price at which the clearing organization clears all trades and settles all accounts between clearing members for each contract month; it is the benchmark used for marking positions to market, computing margin calls, and invoicing deliveries.
Intuition: The daily settlement price is the exchange's official 'score' for the day: everyone's futures P&L and margin requirements are recomputed against it every session.
Mechanics: Exchanges derive it from trading activity near the close (e.g., a volume-weighted average over a designated closing period, with exchange discretion in illiquid conditions). All open positions are marked to this price daily: gains are credited and losses debited (variation margin), and for physically delivered contracts it feeds the delivery invoice price.
Relationships: Final settlement price, Marking to market, Margin, Daily price limit, Physical settlement
Failure modes: In illiquid or disorderly closes the settlement price may differ from the last trade, so P&L and margin calls can move against a trader even when their executed prices looked favorable; it is also a manipulation target ('banging the close').
Misconceptions: The settlement price is not necessarily the last traded price or the simple closing quote — exchanges use defined closing-period procedures; and daily price limits are measured against the prior day's settlement, not the last trade.
Example: If yesterday's settle on a corn future was 450 cents and today's settle is 460, a long one-contract position is credited 10 cents x 5,000 bushels = $500 of variation margin overnight.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Settlement Price)
Citation: CME Group, A Trader's Guide to Futures — https://www.cmegroup.com/education/files/a-traders-guide-to-futures.pdf (Section 3 (marking positions to market twice daily))
Status: Reviewed

0155. Delivery month
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: The specified month within which a futures contract matures and can be settled by delivery, or within which the delivery period begins, as defined in the contract specification.
Intuition: The delivery month is the contract's calendar label: 'December corn' means the corn future whose obligations fall due in December.
Mechanics: Exchanges list a cycle of delivery months per product (e.g., March, May, July, September, December for many grains). Each month trades as a distinct contract with its own price and open interest; the nearest is the spot/front month, later ones are back months, and prices across months embed carrying costs (contango) or discounts (backwardation).
Relationships: First notice day, Last trading day, Delivery notice, Contract rollover, Contango, Backwardation
Failure modes: Liquidity migrates from the front month to the next month well before expiry, so trading the wrong month late in its life means wide spreads and delivery risk; confusing the delivery month with the last trading day (which usually precedes it) is a common operational error.
Misconceptions: The delivery month is not a single date but a window: the exact first/last trading and notice days are set per product and can fall in the prior month.
Example: A trader long 'ZCZ25' holds December 2025 corn futures; as December approaches, volume and open interest shift to the March 2026 contract, prompting most traders to roll rather than risk delivery.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Delivery Month; Back Months; Spot Month)
Citation: Encyclopaedia Britannica Money: Volume & Open Interest in Futures Trading — https://www.britannica.com/money/futures-volume-open-interest (Identify contract rollover periods)
Status: Reviewed

0156. First notice day
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: The first day on which notices of intent to deliver the actual commodity against open short futures positions can be issued (received by longs); the date varies by commodity and exchange.
Intuition: First notice day is when holding a long futures position stops being purely financial: from then on, a long can be handed a delivery notice and be obliged to pay for and take the goods.
Mechanics: In physically delivered markets, shorts may tender delivery notices from first notice day through the delivery period; the clearing organization assigns them to longs, who must pay the invoice price. First notice day often falls before the delivery month and before the last trading day, so speculators typically exit or roll long positions beforehand.
Relationships: Delivery notice, Delivery month, Last trading day, Physical settlement, Warehouse receipt
Failure modes: Longs who overlook first notice day can be assigned delivery against their will, requiring full contract-value funding and triggering liquidation by brokers who do not support delivery; liquidity also thins as commercials dominate the final sessions.
Misconceptions: First notice day is not the same as the last trading day, and it is not uniform across markets — each contract's calendar sets its own, sometimes weeks before trading ends.
Example: For many CBOT grain contracts, first notice day is the last business day preceding the delivery month, so a speculator long December corn would normally exit by late November to avoid delivery assignment.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (First Notice Day)
Status: Reviewed

0157. Last trading day
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: The final day on which a futures or options contract may be traded on the exchange; after the close of the last trading day, remaining open positions proceed to settlement or delivery.
Intuition: The last trading day is the deadline for closing a position on your own terms — miss it, and the contract's settlement machinery decides the outcome for you.
Mechanics: Each product's specification fixes the last trading day: for standard U.S. equity options it is the expiration Friday (third Friday of the month), while for many European-style index options it is the Thursday before expiration Friday; futures contracts typically stop trading a set number of days before or within the delivery month, after which delivery or final cash settlement occurs.
Relationships: Expiration date, First notice day, Delivery month, Final settlement price, Contract rollover
Failure modes: Positions held past the last trading day lose the ability to be closed competitively and are exposed to the exchange's settlement procedure, which can produce prices far from recent trades; low liquidity on the last day also degrades exit quality.
Misconceptions: The last trading day is not always the same as the expiration date — for many index options trading stops the day before expiration — and it differs by product, so assuming the equity-option convention generalizes is unsafe.
Example: A trader long a European-style index call who wants out must sell by the Thursday before expiration Friday; after that close, only the expiration-day settlement value determines the payoff.
Citation: The Options Industry Council (OIC), FAQ: Options Exercise — https://www.optionseducation.org/referencelibrary/faq/options-exercise (Last trading day conventions for equity and index options)
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Spot Month; Notice Day; Delivery Month)
Status: Reviewed

0158. Delivery notice
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: The written notice given by a futures seller of the intention to make delivery against an open short position on a particular date, delivered through the clearing organization; it is separate and distinct from the warehouse receipt or other instrument used to transfer title.
Intuition: The delivery notice is the short's formal 'I will deliver' declaration — the document that starts the physical settlement process and lands on some long's desk.
Mechanics: Shorts tender delivery notices through their clearing members during the notice period (from first notice day onward); the clearing organization assigns them to longs, typically the oldest outstanding longs, who must then pay the invoice price and receive the delivery instrument. In some markets a long can retender the notice to another long the same day.
Relationships: First notice day, Warehouse receipt, Physical settlement, Delivery month, Daily settlement price
Failure modes: A long assigned a notice must fund the full invoice value promptly; being stopped on a notice when the position was intended as a paper hedge creates financing and logistics burdens, and in some contracts the assigned long can only retender within the same session.
Misconceptions: Receiving a delivery notice is not receiving the commodity itself — the notice initiates invoicing, and the warehouse receipt or shipping certificate that transfers title follows through the clearing process.
Example: A CBOT wheat short tenders a delivery notice on the second business day of the delivery month; the clearing house assigns it to the oldest long, who pays the invoice price and receives the registered warehouse receipt.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Delivery Notice; Retender)
Status: Reviewed

0159. Warehouse receipt
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: A document certifying possession of a commodity in a licensed or exchange-approved warehouse, recognized for delivery purposes in settlement of futures contracts.
Intuition: The warehouse receipt is the paper (or electronic) title to goods sitting in an approved silo or vault — delivering the receipt is delivering the commodity.
Mechanics: Commodities must be stored in exchange-approved facilities and meet deliverable grades; the receipt evidences that stock and circulates through the clearing organization during delivery, transferring ownership from short to long. It functions as a negotiable delivery instrument alongside alternatives such as shipping certificates.
Relationships: Delivery notice, Physical settlement, Delivery month, Deliverable grades, Certified stocks
Failure modes: The system rests on warehouse integrity: fraud, double-pledged receipts, or metal/grain that fails inspection breaks the deliverable supply and can trigger market disruption, as in historical warehouse-receipt scandals.
Misconceptions: A warehouse receipt is not the same as a delivery notice — the notice declares intent to deliver, while the receipt is the title document that actually conveys the commodity.
Example: In a copper futures delivery, the short's clearing member passes a registered LME/CME warehouse receipt for 25 metric tons in an approved warehouse to the assigned long in exchange for the invoice payment.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Warehouse Receipt; Delivery Instrument; Deliverable Stocks)
Status: Reviewed

0160. Notional value
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: The total face or reference value of the underlying exposure controlled by a derivative contract — the amount to which prices, rates, or percentage changes are applied to compute payments or P&L — as distinct from the much smaller premium or margin actually exchanged.
Intuition: Notional value is the size of the position you economically control, not the cash you put up: a small margin deposit can steer a very large notional ship.
Mechanics: For futures, notional value = contract price x contract size (or index level x multiplier), e.g., an E-mini S&P 500 future near 4,500 controls roughly $225,000. For swaps, the notional principal is the amount to which the fixed and floating rates are applied to compute periodic payments; it is typically never exchanged, which is why it is 'notional'.
Formula: Futures notional value = quoted price x contract size (or index level x multiplier); swap periodic payment = notional principal x rate x day-count fraction.
Relationships: Contract size, Contract multiplier, Margin, Leverage, Tick value
Failure modes: Sizing positions by margin posted rather than notional controlled hides true leverage and loss potential; aggregate notional figures (e.g., in derivatives statistics) also overstate economic exposure because notionals gross up offsetting contracts.
Misconceptions: Notional value is not the amount at risk in full for most derivatives — actual loss potential depends on price movement applied to the notional, not on losing the notional itself — yet for leveraged positions losses can still far exceed the margin posted.
Example: An investor posts about $6,000 performance bond to control an E-mini S&P 500 contract worth roughly $67,500 of notional; a 1% index move changes the position value by about $675.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Notional Principal)
Citation: CME Group, A Trader's Guide to Futures — https://www.cmegroup.com/education/files/a-traders-guide-to-futures.pdf (Section 3: What do we mean by leveraged? (E-mini contract value example))
Status: Reviewed

0161. Par value
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: The principal amount of a bond or note that the issuer promises to repay at maturity, and the base on which coupon interest is calculated; the bond trades at a premium, at par, or at a discount depending on whether its price is above, equal to, or below this amount.
Intuition: Par value is the loan amount printed on the bond: whatever the market price does day to day, par is what comes back at the end (absent default).
Mechanics: Coupon payments equal par value x coupon rate (split into periodic installments, typically semiannual). At issuance or in the secondary market, price relative to par reflects the relationship between the coupon rate and the prevailing yield: price < par when yield > coupon, and vice versa.
Formula: Periodic coupon payment = par value x coupon rate / number of payments per year.
Relationships: Coupon rate, Maturity date, Yield to maturity, Accrued interest, Current yield
Failure modes: Par value is repaid only if held to maturity and the issuer performs: default or selling early means the investor realizes the market price or recovery value, not par.
Misconceptions: Par value is not the bond's market value and not a floor on its price; bonds routinely trade above or below par as rates and credit conditions move.
Example: A $1,000-par Treasury note with a 1.75% coupon pays $8.75 every six months and returns the $1,000 par at maturity; it was priced at 98.34 (below par) when its auction yield exceeded the coupon rate.
Citation: TreasuryDirect: Understanding Pricing — https://www.treasurydirect.gov/marketable-securities/understanding-pricing/ (Bonds and Notes (par value and price-yield relationship))
Citation: Investor.gov (SEC Office of Investor Education and Advocacy): Bonds — https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/investment-products/bonds-or-fixed-income-products/bonds (What are bonds?)
Status: Reviewed

0162. Coupon rate
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: The fixed rate of interest a bond pays, stated as a percentage of its principal (par) value per year and typically paid in semiannual installments; it equals the annual coupon divided by the face value.
Intuition: The coupon rate is the bond's built-in paycheck formula, fixed at issuance: it tells you the dollar interest you get each year per $100 of face value, regardless of what the bond's price does later.
Mechanics: Set at issuance (at auction for Treasuries), the coupon rate stays fixed for fixed-rate bonds. Dollar coupon = par x coupon rate, split per payment frequency. The gap between the coupon rate and current market yields drives the bond's price above or below par, and lower-coupon bonds carry greater interest-rate sensitivity, all else equal.
Formula: Coupon rate = annual coupon payment / face value; semiannual payment = face value x coupon rate / 2.
Relationships: Par value, Yield to maturity, Current yield, Accrued interest, Duration
Failure modes: The coupon rate is not the investor's rate of return unless the bond is bought at par and held to maturity; buying at a premium or discount makes yield, not coupon, the return measure.
Misconceptions: A higher coupon rate does not mean a better investment: it usually just compensates for lower price, higher risk, or a higher-rate era — what matters for return is the yield at the purchase price.
Example: A $1,000 bond with a 6% coupon rate pays $60 per year, typically as two $30 semiannual payments, whether its market price is $950 or $1,050.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Coupon (Coupon Rate))
Citation: Hillier et al., Fundamentals of Corporate Finance, Chapter 6: Bond Valuation (McGraw-Hill sample chapter) — https://highered.mheducation.com/sites/dl/free/0077149777/1013655/Sample_Chapter.pdf (6.1 Bond Features and Prices (coupon rate = annual coupon / face value))
Status: Reviewed

0163. Accrued interest
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: Interest earned on a security but not yet paid to the investor; specifically, the portion of the next coupon payment that has accumulated since the last coupon date, which a bond buyer pays to the seller at settlement.
Intuition: Coupons arrive only on payment dates, but interest builds every day: accrued interest is the seller's share of the coming coupon for the days they held the bond.
Mechanics: Accrued interest = coupon payment x (days since last coupon / days in coupon period), using the market's day-count convention (e.g., 30/360 for U.S. corporates, actual/actual for Treasuries). The buyer compensates the seller at settlement, then collects the full coupon on the next payment date; it is also an explicit component of futures invoice prices for deliverable bonds.
Formula: AI = C x (d / D), where C = periodic coupon payment, d = days from last coupon date to settlement, D = days in the coupon period (per the applicable day-count convention).
Relationships: Clean price, Dirty price, Coupon rate, Par value
Failure modes: Accrued interest depends on day-count conventions that differ across bond markets, so a single formula applied across markets miscalculates settlement amounts; it also creates small cash-flow mismatches when hedging coupon-paying bonds with derivatives.
Misconceptions: Accrued interest is not an extra cost or fee: the buyer effectively recovers it in the next full coupon payment, so it is a transfer, not an expense, though it does affect cash outlay at settlement.
Example: Buying a $1,000 bond with a 6% annual coupon (semiannual $30) exactly one-third of the way through the coupon period means paying about $10 of accrued interest to the seller on top of the quoted price.
Citation: Investor.gov Glossary (SEC Office of Investor Education and Advocacy) — https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/glossary (Accrued Interest)
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Conversion Factors (invoice price includes accrued interest))
Status: Reviewed

0164. Clean price
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: The standard quoted market price of a bond, stated net of accrued interest — the price shown on screens and used for price comparison, as distinct from the full amount actually paid at settlement.
Intuition: The clean price strips out the mechanical day-count drift so price changes reflect real market moves, not just time passing between coupon dates.
Mechanics: By market convention bonds are quoted clean; the amount the buyer actually pays is the dirty price = clean price + accrued interest. Quoting clean prevents the sawtooth pattern the dirty price would otherwise show as interest accrues and then drops at each coupon payment.
Formula: Clean price = dirty price - accrued interest.
Relationships: Dirty price, Accrued interest, Coupon rate, Yield to maturity
Failure modes: Computing realized return or cash needs from the clean price alone understates the settlement cash outlay by the accrued interest; comparing yields from dirty cash flows against clean quotes without adjustment creates small pricing inconsistencies.
Misconceptions: The clean price is not the price you pay: settlement always uses the dirty (full) price, so cash planning based on quoted prices alone will be short by the accrued amount.
Example: A bond quoted at 98.50 (clean) with $7.50 accrued interest per $100 face requires a payment of $106.00 per $100 face — the dirty price — at settlement.
Citation: Hillier et al., Fundamentals of Corporate Finance, Chapter 6: Bond Valuation (McGraw-Hill sample chapter) — https://highered.mheducation.com/sites/dl/free/0077149777/1013655/Sample_Chapter.pdf (A Note about Bond Price Quotes)
Status: Reviewed

0165. Dirty price
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: The actual total amount paid for a bond at settlement, equal to the quoted (clean) price plus accrued interest since the last coupon date; also called the full or invoice price.
Intuition: The dirty price is the real check the buyer writes: the quoted price plus the seller's earned-but-unpaid slice of the next coupon.
Mechanics: Dirty price = clean price + accrued interest. It drifts upward between coupon dates as interest accrues and drops by roughly the coupon amount on payment dates, which is why markets quote the clean price for comparison but settle at the dirty price; bond-futures invoice prices likewise add accrued interest to the converted futures price.
Formula: Dirty price = clean price + accrued interest; bond-futures invoice price = contract size x futures settlement price x conversion factor + accrued interest.
Relationships: Clean price, Accrued interest, Coupon rate, Physical settlement
Failure modes: Charting or backtesting dirty prices without adjustment injects artificial sawtooth returns around coupon dates; total-cash mismatches arise when systems quote clean but settle dirty.
Misconceptions: The drop in a bond's full price on the coupon date is not a market loss — it is the mechanical detachment of the coupon just paid, which the clean-price convention exists to filter out.
Example: A bond quoted clean at 101.25 with 45 days of accrued interest of $0.75 per $100 face settles at a dirty price of $102.00 per $100 face.
Citation: Hillier et al., Fundamentals of Corporate Finance, Chapter 6: Bond Valuation (McGraw-Hill sample chapter) — https://highered.mheducation.com/sites/dl/free/0077149777/1013655/Sample_Chapter.pdf (A Note about Bond Price Quotes)
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Conversion Factors (invoice price formula))
Status: Reviewed

0166. Yield to maturity
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: The annual rate of return an investor earns if a bond is bought at its current price and held to maturity, with all coupons reinvested at that same rate; equivalently, the single discount rate that equates the present value of the bond's remaining cash flows to its current price.
Intuition: YTM is the bond's all-in interest rate: it folds the coupon stream and the gain or loss to par into one annualized number, letting different bonds be compared on equal footing.
Mechanics: YTM is found by solving P = sum_t C_t/(1+y)^t + F/(1+y)^T for y given the price — in general only by trial and error or numerical solver. Price and YTM move inversely: when market rates rise, the price of a fixed-rate bond falls and its YTM rises. For semiannual-pay bonds, the periodic rate found is conventionally doubled to quote YTM (bond-equivalent basis).
Formula: P = sum_{t=1..T} C/(1+y)^t + F/(1+y)^T, where P = current price, C = periodic coupon, F = face value, T = number of periods, y = yield to maturity per period (solved numerically).
Relationships: Current yield, Coupon rate, Par value, Duration, Convexity, Clean price
Failure modes: YTM overstates realized return when coupons cannot be reinvested at the same rate, and it is irrelevant for bonds not held to maturity; for callable bonds, YTM assumes a maturity that may never occur (yield-to-worst or yield-to-call is more appropriate).
Misconceptions: YTM is not the coupon rate and not a guaranteed return: it holds only under reinvestment at the YTM and no default, and it says nothing about price risk if the bond is sold early.
Example: A 6-year bond with an 8% coupon and $1,000 face quoted at $955.14 has a yield to maturity of about 9%, found by solving the price equation by trial and error.
Citation: TreasuryDirect: Understanding Pricing — https://www.treasurydirect.gov/marketable-securities/understanding-pricing/ (Bonds and Notes (yield to maturity vs interest rate and price))
Citation: Hillier et al., Fundamentals of Corporate Finance, Chapter 6: Bond Valuation (McGraw-Hill sample chapter) — https://highered.mheducation.com/sites/dl/free/0077149777/1013655/Sample_Chapter.pdf (6.1 Bond Values and Yields; Finding the Yield to Maturity)
Status: Reviewed

0167. Current yield
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: The ratio of a bond's annual interest (coupon) payments to its current market price, stated as a percentage — a simple income-on-price measure that ignores the gain or loss to par at maturity.
Intuition: Current yield answers only 'how much income per dollar of price right now?' — like a dividend yield for bonds, with no regard for what you get back at the end.
Mechanics: Current yield = annual coupon / current price. It exceeds the coupon rate when the bond trades below par and falls below it above par; for discount bonds it understates total return (missing the pull to par), and for premium bonds it overstates it.
Formula: Current yield = annual coupon payment / current market price (e.g., $80 / $955.14 = 8.38%).
Relationships: Yield to maturity, Coupon rate, Par value, Clean price
Failure modes: Because it ignores time value and the terminal capital gain or loss, current yield misranks bonds of different maturities or prices; it is especially misleading for deep-discount, premium, or callable bonds.
Misconceptions: Current yield is not the bond's expected return: for a discount bond the true yield to maturity is higher (current yield misses the built-in gain), and for a premium bond it is lower.
Example: A bond paying $80 annually and priced at $955.14 has a current yield of about 8.38%, below its 9% yield to maturity because the current yield omits the $44.86 discount that accrues to par.
Citation: Investor.gov Glossary (SEC Office of Investor Education and Advocacy) — https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/glossary (Current Yield)
Citation: Hillier et al., Fundamentals of Corporate Finance, Chapter 6: Bond Valuation (McGraw-Hill sample chapter) — https://highered.mheducation.com/sites/dl/free/0077149777/1013655/Sample_Chapter.pdf (6.1 Finding the Yield to Maturity (current yield contrast))
Status: Reviewed

0168. Duration
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: A measure of a bond's price sensitivity to changes in interest rates, expressed in years; formally, the Macaulay duration is the present-value-weighted average time to receipt of the bond's cash flows, and it serves as the basis for the price-sensitivity (modified duration) measure.
Intuition: Duration compresses maturity, coupon, and yield into one number that approximates how many percent a bond's price moves when rates move one percent — the bond's interest-rate speedometer.
Mechanics: Macaulay duration = sum over t of [t x PV(CF_t)] / price. Longer maturities and lower coupons raise duration; a zero-coupon bond's duration equals its maturity, while coupon bonds always have duration below maturity. Approximate percentage price change = -duration (modified) x yield change.
Formula: Macaulay duration D = [ sum_t t x CF_t / (1+y)^t ] / P, where CF_t = cash flow at time t, y = yield per period, P = bond price.
Relationships: Modified duration, Convexity, Yield to maturity, Maturity date, Coupon rate
Failure modes: Duration is a linear (first-order) approximation that degrades for large rate moves (where convexity matters) and assumes parallel yield-curve shifts; for callable or mortgage-backed bonds, changing cash flows make static duration unreliable (effective duration is used instead).
Misconceptions: Duration is not the same as maturity: except for zero-coupon bonds it is shorter than maturity, and it is a risk measure, not a waiting period; nor is it constant — it drifts with time, yield, and coupon changes.
Example: A 10-year bond with a 5% coupon might have a duration near 8-9 years, so a 1% rise in rates implies roughly an 8-9% price decline, versus under 1% for a 6-month bond.
Citation: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Duration)
Citation: Fidelity Investments: Duration — Understanding the Relationship Between Bond Prices and Interest Rates — https://www.fidelity.com/learning-center/investment-products/fixed-income-bonds/duration (Using a bond's duration to gauge interest rate risk)
Status: Reviewed

0169. Modified duration
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: The Macaulay duration adjusted for the bond's yield, giving the approximate percentage change in a bond's full price for a one-percent (100 basis point) change in yield to maturity — the direct price-sensitivity measure used in practice.
Intuition: If duration is the weighted-average timing of cash flows, modified duration is the translation of that timing into an actual price-risk number: MD 5 means roughly 5% price change per 1% rate change.
Mechanics: Modified duration = Macaulay duration / (1 + y/m), where y is the yield to maturity and m the number of compounding periods per year. The first-order price approximation is dP/P ≈ -MD x dy; portfolio managers use MD (and its dollar version, DV01 = MD x price x 0.0001) to size interest-rate exposure.
Formula: MD = D_mac / (1 + y/m); dP/P ≈ -MD x dy, where D_mac = Macaulay duration, y = yield to maturity, m = payments per year, dy = change in yield.
Relationships: Duration, Convexity, Yield to maturity, DV01, Basis point
Failure modes: Being linear, MD overstates losses and understates gains for large yield moves (corrected by adding the convexity term); it presumes a parallel shift and fixed cash flows, so it misstates risk for callable, putable, or mortgage-backed securities and during non-parallel curve moves.
Misconceptions: Modified duration is not measured in years in the economic sense that matters for hedging — it is a percentage-sensitivity figure; and it does not predict price changes from credit-spread moves, only from yield changes.
Example: A bond with modified duration 8.87 would be expected to lose about 8.87% of value if yields rise 1%, and to gain roughly 18% if yields fall 2% (ignoring convexity).
Citation: Fidelity Investments: Duration — Understanding the Relationship Between Bond Prices and Interest Rates — https://www.fidelity.com/learning-center/investment-products/fixed-income-bonds/duration (Using a bond's duration to gauge interest rate risk)
Status: Reviewed

0170. Convexity
Domain: Contract mechanics
Definition: The curvature in the relationship between a bond's price and its yield: the second-order measure of how a bond's duration itself changes as yields change, quantifying the error in the linear duration approximation.
Intuition: Duration draws a straight line through a curved price-yield relationship; convexity measures the bend, and positive convexity means the bond falls less than duration predicts when rates rise and gains more when rates fall.
Mechanics: The price-yield curve is convex for plain-vanilla bonds, so the second-order approximation is dP/P ≈ -MD x dy + 0.5 x Convexity x (dy)^2. Convexity rises with maturity and falls with coupon size; callable and mortgage-backed bonds can exhibit negative convexity, where price appreciation is capped as yields fall because expected cash flows shorten.
Formula: dP/P ≈ -MD x dy + 0.5 x C x (dy)^2, where MD = modified duration, C = convexity = [sum_t CF_t x t x (t+1/m) / (1+y/m)^(t+2)] / P (m = payments per year), dy = change in yield.
Relationships: Modified duration, Duration, Yield to maturity, Callable bond
Failure modes: Ignoring convexity misestimates price changes for large rate moves and for long-duration, low-coupon bonds; assuming positive convexity fails for callable bonds and MBS, whose prepayment or call options flip the curvature negative near rate lows.
Misconceptions: Higher convexity is not a free lunch guaranteeing outperformance — it is a priced characteristic (investors pay for it via lower yield), and it only describes rate sensitivity, not credit or liquidity risk.
Example: For a 2% rate rise, a bond with MD 9 and convexity 0.8 is estimated to change by about -9 x 0.02 + 0.5 x 0.8 x 0.0004 = -17.98% instead of the -18% the duration-only estimate gives, a gap that widens with the size of the rate move.
Citation: Fidelity Investments: Duration — Understanding the Relationship Between Bond Prices and Interest Rates — https://www.fidelity.com/learning-center/investment-products/fixed-income-bonds/duration (Using a bond's convexity to gauge interest rate risk)
Status: Reviewed

0236. Quoted spread
Domain: Microstructure
Definition: The difference between the best (lowest) quoted offer and the best (highest) quoted bid for a security at a point in time, i.e. the round-trip cost of immediacy at displayed prices. SEC Rule 600(b)(12) of Regulation NMS defines the average quoted spread as the share-weighted average of the national best offer minus the national best bid at the time of order receipt.
Intuition: It measures how far apart the best standing buy and sell prices are; the narrower the gap, the cheaper it is to trade immediately in small size.
Mechanics: Computed from the inside market (best bid and offer, or the NBBO nationally) each time quotes update; expressed in absolute currency terms or relative to the quote midpoint. It reflects posted liquidity only and changes continuously with order submissions, cancellations, and executions.
Formula: QS = A - B, where A is the best ask and B the best bid; relative quoted spread = (A - B) / M with midpoint M = (A + B) / 2.
Relationships: Bid-ask spread, Midpoint, Best bid, Best ask, Effective spread, Tightness
Failure modes: It says nothing about available depth or hidden liquidity, so it can look deceptively tight when displayed size is tiny or when the minimum tick constrains prices. It also overstates the cost actually paid when executions receive price improvement inside the quotes.
Misconceptions: The quoted spread is not the transaction cost actually incurred; realized costs are captured by the effective spread and can be lower after price improvement or higher after market impact on large orders.
Example: With a national best bid of $100.00 and national best offer of $100.02, the quoted spread is $0.02, or about 2 basis points of the $100.01 midpoint.
Citation: 17 CFR 242.600 - NMS security designation and definitions (Regulation NMS Rule 600) — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/chapter-II/part-242/section-242.600 (paragraph (b)(12) Average quoted spread)
Status: Reviewed

0237. Effective spread
Domain: Microstructure
Definition: A measure of the execution cost actually paid, defined relative to the midpoint of the national best bid and offer at the time of order receipt: for buy orders, twice the difference between the execution price and the midpoint; for sell orders, twice the difference between the midpoint and the execution price (SEC Rule 600(b)(8)).
Intuition: It captures what a liquidity demander really paid against the pre-trade benchmark price, so price improvement inside the quotes shows up as a smaller spread.
Mechanics: Computed per execution using the NBBO midpoint at order receipt, then share-weighted across executions (average effective spread); dividing by the midpoint gives the percentage effective spread. It is a standard output of SEC Rule 605 execution-quality reports.
Formula: ES_buy = 2(P_exec - M); ES_sell = 2(M - P_exec), where M is the NBBO midpoint at the time of order receipt.
Relationships: Quoted spread, Realized spread, Midpoint, National best bid and offer, Price improvement
Failure modes: The midpoint benchmark can be stale or misleading in fast markets and wide-spread stocks, and the measure depends on the order-receipt time convention. It also ignores the market impact of large orders that walk the book and the opportunity cost of unfilled orders.
Misconceptions: A low effective spread does not mean trading was free; it excludes commissions, fees, delay costs, and impact beyond the first execution.
Example: NBBO midpoint is $100.01 at order receipt; a buy executes at $100.02, giving an effective spread of $0.02, equal to the quoted spread; execution at $100.01 gives $0.00.
Citation: 17 CFR 242.600 - NMS security designation and definitions (Regulation NMS Rule 600) — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/chapter-II/part-242/section-242.600 (paragraph (b)(8) Average effective spread)
Status: Reviewed

0238. Realized spread
Domain: Microstructure
Definition: The execution cost measure recomputed with the NBBO midpoint at a specified interval after execution rather than at order receipt: for buys, twice the execution price minus the later midpoint; for sells, twice the later midpoint minus the execution price (SEC Rule 600(b)(13)). It estimates what a liquidity provider retains after prices adjust to the trade.
Intuition: It separates the liquidity provider's compensation from its losses to better-informed traders: if the price moves against the provider after the trade, the realized spread shrinks below the effective spread.
Mechanics: Computed like the effective spread but with the midpoint at a fixed post-trade horizon (e.g. minutes later); the gap between effective and realized spread approximates the price impact or information content of the trade.
Formula: RS_buy = 2(P_exec - M_{t+D}); RS_sell = 2(M_{t+D} - P_exec), where M_{t+D} is the NBBO midpoint at a specified interval D after execution.
Relationships: Effective spread, Quoted spread, Adverse selection, Price impact, Midpoint
Failure modes: Results are highly sensitive to the choice of horizon D, and unrelated news arriving during the interval contaminates the measurement. A negative realized spread can reflect general market movement rather than counterparty informativeness.
Misconceptions: The realized spread is not the market maker's profit; it ignores hedging costs, inventory risk, fees, rebates, and operating costs.
Example: A buy executes at $100.02 with a $100.01 midpoint at receipt (effective spread $0.02); five minutes later the midpoint is $100.015, so the realized spread is $0.01 - half the effective spread was given back to adverse price movement.
Citation: 17 CFR 242.600 - NMS security designation and definitions (Regulation NMS Rule 600) — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/chapter-II/part-242/section-242.600 (paragraph (b)(13) Average realized spread)
Status: Reviewed

0239. Midpoint
Domain: Microstructure
Definition: The arithmetic mean of the best bid and best offer, conventionally computed from the NBBO; Regulation NMS uses the NBBO midpoint as the reference price for effective and realized spread calculations. It is the standard benchmark for the unobserved transaction-cost-free value of a security between trades.
Intuition: It is the neutral point splitting the spread - neither side's concession - so it serves as the default fair-value reference for measuring execution quality.
Mechanics: Recomputed on every change to the best bid or offer; used as the peg for midpoint orders, as the benchmark in spread and price-improvement statistics, and as the reference in trade-classification rules such as the quote rule.
Formula: M = (B + A) / 2, where B is the best (national best) bid and A the best (national best) offer.
Relationships: Quoted spread, Effective spread, National best bid and offer, Microprice, Quote rule
Failure modes: When the spread is wide, one side is thin, or prices are tick-constrained, the midpoint is a poor value estimate; it also ignores the size imbalance between bid and ask, which the microprice corrects.
Misconceptions: The midpoint is a benchmark, not a tradable price and not necessarily the market's true valuation; executions at the midpoint are a convention, not a law.
Example: With the NBBO at $100.00 x $100.04, the midpoint is $100.02; a buy executed at $100.03 shows $0.02 of effective spread (2 x (100.03 - 100.02)).
Citation: 17 CFR 242.600 - NMS security designation and definitions (Regulation NMS Rule 600) — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/chapter-II/part-242/section-242.600 (paragraphs (b)(8)-(b)(13), spread definitions referencing the NBBO midpoint)
Status: Reviewed

0240. Last traded price
Domain: Microstructure
Definition: The price of the most recently reported transaction in a security. Regulation NMS defines last sale data as price and volume data associated with a transaction, and consolidated last sale information as the price, volume, and market identification of the most recent transaction report disseminated under a national market system plan.
Intuition: It records where the asset last changed hands - a fact about the past, not a commitment about the price at which the next trade will occur.
Mechanics: Every executed trade is reported to the consolidated tape under transaction reporting plans, and quote displays update the 'last' field accordingly. In illiquid securities the last trade can be minutes or hours old, and in fast markets it lags the current quotes.
Relationships: Bid, Ask, Midpoint, Transaction report, Consolidated market data
Failure modes: Using it as a value estimate fails in illiquid or fast-moving markets, where it can be far from the currently executable bid and ask; opening, closing, and block prints can also differ systematically from continuous-market prices.
Misconceptions: The last traded price is not the price at which a new order will execute; market orders transact at the current bid or ask, not at the last print.
Example: A stock last printed at $50.10, but news has moved the quotes to $50.00 x $50.20; a market buy executes near $50.20, not $50.10.
Citation: 17 CFR 242.600 - NMS security designation and definitions (Regulation NMS Rule 600) — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/chapter-II/part-242/section-242.600 (paragraphs (b)(23) Consolidated last sale information and (b)(50) Last sale data)
Status: Reviewed

0241. Best bid
Domain: Microstructure
Definition: The highest-priced bid currently quoted for a security; at the level of a single venue it is that market's best bid, and aggregated across protected venues it forms the national best bid. Regulation NMS Rule 600(b)(15) defines best bid and best offer as the highest priced bid and the lowest priced offer.
Intuition: It is the most any displayed buyer is currently willing to pay - the price a seller can execute against immediately, up to the quoted size.
Mechanics: Sits at the top of the bid side of the order book with an associated displayed size; it changes whenever a better bid is posted, the existing best bid is cancelled, or it is executed. Under Rule 600(b)(60), ties between identical bids from different market centers are ranked by size, then by time.
Relationships: Best ask, National best bid and offer, Bid, Top of book, Order book
Failure modes: The displayed best bid may be backed by very small size or may flicker in and out within milliseconds, and hidden or iceberg interest means the best truly executable bid can differ from the displayed one.
Misconceptions: The best bid is a firm price only for its quoted size; a seller of larger size will walk down the book and receive progressively worse prices.
Example: Bids rest at $100.00 for 300 shares and $99.99 for 2,000 shares; the best bid is $100.00, available for only 300 shares.
Citation: 17 CFR 242.600 - NMS security designation and definitions (Regulation NMS Rule 600) — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/chapter-II/part-242/section-242.600 (paragraph (b)(15) Best bid and best offer)
Status: Reviewed

0242. Best ask
Domain: Microstructure
Definition: The lowest-priced offer currently quoted for a security; at the level of a single venue it is that market's best offer, and aggregated across protected venues it forms the national best offer. Regulation NMS Rule 600(b)(15) defines best bid and best offer as the highest priced bid and the lowest priced offer.
Intuition: It is the least any displayed seller is currently willing to accept - the price a buyer can execute against immediately, up to the quoted size.
Mechanics: Sits at the top of the offer side of the order book with an associated displayed size; it moves as better offers arrive, are cancelled, or are lifted. Under Rule 600(b)(60), identical offers from different market centers are ranked by size, then by time.
Relationships: Best bid, National best bid and offer, Ask, Top of book, Order book
Failure modes: Displayed size at the best offer can be minimal or fleeting, and reserve or hidden selling interest means the effective best offer can differ from what the tape shows.
Misconceptions: The best ask guarantees the price only for the displayed quantity; larger buys execute through successively higher offer levels.
Example: Offers rest at $100.02 for 200 shares and $100.03 for 1,500 shares; the best ask is $100.02 for 200 shares only.
Citation: 17 CFR 242.600 - NMS security designation and definitions (Regulation NMS Rule 600) — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/chapter-II/part-242/section-242.600 (paragraph (b)(15) Best bid and best offer)
Status: Reviewed

0243. National best bid and offer
Domain: Microstructure
Definition: The highest protected bid and the lowest protected offer for an NMS stock across all national securities exchanges, calculated and disseminated on a current and continuing basis under Regulation NMS; when market centers transmit identical bids or offers, they are ranked first by size, then by time (Rule 600(b)(60)).
Intuition: It is the single national reference for the best available displayed prices in a fragmented market where the same stock trades on many venues.
Mechanics: Computed from the protected (automated, accessible) quotations of exchanges and associations by the plan processor, competing consolidators, or self-aggregators. It anchors the Rule 611 order-protection obligation and the Rule 605 execution-quality statistics.
Formula: NBB = max of protected bids across venues; NBO = min of protected offers across venues.
Relationships: Best bid, Best ask, Trade-through, Protected quotation, Midpoint, Regulation NMS
Failure modes: The consolidated NBBO lags direct exchange data feeds, historically excluded odd lots, and may reference sizes too small to be economically accessible; during locked or crossed conditions it ceases to represent an orderly market.
Misconceptions: The NBBO is not the totality of available liquidity - it excludes book depth beyond the inside, hidden orders, and dark-pool interest.
Example: NYSE quotes $100.00 x $100.03 and Nasdaq quotes $100.01 x $100.02; the NBBO is $100.01 x $100.02, drawing each side from a different venue.
Citation: 17 CFR 242.600 - NMS security designation and definitions (Regulation NMS Rule 600) — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-17/chapter-II/part-242/section-242.600 (paragraph (b)(60) National best bid and national best offer)
Status: Reviewed

0244. Order book
Domain: Microstructure
Definition: The collection of unexecuted buy and sell orders for a security maintained by a trading venue, organized by price level and priority. Its state evolves through order book events - limit-order submissions, market orders, and cancellations - which together drive short-horizon price changes (Cont, Kukanov and Stoikov, 2014).
Intuition: It is the visible queue of supply and demand waiting to trade: who wants to buy, who wants to sell, at what prices, and how much.
Mechanics: Limit orders rest in the book until matched, cancelled, or expired; incoming marketable orders execute against the best opposing prices, removing liquidity. Data feeds disseminate the book as snapshots and event updates, from which quantities like imbalance and depth are derived.
Relationships: Limit order book, Top of book, Depth of market, Order-flow imbalance, Queue position
Failure modes: The displayed book understates true liquidity because of hidden, reserve, and off-exchange interest, and snapshot data miss intra-event dynamics. Book liquidity can also evaporate in stress as quotes are cancelled en masse.
Misconceptions: Size visible in the book is not committed liquidity; orders can be cancelled in milliseconds, so the book is an offer to trade, not a guarantee.
Example: A book shows five price levels per side; a 10,000-share market buy consumes the best offer and the two levels above it, moving the price up two ticks.
Citation: Cont, Kukanov and Stoikov, 'The Price Impact of Order Book Events', Journal of Financial Econometrics 12(1):47-88 (arXiv preprint) — https://arxiv.org/abs/1011.6402 (Abstract and introduction)
Status: Reviewed

0245. Limit order book
Domain: Microstructure
Definition: An order book composed of limit orders ranked by price and by a secondary priority rule (time, size, or pro rata), against which incoming marketable orders are continuously matched - the operating mechanism of a continuous double auction on modern electronic exchanges.
Intuition: It is a standing electronic auction: unfilled limit orders wait in line, and anyone demanding immediacy trades against the front of the opposite queue.
Mechanics: Price priority dominates - the best-priced orders match first; the exchange's matching algorithm (e.g. FIFO or pro rata on CME Globex) then allocates among orders at the same price. Orders lose queue priority when amended in price, increased in quantity, or changed in account.
Relationships: Order book, Price-time priority, Pro rata allocation, Central limit order book, Queue position
Failure modes: Resting orders face adverse selection from better-informed or faster traders, and displayed depth can vanish in volatile periods precisely when it is most needed. Reconstructed books from data feeds can diverge from the exchange's true state.
Misconceptions: The limit order book is not a complete map of market liquidity: iceberg reserve size, hidden orders, and off-book venues all escape it.
Example: On CME Globex, an incoming 250-lot buy at 9711 executes against resting offers at that price in the sequence set by the product's matching algorithm, e.g. FIFO or pro rata.
