Mechanics: Trading venues disseminate trade reports (last sale, size) and quote updates (bid, ask, bid size, ask size) over separate feeds; in the U.S., consolidated tape systems report the latest price and volume of each sale in exchange-listed stocks. Consumers reconstruct sequences via feed handlers and timestamp normalization.
Relationships: OHLCV bar, Tick bar, Consolidated tape, Market data, Trading volume
Failure modes: Raw tick data contains bad prints, out-of-sequence messages, and exchange-specific timestamp quirks that must be cleaned before analysis. Volume is enormous (millions of events per day for active instruments), creating storage and processing burdens.
Misconceptions: A 'tick' in tick data is any recorded event, not the minimum price increment (tick size) — the two uses of the word are unrelated. Also, the consolidated tape is not identical to any single exchange's feed.
Example: A single second of AAPL tick data might contain 40 trade prints across NYSE, Nasdaq, and other venues plus hundreds of bid/ask updates — all collapsed into one OHLCV bar if aggregated per second.
Citation: Wikipedia: Market data — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Market_data (Data structure (trade data and quote data feeds))
Citation: SEC Investor.gov Glossary — https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/glossary (Consolidated Tape)
Status: Reviewed

0329. Time bar
Domain: Market data
Definition: A time bar is an OHLC(V) bar built by aggregating all trades within a fixed clock interval (1 minute, 1 hour, 1 day, etc.). It is the default sampling scheme in market data, in which bars are produced at uniform points in time regardless of how much trading occurred.
Intuition: Time bars chop the trading day into equal clock slices and summarize each slice — whether it contained three trades or three thousand.
Mechanics: Define a fixed interval Δt; group all ticks with timestamps in [t, t+Δt) and reduce to OHLCV. López de Prado notes that time bars oversample information-poor (quiet) periods and undersample information-rich (busy) periods, and exhibit serial correlation, heteroskedasticity, and non-normality of returns — motivating activity-based alternatives like tick, volume, and dollar bars.
Relationships: OHLCV bar, Tick bar, Volume bar, Dollar bar, Tick data
Failure modes: Statistical properties of time-bar returns (normality, homoskedasticity) are poor, which degrades many ML and econometric methods applied directly to them. Bars also align to arbitrary clock boundaries, splitting coherent bursts of activity.
Misconceptions: Uniform clock sampling does not produce uniform information sampling — a 1-minute bar at the open and one at lunch carry very different amounts of market information.
Example: A 1-minute time-bar series of EUR/USD produces 1,440 bars per day even though overnight bars may contain a handful of trades while London-open bars contain thousands.
Citation: López de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning (Wiley, 2018) — https://www.wiley.com/en-us/Advances+in+Financial+Machine+Learning-p-9781119482086 (Chapter 2: Financial Data Structures (time bars))
Status: Reviewed

0330. Tick bar
Domain: Market data
Definition: A tick bar is an OHLCV bar built by aggregating a fixed number of consecutive trades (e.g., every 1,000 transactions), rather than a fixed clock interval. Sampling in transaction time aligns bar formation with market activity instead of the clock.
Intuition: A new bar appears after every N trades — busy markets produce bars rapidly, quiet markets slowly, so each bar contains a comparable amount of trading activity.
Mechanics: Count executed trades from the tick stream; every time the count reaches N, reduce those N trades to OHLCV and start a new bar. Returns sampled this way are statistically better behaved (closer to i.i.d. and normal) than time-bar returns, per López de Prado.
Relationships: Time bar, Volume bar, Dollar bar, Tick data
Failure modes: Tick bars are sensitive to trade-count fragmentation: the same order flow split into more prints (by algo slicing or venue rules) produces more bars without more information, so bar frequency is not comparable across regimes or venues.
Misconceptions: A tick bar is not one bar per tick — it aggregates N trades, and 'tick' here means transaction, not minimum price increment.
Example: With 1,000-trade tick bars on ES futures, a bar may complete in seconds around the U.S. open but take minutes overnight.
Citation: López de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning (Wiley, 2018) — https://www.wiley.com/en-us/Advances+in+Financial+Machine+Learning-p-9781119482086 (Chapter 2: Financial Data Structures (tick bars))
Status: Reviewed

0331. Volume bar
Domain: Market data
Definition: A volume bar is an OHLCV bar built by aggregating trades until a fixed cumulative quantity (e.g., 10,000 shares or 100 BTC) has traded. Bars are thus sampled in units of traded volume rather than time or trade count.
Intuition: Each bar represents the same amount of actual participation — the market 'votes' with quantity, and a new bar is cast once the vote count reaches the threshold.
Mechanics: Accumulate traded quantities from the tick stream; when cumulative volume reaches the threshold V*, reduce the accumulated trades to OHLCV and reset. Volume bars sample more frequently when large traders are active and partially mitigate the trade-fragmentation distortion of tick bars, since splitting an order into more prints does not change total volume.
Relationships: Tick bar, Dollar bar, Time bar, Trading volume, OHLCV bar
Failure modes: A single block trade larger than the threshold straddles multiple bars or forces an oversized bar, depending on implementation, so bar-level volume is not exactly constant in practice. The threshold is arbitrary and not comparable across instruments of different liquidity.
Misconceptions: Volume bars do not have identical volumes in strict tick-level implementations unless trades are allowed to be split; many charting platforms approximate them from already-aggregated data, distorting the construction.
Example: With 50,000-share volume bars, if the tape prints 30k, 15k, and then 10k shares, the bar closes partway through the third print after exactly 50k shares have traded.
Citation: López de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning (Wiley, 2018) — https://www.wiley.com/en-us/Advances+in+Financial+Machine+Learning-p-9781119482086 (Chapter 2: Financial Data Structures (volume bars))
Status: Reviewed

0332. Dollar bar
Domain: Market data
Definition: A dollar bar is an OHLCV bar built by aggregating trades until a fixed cumulative dollar value (price × quantity, e.g., $1,000,000) has traded. Sampling in money terms keeps bar information content comparable even as an instrument's price level changes over time.
Intuition: Each bar represents the same amount of cash changing hands, which keeps the sampling meaningful across years during which the share price may have multiplied.
Mechanics: Accumulate p_i·q_i over consecutive trades; when the running sum reaches the dollar threshold, emit an OHLCV bar and reset. López de Prado advocates dollar bars over share-volume bars because a fixed share count corresponds to very different economic significance as prices move, and suggests periodically adjusting the threshold for changes in free float or outstanding shares.
Relationships: Volume bar, Tick bar, Time bar, Dollar volume, OHLCV bar
Failure modes: The threshold must be maintained: corporate actions, price trends, and changing float can make a once-reasonable dollar threshold inappropriate, and implementations that cannot split block trades produce inexact bar values. Thresholds are not portable across instruments.
Misconceptions: Dollar bars are not just volume bars at a different scale — because they normalize by value, they remain economically comparable across price levels where share-volume bars do not.
Example: With $5M dollar bars on a large-cap stock, about 20 bars form on a $100M day, versus only 4 on a quiet $20M day.
Citation: López de Prado, Advances in Financial Machine Learning (Wiley, 2018) — https://www.wiley.com/en-us/Advances+in+Financial+Machine+Learning-p-9781119482086 (Chapter 2: Financial Data Structures (dollar bars))
Status: Reviewed

0333. Range bar
Domain: Market data
Definition: A range bar is a price-based chart element in which a new bar is created only after the price has moved by a user-specified fixed range, regardless of how much time passes. Every completed bar therefore has the same high-low span, and time is eliminated as a construction variable.
Intuition: Range bars print one bar per fixed price excursion — the chart advances only when price actually travels, so flat markets produce almost no bars.
Mechanics: Choose a range in ticks (1 range unit equals one minimum price change). Track the running high-low of the forming bar; when the span reaches the configured range, close the bar at that boundary and open a new one. Because bars complete at irregular times, the time axis is non-uniform.
Relationships: Renko bar, Point-and-figure chart, Time bar, True range
Failure modes: Fast markets and gaps can blow through a bar's boundary, so the recorded bar may not reflect tradeable prices within it. As an analytical framework, range bars filter noise but discard time and usually volume information, and results are sensitive to the chosen range.
Misconceptions: Equal-sized bars do not imply equal information per bar, and a range bar's tidy structure is a construction artifact, not evidence of orderly market behavior.
Example: With a 10-tick range setting on crude oil futures, each bar closes once price has traveled $0.10 from its open extreme, whether that takes two seconds or two hours.
Citation: TradingView Support: Understanding range charts — https://www.tradingview.com/support/solutions/43000474007-understanding-range-charts/ (What are range bars)
Status: Reviewed

0334. Renko bar
Domain: Market data
Definition: A Renko chart is a Japanese-origin price chart built of fixed-size 'bricks': a new brick is drawn in the direction of the move only when price surpasses the previous brick's boundary by the brick size, and never adjacent on the same line. Like point-and-figure, time plays no role; it is a technical-analysis framework for filtering noise, not a proven predictive method.
Intuition: Renko stacks identical bricks in the direction of travel — you see a clean staircase of meaningful moves while small wiggles never make it onto the chart.
Mechanics: Fix a brick size (e.g., 10 points). When price exceeds the last brick's upper or lower boundary by the brick size, draw a new brick offset to the right; moves larger than one brick add multiple bricks, and partial bricks are not plotted. Classic Renko uses only closing prices of the chosen time frame; a reversal conventionally requires a move of two brick sizes from the last brick's close.
Relationships: Point-and-figure chart, Range bar, Kagi chart, OHLC bar
Failure modes: Brick-size selection completely determines the chart: too small reintroduces noise, too large misses structure. Discarding time and volume removes context, and bricks drawn from closes can lag sharply in fast reversals.
Misconceptions: Renko 'signals' are a repackaging of price movement, not independent confirmation — and because bricks form only after the required move, entries shown on the chart were not available at the brick's open price.
Example: With a $1 brick size on a stock closing at 50.00, 50.40, 51.10, 51.30, two up-bricks are drawn (50→51, 51→52 requires 52.00, so only one) — only the 50→51 brick prints.
Citation: Wikipedia: Renko chart — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renko_chart (Construction rules)
Status: Reviewed

0335. Point-and-figure chart
Domain: Market data
Definition: Point-and-figure is a century-old technical-analysis charting technique that plots price against changes in direction rather than against time: rising prices are drawn as columns of Xs and falling prices as columns of Os, with columns reversing only after a set reversal amount. It is an analytical framework for trend and pattern study, not a proven predictive law.
Intuition: P&F ignores the clock and minor wiggles entirely — the chart only grows when price moves by a full box, and switches columns only on a meaningful reversal.
Mechanics: Choose a box size (price increment per X/O) and a reversal criterion (traditionally 1 box, commonly 3). Add Xs upward as price rises by box increments and Os downward as it falls; move to a new column only when price reverses by the reversal number of boxes. Price changes smaller than the box size are filtered out, and if no significant move occurs, no new data is plotted.
Relationships: Renko bar, Kagi chart, Range bar, OHLC bar
Failure modes: Results are highly sensitive to box size and reversal settings, and discarding time and volume removes execution-relevant context. Classic P&F price targets (vertical/horizontal counts) are heuristics without reliable out-of-sample validation.
Misconceptions: P&F columns are not time periods — a column can span days or minutes — and the filtered chart understates how much price action actually occurred.
Example: With a $1 box and 3-box reversal, a stock rising from $50 to $54 draws four Xs; it must fall to $51 before a column of Os begins.
Citation: Wikipedia: Point and figure chart — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Point_and_figure_chart (Construction and history)
Status: Reviewed

0336. Heikin-Ashi candle
Domain: Market data
Definition: Heikin-Ashi (Japanese for 'average bar') is a candlestick variant in which each candle's OHLC values are computed as weighted averages of actual prices and the previous Heikin-Ashi candle, smoothing the displayed price series. It is a visualization/analytical technique for highlighting trend; its displayed values are not actual traded prices.
Intuition: Heikin-Ashi candles are 'pre-smoothed' candlesticks: trends look cleaner and reversals stand out, because each bar is averaged with its predecessor.
Mechanics: HA-Close = (O+H+L+C)/4 of the real bar; HA-Open = (previous HA-Open + previous HA-Close)/2; HA-High = max(real high, HA-Open, HA-Close); HA-Low = min(real low, HA-Open, HA-Close). The recursion means each candle depends on the prior one, introducing lag.
Formula: HA_C = (O+H+L+C)/4; HA_O = (HA_O_prev + HA_C_prev)/2; HA_H = max(H, HA_O, HA_C); HA_L = min(L, HA_O, HA_C), where O,H,L,C are the real bar's prices.
Relationships: OHLC bar, OHLCV bar, Average price, Candlestick chart
Failure modes: Because HA values are synthetic averages, the current HA close does not equal the market price, so signals based on HA levels lag and cannot be executed at displayed prices. Smoothing also erases gap information that matters for risk management.
Misconceptions: Heikin-Ashi candles cannot be traded directly — a strategy backtested on HA prices uses prices that never existed. Fewer red candles in an uptrend is a smoothing artifact, not new information about the trend.
Example: If a real bar is O=100, H=103, L=99, C=102 and the prior HA candle had HA_O=99, HA_C=100.5, then HA_C=101.0 and HA_O=99.75 — not equal to any real print.
Citation: Wikipedia: Candlestick chart — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_chart (Heikin-Ashi candlesticks)
Status: Reviewed

0337. Typical price
Domain: Market data
Definition: The typical price is the arithmetic mean of a bar's high, low, and close: (H+L+C)/3. It is a standard single-price summary of a trading bar, used as the price input of indicators such as the Money Flow Index and the Commodity Channel Index.
Intuition: Typical price collapses a bar into one number that represents where trading happened, giving equal weight to the extremes and the close.
Mechanics: Compute (High + Low + Close)/3 for each bar and optionally smooth the resulting series (e.g., with a moving average) for trend display. It serves as the price input in MFI's raw money flow (typical price × volume) and CCI's deviation calculations.
Formula: TP = (H + L + C) / 3, where H, L, C are the bar's high, low, and close.
Relationships: Median price, Weighted close, Average price, Money flow index, Commodity channel index, OHLC bar
Failure modes: Equal weighting of high and low lets a single extreme print shift the summary as much as the close, while ignoring the open and the volume distribution within the bar. It is a convention, not a statistically optimal bar summary.
Misconceptions: The typical price is not the price at which most volume traded (that would be closer to VWAP) and not necessarily near the close — treating it as 'the' bar price is a modeling choice.
Example: For a bar with H=105, L=100, C=103, the typical price is (105+100+103)/3 = 102.67.
Citation: StockCharts ChartSchool: Typical Price — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/technical-indicators-and-overlays/technical-indicators/typical-price (Calculating the Typical Price Indicator)
Status: Reviewed

0338. Median price
Domain: Market data
Definition: The median price is the midpoint of a bar's trading range: (H+L)/2. It summarizes a bar by the center of its extremes and, when averaged over periods, forms a smoother trend line than close-based averages because it is less affected by close-to-close fluctuations and outliers.
Intuition: Median price is the halfway point of the bar's range — a quick measure of the bar's center of gravity that ignores where within the range the close landed.
Mechanics: Compute (High + Low)/2 per bar; charting platforms typically then average the per-bar median prices over N periods (e.g., 14) to plot the Median Price indicator as a trend line or overlay.
Formula: MP = (H + L) / 2, where H and L are the bar's high and low.
Relationships: Typical price, Weighted close, Average price, OHLC bar
Failure modes: Ignoring open and close discards the most decision-relevant prints, and the midpoint is dominated by outlier extremes in volatile bars. Like all averages it lags, and it produces misleading signals in choppy, non-trending markets.
Misconceptions: Despite the name, it is the midrange, not the statistical median of all trade prices in the bar — no trade-level distribution is involved.
Example: For a bar with H=48.20 and L=46.80, the median price is 47.50 regardless of whether the close was 47.00 or 48.10.
Citation: StockCharts ChartSchool: Median Price — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/technical-indicators-and-overlays/technical-indicators/median-price (How Is the Median Price Indicator Calculated?)
Status: Reviewed

0339. Weighted close
Domain: Market data
Definition: The weighted close is the average of a bar's high, low, and close with the close counted twice: (H+L+2C)/4. It is a bar-summary price that emphasizes the close — reflecting its importance for mark-to-market — over the bar's extremes.
Intuition: Weighted close is the typical price with extra weight on the closing print, on the view that where the bar settled matters more than where it wandered.
Mechanics: Compute (High + Low + Close×2)/4 for each bar and plot as a line or overlay; it is commonly combined with moving averages, using crossovers as trend signals.
Formula: WC = (H + L + 2C) / 4, where H, L, C are the bar's high, low, and close.
Relationships: Typical price, Median price, Average price, Close price, OHLC bar
Failure modes: The 2× weight on the close is an arbitrary convention, and the measure still ignores the open and intra-bar volume distribution. As with other smoothed price lines, crossover signals lag and whipsaw in sideways markets.
Misconceptions: Weighted close is not a volume-weighted measure — 'weighted' refers only to the doubled close in the average, not to traded volume.
Example: For a bar with H=210, L=200, C=206, the weighted close is (210+200+2×206)/4 = 205.50.
Citation: StockCharts ChartSchool: Weighted Close — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/technical-indicators-and-overlays/technical-indicators/weighted-close (How To Calculate the Weighted Close Indicator)
Status: Reviewed

0340. Average price
Domain: Market data
Definition: In bar data, the average price is the arithmetic mean of a bar's four OHLC prices: (O+H+L+C)/4. It is the most neutral single-number summary of a bar — it is, for example, exactly the Heikin-Ashi close — though in session-level contexts 'average price' can instead mean a volume-weighted average over the period.
Intuition: Average price treats all four of a bar's reference prices equally, giving a balanced 'center' of the period's action.
Mechanics: Compute (Open + High + Low + Close)/4 per bar. The same construction appears as the close of a Heikin-Ashi candle; exchanges and vendors also publish session average prices, sometimes volume-weighted, so the exact convention must be checked per data source.
Formula: AP = (O + H + L + C) / 4, where O, H, L, C are the bar's four prices.
Relationships: Typical price, Median price, Weighted close, Heikin-Ashi candle, OHLC bar
Failure modes: The unweighted mean ignores where volume concentrated inside the bar, so it can sit far from the prices at which most trading occurred. The term is ambiguous across sources (OHLC/4 vs VWAP vs average of period closes), which causes silent data mismatches.
Misconceptions: Average price (OHLC/4) is not VWAP — no volume weighting is involved — and it is not the same as a moving average of closes.
Example: For a bar with O=100, H=103, L=99, C=102, the average price is (100+103+99+102)/4 = 101.00, which is also that bar's Heikin-Ashi close.
Citation: Wikipedia: Candlestick chart — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_chart (Heikin-Ashi candlesticks (Close = (open+high+low+close)/4))
Citation: Binance Spot API documentation (rest-api.md) — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/binance/binance-spot-api-docs/master/rest-api.md (Current average price endpoint)
Status: Reviewed

0341. True range
Domain: Market data
Definition: True range is a volatility measure introduced by J. Welles Wilder Jr. (1978) that extends the bar's high-low range to capture gaps relative to the previous close. It is the largest of: current high minus low, |high − previous close|, and |low − previous close|; its smoothed average is the Average True Range (ATR).
Intuition: Plain range misses overnight gaps. True range asks: how far did price actually travel, including any jump from yesterday's close to today's extremes?
Mechanics: Compute the three candidate distances per bar and take the maximum: when the previous close lies inside today's range this reduces to high − low; gaps up or down are captured by the two absolute-value terms. Wilder smoothed TR with a 14-period smoothed moving average to obtain ATR.
Formula: TR_t = max(H_t − L_t, |H_t − C_{t−1}|, |L_t − C_{t−1}|), where H_t, L_t are the current high and low and C_{t−1} is the previous close.
Relationships: Average true range, High price, Low price, Close price, OHLC bar
Failure modes: True range measures magnitude only — it carries no directional information, and a single gap bar permanently elevates the smoothed ATR for the smoothing horizon. Because it is computed from price differences, its interpretation shifts with the instrument's price level.
Misconceptions: A high true range does not signal a trend or a breakout direction — it only marks volatility. ATR is not a percentage volatility measure unless normalized by price.
Example: If yesterday closed at 50 and today trades between 48 and 49, plain range is 1 but true range is max(1, 2, 1) = 2, capturing the gap down.
Citation: Wikipedia: Average true range — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Average_true_range (True range definition (citing Wilder, New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems, 1978))
Status: Reviewed

0342. Rolling maximum
Domain: Market data
Definition: The rolling maximum is the highest value of a series within a trailing window of fixed length that slides forward one observation at a time. It underlies channel indicators such as Donchian channels and breakout systems.
Intuition: At each point, look back over the last N bars and ask: what was the highest price seen? That level moves as old extremes drop out of the window.
Mechanics: For window length w, compute max over observations x_{t−w+1}…x_t and repeat for each t; standard implementations (e.g., pandas rolling().max()) label the result at the window's right edge and return NaN until the window is full unless min_periods is set.
Formula: RMax_t = max(x_{t−w+1}, …, x_t), where w is the window length.
Relationships: Rolling minimum, Donchian channel, High price, Rolling mean
Failure modes: The statistic is window-sensitive and jumps discontinuously when an old extreme exits the window, creating artificial 'breakdowns' of the level. Centering the window introduces lookahead bias into backtests.
Misconceptions: A break above the rolling maximum is a mechanical event defined by the window choice, not independent evidence of a meaningful breakout.
Example: With a 20-day rolling maximum on daily highs, if the highest high of the last 20 days is 112.30, today's upper Donchian line sits at 112.30.
Citation: pandas User Guide: Windowing operations — https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/window.html (Rolling window (supported aggregations incl. max))
Status: Reviewed

0343. Rolling minimum
Domain: Market data
Definition: The rolling minimum is the lowest value of a series within a trailing window of fixed length that slides forward one observation at a time. Together with the rolling maximum it defines the lower boundary of channel indicators such as Donchian channels.
Intuition: At each point, look back over the last N bars and ask: what was the lowest price seen? The level ratchets as time passes and old lows expire from the window.
Mechanics: For window length w, compute min over observations x_{t−w+1}…x_t at each t; implementations such as pandas rolling().min() label at the window's right edge and produce NaN until the window fills unless min_periods is set.
Formula: RMin_t = min(x_{t−w+1}, …, x_t), where w is the window length.
Relationships: Rolling maximum, Donchian channel, Low price, Rolling median
Failure modes: Like the rolling maximum, it jumps discontinuously when an extreme exits the window and is entirely defined by the chosen window length; centered windows leak future data into the past.
Misconceptions: The rolling minimum is not a support level in any market-microstructure sense — it is purely the trailing extreme over an arbitrary lookback.
Example: With a 20-day rolling minimum on daily lows, if the lowest low of the last 20 days is 96.10, the lower Donchian line sits at 96.10 today.
Citation: pandas User Guide: Windowing operations — https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/window.html (Rolling window (supported aggregations incl. min))
Status: Reviewed

0344. Rolling mean
Domain: Market data
Definition: The rolling mean is the arithmetic average of a series over a trailing window of fixed length that slides forward one observation at a time. Applied to prices it is the simple moving average (SMA), the most common trend-smoothing statistic in market analysis.
Intuition: The rolling mean smooths out bar-to-bar noise by averaging the last N values, so the line rises when recent values are generally higher than the ones dropping out.
Mechanics: For window length w, sum the last w observations and divide by w at each step. pandas rolling(window).mean() labels the result at the right edge of the window and returns NaN for the first w−1 points by default (min_periods=w for fixed windows).
Formula: μ_t = (1/w) Σ_{i=0}^{w−1} x_{t−i}, where w is the window length.
Relationships: Rolling median, Rolling standard deviation, Moving average, Rolling z-score
Failure modes: The mean lags the series by roughly half the window and is distorted by outliers, since each extreme pulls the average for w periods. Equal weighting of the oldest and newest observations is arbitrary; window changes can flip signals.
Misconceptions: A moving-average crossover is a descriptive smoothing artifact, not a proven predictive signal; and the SMA is not 'the fair price' — it is a trailing average.
Example: A 5-day rolling mean of closes 100, 102, 101, 103, 104 is (100+102+101+103+104)/5 = 102.0 on the fifth day.
Citation: pandas User Guide: Windowing operations — https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/window.html (Rolling window (mean aggregation))
Status: Reviewed

0345. Rolling median
Domain: Market data
Definition: The rolling median is the median value of a series over a trailing window of fixed length that slides forward one observation at a time. It is a robust alternative to the rolling mean, insensitive to extreme values within the window.
Intuition: Instead of averaging the last N bars, take the middle one — a single spike can pull a mean around but cannot move the median much.
Mechanics: For window length w, sort the last w observations and take the middle value (average of the two middle values for even w) at each step. pandas supports rolling(window).median(), with the same right-edge labeling and min_periods conventions as other rolling aggregations.
Formula: RMed_t = median(x_{t−w+1}, …, x_t), where w is the window length.
Relationships: Rolling mean, Median price, Rolling maximum, Rolling minimum
Failure modes: The median is a coarse, step-like statistic that can sit unchanged for many bars and then jump, which makes derivative-based signals awkward. It is also computationally heavier than the mean and still lagged by the window.
Misconceptions: Robustness to outliers is not always desirable — in return series, extreme moves are often the information, and median-filtering them away changes the risk picture.
Example: For the last 5 closes 100, 101, 99, 130, 102, the rolling median is 101 while the rolling mean is 106.4, showing the median's immunity to the 130 spike.
Citation: pandas User Guide: Windowing operations — https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/window.html (Rolling window (median aggregation))
Status: Reviewed

0346. Rolling standard deviation
Domain: Market data
Definition: The rolling standard deviation is the sample (or population) standard deviation of a series over a trailing window of fixed length that slides forward one observation at a time. Applied to returns it is the standard estimator of realized volatility and the width driver of Bollinger Bands.
Intuition: It measures how spread out the last N returns (or prices) were — a live gauge of how violently the market has been moving recently.
Mechanics: For window w, compute σ over the last w observations at each step; pandas rolling(window).std() uses the sample (unbiased, ddof=1) convention by default and labels at the window's right edge. On returns, annualization scales by √T (e.g., √252 for daily data).
Formula: σ_t = sqrt( (1/(w−1)) Σ_{i=0}^{w−1} (x_{t−i} − μ_t)² ), where μ_t is the rolling mean over the same window (use 1/w for the population convention).
Relationships: Rolling mean, Rolling z-score, Bollinger Bands, Average true range, Volatility
Failure modes: The estimate assumes the window's observations come from one stable regime; volatility clustering makes short windows noisy and long windows slow to react. Squaring returns gives extreme observations outsized influence, and with w−1 denominators small windows are unreliable.
Misconceptions: Rolling std of prices is not comparable across instruments or time as price levels drift — volatility is conventionally computed on returns, not price levels.
Example: The 20-day rolling std of daily log returns at 0.015 (1.5%) annualizes to roughly 0.015 × √252 ≈ 23.8%.
Citation: pandas User Guide: Windowing operations — https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/window.html (Rolling window (std aggregation; numerical notes))
Status: Reviewed

0347. Rolling correlation
Domain: Market data
Definition: Rolling correlation is the Pearson correlation coefficient between two series computed over a trailing window of fixed length that slides forward one observation at a time. It tracks how the co-movement of two assets (typically their returns) evolves through time.
Intuition: Instead of one correlation number for the whole history, you get a time series showing when two markets moved together and when they decoupled.
Mechanics: For window w, compute the Pearson coefficient over the paired observations in the last w points at each t; pandas rolling().corr() supports Series–Series and pairwise DataFrame computations, ignoring missing values pairwise. Correlations are typically computed on returns, not price levels.
Formula: ρ_t = Σ (x_i − μ_x)(y_i − μ_y) / sqrt( Σ (x_i − μ_x)² Σ (y_i − μ_y)² ), sums over the trailing w paired observations.
Relationships: Rolling beta, Rolling covariance, Rolling standard deviation, Correlation
Failure modes: Short windows produce wildly unstable estimates that swing between −1 and +1 on noise; correlation computed on trending price levels is spuriously high. Crisis periods reveal that correlations estimated in calm windows understate co-movement exactly when diversification is needed.
Misconceptions: A high rolling correlation over a window does not establish a stable relationship — window choice can manufacture or erase apparent correlation, and correlation is not causation.
Example: A 60-day rolling correlation between SPY and TLT daily returns hovering near −0.4 that jumps toward +0.2 signals a regime shift in the stock-bond relationship.
Citation: pandas User Guide: Windowing operations — https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/window.html (Binary window functions (corr) and rolling pairwise covariances/correlations)
Status: Reviewed

0348. Rolling beta
Domain: Market data
Definition: Rolling beta is the regression slope of an asset's returns on a benchmark's returns — covariance divided by benchmark variance — estimated over a trailing window that slides forward one observation at a time. It tracks how an asset's market sensitivity evolves rather than assuming a single static beta.
Intuition: Beta asks 'when the market moves 1%, how much does this asset typically move?'; rolling beta shows that answer changing through time as the asset's risk profile shifts.
Mechanics: For window w, compute β_t = Cov_w(r_asset, r_market) / Var_w(r_market) over the last w paired return observations at each t; pandas rolling().cov() and rolling().var() provide the components. The result is the CAPM-style beta estimated on the trailing sample.
Formula: β_t = Cov_w(r_i, r_m) / Var_w(r_m), where r_i and r_m are the asset's and benchmark's returns over the trailing window of length w.
Relationships: Rolling correlation, Rolling standard deviation, Beta, CAPM
Failure modes: Beta estimates are regime-dependent: a window spanning a volatility spike or structural break blends incompatible regimes, and short windows give noisy, unstable slopes. Rolling beta is backward-looking and often fails to anticipate beta shifts at market turning points.
Misconceptions: Beta is not correlation — it scales correlation by relative volatility — and a low trailing beta does not guarantee low future market sensitivity, especially for assets with option-like payoffs.
Example: If over the last 252 days Cov(r_stock, r_S&P500) = 0.0030 and Var(r_S&P500) = 0.0020, the stock's rolling 1-year beta is 1.5.
Citation: pandas User Guide: Windowing operations — https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/window.html (Binary window functions (cov) and rolling pairwise covariances)
Status: Reviewed

0349. Rolling z-score
Domain: Market data
Definition: The rolling z-score standardizes each observation of a series by the rolling mean and rolling standard deviation of its trailing window: how many recent-standard-deviations the current value sits from the recent mean. It converts levels into a locally normalized scale used by mean-reversion and Bollinger-style analyses.
Intuition: A z-score of +2 says 'today's value is unusually high compared with the recent past' — unusual measured in units of the recent volatility, not absolute price.
Mechanics: At each t compute z_t = (x_t − μ_t)/σ_t, where μ_t and σ_t are the rolling mean and rolling standard deviation over the trailing window of length w. pandas rolling().mean() and rolling().std() supply the components; care is needed on whether the current observation is included in the window.
Formula: z_t = (x_t − μ_t) / σ_t, with μ_t and σ_t the rolling mean and rolling standard deviation over the trailing window of length w.
Relationships: Rolling mean, Rolling standard deviation, Bollinger Bands, Mean reversion
Failure modes: Z-scores assume approximate local normality and stationarity; in trending or fat-tailed series, |z| > 2 events are far more common than the Gaussian 5%, so 'extreme' readings are not reliable reversal signals. The statistic also inherits the window sensitivity of its mean and std components.
Misconceptions: A high z-score is not automatically an overbought signal — in a persistent trend, price can hold z > 2 for long stretches. The z-score is relative to an arbitrary lookback, not to any fundamental anchor.
Example: If the 20-day rolling mean of a spread is 1.20 with rolling std 0.15 and today's spread is 1.65, the z-score is (1.65 − 1.20)/0.15 = +3.0.
Citation: pandas User Guide: Windowing operations — https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/user_guide/window.html (Rolling window (mean and std aggregations))
Status: Reviewed

0350. Simple return
Domain: Statistics and probability
Definition: The fractional change in value of an investment over a single period: the difference between final and initial value divided by the initial value, including any income such as dividends in the final value. It is the standard per-period return measure in empirical finance.
Intuition: It answers 'by what percentage did my money grow this period?' A 5% simple return means $100 became $105.
Mechanics: Divide the change in value (final plus distributions minus initial) by the initial value. Simple returns aggregate across assets by value-weighted averaging (portfolio return is the weighted sum of asset returns) but compound, not add, across time.
Formula: R_t = (V_t + D_t - V_{t-1}) / V_{t-1}, where V_t is the end-of-period value, V_{t-1} the initial value, and D_t any distributions (dividends, interest) received during the period.
Relationships: Log return, Gross return, Cumulative return, Annualized return, Geometric mean
Failure modes: Simple returns do not add across time - summing them over multiple periods overstates compounded growth when returns are volatile. They are also bounded below by -100%, which complicates symmetric statistical models.
Misconceptions: A +50% gain followed by a -50% loss does not net to zero: (1.5)(0.5) = 0.75, a 25% cumulative loss. Arithmetic averaging of simple returns is not the rate at which capital actually compounds.
Example: A stock bought at $100 that pays a $2 dividend and ends the period at $105 has simple return R = (105 + 2 - 100)/100 = 7%.
Citation: Wikipedia, 'Rate of return' — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rate_of_return (Calculation (single period))
Status: Reviewed

0351. Log return
Domain: Statistics and probability
Definition: The natural logarithm of the gross return (price ratio) over a period, equivalent to the continuously compounded rate of return. Its key property is time-additivity: multi-period log returns are the sum of single-period log returns.
Intuition: Log returns convert compounding into addition. Gains and losses become symmetric: +10% and -10% log returns cancel exactly to zero, unlike simple returns.
Mechanics: Take the natural log of the ratio of final to initial value. Because log returns add across periods, they are preferred for statistical modeling, aggregation over time, and continuous-time finance; they approximate simple returns closely when the period change is small.
Formula: r_t = ln(V_t / V_{t-1}) = ln(1 + R_t), where V_t and V_{t-1} are the final and initial values and R_t is the simple return. Multi-period: r_{1..T} = SUM r_t = ln(V_T / V_0).
Relationships: Simple return, Gross return, Cumulative return, Lognormal distribution, Geometric mean
Failure modes: Log returns are undefined for a final value of zero or negative and diverge to minus infinity as value approaches zero, so they behave badly for instruments that can hit zero. Portfolio-level log returns are not the weighted sum of asset log returns (that property holds only for simple returns), so they must be converted back before portfolio aggregation.
Misconceptions: Log returns are not identical to simple returns except approximately for small changes: +50% simple corresponds to 40.55% log, and -50% simple to -69.31% log. Treating a mean log return as an arithmetic mean return understates or overstates expected growth if conversion is skipped.
Example: A stock closes at $3.570 one day and $3.575 the next; the daily log return is ln(3.575/3.570) = 0.0014, or 0.14%.
Citation: Wikipedia, 'Rate of return' — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rate_of_return (Logarithmic or continuously compounded return)
Status: Reviewed

0352. Gross return
Domain: Statistics and probability
Definition: Two usages coexist: (1) in asset-pricing mathematics, the gross return is the growth factor of an investment over a period, i.e., final value divided by initial value, equal to one plus the simple return; (2) in performance reporting, gross return is the return before deduction of fees, commissions, and taxes (gross of costs), as opposed to net return.
Intuition: In sense (1), it is 'what $1 becomes' - a multiplier like 1.07 for a 7% gain. In sense (2), it is what the investment earned before anyone took their cut.
Mechanics: As a growth factor, gross returns multiply across periods, which is why cumulative performance is computed as their product. As a reporting concept, gross-of-fees return subtracts no management fees or trading costs, while net return is gross return minus those costs.
Formula: G_t = V_t / V_{t-1} = 1 + R_t, where V_t and V_{t-1} are final and initial values and R_t is the simple (net) return; log return r_t = ln(G_t).
Relationships: Simple return, Log return, Cumulative return, Total return
Failure modes: The term is ambiguous across literatures: confusing the growth-factor sense (1.07) with the percentage sense (7%) corrupts compounding calculations, and gross-of-fees performance systematically overstates what an investor actually receives.
Misconceptions: Gross return is not 'the return in gross dollar terms' nor simply the simple return restated; in reporting contexts it differs from net return precisely by fees and taxes, which can be several percentage points per year for active funds.
Example: An index fund reports a 9.0% gross annual return but a 0.8% expense ratio and transaction costs reduce the investor's net return to about 8.2%; meanwhile the year's gross return as a growth factor is 1.09.
Citation: Investopedia, 'What Is a Return?' — https://www.investopedia.com/terms/r/return.asp (What Are Gross Return and Net Return?)
Citation: Wikipedia, 'Rate of return' — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rate_of_return (Returns over multiple periods (growth factor))
Status: Reviewed

0353. Cumulative return
Domain: Statistics and probability
Definition: The total return of an investment over a multi-period horizon, obtained by compounding (geometrically linking) the single-period returns, assuming gains are reinvested. It measures the full change in value from the start to the end of the holding period.
Intuition: It is the answer to 'if I invested $1 at the start and reinvested everything, what fraction do I have now, minus one?' It compounds, so it is not the sum of the periodic returns.
Mechanics: Multiply the gross returns (growth factors) of each sub-period together and subtract one. Equivalently, sum the log returns over the horizon and exponentiate minus one.
Formula: R_cum = PRODUCT_{t=1..T} (1 + R_t) - 1, where R_t are the per-period simple returns; equivalently R_cum = exp(SUM r_t) - 1 using log returns r_t.
Relationships: Simple return, Gross return, Log return, Annualized return, Geometric mean
Failure modes: Cumulative returns are path-dependent with respect to cash flows: with deposits and withdrawals, the simple compounded figure misstates performance and time-weighted or money-weighted methods are needed. Long cumulative figures also conceal interim drawdowns.
Misconceptions: Cumulative return is not the sum or arithmetic average of periodic returns: four annual returns of +50%, -20%, +30%, -40% sum to +20% but compound to a cumulative return of 1.5*0.8*1.3*0.6 - 1 = -6.4%.
Example: Monthly returns of +2%, -1%, and +3% give a cumulative return of 1.02 * 0.99 * 1.03 - 1 = 4.03% over the quarter.
Citation: Wikipedia, 'Rate of return' — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rate_of_return (Returns over multiple periods (time-weighted / geometric linking))
Status: Reviewed

0354. Annualized return
Domain: Statistics and probability
Definition: The constant per-year rate of return that, compounded over the holding period, would produce the observed cumulative return. It converts returns measured over periods longer or shorter than a year to a comparable yearly basis.
Intuition: It answers 'what steady yearly growth rate would have gotten me to the same final value?' It lets you compare a 9-month return with a 5-year return on one scale.
Mechanics: Take the cumulative gross return, raise it to the power 1/T where T is the holding period in years, and subtract one. For volatility-style annualization of average per-period returns, the compounded convention (1+R_period)^k - 1 is used, not simple multiplication by k.
Formula: R_ann = (1 + R_cum)^(1/T) - 1 = (PRODUCT (1 + R_t))^(1/T) - 1, where R_cum is the cumulative return and T is the horizon in years.
Relationships: Cumulative return, Geometric mean, Simple return, Log return
Failure modes: Annualizing short or volatile track records extrapolates a possibly unrepresentative period to a full year; CFA Institute GIPS prohibit annualizing returns for periods shorter than one year because such figures project an unverified rate onto the remainder of the year. Annualized returns also smooth over the path and hide drawdowns.
Misconceptions: Annualized return is not the arithmetic average of yearly returns: +10% then -10% averages to 0% arithmetically but annualizes to (0.99)^(1/2) - 1 = -0.5% per year. The gap between arithmetic and annualized (geometric) return grows with volatility.
Example: A cumulative return of 33.1% over 3 months annualizes to (1.331)^(12/3) - 1 = 214% if naively compounded, which is why sub-year annualization is discouraged; a 21% return over 2 years annualizes to (1.21)^(1/2) - 1 = 10% per year.
Citation: Wikipedia, 'Rate of return' — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rate_of_return (Annualization; Annual returns and annualized returns)
Citation: Investopedia, 'What Is a Return?' — https://www.investopedia.com/terms/r/return.asp (Understanding a Return (annualization))
Status: Reviewed

0355. Arithmetic mean
Domain: Statistics and probability
Definition: The sum of a set of values divided by their count; the most common measure of central tendency (location). It is the value that minimizes the sum of squared deviations from the data.
Intuition: It is the 'fair share' value: if every observation were replaced by the mean, the total would stay the same. It balances the data like a center of gravity.
Mechanics: Add all observations and divide by the number of observations. Every value, including extremes, contributes fully, which makes the mean efficient for well-behaved data but sensitive to outliers.
Formula: x_bar = (1/N) * SUM_{i=1..N} x_i, where x_i are the observations and N is their count.
Relationships: Median, Mode, Geometric mean, Expected value, Sample mean, Population mean
Failure modes: Extreme tail values can pull the mean far from the bulk of the data (NIST illustrates this with Cauchy data, where the mean is useless as a location estimate). For multiplicative processes such as compounded returns, the arithmetic mean overstates the actual growth rate.
Misconceptions: The arithmetic mean is not always the 'typical' value: for skewed distributions like income or returns it sits above the median. Averaging periodic returns arithmetically does not give the compounded growth rate - that requires the geometric mean.
Example: Monthly returns of +5%, -3%, and +7% have arithmetic mean (5 - 3 + 7)/3 = 3% per month; the compounded monthly growth is slightly lower at the geometric mean of about 2.9%.
Citation: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods — https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda351.htm (1.3.5.1, 'Measures of Location')
Status: Reviewed

0356. Geometric mean
Domain: Statistics and probability
Definition: The nth root of the product of n positive numbers; the central-tendency measure appropriate when quantities combine multiplicatively rather than additively. In finance, the geometric mean of period growth factors gives the constant per-period growth rate that reproduces the compounded result.
Intuition: It is the average growth rate that actually compounds to the observed total. Where the arithmetic mean answers 'average change', the geometric mean answers 'average multiplier'.
Mechanics: Multiply the n values and take the nth root; equivalently average their natural logarithms and exponentiate. It is always less than or equal to the arithmetic mean, with equality only when all values are identical (AM-GM inequality), so the gap widens with dispersion.
Formula: GM = (PRODUCT_{i=1..n} a_i)^(1/n) = exp( (1/n) * SUM ln(a_i) ), for a_i > 0. For returns, apply it to gross returns: g = (PRODUCT (1 + R_t))^(1/n) - 1.
Relationships: Arithmetic mean, Cumulative return, Annualized return, Log return, Lognormal distribution
Failure modes: It is defined only for positive values, so it cannot be applied to raw returns that can be negative - one must average gross returns (1 + R) instead. A single zero value makes the whole product zero, and highly volatile return sequences push it far below the arithmetic mean (volatility drag).
Misconceptions: The geometric mean of returns is not interchangeable with the arithmetic mean: for +50% and -50% the arithmetic mean is 0% but the geometric mean of 1.5 and 0.5 is about -13.4% per period, which is what the capital actually did. It is also wrong to apply it to negative raw returns directly.
Example: An investment with annual returns of +10%, -12%, +90%, -30%, +25% ends at 1.609 times its start; the geometric mean growth factor is 1.0998, i.e., about 9.98% per year, versus a 16.6% arithmetic mean that does not reproduce the final value.
Citation: Wikipedia, 'Geometric mean' — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geometric_mean (Definition; Average proportional growth rate)
Status: Reviewed

0357. Median
Domain: Statistics and probability
Definition: The middle value of an ordered data set: the point with half the observations below it and half above. For an even number of observations it is conventionally the average of the two central values.
Intuition: It is the 'typical middle' value that ignores how extreme the tails are. Half the data lies on each side, by construction.
Mechanics: Sort the data ascending; if N is odd, take the ((N+1)/2)th value; if N is even, average the (N/2)th and (N/2 + 1)th values. Because it depends only on ranks, it is robust to outliers and skew.
Formula: For ordered data Y_(1) <= ... <= Y_(N): median = Y_((N+1)/2) if N is odd; median = (Y_(N/2) + Y_(N/2 + 1))/2 if N is even.
Relationships: Arithmetic mean, Mode, Quantile, Percentile, Interquartile range
Failure modes: By discarding magnitude information, the median can hide important tail behavior - two return series with the same median can have very different crash risk. It is also less statistically efficient than the mean when data truly are normal.
Misconceptions: The median is not necessarily a member of the data set, and it equals the mean only for symmetric distributions; for skewed data they differ systematically, with the mean pulled toward the long tail.
Example: For trade P&Ls of -50, -20, 10, 30, 400, the median is 10 while the mean is 74; the single large win dominates the mean but leaves the median unchanged.
Citation: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods — https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda351.htm (1.3.5.1, 'Measures of Location')
Status: Reviewed

0358. Mode
Domain: Statistics and probability
Definition: The value that occurs with the greatest frequency in a data set, or the location of the peak of a probability distribution. A distribution may have one mode (unimodal), several modes (multimodal), or no well-defined mode.
Intuition: It is the most common outcome - the value you would bet on if you had to guess exactly one number.
Mechanics: For discrete data, count frequencies and select the most frequent value; for continuous data, values essentially never repeat, so the mode is taken as the peak of a histogram or density estimate (e.g., the midpoint of the tallest histogram bin).
Relationships: Arithmetic mean, Median, Probability distribution
Failure modes: For continuous data the sample mode is unstable and depends on histogram binning, and multimodal data make 'the mode' ambiguous. The mode ignores all non-peak values, so it carries no information about spread or tails.
Misconceptions: The mode is not the same as the mean or median and is not necessarily near the center of the data - in a right-skewed distribution it sits below both. A data set can legitimately have more than one mode or none.
Example: For a normal sample the mean, median, and mode nearly coincide, while for a lognormal sample NIST reports mode 0.68, median 0.99, mean 1.68 - the mode sits at the peak of the right-skewed density.
Citation: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods — https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda351.htm (1.3.5.1, 'Measures of Location')
Status: Reviewed

0359. Covariance
Domain: Statistics and probability
Definition: A measure of the joint variability of two random variables: the expected product of their deviations from their respective means. Its sign indicates the direction of the linear relationship (positive: variables tend to move together; negative: oppositely), and its magnitude depends on the units of the variables.
Intuition: It is the raw, unstandardized version of correlation: it tells you whether two variables move together and by how much in squared unit terms, but you cannot compare covariances across different unit scales.
Mechanics: For each paired observation, multiply the deviation of x from its mean by the deviation of y from its mean, then average these products. Normalizing covariance by the product of the standard deviations yields the Pearson correlation coefficient; in portfolio theory, asset covariances determine portfolio variance.
Formula: cov(X,Y) = E[(X - E[X])(Y - E[Y])] = E[XY] - E[X]E[Y]; sample estimate: q = SUM_{i=1..N}(x_i - x_bar)(y_i - y_bar) / (N - 1).
Relationships: Correlation, Pearson correlation, Variance, Portfolio variance, Beta
Failure modes: Because covariance carries units of x times y, its magnitude is not comparable across variable pairs or scales - only its sign and the normalized correlation are interpretable. Zero covariance rules out linear dependence but not nonlinear dependence (e.g., X uniform on [-1,1] and Y = X^2 have covariance zero yet are perfectly dependent).
Misconceptions: Uncorrelated does not mean independent, except under joint normality. Also, a large absolute covariance does not by itself imply a strong relationship - it may just reflect large units or variances.
Example: If two stocks have daily returns with variances 0.0004 and 0.0009 and covariance 0.0003, their correlation is 0.0003 / sqrt(0.0004*0.0009) = 0.5; the covariance value alone says nothing without that normalization.
Citation: Wikipedia, 'Covariance' — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Covariance (Definition; Calculating the sample covariance)
Status: Reviewed

0360. Pearson correlation
Domain: Statistics and probability
Definition: The standardized measure of linear association between two variables, equal to their covariance divided by the product of their standard deviations, ranging from -1 (perfect negative linear) to +1 (perfect positive linear). Developed by Karl Pearson around the early 1900s.
Intuition: It measures how well a straight line describes the relationship: +1 or -1 means all points lie exactly on a line, 0 means no linear pattern at all.
Mechanics: Standardize each variable (subtract its mean, divide by its standard deviation), multiply the paired standardized values, and average. The sign matches the slope of the least-squares regression line, and r^2 is the share of variance in y explained linearly by x.
Formula: r = [n*SUM(xy) - (SUM x)(SUM y)] / sqrt( [n*SUM x^2 - (SUM x)^2] * [n*SUM y^2 - (SUM y)^2] ), where n is the number of paired observations.
Relationships: Correlation, Covariance, Spearman rank correlation, Kendall rank correlation, Coefficient of determination, Linear regression
Failure modes: It detects only linear structure: U-shaped, cyclical, or threshold relationships can yield r near 0 despite perfect dependence. It is also non-robust - one outlier can inflate or destroy r - and it presumes the relationship is stable over the sample.
Misconceptions: r = 0 does not mean 'no relationship', only no linear one. Squaring r gives variance explained, so r = 0.5 means only 25% shared variance, not '50% association'; and strong correlation still does not imply causation.
Example: For 11 students' third-exam and final-exam scores, OpenStax computes r = 0.6631, so r^2 = 0.44: about 44% of the variation in final scores is linearly explained by third-exam scores.
Citation: OpenStax, Introductory Statistics — https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics/pages/12-3-the-regression-equation (12.3, 'The Correlation Coefficient r')
Status: Reviewed

0361. Spearman rank correlation
Domain: Statistics and probability
Definition: A nonparametric measure of monotonic association between two variables, defined as the Pearson correlation coefficient computed on the ranks of the observations rather than their raw values. It ranges from -1 to +1 and detects any consistent monotonic relationship, linear or not.
Intuition: It asks 'do bigger x values reliably come with bigger y values?' regardless of how big the steps are. Only the ordering matters, so outliers can do no more damage than their rank allows.
Mechanics: Rank each variable separately (averaging ranks for ties), then compute the Pearson correlation of the rank pairs. With no ties, a simplified formula in the squared rank differences d_i applies; with ties, the general Pearson-on-ranks form must be used.
Formula: rs = 1 - 6*SUM(d_i^2) / (n*(n^2 - 1)), where d_i is the difference between the two ranks of observation i and n is the sample size; valid only when all ranks are distinct (no ties).
Relationships: Pearson correlation, Kendall rank correlation, Correlation, Rank statistics
Failure modes: The simplified d^2 formula gives wrong values when ties are present. Like all correlation measures it does not imply causation, and it quantifies monotone association only - a non-monotonic (e.g., inverted-U) dependence can score near zero. With small samples, significance is hard to establish.
Misconceptions: A perfect Spearman coefficient does not require a linear relationship - any strictly monotonic one gives +/-1, so Spearman = 1 is weaker evidence than Pearson = 1. Nor is Spearman simply 'Pearson with outliers removed'; it answers a different question (monotonic vs. linear).
Example: Ranking 10 people by IQ and by weekly TV hours yields SUM d_i^2 = 58 and n = 10, giving rho = 1 - 6*58/(10*99) = -0.176, a weak negative monotonic association.
Citation: Wikipedia, 'Spearman's rank correlation coefficient' — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spearman%27s_rank_correlation_coefficient (Definition and calculation)
Status: Reviewed

0362. Kendall rank correlation
Domain: Statistics and probability
Definition: A nonparametric measure of ordinal association between two variables, computed from the difference between the number of concordant and discordant observation pairs, normalized by the total number of pairs. It ranges from -1 (perfectly reversed rankings) to +1 (identical rankings) and was introduced by Maurice Kendall in 1938.
Intuition: Pick any two observations; the pair is 'concordant' if both variables rank them in the same order. Tau is essentially the probability of concordance minus the probability of discordance.
Mechanics: For all n(n-1)/2 pairs, count pairs where the x-order and y-order agree (concordant) minus those where they disagree (discordant), and divide by the number of pairs. Variants tau-b and tau-c adjust the denominator for ties; under the null of independence, tau has mean zero and an approximately normal sampling distribution for large n.
Formula: tau = (n_C - n_D) / (n(n-1)/2) = 1 - 2*n_D / C(n,2), where n_C and n_D are the numbers of concordant and discordant pairs and C(n,2) is the binomial coefficient (number of pairs).
Relationships: Spearman rank correlation, Pearson correlation, Correlation, Rank statistics, Copula
Failure modes: With many tied values, unadjusted tau-a cannot reach +/-1 and the tie-corrected tau-b or tau-c must be used, changing the value. Direct computation is O(n^2), and tau values are systematically smaller in magnitude than Spearman's rho for the same data, so the two are not numerically interchangeable.
Misconceptions: Tau is not 'a worse Spearman': it has a direct probabilistic interpretation (concordance minus discordance) that rho lacks. And like any rank correlation it measures ordinal association only, never causation.
Example: For n = 30 points with 395 concordant and 40 discordant pairs out of 435 total, tau = (395 - 40)/435 = 0.816, indicating strong agreement between the two rankings.
Citation: Wikipedia, 'Kendall rank correlation coefficient' — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kendall_rank_correlation_coefficient (Definition)
Status: Reviewed

0363. Probability distribution
Domain: Statistics and probability
Definition: A mathematical function that assigns probabilities to the possible outcomes of a random variable. For discrete variables it is a probability mass function giving P(X = x) with all masses non-negative and summing to 1; for continuous variables it is a probability density function whose integral over the whole line is 1, with probabilities defined over intervals.
Intuition: It is the complete map of what values a random quantity can take and how likely each is - the 'shape of uncertainty' for a variable such as tomorrow's return.
Mechanics: A discrete PMF p(x) satisfies p(x) >= 0 and SUM p(x) = 1, with P(X = x) = p(x) at each value. A continuous PDF f(x) satisfies f(x) >= 0 and integrates to 1; the probability of any single point is zero and interval probabilities are areas under the curve. The cumulative distribution function F(x) = P(X <= x) gives left-tail probabilities in both cases.
Formula: Discrete: SUM_j p_j = 1, p_j >= 0. Continuous: integral_{-inf}^{+inf} f(x) dx = 1, f(x) >= 0; P(a <= X <= b) = integral_a^b f(x) dx.
Relationships: Normal distribution, Lognormal distribution, Binomial distribution, Poisson distribution, Expected value, Quantile
Failure modes: Real financial return series rarely match any simple parametric distribution exactly - they show skewness, excess kurtosis, volatility clustering, and regime changes - so a fitted distribution understates tail risk if taken literally. For continuous models, treating density height as a probability is a category error.
Misconceptions: A probability density is not a probability: f(x) can exceed 1, and only areas under it are probabilities. Also, knowing a distribution's mean and variance does not determine the distribution - many shapes share the same two moments.
Example: Modeling the number of daily limit-up moves in a year with a binomial distribution and tomorrow's percentage price change with a normal distribution are both choices of a probability distribution; each implies different tail odds.
Citation: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods — https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda361.htm (1.3.6.1, 'What is a Probability Distribution')
Status: Reviewed

0364. Normal distribution
Domain: Statistics and probability
Definition: A continuous, symmetric, single-peaked probability distribution fully determined by its location parameter mu (mean = median = mode) and scale parameter sigma (standard deviation). It is the default modeling distribution in statistics, theoretically justified by the central limit theorem for sums and averages.
Intuition: It is the classic bell curve: most values cluster near the mean and extremes become rapidly rarer, with about 68% of probability within one sigma and 99.7% within three.
Mechanics: The density is fully specified by mu and sigma; the standard normal (mu = 0, sigma = 1) is obtained by z-scoring. Sums and means of many independent contributions converge to it (CLT), which is why many test statistics are normal-based; its CDF has no closed form and is computed numerically.
Formula: f(x) = exp( -(x - mu)^2 / (2*sigma^2) ) / (sigma * sqrt(2*pi)), where mu is the mean and sigma the standard deviation; skewness = 0, kurtosis = 3.
Relationships: Probability distribution, Central limit theorem, Z-score, Student's t-distribution, Lognormal distribution, Standard deviation
Failure modes: Financial returns exhibit heavier tails and skewness than the normal model, so normality assumptions understate the probability of extreme moves (crashes). Tests and intervals built on normality can mislead when applied to fat-tailed or asymmetric data without robustness checks.
Misconceptions: 'Everything averages out to a bell curve' is false for heavy-tailed data - the CLT requires finite variance, and Cauchy-type data never normalize. Also, normality of returns does not follow from price levels being lognormal; they are distinct modeling choices.
Example: Under a normal model with daily mean 0.05% and sigma 1%, a -3% day is a -3.05-sigma event with probability near 0.1% - yet such days occur far more often in real equity returns, illustrating the thin-tail failure.
Citation: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods — https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda3661.htm (1.3.6.6.1, 'Normal Distribution')
Status: Reviewed

0365. Lognormal distribution
Domain: Statistics and probability
Definition: A continuous probability distribution of a positive random variable X whose natural logarithm is normally distributed. It is right-skewed with support on (0, infinity) and is the standard model for asset prices under geometric Brownian motion.
Intuition: If returns compound multiplicatively, prices end up lognormal: the product of many positive random growth factors has a log that is a sum, hence normal by the CLT. Prices cannot go below zero, which the lognormal respects.
Mechanics: If Y = ln(X) ~ N(mu, sigma^2) then X is lognormal; the scale parameter m = exp(mu) is the median of X, and sigma is the standard deviation of log X. The mean exp(mu + sigma^2/2) exceeds the median, reflecting the right skew.
Formula: f(x) = exp( -(ln x - mu)^2 / (2*sigma^2) ) / (x * sigma * sqrt(2*pi)) for x > 0, where mu and sigma are the mean and standard deviation of ln(X); median = exp(mu), mean = exp(mu + sigma^2/2).
Relationships: Normal distribution, Probability distribution, Geometric Brownian motion, Log return, Geometric mean
Failure modes: Real asset prices deviate from lognormality: returns show fat tails, skew, and jumps, so option-pricing and risk models built on strict lognormality (e.g., basic Black-Scholes) misprice tail events. Parameter estimates are also fragile when the data contain outliers.
Misconceptions: Lognormal is not 'the log of a normal variable' (that can be negative) but a variable whose log is normal. And a lognormal price process implies normal log returns - the two statements are equivalent, not competing assumptions.
Example: If a stock's annual log return is N(0.08, 0.2^2), its one-year price ratio is lognormal with median exp(0.08) = 1.083 and mean exp(0.08 + 0.02) = 1.105 - the mean outcome is pulled above the median by upside compounding.
Citation: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods — https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda3669.htm (1.3.6.6.9, 'Lognormal Distribution')
Status: Reviewed

0366. Student's t-distribution
Domain: Statistics and probability
Definition: A symmetric, bell-shaped probability distribution with heavier tails than the normal, parameterized by the degrees of freedom nu. It is the exact sampling distribution of the standardized sample mean when the population standard deviation is estimated from a small sample, and it converges to the normal distribution as nu grows.
Intuition: It is the 'cautious normal': when you estimate spread from limited data, the extra uncertainty fattens the tails, so extreme values are more likely than the bell curve suggests.
Mechanics: With shape parameter nu (a positive integer in testing contexts), the t density resembles the normal but with tail weight decreasing as nu increases; nu = 1 gives the Cauchy distribution and nu > 30 is practically normal. Its variance nu/(nu-2) exists only for nu > 2, and kurtosis only for nu > 4.
Formula: f(x) = (1 + x^2/nu)^(-(nu+1)/2) / (B(0.5, 0.5*nu) * sqrt(nu)), where nu is the degrees-of-freedom parameter and B is the beta function; variance = nu/(nu-2) for nu > 2.
Relationships: Normal distribution, Confidence interval, Student's t-test, Standard error, Excess kurtosis
Failure modes: Low degrees of freedom imply very heavy tails - the mean is undefined at nu = 1 and the variance at nu <= 2 - so low-nu t models can break variance-based risk metrics. As a model for returns it captures symmetric fat tails but not skewness or volatility clustering.
Misconceptions: The t distribution is not just a small-sample curiosity: in finance it is used deliberately as a fat-tailed return model. Nor does 't-distributed test statistic' require the raw data to be t-distributed - it arises from normal data with estimated variance.
Example: A 95% confidence interval for a mean from n = 20 observations uses the t critical value with 19 degrees of freedom (about 2.09) instead of the normal 1.96, widening the interval to account for the estimated standard deviation.
Citation: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods — https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda3664.htm (1.3.6.6.4, 't Distribution')
Status: Reviewed

0367. Bernoulli distribution
Domain: Statistics and probability
Definition: The probability distribution of a single trial with exactly two outcomes, conventionally 'success' (X = 1) with probability p and 'failure' (X = 0) with probability 1 - p. It is the building block of the binomial distribution, which counts successes across n independent Bernoulli trials.
Intuition: It models any one-shot yes/no event: will this trade close in profit, will this coin land heads? Only one number - p - fully describes it.
Mechanics: The random variable takes value 1 with probability p and 0 with probability q = 1 - p. Its mean is p and variance is p(1 - p); summing n independent Bernoulli variables with the same p gives a Binomial(n, p) variable.
Formula: P(X = 1) = p, P(X = 0) = 1 - p; E[X] = p; Var(X) = p(1 - p), where p is the success probability.
Relationships: Binomial distribution, Probability distribution, Expected value
Failure modes: It only fits single binary trials with a fixed success probability; applying it to sequences requires independence and constant p, both of which often fail in trading (regime shifts, path dependence). It carries no information about magnitude - a 'win' of 1% and 50% are the same event.
Misconceptions: A Bernoulli trial is not any two-outcome situation: the probabilities must be fixed and, for sequences, the trials independent - drawing without replacement violates the setup. Also, p = 0.5 is not required; 'binary' does not mean 'fair'.
Example: Modeling one trade as a Bernoulli variable with win probability p = 0.55 gives expected value 0.55 and variance 0.2475; a 20-trade win count then follows a Binomial(20, 0.55) distribution.
Citation: OpenStax, Introductory Statistics — https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics/pages/4-3-binomial-distribution (4.3 (Bernoulli trial definition))
Status: Reviewed

0368. Binomial distribution
Domain: Statistics and probability
Definition: The discrete probability distribution of the number of successes in n independent trials, each with exactly two outcomes and the same success probability p. It is the sum of n independent Bernoulli variables and is probably the most commonly used discrete distribution.
Intuition: It answers: 'If each trade wins with probability p, what are the chances of exactly x wins in n trades?' The win count, not the order of wins, is what matters.
Mechanics: The probability of x successes equals the number of ways to choose which x trials succeed (the binomial coefficient) times p^x(1-p)^(n-x). It requires a fixed number of trials, two outcomes per trial, constant p, and independence; the maximum likelihood estimate of p from data is x/n.
Formula: P(X = x) = C(n,x) * p^x * (1-p)^(n-x) for x = 0..n, where C(n,x) = n!/(x!(n-x)!); mean = np, variance = np(1-p).
Relationships: Bernoulli distribution, Poisson distribution, Probability distribution, Normal distribution
Failure modes: The independence and constant-p assumptions fail under regime changes, serial correlation, or sampling without replacement, in which case binomial probabilities misstate tail odds. For large n and small p it is better approximated by the Poisson distribution, and for large n with moderate p by the normal.
Misconceptions: The binomial counts successes without regard to order or payoff size - it cannot price P&L, only event counts. And 'more wins than expected' over n trades is not proof of skill; with p = 0.5, 12+ wins in 20 trials still occurs about 25% of the time.
Example: A strategy wins with p = 0.55 per trade; the probability of exactly 15 wins in 20 trades is C(20,15) * 0.55^15 * 0.45^5, about 0.037.
Citation: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods — https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda366i.htm (Gallery of Distributions, 'Binomial Distribution')
Citation: OpenStax, Introductory Statistics — https://openstax.org/books/introductory-statistics/pages/4-3-binomial-distribution (4.3)
Status: Reviewed

0369. Poisson distribution
Domain: Statistics and probability
Definition: The discrete probability distribution of the number of events occurring in a fixed interval of time or space when events occur independently at a constant average rate lambda. Both its mean and its variance equal lambda.
Intuition: It models rare, independent arrivals: 'If on average 2 news shocks hit per day, what is the chance of 5 tomorrow?' One rate parameter determines everything.
Mechanics: The probability of x events decays factorially in x: e^(-lambda) lambda^x / x!. Key properties: mean = variance = lambda, standard deviation sqrt(lambda), and the maximum likelihood estimate of lambda is the sample mean of counts; inter-arrival times follow the exponential distribution.
Formula: P(X = x) = e^(-lambda) * lambda^x / x! for x = 0, 1, 2, ..., where lambda is the average number of events per interval; mean = lambda, variance = lambda.
Relationships: Exponential distribution, Binomial distribution, Probability distribution, Poisson process
Failure modes: It assumes a constant rate and independence, so clustered events - such as volatility spikes or order-flow bursts that bunch together - are badly fit: real count data often show variance exceeding the mean (overdispersion), which Poisson cannot represent.
Misconceptions: Poisson is not a model for any count data: if events cluster or the rate varies over time (non-stationarity), the equal mean-variance property breaks. Also, lambda need not be small - the distribution works for large rates too and approaches normality as lambda grows.
Example: If a stock experiences on average lambda = 3 price gaps per month, the probability of a month with zero gaps is e^(-3) = 0.0498, about 5%.
Citation: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods — https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda366j.htm (1.3.6.6.19, 'Poisson Distribution')
Status: Reviewed

0370. Exponential distribution
Domain: Statistics and probability
Definition: A continuous probability distribution on the non-negative reals modeling the waiting time between events that occur at a constant rate, with a constant hazard function. It is the unique continuous memoryless distribution: the probability of waiting t more time units is independent of time already waited.
Intuition: It answers 'how long until the next event?' when events strike at a steady average rate. Past waiting tells you nothing about remaining waiting - the process has no memory.
Mechanics: With scale parameter beta (mean waiting time), the density decays exponentially from its start; mean and standard deviation both equal beta and the hazard rate is the constant 1/beta. It is the inter-arrival-time distribution of a Poisson process and is widely used in reliability and duration modeling.
Formula: f(x) = (1/beta) * exp(-x/beta) for x >= 0, where beta > 0 is the scale parameter (mean waiting time); CDF F(x) = 1 - exp(-x/beta); mean = SD = beta. (Rate form: lambda = 1/beta.)
Relationships: Poisson distribution, Probability distribution, Hazard rate, Poisson process
Failure modes: The constant-hazard (memoryless) assumption fails whenever risk changes with age or state - trade durations and default times typically show time-varying hazard, making Weibull or other models more appropriate. It also cannot represent zero-inflated or multi-modal waiting data.
Misconceptions: Memorylessness does not mean events are 'due' after a long quiet period - the gambler's-fallacy intuition contradicts the model. And the exponential distribution is not 'the distribution of an exponential trend'; it describes random waiting times.
Example: If order-book price changes arrive at an average rate of one every beta = 30 seconds, the probability that the next change takes more than 60 seconds is exp(-60/30) = e^(-2) = 0.135.
Citation: NIST/SEMATECH e-Handbook of Statistical Methods — https://www.itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda3667.htm (1.3.6.6.7, 'Exponential Distribution')
Status: Reviewed

0371. Skewness
Domain: Statistics and probability
Definition: A measure of the asymmetry of a distribution about its mean, defined as the third standardized moment. Zero indicates symmetry, positive values indicate a longer right tail, and negative values a longer left tail.
Intuition: It tells you which side the surprises live on: negatively skewed returns have occasional large crashes amid small gains; positively skewed returns have occasional large wins amid small losses.
Mechanics: Average the cubed deviations from the mean and divide by the cube of the standard deviation; cubing preserves sign, so the heavy tail determines the sign. Software typically reports the sample-size-adjusted Fisher-Pearson coefficient, with the correction factor approaching 1 for large N.
Formula: g1 = [SUM_{i=1..N}(Y_i - Y_bar)^3 / N] / s^3, where Y_bar is the mean and s is the standard deviation computed with N in the denominator; adjusted version G1 = [sqrt(N(N-1))/(N-2)] * g1.
