Definition: A charting technique that projects levels beyond the prior swing — conventionally 100%, 161.8%, and 261.8% of the measured move — as candidate profit-target or exhaustion zones once the trend resumes. Like retracements, it is an analytical convention, not a validated forecasting law.
Intuition: If the retracement yardstick measures how far price pulls back, the extension yardstick guesses how far the next leg might reach.
Mechanics: Applied after a trend resumes: the prior swing's range (or the swing plus its retracement, in three-point projection tools) is multiplied by extension ratios and projected past the old extreme. The 161.8% projection is the most widely watched target.
Formula: Extension level (up-move) = Low + e x (High - Low) with e > 1 (e.g., 1.618); three-point variant: target = RetracementLow + e x (High - Low).
Relationships: Fibonacci retracement, Retracement, Uptrend, Downtrend
Failure modes: All the subjectivity of retracements applies, compounded by the choice of anchor points; trends frequently stop well short of, or blow through, projected extensions.
Misconceptions: That extension targets are high-probability exit prices; they are reference zones at best, and many moves never reach the 161.8% projection.
Example: After a stock rallies 40 to 50 and resumes upward from a 46 pullback, the 161.8% extension of the 40-50 leg projects a target zone near 62.2 (46 + 1.618 x 10).
Citation: Investopedia — Fibonacci Retracement Levels Explained — https://www.investopedia.com/terms/f/fibonacciretracement.asp (Applications in Trading (extensions))
Status: Reviewed

0623. Pivot point
Domain: Price action and technical analysis
Definition: A calculated price level derived from the prior period's high, low, and close, used to frame the current period's directional bias and to derive support/resistance levels. Originating with floor traders, pivot points are deterministic calculations; their use as turning-point levels is a convention, not a validated edge.
Intuition: Yesterday's average price becomes today's line in the sand: above it leans bullish, below it leans bearish.
Mechanics: The base pivot P = (High + Low + Close)/3 of the prior period; derived levels include S1 = 2P - High, S2 = P - (High - Low), R1 = 2P - Low, R2 = P + (High - Low). Levels are computed once per period and remain fixed; variants include Fibonacci and Demark pivots.
Formula: P = (H + L + C)/3; S1 = 2P - H; S2 = P - (H - L); R1 = 2P - L; R2 = P + (H - L), where H, L, C are the prior period's high, low, close.
Relationships: Daily pivot, Weekly pivot, Monthly pivot, Support, Resistance
Failure modes: In strongly trending periods price may never interact with the pivot, and in whippy markets it slices through the levels repeatedly; the levels have no inherent causal force.
Misconceptions: That pivot levels are precise reversal points; ChartSchool treats them as a framework to be confirmed with price action and other indicators.
Example: Yesterday's H/L/C are 105, 99, 102: P = 102, R1 = 105, S1 = 99. A move above 102 early today is read as positive, targeting R1 at 105.
Citation: StockCharts ChartSchool — Pivot Points — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/technical-indicators-and-overlays/technical-overlays/pivot-points (What Are Pivot Points? / Standard Pivot Points)
Status: Reviewed

0624. Daily pivot
Domain: Price action and technical analysis
Definition: A pivot point computed from the previous trading day's high, low, and close, applied to the current day's trading — the original floor-trader usage. On StockCharts' convention, pivots for 1- to 15-minute intraday charts use the prior day's data and remain fixed all day.
Intuition: Yesterday's H/L/C distill into today's map of where buyers and sellers are expected to contest control.
Mechanics: Computed at the start of the day as P = (prior day H + L + C)/3 with the standard derived S1/S2/R1/R2 levels; the levels do not change intraday and are used as bias filter (price above or below P) and as support/resistance references.
Formula: P = (H_prev_day + L_prev_day + C_prev_day)/3; S1 = 2P - H; R1 = 2P - L; S2 = P - (H - L); R2 = P + (H - L).
Relationships: Pivot point, Weekly pivot, Monthly pivot, Support, Resistance
Failure modes: Gap openings can start the day far beyond the pivot, making the levels irrelevant; quiet range days slice back and forth across P, generating noise.
Misconceptions: That daily pivots are intraday reversal guarantees; they are reference levels whose reactions must be confirmed.
Example: An index future closes at 5000 with a 5030 high and 4970 low; today's daily pivot set is P = 5000, R1 = 5030, S1 = 4970, watched on the 5-minute chart all session.
Citation: StockCharts ChartSchool — Pivot Points — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/technical-indicators-and-overlays/technical-overlays/pivot-points (Timeframes for Pivot Points)
Status: Reviewed

0625. Weekly pivot
Domain: Price action and technical analysis
Definition: A pivot point computed from the previous calendar week's high, low, and close, applied to the current week. On StockCharts' convention, pivots for 30- to 120-minute charts use the prior week's data and remain fixed for the entire week.
Intuition: Last week's price action condenses into this week's bias line and outer reference levels.
Mechanics: Computed at the week's start as P = (prior week H + L + C)/3 with derived S/R levels; fixed for the week and recalculated on the first trading day of the next week.
Formula: P = (H_prev_week + L_prev_week + C_prev_week)/3; S1 = 2P - H; R1 = 2P - L; S2 = P - (H - L); R2 = P + (H - L).
Relationships: Pivot point, Daily pivot, Monthly pivot, Support, Resistance
Failure modes: Same structural limits as all pivots: strong weekly trends can leave the pivot behind on day one, and holiday-shortened weeks distort the inputs.
Misconceptions: That weekly pivots are more 'reliable' than daily ones by nature; they are merely slower-moving references with the same heuristic status.
Example: Last week a stock printed H 110, L 100, C 108: this week's weekly pivot is P = 106, with R1 = 112 and S1 = 102 on the 60-minute chart.
Citation: StockCharts ChartSchool — Pivot Points — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/technical-indicators-and-overlays/technical-overlays/pivot-points (Timeframes for Pivot Points)
Status: Reviewed

0626. Monthly pivot
Domain: Price action and technical analysis
Definition: A pivot point computed from the previous month's high, low, and close, applied to the current month. On StockCharts' convention, pivots displayed on daily charts use the prior month's data and remain fixed for the whole month (weekly and monthly charts use the prior year's data).
Intuition: Last month's range and close set this month's reference grid for where longer-term buyers and sellers may engage.
Mechanics: Computed on the first trading day of the month as P = (prior month H + L + C)/3 with derived S/R levels; fixed until the next month begins, and used on daily charts as slower bias and support/resistance references.
Formula: P = (H_prev_month + L_prev_month + C_prev_month)/3; S1 = 2P - H; R1 = 2P - L; S2 = P - (H - L); R2 = P + (H - L).
Relationships: Pivot point, Daily pivot, Weekly pivot, Support, Resistance
Failure modes: Monthly levels are coarse on volatile instruments, often sitting far from price and untouched for weeks; gaps between months can strand the grid entirely.
Misconceptions: That monthly pivots carry institutional weight by construction; they are arithmetic averages of last month's range, watched only by those who choose to watch them.
Example: A stock printed H 120, L 100, C 115 in May: June's monthly pivot is P = 111.67, plotted on the daily chart for all of June.
Citation: StockCharts ChartSchool — Pivot Points — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/technical-indicators-and-overlays/technical-overlays/pivot-points (Timeframes for Pivot Points)
Status: Reviewed

0627. Market structure break
Domain: Price action and technical analysis
Definition: In price-structure analysis, a break of the swing sequence defining the current trend: in an uptrend, a close below the most recent higher low (or, in continuation terms, a close above the prior swing high that extends the structure). SMC/ICT usage distinguishes a trend-continuing break of structure from a counter-trend structure shift; the terminology is a discretionary convention without a single canonical authority.
Intuition: The market's staircase pattern breaks a step — the rhythm of higher floors or lower ceilings is violated, so the structure may be changing.
Mechanics: Map swing highs and lows; a trend-continuing BOS prints when price exceeds the last swing high in an uptrend (or undercuts the last swing low in a downtrend), while a structure break against the trend prints when the last higher low (or lower high) is taken out. Confirmation conventions vary: some require a close beyond the swing, others a wick.
Relationships: Change of character, Swing high, Swing low, Uptrend, Downtrend, Liquidity sweep, Reversal
Failure modes: Marginal wick-throughs of a swing look like structure breaks but resolve as stop runs; and without a fixed swing-definition rule, two analysts mark different structures on the same chart.
Misconceptions: That a single broken swing proves trend reversal; a wick through a level that closes back inside is a sweep, not a break — acceptance beyond the level is the distinguishing test.
Example: An uptrend with higher lows at 50, 52, 54 breaks down when price closes below 54: the structure break flips bias from buying dips to selling rallies.
Citation: LuxAlgo Library — Smart Money Concepts — https://www.luxalgo.com/library/concept/smart-money-concepts/ (What are Smart Money Concepts?)
Citation: LuxAlgo Library — Liquidity Sweep — https://www.luxalgo.com/library/concept/liquidity-sweep/ (Liquidity sweep vs similar concepts (Break of Structure))
Status: Reviewed

0628. Change of character
Domain: Price action and technical analysis
Definition: In SMC/ICT vocabulary, the first structural break against the prevailing trend — e.g., in an uptrend, the first close below a higher low — read as an early signal that order flow may be shifting. It is the counter-trend counterpart of a trend-continuing break of structure; a discretionary convention with no canonical authority.
Intuition: The first crack in the trend's rhythm: the market does something it hasn't been doing, hinting the character of the move is changing.
Mechanics: After establishing the trend's swing sequence, mark the most recent higher low (uptrend) or lower high (downtrend); a decisive break of that pivot against the trend is the change of character. SMC models typically require a preceding liquidity sweep and subsequent displacement before treating it as tradable evidence.
Relationships: Market structure break, Liquidity sweep, Order block, Reversal, Swing high, Swing low
Failure modes: CHoCH signals proliferate on lower timeframes and most are noise within higher-timeframe trends; deep pullbacks routinely trigger counter-trend structure breaks without reversing the main trend.
Misconceptions: That a CHoCH is a sell/buy signal by itself; within SMC it is context requiring confirmation (displacement, a return to an order block or gap), not an entry trigger.
Example: After a sweep of the prior high, an uptrending pair closes below its last higher low on the 15-minute chart — a CHoCH that SMC traders take as the first evidence of a possible short-side shift.
Citation: LuxAlgo Library — Smart Money Concepts — https://www.luxalgo.com/library/concept/smart-money-concepts/ (What are Smart Money Concepts?)
Citation: LuxAlgo Library — Liquidity Sweep — https://www.luxalgo.com/library/concept/liquidity-sweep/ (What is a Liquidity Sweep?)
Status: Reviewed

0629. Liquidity sweep
Domain: Price action and technical analysis
Definition: In SMC/ICT vocabulary, a run through a level where resting orders cluster — stop-losses and breakout entries just beyond an obvious high or low — followed by failure to hold beyond it: price trades through, fills those orders, and closes back inside the prior range. The same chart event is called a false breakout in classical TA; 'sweep' adds an interpretation (order collection) that a chart cannot prove.
Intuition: Price pokes through an obvious level, triggers the crowd's stops, then snaps back — the level was the target of the move, not an obstacle in its way.
Mechanics: Identification is a two-part check: mark pools where stops cluster (prior swing highs/lows, equal highs/lows, session extremes), then require the failure — a trade through the level (often on a wick) followed by a close back inside the old range. A close that holds beyond the level with continuation is a breakout, not a sweep.
Relationships: Stop run, False breakout, Market structure break, Change of character, Order block, Fair value gap
Failure modes: At the moment of the break a sweep and a genuine breakout are indistinguishable — only the close and follow-through separate them, so acting early means sometimes fading real breakouts.
Misconceptions: That sweeps prove a market maker deliberately hunted retail stops; order-flow research documents stop clustering at predictable levels, but intent is narrative, not observable fact.
Example: Price wicks above a prior swing high where buy stops rest, immediately rejects, and closes back inside the range; SMC traders read the level as swept and look for short setups on the retrace.
Citation: LuxAlgo Library — Liquidity Sweep — https://www.luxalgo.com/library/concept/liquidity-sweep/ (What is a Liquidity Sweep?)
Citation: LuxAlgo Library — Smart Money Concepts — https://www.luxalgo.com/library/concept/smart-money-concepts/ (What are Smart Money Concepts?)
Status: Reviewed

0630. Stop run
Domain: Price action and technical analysis
Definition: A move that pushes price through a level where stop-loss orders are known or presumed to cluster, triggering them, often followed by a quick reversal. In SMC vocabulary this is the liquidity sweep; in classical terms it overlaps with the false breakout. The deliberate-targeting framing is an inference, not an observable fact.
Intuition: Obvious levels have crowds of stops parked behind them; a push through sets off that cascade in one quick burst.
Mechanics: Identified by the footprint: a fast trade through a well-watched swing high/low or round number, a burst of activity as stops execute, and (in the sweep reading) failure to hold beyond the level. Buy stops sit above highs, sell stops below lows, so the run direction names the pool being executed.
Relationships: Liquidity sweep, False breakout, Support, Resistance, Swing high, Swing low
Failure modes: Not every run through a level reverses — sometimes the stop cascade fuels a genuine breakout; distinguishing the two requires waiting for the close and follow-through.
Misconceptions: That brokers or market makers visibly hunt individual retail stops; academic work documents stop clustering and unusual behavior at such levels, but the personalized stop-hunt story is contested.
Example: A pair trades two ticks below an obvious equal-lows level, triggering clustered sell stops, then closes back above the level within the same bar — a classic stop-run footprint.
Citation: LuxAlgo Library — Liquidity Sweep — https://www.luxalgo.com/library/concept/liquidity-sweep/ (What is a Liquidity Sweep?)
Citation: LuxAlgo Library — Smart Money Concepts — https://www.luxalgo.com/library/concept/smart-money-concepts/ (What are Smart Money Concepts?)
Status: Reviewed

0631. Supply zone
Domain: Price action and technical analysis
Definition: A price band marking the base from which a strong decline launched, drawn (in supply-and-demand methodology) around the small consolidation preceding the impulsive drop. It is treated as potential resistance on a return, on the hypothesis that unfilled sell interest remains there — a discretionary zone framework related to, but looser than, classical resistance.
Intuition: Price paused, then fell out of bed; the pause zone is where sellers were last in control, so the first return there may meet them again.
Mechanics: Identify an impulsive decline; step back to the small base candles just before it. Draw the zone around the base — proximal line at the edge nearest current price, distal line at the base's extreme — and extend it right. Reversal zones (rally-base-drop) form at swing turns; continuation zones (drop-base-drop) form mid-swing.
Relationships: Demand zone, Resistance, Order block, Consolidation, Breakdown
Failure modes: Zones are re-drawn to fit hindsight, and price trades straight through many of them; continuation-type (RBR/DBD) zones are documented by practitioners as weaker than reversal-type zones.
Misconceptions: That a supply zone is proof of institutional sell orders waiting there; the zone marks where price left a base impulsively, and the unfilled-orders story is an inference, not an observation.
Example: EUR/USD pauses for three small candles at 1.0850-1.0860, then drops 100 pips; the base is drawn as a supply zone and watched for a short entry on the first return.
Citation: PriceActionNinja — Trading Rally-Base-Rally/Drop-Base-Drop Zones (Complete Guide) — https://priceactionninja.com/trading-rally-base-rally-drop-base-drop-zones-complete-guide/ (What Are Rally-Base-Rally & Drop-Base-Drop Zones? / Drawing RBR/DBD Zones)
Citation: StockCharts ChartSchool — Support & Resistance — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/chart-analysis/support-and-resistance (Support and Resistance—In Simple Words)
Status: Reviewed

0632. Demand zone
Domain: Price action and technical analysis
Definition: A price band marking the base from which a strong advance launched, drawn (in supply-and-demand methodology) around the small consolidation preceding the impulsive rally. It is treated as potential support on a return, on the hypothesis that unfilled buy interest remains there — a discretionary zone framework related to, but looser than, classical support.
Intuition: Price paused, then took off upward; the pause zone is where buyers were last in control, so the first return there may attract them again.
Mechanics: Identify an impulsive rally; step back to the small base candles just before it and box the base (proximal edge nearest current price, distal edge at the base extreme). Reversal zones (drop-base-rally) form at swing lows; continuation zones (rally-base-rally) form mid-swing and are regarded by practitioners as weaker.
Relationships: Supply zone, Support, Order block, Consolidation, Breakout
Failure modes: Zone boundaries are subjective and hindsight-fitted; price frequently slices through demand zones without reacting, especially continuation-type zones formed mid-swing.
Misconceptions: That an untouched ('fresh') demand zone must hold on first test; freshness heuristics are practitioner rules of thumb without validated statistics.
Example: GBP/JPY bases at 182.00-182.30, then rallies sharply; the base is drawn as a demand zone, and a later retracement into it produces a bullish engulfing entry.
Citation: PriceActionNinja — Trading Rally-Base-Rally/Drop-Base-Drop Zones (Complete Guide) — https://priceactionninja.com/trading-rally-base-rally-drop-base-drop-zones-complete-guide/ (What Are Rally-Base-Rally & Drop-Base-Drop Zones? / Drawing RBR/DBD Zones)
Citation: StockCharts ChartSchool — Support & Resistance — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/chart-analysis/support-and-resistance (Support and Resistance—In Simple Words)
Status: Reviewed

0633. Order block
Domain: Price action and technical analysis
Definition: In SMC/ICT vocabulary, the last opposite-direction candle (or consecutive cluster of them) before an impulsive move — the final down candle before a rally (bullish) or the final up candle before a decline (bearish) — marked as a zone that may be defended on a return. It is read as the footprint of institutional position-building; that reading is an interpretation, since the candle alone shows only price, not orders.
Intuition: The last place price sat before the big move launched is treated as the move's origin — and origins are where defenders may remain.
Mechanics: Find the displacement first (an impulsive leg that breaks structure or sweeps a swing, ideally leaving a fair value gap), then step back to the last opposite close and box its range — conventions include full high-low, body only, or the 50% mean threshold. A decisive close through the whole zone invalidates it; the failed zone is then watched as a 'breaker' from the other side.
Relationships: Fair value gap, Supply zone, Demand zone, Market structure break, Liquidity sweep, Change of character
Failure modes: Candidate blocks are everywhere, so most are meaningless; price trades straight through a large share of them, and there is no reliable published hit rate for the concept.
Misconceptions: That an order block visibly shows institutional orders; only the candle is observable, and the institutional-footprint narrative cannot be verified from the chart.
Example: A pair sweeps a low, then rallies impulsively through the prior swing high; the last down-close candle before that leg is boxed as a bullish order block, watched for longs on the retrace (mitigation).
Citation: LuxAlgo Library — Bullish/bearish Order Block — https://www.luxalgo.com/library/concept/bullish-bearish-order-block/ (What is a Bullish/bearish Order Block? / How to identify)
Citation: LuxAlgo Library — Smart Money Concepts — https://www.luxalgo.com/library/concept/smart-money-concepts/ (What are Smart Money Concepts?)
Status: Reviewed

0634. Fair value gap
Domain: Price action and technical analysis
Definition: In SMC/ICT vocabulary, a three-candle pattern in which the middle candle's range does not overlap with the wicks of its neighbors — the low of the third candle sits above the high of the first (bullish FVG), or the high of the third sits below the low of the first (bearish FVG) — leaving a span price crossed in a single fast pass. It is read as an inefficiency that price may later revisit; that expectation is a hypothesis, not an established regularity.
Intuition: The middle candle moved so fast that a slice of prices was skipped; the gap marks the skipped slice.
Mechanics: Scan consecutive three-candle sequences: for a bullish FVG, check whether candle 3's low exceeds candle 1's high — the gap is the void between them. Traders mark the span (sometimes refined to its midpoint, the 'consequent encroachment') and watch for a retracement into it as entry context, with invalidation beyond the gap's far edge.
Formula: Bullish FVG exists when Low(candle3) > High(candle1); gap span = [High(candle1), Low(candle3)]. Bearish FVG exists when High(candle3) < Low(candle1); span = [High(candle3), Low(candle1)].
Relationships: Imbalance zone, Order block, Gap, Liquidity sweep, Change of character
Failure modes: FVGs are extremely common, especially on low timeframes, so most carry no information; many are never filled, and 'price returns to balance inefficiencies' is an untested slogan rather than a documented tendency.
Misconceptions: That an FVG must be filled; unlike session gaps (where 'gap fill' at least has a mechanical definition), there is no validated fill-rate for FVGs, and the concept repackages older notions of price vacuums.
Example: Candle 1 tops at 100.20, candle 2 surges to close at 102, and candle 3 bottoms at 101.50: the 100.20-101.50 span is a bullish fair value gap watched for support on a retrace.
Citation: LuxAlgo Library — Bullish/bearish Order Block — https://www.luxalgo.com/library/concept/bullish-bearish-order-block/ (Order block vs neighboring concepts (Fair Value Gap, Supply & Demand Zones))
Citation: LuxAlgo Library — Smart Money Concepts — https://www.luxalgo.com/library/concept/smart-money-concepts/ (What are Smart Money Concepts?)
Status: Reviewed

0635. Imbalance zone
Domain: Price action and technical analysis
Definition: A chart region where price moved so quickly in one direction that little two-sided trading occurred — operationalized in SMC/ICT practice chiefly as the fair value gap, the three-candle non-overlap span. The zone is hypothesized to attract a later revisit ('rebalancing'); the hypothesis is discretionary and unproven.
Intuition: A one-sided stampede leaves thin ice on the chart — a stretch where almost no business was done.
Mechanics: Identified as the span between the first and third candles' non-overlapping wicks in a fast three-candle move (the FVG definition), or more loosely as any fast, one-directional price leg with minimal overlap. Marked as a zone and watched for retracement entries in the direction of the originating move.
Relationships: Fair value gap, Order block, Gap, Volatility expansion
Failure modes: The 'imbalance gets rebalanced' expectation fails constantly; trends leave trails of unfilled imbalances behind them, and the term is vague enough to be fitted to almost any fast move.
Misconceptions: That an imbalance is a market defect the price must repair; markets have no obligation to revisit thinly traded spans, and session gaps (a different phenomenon) are often conflated with this concept.
Example: During a news-driven spike, three consecutive 5-minute candles leave a 15-point span untouched between the first candle's high and the third's low — an imbalance zone marked for a possible retrace entry.
Citation: LuxAlgo Library — Smart Money Concepts — https://www.luxalgo.com/library/concept/smart-money-concepts/ (What are Smart Money Concepts?)
Citation: LuxAlgo Library — Bullish/bearish Order Block — https://www.luxalgo.com/library/concept/bullish-bearish-order-block/ (Order block vs neighboring concepts (Fair Value Gap, Supply & Demand Zones))
Status: Reviewed

0636. Premium zone
Domain: Price action and technical analysis
Definition: In SMC/ICT vocabulary, the upper half of a 'dealing range' — the leg between a significant swing low and swing high — i.e., everything above the 50% midpoint. The convention frames longs taken in premium as poor value and shorts in premium as acceptable value; it is a positioning heuristic, not a valuation measure.
Intuition: Split the range in half; buying in the top half means paying up relative to where the market has just been.
Mechanics: Anchor the dealing range at a meaningful swing low and high; the midpoint is equilibrium and the region above it is premium. SMC models look for sell-side setups (bearish order blocks, bearish FVGs) located in premium, aligned with the higher-timeframe bias.
Formula: Equilibrium = (range high + range low) / 2; premium zone = prices above that midpoint within the dealing range.
Relationships: Discount zone, Equilibrium level, Order block, Fair value gap, Fibonacci retracement
Failure modes: In strong trends price lives in premium for long stretches, so 'expensive' stays expensive; the framework also depends entirely on which swing anchors are chosen.
Misconceptions: That premium means overvalued in any fundamental sense; it is purely a relative position within one analyst-chosen range.
Example: With a dealing range of 1800-1900, equilibrium sits at 1850; a bearish order block at 1875 lies in premium, qualifying it — under SMC convention — as a short-entry zone.
Citation: LuxAlgo Library — Premium & Discount — https://www.luxalgo.com/library/concept/premium-and-discount/ (What is Premium & Discount?)
Citation: LuxAlgo Library — Smart Money Concepts — https://www.luxalgo.com/library/concept/smart-money-concepts/ (What are Smart Money Concepts?)
Status: Reviewed

0637. Discount zone
Domain: Price action and technical analysis
Definition: In SMC/ICT vocabulary, the lower half of a 'dealing range' — the leg between a significant swing low and swing high — i.e., everything below the 50% midpoint. The convention frames longs taken in discount as acceptable value and shorts in discount as poor value; a positioning heuristic, not a valuation measure.
Intuition: Split the range in half; buying in the bottom half means paying less than the range's typical price.
Mechanics: Anchor the dealing range at a meaningful swing low and high; the midpoint is equilibrium and the region below it is discount. SMC models look for buy-side setups (bullish order blocks, bullish FVGs) located in discount, aligned with the higher-timeframe bias.
Formula: Equilibrium = (range high + range low) / 2; discount zone = prices below that midpoint within the dealing range.
Relationships: Premium zone, Equilibrium level, Order block, Fair value gap, Fibonacci retracement
Failure modes: In strong downtrends price keeps getting 'cheaper' without bouncing, so discount buys can average into a falling market; results hinge on discretionary anchor selection.
Misconceptions: That discount means undervalued or due to rise; it only means 'below the midpoint of the chosen range', which says nothing about where price goes next.
Example: With a dealing range of 1800-1900, a bullish order block at 1825 lies in discount (below the 1850 equilibrium), qualifying it — under SMC convention — as a long-entry zone.
Citation: LuxAlgo Library — Premium & Discount — https://www.luxalgo.com/library/concept/premium-and-discount/ (What is Premium & Discount?)
Citation: LuxAlgo Library — Smart Money Concepts — https://www.luxalgo.com/library/concept/smart-money-concepts/ (What are Smart Money Concepts?)
Status: Reviewed

0638. Equilibrium level
Domain: Price action and technical analysis
Definition: In SMC/ICT vocabulary, the 50% midpoint of a dealing range (a significant swing low to swing high), separating the premium half above from the discount half below. It serves as the reference for the methodology's value heuristic; outside SMC, a 50% midpoint is simply the midpoint of a range (also a Dow Theory retracement convention).
Intuition: The range's center of gravity: above it price is relatively expensive, below it relatively cheap, within that range.
Mechanics: Computed as (swing high + swing low)/2 of the chosen dealing range and drawn as a horizontal reference. SMC models use it to filter setups (longs below, shorts above) and as a mean-threshold reference on individual candles and gaps.
Formula: Equilibrium = (range high + range low) / 2.
Relationships: Premium zone, Discount zone, Fibonacci retracement, Trading range, Swing high, Swing low
Failure modes: The level moves whenever the analyst re-anchors the range, so it is unstable as a signal; price shows no documented obligation to react at a range midpoint.
Misconceptions: That equilibrium is a supply-demand balance price the market returns to; it is an arithmetic midpoint of an arbitrarily chosen range, not an economic equilibrium.
Example: A dealing range from 1800 to 1900 puts equilibrium at 1850; price stalls near 1850 on its way from the discount half toward the range high.
Citation: LuxAlgo Library — Premium & Discount — https://www.luxalgo.com/library/concept/premium-and-discount/ (What is Premium & Discount?)
Citation: LuxAlgo Library — Smart Money Concepts — https://www.luxalgo.com/library/concept/smart-money-concepts/ (What are Smart Money Concepts?)
Status: Reviewed

0639. Doji
Domain: Candlestick patterns
Definition: A single-candlestick formation in which the open and close are equal or virtually equal, producing a very small or nonexistent real body. In technical analysis it is read as a sign of indecision between buyers and sellers; as with all candlestick patterns, it is an interpretive framework, not a proven predictive law.
Intuition: Buyers and sellers fought to a draw during the period: price traveled up and down but ended essentially where it started, so neither side is in control.
Mechanics: Computed directly from OHLC data: the real body |close - open| is at or near zero relative to the period's range (a common convention classifies a candle as a doji when the body is no more than a few percent of the high-low range). The position of the open/close within the range defines subtypes (long-legged, dragonfly, gravestone).
Formula: Doji when |C - O| <= epsilon * (H - L), where O, H, L, C are the period's open, high, low, close and epsilon is a small threshold (often ~0.05).
Relationships: Long-legged doji, Dragonfly doji, Gravestone doji, Spinning top, Harami cross, Morning doji star, Evening doji star
Failure modes: A lone doji is a neutral indicator with little information content; it appears frequently in sideways markets where it says nothing about direction. Reversal interpretations often fail without confirmation from the next candle or other indicators.
Misconceptions: A doji does not by itself signal a reversal; it signals indecision, and the prevailing trend can just as easily continue. It is also not rare in the absolute sense on low-liquidity or very short timeframes.
Example: A stock rallies for a week, then prints a daily candle that opens at 50.10 and closes at 50.12 with a high of 51.00 and low of 49.20. Analysts read the doji as waning buying momentum and wait for a bearish confirmation candle before treating it as a reversal warning.
Citation: Investopedia, "Doji" — https://www.investopedia.com/terms/d/doji.asp (What Is a Doji?)
Citation: Wikipedia, "Candlestick pattern" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_pattern (Simple patterns)
Status: Reviewed

0640. Long-legged doji
Domain: Candlestick patterns
Definition: A doji variant with long upper and lower shadows and open and close at or near the same price, typically near the middle of the period's range. It is interpreted in technical analysis as strong two-sided pressure ending in a standoff, often read as a sign that the prior trend is losing conviction.
Intuition: Price was pushed far up and far down during the period, but neither side could hold its gains; the market ended exactly where it began after a wide-ranging battle.
Mechanics: Identified from OHLC data as a candle with a near-zero real body (open approximately equal to close) whose upper and lower shadows are both long relative to the body and typically to recent candles. No strict numerical threshold is canonical; charting packages apply their own body/range rules.
Relationships: Doji, Dragonfly doji, Gravestone doji, Spinning top
Failure modes: It only shows indecision, not direction; in choppy or low-volume markets long-legged dojis are common and meaningless. Treating it as a standalone reversal signal produces frequent false positives.
Misconceptions: It is not inherently bearish or bullish; its meaning depends entirely on the preceding trend and on confirmation from subsequent candles.
Example: After a two-week uptrend, a stock opens at 100, trades between 95 and 105, and closes at 100.05. The long-legged doji marks exhaustion of both sides; traders watch the next session to see which way the stalemate resolves.
Citation: Investopedia, "Doji" — https://www.investopedia.com/terms/d/doji.asp (What Is a Long-Legged Doji Candle?)
Citation: Wikipedia, "Candlestick pattern" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_pattern (Simple patterns)
Status: Reviewed

0641. Dragonfly doji
Domain: Candlestick patterns
Definition: A doji variant in which the open, high, and close are equal or nearly equal, leaving a long lower shadow and little or no upper shadow (a T shape). Technical analysts read it as intraperiod selling that was fully absorbed by buyers, and treat it as a possible bullish reversal sign when it appears after a decline; it is an interpretive framework, not a validated predictor.
Intuition: Sellers drove price sharply lower during the period, but buyers pushed it all the way back to the opening level, showing demand underneath the market.
Mechanics: From OHLC data: open, high, and close cluster at or near the same price (small tolerance), while the low sits far below, so the lower shadow dominates the range. It is the single-candle mirror of the gravestone doji.
Relationships: Doji, Gravestone doji, Long-legged doji, Hammer
Failure modes: Its reversal implication fails often in strong downtrends, where the bounce back to the open is only temporary short covering. In quiet markets it occurs frequently and carries no signal.
Misconceptions: A dragonfly doji is not automatically bullish; after an advance it can mark exhaustion instead. It requires confirmation from the following candle before it supports any directional hypothesis.
Example: In a downtrend, a stock opens at 40.00, falls to 37.50 intraday, then recovers to close at 40.00. The resulting dragonfly doji suggests sellers failed to hold the lows, and traders watch for a higher close the next day as confirmation.
Citation: Investopedia, "Doji" — https://www.investopedia.com/terms/d/doji.asp (What Is a Dragonfly Doji Candle?)
Citation: Wikipedia, "Candlestick pattern" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_pattern (Simple patterns)
Status: Reviewed

0642. Gravestone doji
Domain: Candlestick patterns
Definition: A doji variant in which the open, low, and close are equal or nearly equal, leaving a long upper shadow and little or no lower shadow (an inverted T). Technical analysts read it as intraperiod buying that was fully rejected by sellers, and treat it as a possible bearish reversal sign when it appears after an advance; it is an interpretive framework, not a validated predictor.
Intuition: Buyers drove price sharply higher during the period, but sellers forced it all the way back down to the opening level, showing supply sitting above the market.
Mechanics: From OHLC data: open, low, and close cluster at or near the same price (small tolerance), while the high sits far above, so the upper shadow dominates the range. It is the single-candle mirror of the dragonfly doji.
Relationships: Doji, Dragonfly doji, Long-legged doji, Shooting star
Failure modes: In strong uptrends the rejection is often temporary profit-taking and the trend resumes, so reversal readings fail. It is also common and meaningless in flat, low-volume sessions.
Misconceptions: A gravestone doji is not automatically a sell signal; after a decline it can instead mark seller exhaustion. It needs bearish confirmation from the next candle.
Example: After a rally, a stock opens at 60.00, spikes to 63.00, and is sold back down to close at 60.00. The gravestone doji shows the highs were rejected; traders look for a lower close the following session before acting on a bearish reading.
Citation: Investopedia, "Doji" — https://www.investopedia.com/terms/d/doji.asp (What Is a Gravestone Doji Candle?)
Citation: Wikipedia, "Candlestick pattern" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_pattern (Simple patterns)
Status: Reviewed

0643. Spinning top
Domain: Candlestick patterns
Definition: A single candlestick with a small real body vertically centered between upper and lower shadows that are both noticeably longer than the body. Like the doji, it is read as indecision between buyers and sellers and is treated in technical analysis as a possible sign of trend exhaustion when it follows an extended move; it is a hypothesis requiring confirmation, not a predictive law.
Intuition: Both bulls and bears pushed price around during the period, but neither could keep it anywhere; the close near the open shows the tug-of-war ended in a draw.
Mechanics: Identified from OHLC data: the real body |close - open| is small relative to the total range (larger than a doji's near-zero body; a common convention allows up to roughly 5% of the range before calling it a doji instead), with meaningful shadows on both sides. The close may be above or below the open.
Relationships: Doji, Long-legged doji, High wave
Failure modes: Spinning tops are extremely common, so most occurrences are inconsequential, especially within ranges. Even after extended trends, many spinning tops are followed by continuation rather than reversal.
Misconceptions: A spinning top does not predict a reversal on its own; the following candle must confirm. It is also not the same as a doji: its body is small but visible.
Example: After a long advance, a stock opens at 80.00, trades between 78.50 and 81.50, and closes at 80.20. The spinning top hints that buyers are losing control; a strong down candle the next day would confirm a reversal reading.
Citation: Investopedia, "Spinning Top Candlestick" — https://www.investopedia.com/terms/s/spinning-top.asp (What Does a Spinning Top Candlestick Tell You?)
Citation: Wikipedia, "Candlestick pattern" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_pattern (Simple patterns)
Status: Reviewed

0644. Marubozu
Domain: Candlestick patterns
Definition: A long-bodied candlestick with no (or almost no) shadows, so that the open and close coincide with the period's extreme prices: a white/green marubozu opens at the low and closes at the high, and a black/red marubozu opens at the high and closes at the low. It is read as one-sided dominance throughout the period and is usually interpreted as a continuation signal.
Intuition: One side controlled the entire session from the first trade to the last: buyers never let price dip below the open (bullish marubozu) or sellers never let it rise above the open (bearish marubozu).
Mechanics: From OHLC data: the real body spans essentially the full high-low range, with upper and lower shadows at or near zero. Partial variants exist: an opening marubozu lacks a shadow only at the open side, a closing marubozu only at the close side.
Relationships: Kicker pattern, Three white soldiers, Three black crows
Failure modes: A single marubozu late in an extended move can mark exhaustion (a climactic final push) rather than continuation. On very short timeframes or illiquid instruments, shadowless candles occur routinely and carry little information.
Misconceptions: It is not a guarantee the trend continues; context matters, and a marubozu into strong resistance or support often precedes a pullback rather than immediate follow-through.
Example: A stock opens at 25.00, its session low, and grinds upward all day to close at 26.40, its session high. This white marubozu shows uninterrupted buying pressure and is read as supporting continuation of the advance.
Citation: Wikipedia, "Candlestick pattern" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_pattern (Simple patterns)
Status: Reviewed

0645. Hammer
Domain: Candlestick patterns
Definition: A single candlestick with a small real body near the top of the period's range, a long lower shadow (conventionally at least twice the body length), and little or no upper shadow, appearing after a downtrend. Technical analysts interpret it as a potential bullish reversal signal because sellers drove price down but buyers recovered nearly all of the loss; it is a hypothesis that requires confirmation.
Intuition: Sellers smashed price down during the period, but buyers hammered it back up to close near the open, showing the decline was rejected.
Mechanics: From OHLC data: the lower shadow (min(O, C) - L) is at least about twice the real body |C - O|, the upper shadow (H - max(O, C)) is very small, and the body sits near the high. The identical shape after an uptrend is called a hanging man; trend context, not shape, distinguishes them.
Formula: Hammer heuristic: (min(O, C) - L) >= 2 * |C - O| and (H - max(O, C)) <= |C - O|, after a downtrend.
Relationships: Hanging man, Inverted hammer, Shooting star, Pin bar, Dragonfly doji
Failure modes: In a strong downtrend a hammer is often just a pause before further declines, so unconfirmed long entries fail frequently. Its reliability also drops on low volume or away from support levels.
Misconceptions: The body color is not decisive (a green close is modestly stronger, but a red hammer is still a hammer), and the shape alone is not the pattern: without a preceding downtrend it is not a hammer.
Example: After a month-long slide, a stock opens at 30.00, falls to 27.50, then rallies to close at 29.90. The next day a strong white candle closes above 30.50, confirming the hammer and prompting reversal-focused traders to go long with a stop below 27.50.
Citation: Investopedia, "Hammer Candlestick" — https://www.investopedia.com/terms/h/hammer.asp (Understanding Hammer Candlesticks)
Citation: Wikipedia, "Candlestick pattern" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_pattern (Simple patterns)
Status: Reviewed

0646. Hanging man
Domain: Candlestick patterns
Definition: A single candlestick with a small real body near the top of the range, a long lower shadow (conventionally two or more times the body), and little or no upper shadow, appearing after an uptrend. It has the same shape as a hammer; technical analysts read it as a potential bearish reversal warning because the deep intraperiod selloff revealed latent selling pressure, though the reading requires bearish confirmation.
Intuition: Price was dumped hard during the session and only partly recovered; the fact that sellers could push it that low at all, after a long rise, is taken as a crack in the uptrend.
Mechanics: From OHLC data: identical geometry to the hammer (small body near the high, lower shadow >= ~2x body, minimal upper shadow); the distinguishing feature is context, since it must follow an advance. Confirmation is typically a lower close on the following candle.
Relationships: Hammer, Shooting star, Inverted hammer
Failure modes: The recovery to near the open shows buyers are still active, so many hanging men are followed by further gains; acting short without confirmation has a high failure rate. In strong trends it repeatedly fails as a topping signal.
Misconceptions: The shape alone does not make a hanging man: the same candle after a decline is a hammer, a bullish sign. Nor is a hanging man an immediate sell signal; it is a warning that needs a confirming down candle.
Example: After a steady six-week climb, a stock opens at 70.00, plunges to 66.00 intraday, and closes at 69.80. Chartists flag the hanging man and wait; a close below 68.50 the next day would confirm the bearish reading.
Citation: Wikipedia, "Candlestick pattern" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_pattern (Simple patterns)
Status: Reviewed

0647. Inverted hammer
Domain: Candlestick patterns
Definition: A single candlestick with a small real body near the bottom of the range, a long upper shadow, and little or no lower shadow, appearing after a downtrend. Technical analysts interpret it as a potential bullish reversal signal: buyers mounted an intraperiod rally that sellers could not fully erase, hinting that demand is emerging; confirmation by a higher close next period is normally required.
Intuition: In a falling market, buyers finally staged a real push upward during the session; even though it was sold back toward the open, the attempt shows bulls are waking up.
Mechanics: From OHLC data: the upper shadow (H - max(O, C)) is at least about twice the real body |C - O|, the lower shadow (min(O, C) - L) is very small, and the body sits near the low, after a preceding decline. The same shape after an uptrend is a shooting star.
Relationships: Hammer, Shooting star, Hanging man
Failure modes: Because it closes near its low, the inverted hammer by itself still shows sellers winning the session, and downtrends often continue. Without bullish confirmation it is one of the weaker single-candle reversal candidates.
Misconceptions: It is not a shooting star: the two have identical geometry but opposite context and meaning. And it is not a buy signal on its own; the standard use requires the next candle to close higher.
Example: In a downtrend, a stock opens at 15.00, spikes to 16.20, and settles back to close at 15.05. A close above 15.50 the next session would be taken as confirmation that the inverted hammer marked a bottoming attempt.
Citation: Wikipedia, "Candlestick pattern" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_pattern (Simple patterns)
Status: Reviewed

0648. Shooting star
Domain: Candlestick patterns
Definition: A single candlestick with a small real body near the bottom of the range, a long upper shadow, and little or no lower shadow, appearing after an uptrend. Technical analysts read it as a potential bearish reversal signal: buyers drove price sharply higher intraperiod but sellers forced it back near the open, showing the rally was rejected; it is a hypothesis that needs confirmation.
Intuition: The market shot up during the session but fell back to earth before the close, leaving a long tail that shows buyers could not hold the highs.
Mechanics: From OHLC data: the upper shadow is at least about twice the real body, the lower shadow is minimal, and the body sits near the period's low, after a preceding advance. Its geometry is identical to the inverted hammer; the uptrend context is what makes it a shooting star.
Relationships: Inverted hammer, Hanging man, Gravestone doji
Failure modes: In strong bull trends shooting stars frequently mark only brief pauses before new highs. A close near the high of the next candle negates the pattern entirely.
Misconceptions: A shooting star is not confirmed bearish until the next candle closes lower; the pattern alone shows rejection, not a completed reversal. It also cannot exist without a preceding uptrend.
Example: After a two-week rally, a stock opens at 90.00, surges to 94.00, and closes at 90.20. Traders flag the shooting star and treat a close below 89.00 the next day as confirmation of a downside reversal.
Citation: Wikipedia, "Candlestick pattern" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_pattern (Simple patterns)
Status: Reviewed

0649. Bullish engulfing
Domain: Candlestick patterns
Definition: A two-candlestick pattern in which a small black (down) body is followed by a larger white (up) body whose real body completely contains the prior real body, appearing after a downtrend. Technical analysts treat it as a potential major bottom reversal signal because buyers overwhelmed the prior session's entire price range; it is an interpretive framework, not a proven predictor.
Intuition: After a falling session, buyers arrived with enough force to open lower and close above where the previous session opened, swallowing the sellers' progress whole.
Mechanics: From OHLC data: C1 < O1 (down candle), then O2 < C1 and C2 > O1, so the second real body engulfs the first. Engulfing is defined on bodies, not shadows (when the full high-low range is engulfed it is an outside bar). Confirmation is sought in follow-through buying on the next candle.
Formula: Bullish engulfing when C1 < O1, C2 > O2, O2 <= C1, C2 >= O1 (bodies strictly compared per convention).
Relationships: Bearish engulfing, Three outside up, Outside bar, Piercing line, Bullish harami
Failure modes: In persistent downtrends many bullish engulfing patterns mark only one-day short-covering bounces before new lows. Signals formed in choppy, range-bound markets are especially unreliable.
Misconceptions: The shadows do not need to be engulfed; only the real bodies matter for the classic definition. It is also not a standalone buy signal; practitioners typically demand confirmation or confluence with support.
Example: A stock in a downtrend closes at 48.00 after opening at 49.00; the next day it opens at 47.50 and closes at 49.50. The white body engulfs the prior black body, and traders watch for follow-through above 49.50 as confirmation.
Citation: Wikipedia, "Candlestick pattern" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_pattern (Complex patterns)
Status: Reviewed

0650. Bearish engulfing
Domain: Candlestick patterns
Definition: A two-candlestick pattern in which a small white (up) body is followed by a larger black (down) body whose real body completely contains the prior real body, appearing after an uptrend. Technical analysts treat it as a potential major top reversal signal because sellers overwhelmed the prior session's entire price range; it is an interpretive framework, not a proven predictor.
Intuition: After a rising session, sellers hit the market hard enough to open higher and close below where the previous session opened, erasing the buyers' progress in one move.
Mechanics: From OHLC data: C1 > O1 (up candle), then O2 > C1 and C2 < O1, so the second real body engulfs the first. Only the bodies must overlap; shadow containment is not required. Follow-through weakness on the next candle is used as confirmation.
Formula: Bearish engulfing when C1 > O1, C2 < O2, O2 >= C1, C2 <= O1 (bodies strictly compared per convention).
Relationships: Bullish engulfing, Three outside down, Outside bar, Dark cloud cover, Bearish harami
Failure modes: In strong bull markets bearish engulfing patterns often mark one-day profit-taking before the advance resumes. They are also common noise in sideways ranges where neither direction follows through.
Misconceptions: The pattern does not require the second candle's shadows to engulf the first candle's range. And it is not an automatic short signal; context (resistance, volume, prior trend maturity) and confirmation matter.
Example: A stock in an uptrend closes at 55.00 after opening at 54.00; the next day it opens at 55.50 and closes at 53.50. The black body engulfs the prior white body, and a lower close the following day would confirm the bearish reading.
Citation: Wikipedia, "Candlestick pattern" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_pattern (Complex patterns)
Status: Reviewed

0651. Piercing line
Domain: Candlestick patterns
Definition: A two-candlestick pattern in a downtrend: a long black candle is followed by a white candle that opens below the prior low (ideally with a gap) and closes more than halfway up into the prior black body. Technical analysts read it as a potential bottom reversal signal, a weaker cousin of the bullish engulfing pattern.
Intuition: Sellers gapped the market down at the open, but buyers drove price back up through more than half of the previous session's losses, piercing deep into their territory.
Mechanics: From OHLC data: candle 1 is a long black body; candle 2 opens at or below L1 and closes above the midpoint (O1 + C1) / 2 of the first body but below O1 (otherwise it would be a bullish engulfing). The deeper the close into the first body, the stronger the conventional reading.
Formula: Piercing line when C1 < O1, O2 <= L1, and (O1 + C1)/2 < C2 < O1.
Relationships: Dark cloud cover, Bullish engulfing, Bullish harami
Failure modes: A close that only just passes the midpoint is weak and often fails, especially in strong downtrends. On 24-hour markets like forex where gaps are rare, the opening-gap requirement is often relaxed, which dilutes the pattern.
Misconceptions: Closing above the prior candle's high or open turns it into an engulfing pattern, not a piercing line; the close must stop within the first body. It is also not a confirmed reversal without follow-through.
Example: A stock falls, printing a candle from 44.00 open to 42.00 close (low 41.80). The next day opens at 41.50 and closes at 43.50, above the 43.00 midpoint of the prior body: a piercing line that bulls read as a bottoming attempt.
Citation: Wikipedia, "Candlestick pattern" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_pattern (Complex patterns)
Status: Reviewed

0652. Dark cloud cover
Domain: Candlestick patterns
Definition: A two-candlestick pattern in an uptrend: a long white candle is followed by a black candle that opens above the prior high (ideally with a gap) and closes more than halfway down into the prior white body. Technical analysts read it as a potential top reversal signal, the bearish mirror of the piercing line and a weaker cousin of the bearish engulfing pattern.
Intuition: Buyers gapped the market up at the open, but sellers dragged price back down through more than half of the previous session's gains, casting a dark cloud over the rally.
Mechanics: From OHLC data: candle 1 is a long white body; candle 2 opens at or above H1 and closes below the midpoint (O1 + C1) / 2 of the first body but above O1 (otherwise it would be a bearish engulfing). Deeper penetration of the first body strengthens the conventional bearish reading.
Formula: Dark cloud cover when C1 > O1, O2 >= H1, and O1 < C2 < (O1 + C1)/2.
Relationships: Piercing line, Bearish engulfing, Bearish harami
Failure modes: Shallow penetration (barely past the midpoint) frequently fails, particularly in strong uptrends where the dip is bought. In gapless 24-hour markets the opening-gap condition is usually relaxed, weakening selectivity.
Misconceptions: If the second candle closes below the first candle's open, the pattern is a bearish engulfing, not dark cloud cover. The name refers only to the partial-penetration configuration, and confirmation is still required.
Example: A stock rises, printing a candle from 60.00 open to 62.00 close (high 62.20). The next day opens at 62.50 and closes at 60.50, below the 61.00 midpoint of the prior body: dark cloud cover, read as a warning of an impending top.
Citation: Wikipedia, "Candlestick pattern" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_pattern (Complex patterns)
Status: Reviewed

0653. Morning star
Domain: Candlestick patterns
Definition: A three-candlestick bottom reversal pattern: a long black body is followed by a small-bodied candle (the star, of either color) that gaps below the first body, and then a long white body that closes well into the first candle's real body. Technical analysts treat it as a major bottom reversal signal marking a shift from selling to indecision to buying.
Intuition: Sellers push hard, then the market stalls in a small indecisive candle, then buyers take over and recover most of the lost ground, like dawn after a dark night.
Mechanics: From OHLC data: candle 1 is a long black body in a downtrend; candle 2 has a small real body (ideally gapping below body 1); candle 3 is a long white body closing above the midpoint of body 1. The gap between bodies 1 and 2 (and ideally between 2 and 3) is the classic requirement, often relaxed in gap-poor markets.
Relationships: Evening star, Morning doji star, Abandoned baby, Bullish engulfing
Failure modes: In gapless markets (spot forex, crypto) the pattern is frequently identified without true gaps, which weakens it. A weak third candle that fails to close deep into the first body often precedes renewed decline.
Misconceptions: The star need not be a doji; any small body qualifies (when it is a doji the pattern is specifically a morning doji star). The pattern is also not complete, and not actionable by convention, until the third candle closes.
Example: A stock slides, printing a long black candle (52.00 to 50.00), then a tiny-bodied candle around 49.60-49.80, then a long white candle closing at 51.50, deep into the first body. Chartists read the morning star as a bottom reversal signal.
Citation: Wikipedia, "Candlestick pattern" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_pattern (Complex patterns)
Status: Reviewed

0654. Evening star
Domain: Candlestick patterns
Definition: A three-candlestick top reversal pattern: a long white body is followed by a small-bodied candle (the star, of either color) that gaps above the first body, and then a long black body that closes well into the first candle's real body. Technical analysts treat it as a major top reversal signal marking a shift from buying to indecision to selling; it is the bearish mirror of the morning star.
Intuition: Buyers push hard, then the market stalls in a small indecisive candle near the highs, then sellers seize control and erase much of the advance, like nightfall after a bright day.
Mechanics: From OHLC data: candle 1 is a long white body in an uptrend; candle 2 has a small real body (ideally gapping above body 1); candle 3 is a long black body closing below the midpoint of body 1. Classic definitions want gaps around the star; these are commonly relaxed in gap-poor markets.
Relationships: Morning star, Evening doji star, Abandoned baby, Bearish engulfing
Failure modes: In strong bull trends the third candle's dip is often bought, and the uptrend resumes. In 24-hour markets without gaps, loosely matched 'evening stars' generate many false tops.
Misconceptions: The star candle can be either color and need not be a doji (a doji star makes it an evening doji star). The signal is only conventionally valid once the third candle has closed deep into the first body.
Example: A stock climbs, printing a long white candle (70.00 to 72.00), then a tiny-bodied candle around 72.30-72.50, then a long black candle closing at 70.50. The evening star is read as a top reversal warning.
Citation: Wikipedia, "Candlestick pattern" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_pattern (Complex patterns)
Status: Reviewed

0655. Morning doji star
Domain: Candlestick patterns
Definition: A three-candlestick bottom reversal pattern: a long black body is followed by a doji that gaps below it (the doji star), and then a long white body that closes well into the first candle's real body. It is the morning star with a doji as the middle candle, conventionally regarded as a stronger reversal signal because the doji marks a more complete stall in selling.
Intuition: After heavy selling, the market opens lower but goes absolutely nowhere (a doji), then buyers storm back and reclaim most of the decline; the dead-flat middle candle shows sellers are spent.
Mechanics: From OHLC data: candle 1 is a long black body in a downtrend; candle 2 is a doji whose body (and classically whose range) sits below body 1; candle 3 is a long white body closing above the midpoint of body 1. When the doji also gaps away from both neighbors' shadows, the pattern becomes the rarer bullish abandoned baby.
Relationships: Morning star, Evening doji star, Doji, Abandoned baby
Failure modes: True gap-separated doji stars are rare in 24-hour markets, so relaxed versions are common and less reliable. Even textbook instances fail when the broader downtrend is powerful and the third candle lacks volume.
Misconceptions: It is not interchangeable with the plain morning star; the middle candle must be a doji. It is also distinct from the bullish abandoned baby, which additionally requires the doji's shadows to gap clear of both neighbors.
Example: A stock falls with a long black candle (35.00 to 33.00), then prints a doji near 32.60 after gapping down, then rallies on a long white candle closing at 34.50. The morning doji star is read as a strong bottom reversal signal.
Citation: Wikipedia, "Candlestick pattern" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_pattern (Complex patterns)
Status: Reviewed

0656. Evening doji star
Domain: Candlestick patterns
Definition: A three-candlestick top reversal pattern: a long white body is followed by a doji that gaps above it (the doji star), and then a long black body that closes well into the first candle's real body. It is the evening star with a doji as the middle candle, conventionally regarded as a stronger bearish signal because the doji marks a more complete stall in buying.
Intuition: After heavy buying, the market gaps up but freezes dead flat (a doji), then sellers drive price deep back into the prior gains; the motionless middle candle shows buyers are exhausted.
Mechanics: From OHLC data: candle 1 is a long white body in an uptrend; candle 2 is a doji whose body (and classically whose range) sits above body 1; candle 3 is a long black body closing below the midpoint of body 1. When the doji's shadows also gap clear of both neighbors, the pattern becomes the rarer bearish abandoned baby.
Relationships: Evening star, Morning doji star, Doji, Abandoned baby
Failure modes: Strict gap requirements make genuine instances rare in forex and crypto, and relaxed matches are much less reliable. Strong uptrends often shrug off the pattern after one down candle.
Misconceptions: It is not the same as a plain evening star; the star must be a doji. Nor is it a bearish abandoned baby, which additionally requires the doji's full shadow range to be separated by gaps from both neighbors.
Example: A stock rallies with a long white candle (80.00 to 83.00), gaps up into a doji near 83.40, then prints a long black candle closing at 80.80. The evening doji star is read as a strong top reversal signal.
Citation: Wikipedia, "Candlestick pattern" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_pattern (Complex patterns)
Status: Reviewed

0657. Three white soldiers
Domain: Candlestick patterns
Definition: A three-candlestick bottom reversal pattern consisting of three consecutive long white candles with progressively higher closes, each closing at or near its high and each opening within the prior candle's real body. Technical analysts read it as steady, sustained buying marking a bottom after a decline; it is an interpretive framework, not a validated predictor.
Intuition: Three sessions in a row of determined buying, each marching higher and finishing near its highs, suggests the market has been taken over by confident bulls rather than one-day short covering.
Mechanics: From OHLC data: three long white bodies with C1 < C2 < C3; each candle opens within the previous body (no big gaps) and closes near its high (small upper shadows). Appearing after a downtrend or at support, the pattern's steady structure is meant to distinguish genuine accumulation from a spike.
Relationships: Three black crows, Rising three methods, Marubozu
Failure modes: After three strong up candles the market is often short-term overbought, so the pattern frequently completes right before a pullback; late entry is a common way it 'fails'. Very large first or third candles can also signal exhaustion rather than sustained demand.
Misconceptions: It is not a signal to chase price higher indefinitely; many practitioners use it to time entries on the ensuing retracement rather than buying the third candle's close. Gapped, non-overlapping opens do not form the classic pattern.
Example: After a slide to 45.00, a stock prints three consecutive daily candles closing at 46.20, 47.40, and 48.60, each opening inside the prior body and closing near its high. Chartists read the three white soldiers as evidence of a durable bottom.
Citation: Wikipedia, "Candlestick pattern" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_pattern (Complex patterns)
Status: Reviewed

0658. Three black crows
Domain: Candlestick patterns
Definition: A three-candlestick top reversal pattern consisting of three consecutive long black candles with progressively lower closes, each closing at or near its low and each opening within the prior candle's real body. Technical analysts read it as steady, sustained selling marking a top after an advance; it is the bearish mirror of three white soldiers.
Intuition: Three sessions in a row of relentless selling, each closing near its lows and stepping lower, suggests determined distribution rather than a single day of profit-taking.
Mechanics: From OHLC data: three long black bodies with C1 > C2 > C3; each candle opens within the previous body and closes near its low (small lower shadows). Appearing after an uptrend or at resistance, the stepped structure is meant to distinguish sustained selling from a one-day flush.
Relationships: Three white soldiers, Falling three methods, Marubozu
Failure modes: After three strong down candles the market is often short-term oversold and due for a bounce, so the pattern frequently completes just before a rebound. Shallow or gapped candles that do not meet the stepped structure are weaker and fail more often.
Misconceptions: It is not a signal to short aggressively after completion; the move it 'predicts' has often already happened, so practitioners typically wait for a pullback to enter. Candles with long lower shadows (buying support) do not form a textbook three black crows.
Example: After a rally to 95.00, a stock prints three consecutive daily candles closing at 93.50, 92.00, and 90.50, each opening inside the prior body and closing near its low. The three black crows are read as evidence of a durable top.
Citation: Wikipedia, "Candlestick pattern" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_pattern (Complex patterns)
Status: Reviewed

0659. Harami
Domain: Candlestick patterns
Definition: A two-candlestick pattern in which a small real body is completely contained within the prior session's large real body (the reverse of an engulfing pattern); 'harami' is Japanese for 'pregnant'. Read generically, it marks a sudden loss of momentum in the prevailing trend and is treated in technical analysis as a potential reversal warning, directional (bullish or bearish) according to the trend it interrupts.
Intuition: After a big, confident candle, the market suddenly shrinks to a small candle that fits entirely inside the prior body, as if the trend caught its breath and participants hesitated.
Mechanics: From OHLC data: candle 1 has a large real body; candle 2's open and close both fall strictly inside candle 1's open-close range. Bullish harami: large black body then small body after a decline. Bearish harami: large white body then small body after an advance. If candle 2 is a doji, the pattern is a harami cross.
Formula: Harami when min(O2, C2) > min(O1, C1) and max(O2, C2) < max(O1, C1), with body 1 large relative to recent candles.
Relationships: Bullish harami, Bearish harami, Harami cross, Bullish engulfing, Inside bar, Three inside up
Failure modes: Harami are frequent and low-powered: many are followed by trend continuation, making them one of the weaker reversal families without confirmation. In tight ranges they occur constantly and mean little.
Misconceptions: A harami compares real bodies, not full ranges; a small candle inside the prior candle's full high-low range but not inside its body is an inside bar, a related but distinct concept. It is also a warning of stalling momentum, not a confirmed reversal.
Example: In an uptrend, a stock prints a long white candle (50.00 to 53.00), then a small candle that opens at 52.20 and closes at 51.80, entirely inside the prior body. The harami warns that upside momentum has stalled pending the next candle's direction.
Citation: Wikipedia, "Candlestick pattern" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_pattern (Complex patterns)
Status: Reviewed

0660. Bullish harami
Domain: Candlestick patterns
Definition: A two-candlestick pattern appearing after a downtrend: an unusually large black body is followed by a small white body contained entirely within it. Technical analysts read it as a potential bullish reversal sign, interpreting the sudden contraction of range as selling pressure drying up; confirmation from subsequent candles is normally required.
Intuition: After a big down day, the market can only manage a tiny up day hidden inside the prior body, suggesting sellers have run out of ammunition and buyers are quietly testing the water.
Mechanics: From OHLC data: candle 1 is a long black body; candle 2 is a small white body with both open and close inside body 1's open-close range. The smaller the second body relative to the first, the more pronounced the conventional signal; a doji second candle makes it a (bullish) harami cross.
Relationships: Harami, Bearish harami, Harami cross, Three inside up, Bullish engulfing
Failure modes: As a mild two-candle formation it fails often in strong downtrends, where the small candle is merely a pause before new lows. CandleScanner-style statistics show only moderate predictive efficiency even with confirmation.
Misconceptions: It is not a strong standalone buy signal; practitioners treat it as a warning and typically require the market to break above the first candle's body. The second candle's shadows may protrude beyond body 1; only the body must be contained.
Example: In a downtrend, a stock prints a long black candle (40.00 to 37.00), then a small white candle opening at 37.50 and closing at 38.20. A close above 40.00 within the next sessions would confirm the bullish harami as a three inside up.
Citation: Wikipedia, "Candlestick pattern" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_pattern (Complex patterns)
Status: Reviewed

0661. Bearish harami
Domain: Candlestick patterns
Definition: A two-candlestick pattern appearing after an uptrend: an unusually large white body is followed by a small black body contained entirely within it. Technical analysts read it as a potential bearish reversal sign, interpreting the sudden contraction of range as buying pressure drying up; it is the bearish mirror of the bullish harami and requires confirmation.
Intuition: After a big up day, the market stalls into a tiny down day nested inside the prior body, suggesting the rally's energy is spent and sellers are probing.
Mechanics: From OHLC data: candle 1 is a long white body; candle 2 is a small black body with both open and close inside body 1's open-close range. A doji second candle turns it into a (bearish) harami cross; a third candle closing below body 1 converts it into the three inside down confirmation pattern.
Relationships: Harami, Bullish harami, Harami cross, Three inside down, Bearish engulfing
Failure modes: In persistent uptrends the small contained candle is usually just consolidation, and the trend resumes higher. Its low standalone reliability means unconfirmed bearish harami shorts fail frequently.
Misconceptions: It is not a confirmed top; the conventional use waits for price to break below the first candle's body. Only the second candle's body must be contained, not its shadows.
Example: In an uptrend, a stock prints a long white candle (65.00 to 68.00), then a small black candle opening at 67.60 and closing at 67.10. Bears treat a subsequent close below 65.00 (a three inside down) as confirmation of the reversal warning.
Citation: Wikipedia, "Candlestick pattern" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_pattern (Complex patterns)
Status: Reviewed

0662. Harami cross
Domain: Candlestick patterns
Definition: A two-candlestick pattern in which a large real body is followed by a doji contained entirely within that body, forming a harami whose second candle is a doji. Technical analysts regard it as a more potent reversal warning than a plain harami because the doji shows the trend's momentum has stalled into outright indecision; it is bullish after declines and bearish after advances.
Intuition: A big confident candle is followed by a session that goes absolutely nowhere and hides inside the prior body, suggesting the driving force behind the trend has abruptly evaporated.
Mechanics: From OHLC data: candle 1 has a large body; candle 2 is a doji (open approximately equal to close) whose body lies inside body 1. Bullish harami cross: large black body then doji after a downtrend. Bearish harami cross: large white body then doji after an uptrend. Confirmation comes from the next candle's direction.
Relationships: Harami, Bullish harami, Bearish harami, Doji, Morning doji star
Failure modes: Doji are common, so harami crosses appear often in directionless markets where they carry no reversal information. Even after trends, many instances resolve as continuation once the indecision breaks the prior way.
Misconceptions: It is not the same as a doji star (morning/evening doji star): there the doji gaps away from the first body, while here it sits inside it. The second candle must be a true near-zero-body doji, not merely a small candle.
Example: After a decline, a stock prints a long black candle (30.00 to 27.00), then a doji opening at 28.10 and closing at 28.12, inside the prior body. The bullish harami cross warns of a possible bottom, pending an up close the next session.
Citation: Wikipedia, "Candlestick pattern" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_pattern (Complex patterns)
Status: Reviewed

0663. Tweezer top
Domain: Candlestick patterns
Definition: A pattern of two or more candlesticks whose highs match (or nearly match), forming an even 'tweezer' line at a price ceiling, typically appearing in an uptrend. Technical analysts read the repeated rejection of the same high as a minor bearish reversal signal, which gains weight when the candles themselves form other reversal shapes.
Intuition: The market probed the exact same ceiling twice and failed both times, as if pinched by tweezers at that price, suggesting sellers are defending that level.
Mechanics: From OHLC data: two or more candles (consecutive or separated) share essentially equal highs; the first is typically a white candle and the second a black candle in the classic uptrend form. The matching highs define an ad-hoc resistance level whose subsequent break invalidates the bearish reading.
Relationships: Tweezer bottom, Shooting star, Hanging man, Bearish engulfing
Failure modes: Matching highs occur constantly by chance, so isolated tweezer tops have low standalone significance. In strong uptrends the double test often precedes a breakout rather than a reversal.
Misconceptions: The candles do not have to be adjacent, and their bodies can be any size; what matters is the matching highs. It is a minor signal on its own, not a major reversal pattern like an evening star.
Example: A stock rallies and prints a white candle with a high of 77.00, then the next session trades up to 77.00 again but closes lower as a black candle. The tweezer top marks 77.00 as resistance and warns of a possible pullback.
Citation: Wikipedia, "Candlestick pattern" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_pattern (Complex patterns)
Status: Reviewed

0664. Tweezer bottom
Domain: Candlestick patterns
Definition: A pattern of two or more candlesticks whose lows match (or nearly match), forming an even 'tweezer' line at a price floor, typically appearing in a downtrend. Technical analysts read the repeated rejection of the same low as a minor bullish reversal signal, the mirror of the tweezer top, which gains weight when combined with other reversal shapes.
Intuition: The market probed the exact same floor twice and held both times, as if supported by tweezers at that price, suggesting buyers are defending that level.
Mechanics: From OHLC data: two or more candles (consecutive or separated) share essentially equal lows; the first is typically a black candle and the second a white candle in the classic downtrend form. The matching lows define an ad-hoc support level whose break invalidates the bullish reading.
Relationships: Tweezer top, Hammer, Bullish engulfing, Piercing line
Failure modes: Matching lows are common by coincidence, so isolated tweezer bottoms carry little weight. In strong downtrends the double bottom at the lows often gives way to further declines.
Misconceptions: The candles need not be adjacent or similar in size; only the lows must match. It is a minor confirmation-level signal, not a major standalone reversal pattern.
Example: A stock falls and prints a black candle with a low of 22.00, then the next session dips to 22.00 again before closing higher as a white candle. The tweezer bottom marks 22.00 as support and hints at a possible bounce.
Citation: Wikipedia, "Candlestick pattern" — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Candlestick_pattern (Complex patterns)
Status: Reviewed

0665. Three inside up
Domain: Candlestick patterns
Definition: A three-candlestick bullish reversal pattern introduced by Gregory Morris as a confirmed bullish harami: a long black body in a downtrend is followed by a small white body contained within it (the harami), and then a third candle closing above the second candle's close. The third candle's higher close is the confirmation that distinguishes it from the unconfirmed two-candle harami.
Intuition: First the trend's selling stalls inside the prior big candle, then the next candle actually closes higher, confirming that buyers, not sellers, won the standoff.
