Example: A stock drops in three accelerating legs from $60 to $22, each bounce weaker, tracing a downward curve through the rally highs; when price finally closes back above the curve at $26 on heavy volume, the capitulation-reversal reading is triggered.
Citation: HowToTrade: How To Trade The Parabolic Pattern — https://howtotrade.com/chart-patterns/parabolic-pattern/ (What is the Parabolic pattern; Bullish or Bearish)
Status: Reviewed

0701. Island reversal
Domain: Chart patterns
Definition: A classical reversal pattern in which a cluster of one or more trading sessions is isolated from the surrounding price action by a gap on each side — typically an exhaustion gap into the cluster and a breakaway gap out of it in the opposite direction. The stranded 'island' marks an abrupt sentiment flip, with island tops (bearish) more common than island bottoms. It is a technical-analysis hypothesis, not a proven predictive law.
Intuition: Price leaps one way, trades in a brief frenzy, then leaps back the other way, leaving the late entrants marooned on an island of prices the market immediately abandoned.
Mechanics: Require a lengthy prior trend, an initial gap (often exhaustion), a compact cluster of sessions trading in a definable range on increased volume, and a final gap in the opposite direction that leaves the cluster isolated. The two gaps are expected not to be filled for some time; the pattern is actionable once the second gap appears. No standard measured target exists.
Relationships: Breakaway gap, Exhaustion gap, Double top, Head and shoulders, Volume confirmation
Failure modes: True islands are rare, and researchers note the pattern often yields poor performance results; many apparent islands get their second gap filled within days, voiding the isolation. In thin or illiquid markets, routine overnight gaps manufacture meaningless 'islands' constantly.
Misconceptions: That all gaps eventually fill quickly — the island reversal is premised on the two flanking gaps staying open; also that a single-day island is required, whereas clusters can span days to weeks.
Example: After a long rally a stock gaps up from $48 to $52, churns between $51 and $53 for five days on heavy volume, then gaps down to $47.50 — stranding the $51–$53 cluster as an island top that precedes a decline.
Citation: Investopedia: Island Reversal — https://www.investopedia.com/terms/i/islandreversal.asp (How to Identify an Island Reversal Pattern)
Citation: Wikipedia: Chart pattern — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chart_pattern (Technical analysis navbox (patterns list))
Status: Reviewed

0702. Simple moving average
Domain: Indicators
Definition: The unweighted arithmetic mean of the last n observations (usually closing prices), recomputed each period as the window slides forward; the most basic trend-following overlay.
Intuition: A rolling average that smooths day-to-day noise so the underlying trend is easier to see. Every observation in the window counts equally.
Mechanics: Sum the last n prices and divide by n; each new bar drops the oldest point and adds the newest, so the average moves through time. Used to define trend direction, support/resistance zones, and as a building block for other indicators such as Bollinger Bands and MACD.
Formula: SMA(n) = (P_1 + P_2 + ... + P_n) / n, where P_i are the last n prices (usually closes) and n is the window length.
Relationships: Exponential moving average, Weighted moving average, Moving average crossover, Bollinger Bands, Golden cross
Failure modes: It is a lagging, trend-following measure: the longer the window the greater the lag, and in sideways, trendless markets price crosses it repeatedly, producing whipsaws.
Misconceptions: A moving average does not predict future prices; it defines the current trend from past data. Nor is any single length (e.g. the 200-day) inherently significant beyond convention and self-reinforcing usage.
Example: Closes of 11, 12, 13, 14, 15 give a 5-day SMA of 13; when the next close is 16, the SMA becomes (12+13+14+15+16)/5 = 14.
Citation: Moving Averages - Simple and Exponential | ChartSchool | StockCharts.com — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/technical-indicators-and-overlays/technical-overlays/moving-averages-simple-and-exponential (Simple Moving Average Formulas)
Status: Reviewed

0703. Exponential moving average
Domain: Indicators
Definition: A recursively computed moving average whose weights decay geometrically with age, giving recent observations more influence and reducing lag relative to a same-length simple moving average.
Intuition: Like a simple average, but today's price counts more than last week's, so it reacts faster to new information.
Mechanics: EMA_t = k*P_t + (1-k)*EMA_{t-1} with k = 2/(n+1), seeded with an SMA. Because each value depends on all previous values, a long history (hundreds of bars) is needed for the series to converge to accurate values.
Formula: EMA_t = k * P_t + (1 - k) * EMA_{t-1}; k = 2/(n+1); P_t = current price; n = period.
Relationships: Simple moving average, MACD line, Double exponential moving average, Smoothed moving average
Failure modes: Still a lagging trend-follower: less lag than an SMA means more sensitivity to noise, so it whipsaws sooner and more often in trading ranges.
Misconceptions: An EMA is not inherently better than an SMA — it trades lag for noise sensitivity. Also, early EMA values depend on the seed, so short data histories yield inaccurate values.
Example: A 10-day EMA applies an 18.18% weight (2/11) to the latest close; a 20-day EMA applies 9.52% (2/21).
Citation: Moving Averages - Simple and Exponential | ChartSchool | StockCharts.com — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/technical-indicators-and-overlays/technical-overlays/moving-averages-simple-and-exponential (Exponential Moving Average Formulas)
Status: Reviewed

0704. Weighted moving average
Domain: Indicators
Definition: A moving average that weights observations linearly by recency — the newest price gets weight n, the next n-1, down to 1 — so recent data dominates while the window length stays fixed.
Intuition: A compromise between the SMA and EMA: recent prices matter more, but the weights decline in a straight line rather than exponentially.
Mechanics: Multiply each of the last n prices by its recency rank, sum the products, and divide by the sum of the weights n(n+1)/2. Recomputed fresh each bar; not recursive.
Formula: WMA(n) = sum(i * P_i, i=1..n) / sum(i, i=1..n), with P_n the most recent price; the denominator equals n(n+1)/2.
Relationships: Simple moving average, Exponential moving average, Hull moving average, Triangular moving average
Failure modes: Lags like all averages and whipsaws in ranges; the abrupt weight cutoff at the window edge makes it twitchy when a large old value exits the window.
Misconceptions: A WMA is not an EMA: WMA weights decline linearly over a fixed window, whereas EMA weights decay exponentially over an effectively infinite history.
Example: With closes 10, 11, 12, the 3-period WMA = (1*10 + 2*11 + 3*12)/6 = 68/6 = 11.33, versus an SMA of 11.
Source authority: Authoritative domain source / exact citation pending
Status: Provisional

0705. Smoothed moving average
Domain: Indicators
Definition: A recursive moving average (also called modified or running moving average) equivalent to an EMA with smoothing constant 1/n, so it smooths far more heavily than a same-length standard EMA.
Intuition: The gentlest common average: each new price is absorbed at only 1/n weight, so the line moves slowly and filters a great deal of noise.
Mechanics: Seeded with an n-period SMA; thereafter SMMA_t = (SMMA_{t-1}*(n-1) + P_t)/n. This is the smoothing Welles Wilder used for RSI, ATR, and ADX, and the average used in Bill Williams' Alligator lines.
Formula: SMMA_t = (SMMA_{t-1} * (n - 1) + P_t) / n; first value = SMA of the first n prices.
Relationships: Exponential moving average, Simple moving average, Alligator indicator, Average true range
Failure modes: Very heavy lag; early values depend strongly on the seed and need long histories to stabilize, so short data sets give unreliable readings.
Misconceptions: SMMA(n) is not the same as EMA(n): its alpha is 1/n rather than 2/(n+1), so a 14-period SMMA responds roughly like a 27-period standard EMA.
Example: If the prior 14-period SMMA is 50 and the new close is 52, SMMA = (50*13 + 52)/14 = 50.14.
Source authority: Authoritative domain source / exact citation pending
Status: Provisional

0706. Hull moving average
Domain: Indicators
Definition: Alan Hull's moving average (2005), engineered to nearly eliminate lag while retaining smoothness by combining weighted moving averages of different lengths with a lag-canceling correction term.
Intuition: An average designed to hug price closely without becoming jagged — fast like a short WMA, smooth like a long one.
Mechanics: Compute WMA(n/2) and WMA(n) of price, form the raw series 2*WMA(n/2) - WMA(n) to cancel lag, then smooth the result with a WMA of length sqrt(n), rounding non-integer periods to whole numbers.
Formula: HMA(n) = WMA( 2*WMA(P, n/2) - WMA(P, n), sqrt(n) ), where WMA(P, m) is the m-period weighted moving average of price.
Relationships: Weighted moving average, Zero-lag exponential moving average, Double exponential moving average
Failure modes: Reduced lag means reduced noise filtering: it whipsaws in sideways markets and remains a trend-follower, not a predictor.
Misconceptions: Hull himself advises against HMA crossover systems — crossovers exploit lag differences that the HMA was built to remove; use turns in the HMA's direction instead.
Example: For an 11-period HMA, use WMA(6) and WMA(11) for the raw line, then smooth with a 3-period WMA (sqrt(11) = 3.3 rounds to 3).
Citation: Hull Moving Average (HMA) | ChartSchool | StockCharts.com — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/technical-indicators-and-overlays/technical-overlays/hull-moving-average-hma (Calculation)
Status: Reviewed

0707. Triangular moving average
Domain: Indicators
Definition: A double-smoothed simple moving average — an SMA of an SMA — whose effective weights form a triangle that peaks at the middle of the window, giving mid-window data the most influence.
Intuition: Averaging an average: extra smooth at the cost of extra lag, with the middle of the window weighted most.
Mechanics: TMA(n) = SMA( SMA(P, m1), m2 ) with m1 = ceil((n+1)/2) and m2 = floor((n+1)/2); equivalently a single convolution with triangular weights 1, 2, ..., m, ..., 2, 1.
Formula: TMA(n) = SMA( SMA(P, ceil((n+1)/2)), floor((n+1)/2) ).
Relationships: Simple moving average, Weighted moving average
Failure modes: Twice the smoothing means roughly twice the lag of its component SMA, so it is poor for timing and usable mainly as a slow trend reference.
Misconceptions: Despite the peaked weighting it is not centered in the signal sense — it uses past data only and still lags; a true centered moving average uses future data and cannot be computed in real time.
Example: A 5-period TMA = SMA(SMA(P, 3), 3); if the last three 3-period SMA values are 10, 11, 12, the TMA is 11.
Source authority: Authoritative domain source / exact citation pending
Status: Provisional

0708. Variable index dynamic average
Domain: Indicators
Definition: Tushar Chande's Variable Index Dynamic Average: an exponential-style moving average whose smoothing constant is scaled each bar by a volatility index — the absolute Chande Momentum Oscillator — so it reacts faster in decisive, volatile markets and slower in quiet ones.
Intuition: An adaptive average that automatically speeds up when the market is moving decisively and slows down when it is drifting.
Mechanics: VIDYA_t = VIDYA_{t-1} + alpha * |CMO_t|/100 * (P_t - VIDYA_{t-1}), with alpha = 2/(n+1). When |CMO| nears 100 (one-way market) VIDYA behaves like a fast EMA; when CMO nears 0 it barely moves.
Formula: VIDYA_t = VIDYA_{t-1} + alpha * (|CMO_t|/100) * (P_t - VIDYA_{t-1}); alpha = 2/(n+1); CMO = 100*(Su - Sd)/(Su + Sd) with Su, Sd the sums of up and down close-to-close changes over the look-back.
Relationships: Exponential moving average, Kaufman adaptive moving average, Chande momentum oscillator
Failure modes: In choppy markets CMO hovers near zero and VIDYA effectively freezes, missing genuine moves; results are sensitive to the CMO look-back choice.
Misconceptions: VIDYA is not the same as KAMA: KAMA adapts via an efficiency ratio (net change over path length), while VIDYA adapts via a momentum-volatility index.
Example: If alpha = 0.2 and the CMO reads +60, the effective smoothing constant is 0.12; at CMO = +10 it falls to 0.02.
Source authority: Authoritative domain source / exact citation pending
Status: Provisional

0709. Kaufman adaptive moving average
Domain: Indicators
Definition: Perry Kaufman's adaptive moving average, which varies its smoothing constant with an Efficiency Ratio measuring how directional (versus noisy) recent price movement has been, hugging price in trends and going flat in chop.
Intuition: An average that asks how much of the recent movement is real trend versus random wiggle, and speeds up only when the answer is mostly trend.
Mechanics: ER = |Close - Close_n| / sum|Close - prior Close| over n bars (0 to 1); SC = [ER*(fast - slow) + slow]^2 with fast = 2/(2+1) and slow = 2/(30+1); KAMA_t = KAMA_{t-1} + SC*(P_t - KAMA_{t-1}). Recommended settings KAMA(10,2,30); the first value is seeded with an SMA.
Formula: ER = |P_t - P_{t-n}| / sum(|P_i - P_{i-1}|, i=t-n+1..t); SC = [ER*(2/3 - 2/31) + 2/31]^2; KAMA_t = KAMA_{t-1} + SC*(P_t - KAMA_{t-1}).
Relationships: Exponential moving average, Variable index dynamic average, Efficiency ratio
Failure modes: A simple price/KAMA crossover system still whipsaws without price or time filters, and in persistently choppy markets ER stays low, leaving KAMA flat and uninformative.
Misconceptions: Lengthening the ER look-back does not necessarily improve the indicator — the documented guidance is to adjust the fast (middle) parameter for smoothing, not the ER period.
Example: If price rises for 10 straight bars, change equals volatility so ER = 1 and KAMA tracks a 2-period EMA; if price ends unchanged after 10 choppy bars, ER is near 0 and KAMA barely moves.
Citation: Kaufman's Adaptive Moving Average (KAMA) | ChartSchool | StockCharts.com — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/technical-indicators-and-overlays/technical-overlays/kaufmans-adaptive-moving-average-kama (Calculation)
Status: Reviewed

0710. Zero-lag exponential moving average
Domain: Indicators
Definition: A lag-corrected EMA (John Ehlers and Ric Way, 'Zero Lag (Well, Almost)', TASC 2010): an EMA applied to de-lagged data — price plus the difference between the current price and the price (n-1)/2 bars ago — compensating for the EMA's inherent lag.
Intuition: Pre-correct the data for the lag you know the EMA will add, so the smoothed output lands close to the current price.
Mechanics: Form the adjusted series Z_t = P_t + (P_t - P_{t-lag}) with lag = floor((n-1)/2), then take a standard n-period EMA of Z. The construction is related to Mulloy's DEMA/TEMA lag-cancellation idea.
Formula: lag = floor((n-1)/2); Z_t = P_t + (P_t - P_{t-lag}); ZLEMA_t = EMA_n(Z)_t with k = 2/(n+1).
Relationships: Exponential moving average, Double exponential moving average, Hull moving average
Failure modes: The de-lagging term amplifies noise and overshoots on sharp reversals; in sideways markets it whipsaws more than a plain EMA.
Misconceptions: Zero lag is aspirational: the correction removes the systematic EMA lag in smooth trends but cannot anticipate turning points, where lag remains.
Example: For n = 10, lag = 4; if P_t = 105 and P_{t-4} = 100, the EMA is applied to 110 instead of 105, pulling the average up toward the trending price.
Source authority: Authoritative domain source / exact citation pending
Status: Provisional

0711. Double exponential moving average
Domain: Indicators
Definition: Patrick Mulloy's Double Exponential Moving Average (Technical Analysis of Stocks & Commodities, January 1994): a composite of a single and a double EMA that subtracts the extra lag of the double-smoothed series from the single-smoothed one to track price more closely.
Intuition: Measure how much double-smoothing lags single-smoothing, and add that gap back to the fast EMA as a correction.
Mechanics: EMA1 = EMA(price), EMA2 = EMA(EMA1); DEMA = 2*EMA1 - EMA2. The double-smoothed EMA2 serves only as a lag-correction term, not as the output. Default 20 periods; signals via price/line crosses or fast/slow DEMA crossovers, which occur earlier than equivalent EMA crossovers.
Formula: DEMA = 2*EMA_n(P) - EMA_n(EMA_n(P)).
Relationships: Exponential moving average, Triple exponential moving average, Zero-lag exponential moving average
Failure modes: Greater responsiveness means more noise and more false signals in choppy markets; long-term investors may be better served by a traditional, smoother average.
Misconceptions: DEMA is not simply the EMA of an EMA — that double-smoothed series alone would lag more, not less; the output is 2*EMA1 - EMA2.
Example: If EMA1 = 50 and EMA2 = 48, DEMA = 2*50 - 48 = 52, pulling the average above EMA1 toward current price.
Citation: Double Exponential Moving Average (DEMA) | ChartSchool | StockCharts.com — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/technical-indicators-and-overlays/technical-overlays/double-exponential-moving-average-dema (Calculation)
Status: Reviewed

0712. Triple exponential moving average
Domain: Indicators
Definition: Patrick Mulloy's Triple Exponential Moving Average, which extends DEMA with a third smoothing layer, combining single, double, and triple EMAs to remove even more lag for short-term trading.
Intuition: DEMA with one more correction term — closer still to price, noisier still.
Mechanics: TEMA = 3*EMA1 - 3*EMA2 + EMA3, where EMA2 = EMA(EMA1) and EMA3 = EMA(EMA2). Used via price crosses or fast/slow TEMA crossovers, which fire earlier than equivalent DEMA or EMA crosses; default 20 periods.
Formula: TEMA = 3*EMA_n(P) - 3*EMA_n(EMA_n(P)) + EMA_n(EMA_n(EMA_n(P))).
Relationships: Double exponential moving average, Exponential moving average, TRIX
Failure modes: Minimal lag means minimal noise filtering — it whipsaws the most of the EMA family in sideways markets, and some lag is actually useful for longer-term analysis.
Misconceptions: Faster is not universally better: TEMA's responsiveness amplifies noise, so it is not a straight upgrade over EMA or DEMA. Also, TEMA is not TRIX — TRIX is the 1-period rate of change of a triple EMA.
Example: If EMA1 = 50, EMA2 = 48, EMA3 = 46, TEMA = 3*50 - 3*48 + 46 = 52.
Citation: Triple Exponential Moving Average (TEMA) | ChartSchool | StockCharts.com — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/technical-indicators-and-overlays/technical-overlays/triple-exponential-moving-average-tema (Calculation)
Status: Reviewed

0713. Moving average crossover
Domain: Indicators
Definition: A signal framework in which a shorter-period moving average crossing a longer-period one (or price crossing a moving average) is read as a shift in trend direction; John Murphy calls the two-average version the double crossover method. It is an analytical convention, not a proven predictive law.
Intuition: When the fast average overtakes the slow one, recent prices have moved enough to bend the trend measure — a simple, mechanical trend-change rule.
Mechanics: Bullish signal: the short MA crosses above the long MA; bearish: short crosses below. Common pairs are 5/35 (short-term) and 50/200 (long-term); a triple-crossover variant uses three averages. MACD(12,26,1) quantifies EMA crossovers as the fast-minus-slow difference.
Relationships: Golden cross, Death cross, Simple moving average, Moving average convergence divergence
Failure modes: Both averages lag, so signals are late by construction and whipsaw repeatedly in trendless markets; the documented Home Depot example shows three whipsaws before one successful 20%+ signal.
Misconceptions: A crossover describes what has already happened; it does not predict continuation. Unfiltered crossover systems are unreliable — price or time filters are typically needed.
Example: A 10-day EMA crossing above a 50-day EMA is a bullish crossover; with MACD(10,50,1), the MACD line crossing zero marks the same event.
Citation: Moving Averages - Simple and Exponential | ChartSchool | StockCharts.com — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/technical-indicators-and-overlays/technical-overlays/moving-averages-simple-and-exponential (Double Moving Average Crossovers)
Status: Reviewed

0714. Golden cross
Domain: Indicators
Definition: A bullish moving-average crossover — classically the 50-day SMA crossing above the 200-day SMA — interpreted by technicians as confirmation of a long-term uptrend. It is a widely watched analytical convention, not a proven predictive law.
Intuition: The market's medium-term average climbing above its long-term average suggests that upward momentum has been sustained long enough to matter.
Mechanics: Identified on daily charts when the shorter (typically 50-day) moving average crosses up through the longer (typically 200-day) one; because both averages lag, the cross usually prints well after the actual low.
Relationships: Death cross, Moving average crossover, Simple moving average
Failure modes: Late by construction and whipsaw-prone in range-bound markets; by the time a golden cross prints, much of the advance has often already occurred.
Misconceptions: It is not a guaranteed buy signal or a law of markets — it records that an advance has been large and persistent; any forward-looking edge is an empirical question, not a property of the construction.
Example: MACD(50,200,1) turning positive marks the same 50/200 EMA golden cross in oscillator form.
Citation: Moving Averages - Simple and Exponential | ChartSchool | StockCharts.com — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/technical-indicators-and-overlays/technical-overlays/moving-averages-simple-and-exponential (Double Moving Average Crossovers)
Status: Reviewed

0715. Death cross
Domain: Indicators
Definition: A bearish moving-average crossover — classically the 50-day SMA crossing below the 200-day SMA — read as confirmation of a long-term downtrend; the mirror image of the golden cross and equally a convention rather than a proven law.
Intuition: The medium-term average sinking below the long-term average suggests the decline has been deep and persistent enough to bend long-term trend measures.
Mechanics: The shorter (typically 50-day) moving average crosses down through the longer (typically 200-day) one; like the golden cross, it lags and typically prints well after the actual top.
Relationships: Golden cross, Moving average crossover, Simple moving average
Failure modes: Late and whipsaw-prone in sideways markets; many historical death crosses have occurred near market lows rather than before extended declines.
Misconceptions: A death cross does not forecast a crash — it records that a decline has already been large enough to pull the 50-day average below the 200-day.
Example: MACD(50,200,1) turning negative marks the same 50/200 EMA death cross in oscillator form.
Citation: Moving Averages - Simple and Exponential | ChartSchool | StockCharts.com — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/technical-indicators-and-overlays/technical-overlays/moving-averages-simple-and-exponential (Double Moving Average Crossovers)
Status: Reviewed

0716. Moving average convergence divergence
Domain: Indicators
Definition: Gerald Appel's Moving Average Convergence/Divergence oscillator (late 1970s): a momentum indicator built from the difference between a fast and a slow EMA (default 12 and 26) with a 9-period EMA signal line, combining trend-following and momentum information in one unbounded oscillator.
Intuition: When the fast average pulls away from the slow one, momentum is accelerating; when they converge, the move is running out of steam.
Mechanics: MACD line = EMA(12) - EMA(26) of closes; signal line = 9-period EMA of the MACD line; histogram = line minus signal. Signals include signal-line crossovers, zero-line (centerline) crossovers — equivalent to the underlying EMA crossover — and divergences with price.
Formula: MACD = EMA_12(Close) - EMA_26(Close); Signal = EMA_9(MACD); Histogram = MACD - Signal.
Relationships: MACD line, MACD signal line, MACD histogram, Exponential moving average, Percentage price oscillator
Failure modes: Signal-line crossovers whipsaw in flat or volatile markets, and crossovers at extremes often mark momentum exhaustion rather than reversal; being unbounded, MACD cannot flag overbought or oversold conditions.
Misconceptions: MACD is not a bounded oscillator, so high readings are not inherently overbought; nor does a signal-line cross guarantee a trend change.
Example: If the 12-day EMA is 102 and the 26-day EMA is 100, MACD = +2; with a 9-day signal line at 1.5, the histogram reads +0.5.
Citation: MACD (Moving Average Convergence/Divergence Oscillator) | ChartSchool | StockCharts.com — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/technical-indicators-and-overlays/technical-indicators/macd-moving-average-convergence-divergence-oscillator (How Do You Calculate the MACD?)
Status: Reviewed

0717. MACD line
Domain: Indicators
Definition: The core series of the MACD: the fast (default 12-period) EMA minus the slow (default 26-period) EMA of closing prices, oscillating around zero as the two averages converge and diverge.
Intuition: The spread between a fast and a slow average: positive and widening means upside momentum is building.
Mechanics: Computed each bar as EMA_12(C) - EMA_26(C); it crosses zero exactly when the two EMAs cross, and its distance from zero measures how far the averages have diverged.
Formula: MACD line = EMA_12(Close) - EMA_26(Close).
Relationships: Moving average convergence divergence, MACD signal line, MACD histogram, Moving average crossover
Failure modes: As an EMA spread it lags and whipsaws in trendless markets; absolute values are price-scale dependent and not comparable across securities (use the PPO for that).
Misconceptions: A falling MACD line is not the same as falling prices — the EMA spread can shrink while prices are still rising, reflecting decelerating momentum only.
Example: A 12-day EMA of 50 and a 26-day EMA of 48 give a MACD line of +2: the fast average sits 2 points above the slow one.
Citation: MACD (Moving Average Convergence/Divergence Oscillator) | ChartSchool | StockCharts.com — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/technical-indicators-and-overlays/technical-indicators/macd-moving-average-convergence-divergence-oscillator (How Do You Calculate the MACD?)
Status: Reviewed

0718. MACD signal line
Domain: Indicators
Definition: A 9-period EMA of the MACD line, plotted alongside it; crossovers of the MACD line through this signal line are the most common MACD trading signal.
Intuition: A moving average of the MACD itself, smoothing its turns so crossovers are easier to read.
Mechanics: Signal_t = EMA_9(MACD line). A bullish crossover occurs when the MACD line rises above the signal line, bearish when it falls below; because it trails the MACD line, it adds a further layer of lag.
Formula: Signal = EMA_9(MACD), where MACD = EMA_12(Close) - EMA_26(Close).
Relationships: MACD line, MACD histogram, Moving average convergence divergence
Failure modes: Adds lag to an already lagging construction, and crossovers occurring at positive or negative extremes often mark exhaustion and reverse quickly.
Misconceptions: The 9-period setting is a convention, not an optimum, and the signal line has no meaning independently of the MACD line it smooths.
Example: If the MACD line is 2.0 and its 9-period EMA is 1.5, the MACD sits above its signal line — a post-crossover bullish state.
Citation: MACD (Moving Average Convergence/Divergence Oscillator) | ChartSchool | StockCharts.com — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/technical-indicators-and-overlays/technical-indicators/macd-moving-average-convergence-divergence-oscillator (Signal Line Crossovers)
Status: Reviewed

0719. MACD histogram
Domain: Indicators
Definition: The bar plot of the MACD line minus its signal line, visualizing the distance between them; it expands and contracts ahead of crossovers and is used to spot momentum shifts early.
Intuition: Instead of waiting for the two MACD lines to cross, watch the gap between them shrink or grow.
Mechanics: Histogram = MACD - Signal; positive when MACD is above its signal line, negative below. It crosses zero exactly at a signal-line crossover, and its peaks and troughs precede the crossovers themselves.
Formula: Histogram = MACD line - Signal line = (EMA_12(C) - EMA_26(C)) - EMA_9(MACD).
Relationships: MACD line, MACD signal line, Moving average convergence divergence
Failure modes: More sensitive than the lines themselves, so it flips sign more often in choppy markets; a shrinking histogram warns of a crossover but says nothing about whether that crossover will matter.
Misconceptions: A declining histogram does not mean prices are falling — only that the MACD's lead over its signal line is narrowing.
Example: MACD = 2.0 with signal = 1.5 gives a histogram of +0.5; if the next bar's MACD is 1.8 and signal 1.6, the histogram shrinks to +0.2, warning that upside momentum is fading.
Citation: MACD (Moving Average Convergence/Divergence Oscillator) | ChartSchool | StockCharts.com — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/technical-indicators-and-overlays/technical-indicators/macd-moving-average-convergence-divergence-oscillator (How Do You Calculate the MACD?)
Status: Reviewed

0720. Relative strength index
Domain: Indicators
Definition: J. Welles Wilder's momentum oscillator (New Concepts in Technical Trading Systems, 1978) comparing smoothed average gains to smoothed average losses over a look-back period (default 14), bounded between 0 and 100.
Intuition: A speedometer for price: it shows how persistently and strongly the market has been closing up versus down.
Mechanics: RS = Average Gain / Average Loss, with first values simple 14-period means and subsequent values Wilder-smoothed ((prior*13 + current)/14); RSI = 100 - 100/(1+RS). Wilder treated readings above 70 as overbought and below 30 as oversold; also used for divergences, failure swings, and centerline analysis.
Formula: RSI = 100 - 100/(1 + RS); RS = AvgGain / AvgLoss; AvgGain_t = (AvgGain_{t-1}*13 + Gain_t)/14 (likewise losses, expressed as positive values).
Relationships: Stochastic RSI, Money flow index, Connors RSI, Stochastic oscillator
Failure modes: In strong trends RSI can stay above 70 or below 30 for extended periods, so fading overbought/oversold readings fails; bearish divergences can recur for months before any reversal.
Misconceptions: Overbought does not mean the price must fall — it can signal strength. RSI is also not a comparison between two securities; that is relative strength (price relative).
Example: If the 14-day average gain is 1.0 and the average loss is 0.5, RS = 2 and RSI = 100 - 100/3 = 66.7.
Citation: Relative Strength Index (RSI) | ChartSchool | StockCharts.com — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/technical-indicators-and-overlays/technical-indicators/relative-strength-index-rsi (RSI Calculation)
Status: Reviewed

0721. Stochastic oscillator
Domain: Indicators
Definition: George Lane's momentum indicator (late 1950s) measuring where the close sits within the high-low range of the look-back period, bounded 0-100 and published in Fast, Slow, and Full versions. Lane's premise: momentum changes direction before price.
Intuition: In an uptrend prices tend to close near the top of their recent range; the stochastic quantifies that tendency.
Mechanics: %K = (C - LL)/(HH - LL)*100 over (default) 14 periods; %D = 3-period SMA of %K acts as the signal line; the Slow version smooths %K once more. Readings above 80 are overbought, below 20 oversold; signals come from %K/%D crosses, divergences, and Lane's bull/bear set-ups.
Formula: %K = 100 * (C - LL_n)/(HH_n - LL_n); %D = SMA_3(%K); HH_n and LL_n are the highest high and lowest low over n periods.
Relationships: Williams percent R, Stochastic RSI, Relative strength index
Failure modes: Can remain overbought or oversold through an entire strong trend, so counter-trend signals fail repeatedly; fast versions whipsaw, and signals work best in trading ranges or zigzag trends.
Misconceptions: The stochastic does not follow price or volume — per Lane it follows the speed (momentum) of price; and an overbought reading alone is not a sell signal.
Example: With a 14-day high of 110, low of 100, and close of 108, %K = (108-100)/(110-100)*100 = 80.
Citation: Stochastic Oscillator (Fast, Slow, and Full) | ChartSchool | StockCharts.com — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/technical-indicators-and-overlays/technical-indicators/stochastic-oscillator-fast-slow-and-full (How Do You Calculate the Stochastic Oscillator?)
Status: Reviewed

0781. Volume analysis
Domain: Volume and order flow
Definition: The study of trading volume — the number of shares or contracts exchanged over a period — and of how that volume behaves relative to price movement, used to gauge the participation and conviction behind a move. In the Wyckoff tradition it is formalized as the effort-versus-result principle: volume is the effort, price change is the result. It is an analytical framework, not a proven predictive law.
Intuition: Price tells you what happened; volume tells you how much conviction was behind it. The same price move means something different on heavy participation than on a thin, uninterested tape.
Mechanics: Practitioners compare absolute and relative volume (against recent averages or prior comparable swings) with price spread and direction, looking for harmony (effort producing a commensurate result) or discrepancy (heavy volume with little progress, or progress on shrinking volume).
Relationships: Price-volume relationship, Volume confirmation, Volume divergence, Climax volume, Dry-up volume
Failure modes: In decentralized markets such as spot forex there is no consolidated volume, so tick or futures-proxy volume can mislead. Volume spikes from contract rollovers, expirations, or index rebalancing are structural and can be mistaken for conviction.
Misconceptions: High volume by itself predicts nothing about direction — it records participation, and every transaction pairs a buyer with a seller, so 'more buyers than sellers' is a category error that volume analysis carefully avoids.
Example: A stock breaks out of a month-long range on volume three times its 20-day average, suggesting broad participation; the identical breakout on half the average volume would be treated as suspect.
Citation: LuxAlgo — Wyckoff Accumulation Schematic (effort vs result logic) — https://www.luxalgo.com/blog/wyckoff-accumulation-a-pattern-essentials-guide/ (What is the Wyckoff Accumulation Schematic?)
Status: Reviewed

0782. Price-volume relationship
Domain: Volume and order flow
Definition: The joint behavior of price change and traded volume, read as the link between effort (volume) and result (price progress). Wyckoff-style analysis treats harmony between the two as trend-confirming and discord between them as a warning that the supply-demand balance is shifting. It is a qualitative framework, not a statistical law.
Intuition: Like a car climbing a hill, a trend needs fuel: rising prices on rising volume look powered, while rising prices on falling volume look like coasting.
Mechanics: Each swing's price spread is compared with its volume: wide spreads on expanding volume show effort producing result; narrowing spread on expanding volume, or wide spread on shrinking volume, flags a mismatch that practitioners interpret as a change in control between buyers and sellers.
Relationships: Volume analysis, Volume confirmation, Volume divergence
Failure modes: The relationship is descriptive and regime-dependent; in news-driven repricing or illiquid markets, volume and price decouple for structural reasons rather than behavioral ones.
Misconceptions: There is no fixed rule that 'volume leads price'; identical price-volume patterns recur with different outcomes, and the relationship is read in context rather than as a mechanical signal.
Example: In an uptrend, each rally leg prints wider ranges on growing volume while pullbacks shrink in both range and volume — a textbook harmonious price-volume structure.
Citation: LuxAlgo — Wyckoff Accumulation Schematic — https://www.luxalgo.com/blog/wyckoff-accumulation-a-pattern-essentials-guide/ (What is the Wyckoff Accumulation Schematic?)
Status: Reviewed

0783. Volume confirmation
Domain: Volume and order flow
Definition: The use of expanding volume to validate a price move: breakouts, trend legs, and reversals are considered more credible when accompanied by above-average participation. Within Wyckoff logic, confirmation is effort (volume) producing a result (price movement) commensurate with it.
Intuition: A price level that the crowd actually had to trade through to break carries more information than one that slipped away in a thin book.
Mechanics: Volume on the signal bar or swing is compared with a recent average and with prior comparable moves; confirmation is present when volume expands in the direction of the move and contracts on counter-moves or pullbacks.
Relationships: Volume analysis, Price-volume relationship, Volume divergence, Buying climax, Selling climax
Failure modes: Volume is only fully known after the bar completes, so demanding confirmation structurally lags the move. Expiration, rebalance, or auction-imbalance volume can fabricate apparent confirmation.
Misconceptions: Confirmed moves still fail regularly; volume confirmation raises the information content of a move but does not certify continuation or improve reward-to-risk by itself.
Example: Price clears a resistance shelf and the breakout bar prints the session's highest volume with follow-through on the next bar; the same breakout on the session's lowest volume would be treated as unconfirmed.
Citation: LuxAlgo — Wyckoff Accumulation Schematic — https://www.luxalgo.com/blog/wyckoff-accumulation-a-pattern-essentials-guide/ (What is the Wyckoff Accumulation Schematic?)
Citation: ATAS — How to read the order flow — https://atas.net/blog/how-to-read-the-order-flow/ (What do traders use order flow for?)
Status: Reviewed

0784. Volume divergence
Domain: Volume and order flow
Definition: A discrepancy in which price registers a new extreme while volume fails to confirm it — for example a higher high made on noticeably lower volume than the prior high — read in Wyckoff and volume-spread practice as diminishing effort behind the trend. It is a warning heuristic, not a stand-alone timing signal.
Intuition: If each new push in the trend direction attracts fewer participants, the move may be running out of fuel even while price still advances.
Mechanics: Volume on successive price extremes in the same direction is compared, or volume on rallies versus reactions across a range; a declining volume trend against advancing price constitutes the divergence and prompts closer scrutiny of subsequent price behavior.
Relationships: Volume analysis, Volume confirmation, Delta divergence, Exhaustion
Failure modes: Trends — especially grinding, low-volatility advances — can persist for long stretches on declining volume, so acting on divergence alone is a classic way to fade strong trends prematurely.
Misconceptions: Volume divergence is not a reversal trigger; practitioners treat it as context that must be confirmed by price behavior such as failure to make further progress or absorption at the extreme.
Example: A future makes three successive swing highs at 4,510, 4,522 and 4,530 while swing volume falls from 1.2M to 0.9M to 0.6M contracts — a bearish volume divergence flagged for monitoring, not an automatic short.
Citation: LuxAlgo — Wyckoff Accumulation Schematic (effort vs result, shrinking-volume declines) — https://www.luxalgo.com/blog/wyckoff-accumulation-a-pattern-essentials-guide/ (What is the Wyckoff Accumulation Schematic?)
Citation: ATAS — How to read the order flow — https://atas.net/blog/how-to-read-the-order-flow/ (Footprint examples)
Status: Reviewed

0785. Climax volume
Domain: Volume and order flow
Definition: An extreme volume surge — typically the heaviest volume in many bars and several times the recent average — occurring after an extended directional move and accompanied by a wide price spread. In Wyckoff analysis it is the volume signature of a buying or selling climax: the terminal effort of a crowd capitulating or chasing.
Intuition: When everyone who was going to trade finally rushes in at once, the burst of activity can mark the end of a move rather than its acceleration.
Mechanics: Identified by comparing bar volume against the recent distribution of volumes together with spread expansion and location after a mature trend; practitioners then watch whether price can make further progress — failure to do so is what retrospectively confirms the climax.
Relationships: Buying climax, Selling climax, Exhaustion, Volume analysis
Failure modes: Climactic volume also occurs on genuine news repricing and on expiration or rebalance days, where it starts new trends rather than ending old ones; the label is dependable only in hindsight once the expected stalling appears.
Misconceptions: The highest-volume bar is not automatically a climax; climax interpretation requires context — a mature preceding move plus subsequent failure of price to continue.
Example: After a six-day selloff, a market prints its widest down bar on triple the 20-day average volume, closes well off the low, and cannot make a new low the next session — classic climax volume at a potential selling climax.
Citation: LuxAlgo — Wyckoff Accumulation Schematic (selling climax as wide, high-volume flush) — https://www.luxalgo.com/blog/wyckoff-accumulation-a-pattern-essentials-guide/ (How to identify Wyckoff accumulation on a chart)
Citation: ATAS — How to read the order flow — https://atas.net/blog/how-to-read-the-order-flow/ (Footprint examples)
Status: Reviewed

0786. Dry-up volume
Domain: Volume and order flow
Definition: A pronounced contraction of volume during a pullback or a test of a prior extreme, interpreted in Wyckoff methodology as a drying up of pressure from the side being tested: secondary tests and springs are expected to occur on markedly lower volume than the climax that preceded them.
Intuition: If price revisits a level and hardly anyone trades, the side that drove it there last time may have run out of ammunition.
Mechanics: Volume on a reaction or retest is compared with the volume of the prior move in the same direction; a dry-up shows volume falling well below both the climax volume and the recent average while price holds the level, suggesting supply (or demand) is spent.
Relationships: Volume analysis, Volume divergence, Selling climax, Absorption
Failure modes: Low volume can reflect simple disinterest, holiday conditions, or a pre-news lull rather than exhausted supply, and a dry-up offers no protection when genuinely new information enters the market.
Misconceptions: A low-volume pullback is not automatically bullish or bearish; it acquires meaning only relative to a prior high-volume event at the same location.
Example: After a selling climax on 2M shares, the retest of the low two weeks later trades only 400K shares and closes unchanged — a dry-up suggesting the selling supply is exhausted.
Citation: LuxAlgo — Wyckoff Accumulation Schematic (secondary tests and springs on light volume) — https://www.luxalgo.com/blog/wyckoff-accumulation-a-pattern-essentials-guide/ (How to identify Wyckoff accumulation on a chart)
Status: Reviewed

0787. Buying climax
Domain: Volume and order flow
Definition: In Wyckoff's distribution schematic, the buying climax (BC) is the terminal event of an advance: a marked expansion of volume and price spread as urgent public buying near the top is filled by professional interests distributing positions. It is a descriptive label for auction behavior, confirmed only when further upside progress fails.
Intuition: The most euphoric buying tends to appear exactly where large operators need that public demand to sell into without depressing the price themselves.
Mechanics: Identified as a wide-spread up bar or cluster on the heaviest volume of the advance following an extended uptrend, often coinciding with good news; the BC high sets the upper boundary of the ensuing trading range, followed by an automatic reaction and secondary tests.
Relationships: Climax volume, Selling climax, Exhaustion, Volume confirmation
Failure modes: Strong trends produce repeated climax-like bars that resolve into continuation rather than distribution, so treating every high-volume up-spike as a buying climax leads to premature shorts.
Misconceptions: A buying climax does not require a collapse to follow; it marks where supply met demand, and the market can also resolve sideways or even grind higher once that supply is absorbed.
Example: A stock rallies 40% in two months, then gaps up on earnings with its widest range and highest volume of the year, closing mid-range; the next two weeks fail to exceed that high, and the spike is labeled the buying climax.
Citation: LuxAlgo — Wyckoff Accumulation Schematic (distribution mirror with a buying climax instead of a selling climax) — https://www.luxalgo.com/blog/wyckoff-accumulation-a-pattern-essentials-guide/ (Wyckoff accumulation vs. related Wyckoff concepts)
Status: Reviewed

0788. Selling climax
Domain: Volume and order flow
Definition: In Wyckoff's accumulation schematic, the selling climax (SC) is the terminal event of a decline: widening spread and climactic selling pressure as panicked public selling is absorbed by large interests near the lows, typically on the heaviest volume of the down-move. It is confirmed only after the automatic rally and a successful secondary test.
Intuition: Capitulation day: when the last fearful sellers dump their positions, stronger hands can finally buy in size without moving the price against themselves.
Mechanics: Marked by a wide-spread down bar on extreme volume after a mature decline; the SC low and the high of the ensuing automatic rally define the initial boundaries of the trading range around which the rest of the schematic (secondary test, spring, sign of strength) develops.
Relationships: Climax volume, Buying climax, Dry-up volume, Absorption
Failure modes: In cascading markets driven by margin spirals or news shocks, apparent climaxes are followed by lower lows; the SC label is provisional until later tests hold.
Misconceptions: The selling climax is not 'the bottom'; it only ends the steepest phase of the decline, and accumulation typically takes weeks or months of range trading afterward.
Example: After a three-week slide, an index future sells off 3% intraday on quadruple average volume, then reverses to close flat; subsequent retests hold above the low on shrinking volume, and the flush is labeled the selling climax.
Citation: LuxAlgo — Wyckoff Accumulation Schematic (PS, SC, AR, ST) — https://www.luxalgo.com/blog/wyckoff-accumulation-a-pattern-essentials-guide/ (What is the Wyckoff Accumulation Schematic?)
Status: Reviewed

0789. Bid volume
Domain: Volume and order flow
Definition: The total traded volume classified as having occurred at the bid price — trades initiated by aggressive sellers whose market or marketable sell orders matched resting buy limit orders. It is the sell-initiated component of bid/ask order-flow analysis.
Intuition: Bid volume measures how much selling was aggressive enough to cross the spread and hit the prices buyers had posted.
Mechanics: Each trade is classified as a bid trade when the exchange feed flags it as executed at the bid, or heuristically when its price is at or below the prevailing bid (or on a downtick when trade and quote data are unsynchronized); classified volumes are then summed per price level, bar, or session.
Relationships: Ask volume, Volume delta, Footprint chart, Time and sales
Failure modes: Classification depends on data quality: feeds without exchange-provided trade-side flags must infer the side from ticks, which misclassifies trades when quote and trade streams are out of sync.
Misconceptions: Bid volume is not net selling that removes ownership — every bid-side trade still has a buyer; it records which side was the aggressor, not a change in net positions.
Example: In a one-minute bar, 800 contracts trade at the bid and 300 at the ask; bid volume of 800 shows sellers were the more aggressive side that minute.
Citation: Sierra Chart — Numbers Bars (Bid Trade / Bid Volume definitions) — https://sierrachart.com/index.php?page=doc/NumbersBars.php (Definitions)
Citation: ATAS — Delta and Cumulative Delta: What are they? — https://atas.net/blog/what-is-delta/ (Delta calculation)
Status: Reviewed

0790. Ask volume
Domain: Volume and order flow
Definition: The total traded volume classified as having occurred at the ask (offer) price — trades initiated by aggressive buyers whose market or marketable buy orders lifted resting sell limit orders. It is the buy-initiated component of bid/ask order-flow analysis.
Intuition: Ask volume shows how urgently buyers were willing to pay the seller's posted price rather than wait for a fill at the bid.
Mechanics: Each trade is classified as an ask trade when the exchange feed flags it as executed at the ask, or heuristically when its price is at or above the prevailing ask (or on an uptick when trade and quote data are unsynchronized); classified volumes are summed per price level, bar, or session.
Relationships: Bid volume, Volume delta, Footprint chart, Cumulative volume delta
Failure modes: Classification depends on data quality: feeds without exchange-provided trade-side flags must infer the side from ticks, which misclassifies trades when quote and trade streams are out of sync.
Misconceptions: Ask volume does not mean there are 'more buyers than sellers' in net terms — every trade pairs one of each; it identifies the initiating, aggressive side of each transaction.
Example: A breakout bar prints 1,500 contracts at the ask versus 600 at the bid; the ask-volume dominance shows buyers lifting offers through the level.
Citation: Sierra Chart — Numbers Bars (Ask Trade / Ask Volume definitions) — https://sierrachart.com/index.php?page=doc/NumbersBars.php (Definitions)
Citation: ATAS — Delta and Cumulative Delta: What are they? — https://atas.net/blog/what-is-delta/ (Delta calculation)
Status: Reviewed

0791. Volume delta
Domain: Volume and order flow
Definition: The net difference between volume traded at the ask (aggressive market buys) and volume traded at the bid (aggressive market sells) over a price level, bar, or period. It measures which side initiated more traded volume, on the premise that market orders are what move prices. It is a descriptive order-flow statistic, not a predictive signal by itself.
Intuition: Delta answers 'who was more impatient — buyers or sellers?' Positive delta means buyers lifted more offers than sellers hit bids.
Mechanics: Every trade is classified as an ask trade (buy-initiated) or bid trade (sell-initiated); delta is then computed per footprint cell, per bar, or per period as ask-traded volume minus bid-traded volume, and displayed numerically or as a signed histogram.
Formula: Delta = V_ask − V_bid, where V_ask is volume traded at the ask (buyer-initiated) and V_bid is volume traded at the bid (seller-initiated)
Relationships: Bid volume, Ask volume, Cumulative volume delta, Delta footprint, Delta divergence
Failure modes: Trade-side classification degrades on feeds without exchange aggressor flags, and delta says nothing about passive limit-order flow — a large passive seller can absorb heavy positive delta while price still falls.
Misconceptions: Positive delta is not synonymous with rising price: bearish candles with positive delta are common when passive sellers absorb aggressive buying, so delta must be read against price response.
Example: A WTI crude trade of 25 contracts executes at the ask (delta +25) followed by 10 contracts at the bid (delta −10); net delta for the sequence is +15.
Citation: ATAS — Delta and Cumulative Delta: What are they? — https://atas.net/blog/what-is-delta/ (Delta calculation)
Citation: Sierra Chart — Numbers Bars (Delta, AskVol/BidVol difference) — https://sierrachart.com/index.php?page=doc/NumbersBars.php (Definitions / Numbers Bars Text Types)
Status: Reviewed

0792. Cumulative volume delta
Domain: Volume and order flow
Definition: The running accumulation of per-bar or per-trade volume delta over a chosen period (typically a session or an entire contract), showing the evolving net balance of aggressive buying versus aggressive selling. It summarizes who has dominated market-order flow since the chosen starting point.
Intuition: If delta is the score of each play, cumulative delta is the scoreboard of the whole game — it shows whether buyers or sellers have been net aggressive all session long.
Mechanics: Starting from zero at the session (or contract) open, each bar's delta is added to the running total; the result is plotted as bars, candles, or a line, and divergences between CVD slope and price are used analytically.
Formula: CVD_t = CVD_{t−1} + Delta_t, with CVD_0 = 0 at the chosen anchor (session or contract start) and Delta_t = V_ask,t − V_bid,t
Relationships: Volume delta, Delta divergence, Ask volume, Bid volume, Footprint chart
Failure modes: Not all markets and feeds transmit reliable trade-side data, so CVD quality varies by venue; CVD also ignores resting liquidity, so strongly positive CVD can coincide with falling prices when passive sellers absorb the flow.
Misconceptions: CVD is not a mechanical signal generator — platform documentation itself stresses it gives no simple buy/sell signals and must be combined with price behavior and context.
Example: During a session, aggressive sells push CVD steadily lower while price refuses to break a prior low; a trader reads the divergence as absorption and watches for longs rather than shorts.
Citation: ATAS — What you should know about Cumulative Delta Analysis — https://atas.net/blog/cumulative-delta-analysis/ (What the Cumulative Delta is?)
Citation: ATAS — Delta and Cumulative Delta: What are they? — https://atas.net/blog/what-is-delta/ (Cumulative delta)
Status: Reviewed

0793. Delta divergence
Domain: Volume and order flow
Definition: A mismatch between price direction and volume delta: for example, price printing a new high while bar delta or cumulative delta fails to make a corresponding new high, indicating that the aggressive order flow no longer supports the price move. Practitioners read it as a warning of weakening initiative or active absorption by the passive side.
Intuition: If price keeps climbing but buyers are swinging less hard each push, someone on the other side may be quietly absorbing their market orders.
Mechanics: Successive price extremes are compared with the corresponding delta or CVD extremes; divergence is flagged when the price extreme is not matched by a delta extreme, often explained by large resting limit orders absorbing market orders so that aggression produces little price progress.
Relationships: Volume delta, Cumulative volume delta, Volume divergence, Absorption, Exhaustion
Failure modes: Delta can diverge for long stretches while the trend continues, and on low-quality data feeds misclassified trades fabricate divergence; the pattern is frequent and far from decisive on its own.
Misconceptions: Delta divergence is not proof of hidden institutional intent — it is equally consistent with ordinary passive liquidity, and it is an observation to be confirmed, not a stand-alone entry signal.
Example: ES pushes to a new session high while the bar's delta prints well below the prior high's delta; the footprint shows big ask volume absorbed at the offer, and price subsequently rotates down.
Citation: ATAS — How to read the order flow — https://atas.net/blog/how-to-read-the-order-flow/ (Footprint examples / Examples with delta and cumulative delta)
Citation: ATAS — What you should know about Cumulative Delta Analysis — https://atas.net/blog/cumulative-delta-analysis/ (How to use the Cumulative Delta?)
Status: Reviewed

0794. Footprint chart
Domain: Volume and order flow
Definition: A chart type that decomposes each price bar into its constituent price levels and displays, for every level, the volume traded there — typically split between bid-side and ask-side trades, or shown as delta. It makes the intra-bar auction visible instead of showing only open, high, low, and close.
Intuition: A candlestick tells you where price went; a footprint shows you the fight that happened at each price along the way.
Mechanics: Built from tick-by-tick exchange data (price, volume, and execution side of each trade), aggregated by price level within each bar; display modes include Bid × Ask, Delta, Volume, Trades, and imbalance highlighting, often with color intensity proportional to activity.
Relationships: Bid-ask footprint, Delta footprint, Volume footprint, Imbalance footprint, Volume delta
Failure modes: Requires high-quality tick data with reliable bid/ask classification; on aggregated or unsynchronized feeds the per-level numbers are inaccurate, and the density of information invites over-reading noise.
Misconceptions: Footprints are not a window into 'hidden' orders — they show executed trades only, not resting intent, and a footprint pattern is context for decisions rather than a stand-alone signal.
Example: On a 5-minute crude oil Bid × Ask footprint, each cell shows contracts sold at the bid on the left and bought at the ask on the right, letting the trader see exactly where sellers overwhelmed buyers inside the bar.
Citation: ATAS — Footprint Charts: What Drives Price Movement — https://atas.net/footprint-charts/ (What is a Footprint in Trading)
Citation: Sierra Chart — Numbers Bars ('Footprint' in other charting programs) — https://sierrachart.com/index.php?page=doc/NumbersBars.php (Introduction)
Status: Reviewed

0795. Bid-ask footprint
Domain: Volume and order flow
Definition: The most common footprint display mode: at every price level inside a bar, two numbers are shown side by side — the volume traded at the bid (seller-initiated) and the volume traded at the ask (buyer-initiated). It exposes where aggressive buying and selling actually occurred within each bar.
Intuition: It is the scoreboard of the intra-bar fight, level by level: how much sellers hit bids versus how much buyers lifted offers at each price.
Mechanics: Tick data are classified by execution side and aggregated per price level per bar; each cell displays 'bid volume × ask volume' (or vice versa), commonly color-coded by which side dominates, and diagonal bid/ask comparisons are used for imbalance analysis.
Relationships: Footprint chart, Bid volume, Ask volume, Imbalance footprint, Volume delta
Failure modes: Same data-quality dependencies as all bid/ask statistics — misclassified ticks distort the per-level split; at very small tick sizes or fast markets the cells become dense and hard to read without aggregation.
Misconceptions: A dominant ask side at a level does not guarantee price will rise from there; it records aggression that has already happened and can mark absorption by passive sellers just as easily as initiative buying.
Example: At a resistance level, a footprint cell shows 320 × 1,450 (bid × ask); the trader sees buyers lifted 1,450 contracts at the offer, then watches whether price advances or stalls on that aggression.
Citation: ATAS — Footprint Charts: What Drives Price Movement (Bid × Ask modes) — https://atas.net/footprint-charts/ (Types of Footprint)
Citation: Sierra Chart — Numbers Bars (Bid Vol x Ask Vol text type) — https://sierrachart.com/index.php?page=doc/NumbersBars.php (Numbers Bars Text Types)
Status: Reviewed

0796. Delta footprint
Domain: Volume and order flow
Definition: A footprint display mode in which each price level inside a bar shows the volume delta at that level — ask-traded volume minus bid-traded volume — rather than the raw bid and ask numbers. It highlights where net aggressive buying or selling was concentrated within the bar.
Intuition: Instead of showing both sides' scores, it shows only who won each price level and by how much.
Mechanics: Per-level delta is computed from classified tick data and displayed as signed numbers (green for positive, red for negative, by convention), with optional background intensity proportional to the magnitude; bar-level totals aggregate the per-level values.
Formula: Per-level delta = V_ask(level) − V_bid(level); bar delta = sum over levels
Relationships: Footprint chart, Volume delta, Cumulative volume delta, Bid-ask footprint
Failure modes: Collapses two-sided information into one signed number, so heavy two-sided trade and light one-sided trade can produce identical deltas; inherits all trade-classification data risks.
Misconceptions: A large positive delta cell is not a buy signal — if price cannot advance on that aggression it evidences absorption by passive sellers, which many traders read as bearish.
Example: Inside a down bar, one level near the low prints delta +900 while price stalls; the trader notes aggressive buying being absorbed at the low and watches for a reversal or continuation break.
Citation: ATAS — Footprint Charts: What Drives Price Movement (Delta footprint modes) — https://atas.net/footprint-charts/ (Types of Footprint)
Citation: Sierra Chart — Numbers Bars (Ask Vol Bid Vol Difference) — https://sierrachart.com/index.php?page=doc/NumbersBars.php (Numbers Bars Text Types)
Status: Reviewed

0797. Volume footprint
Domain: Volume and order flow
Definition: A footprint display mode in which each price level inside a bar shows the total volume traded at that level, regardless of side. It reveals the intra-bar volume distribution — which prices attracted business and which were skipped — rather than the buy/sell split.
Intuition: It answers 'where inside this bar did the market actually do business?', exposing high-volume shelves and low-volume gaps within a single candle.
Mechanics: Tick volume is aggregated per price level per bar and shown as numbers, histograms, or color intensity; the per-bar profile can be read like a miniature volume profile with its own point of control.
Relationships: Footprint chart, Volume profile, Bid-ask footprint, High-volume node
Failure modes: Without the bid/ask split it shows where volume occurred but not who initiated it, so it is weaker for reading aggression; accuracy still depends on complete tick data.
Misconceptions: High intra-bar volume at a level is not automatically support or resistance — it records where trades happened, and only subsequent price behavior shows whether that level matters.
Example: A 15-minute bar shows 60% of its volume concentrated in a three-tick band near its high; the trader marks that band as the bar's high-volume node for the next session.
Citation: ATAS — Footprint Charts: What Drives Price Movement (Volume footprint modes) — https://atas.net/footprint-charts/ (Types of Footprint)
Citation: Sierra Chart — Numbers Bars (Volume text type, Volume Profile background) — https://sierrachart.com/index.php?page=doc/NumbersBars.php (Numbers Bars Text Types / Background Types)
Status: Reviewed

0798. Imbalance footprint
Domain: Volume and order flow
Definition: A footprint analysis mode that flags price levels where one side's traded volume overwhelms the other by a set ratio — commonly 3:1 or more — typically comparing the ask volume at one level diagonally against the bid volume at the level below (and vice versa). It is used to locate levels where aggressive flow was strongly one-sided.
Intuition: An imbalance marks a price where the fight was lopsided: one side hit or lifted with at least several times the force of the other.
Mechanics: For each level, ask volume is compared diagonally with the bid volume of the next lower level, and bid volume with the ask volume of the next higher level (because aggressive buys at price P compete with aggressive sells at P−1 tick); levels exceeding a configurable ratio are highlighted automatically.
Formula: Buy imbalance: V_ask(P) / V_bid(P − 1 tick) ≥ r (commonly r = 3); sell imbalance: V_bid(P) / V_ask(P + 1 tick) ≥ r
Relationships: Stacked imbalance, Bid-ask footprint, Footprint chart, Initiative buying, Initiative selling
Failure modes: The ratio threshold and diagonal convention are platform conventions, not market facts; in thick, slow markets imbalances are rare and in thin markets they are noise, so settings must be adapted per instrument.
Misconceptions: An imbalance is not an unfilled 'gap' that price must revisit — it is a record of one-sided executed aggression whose significance depends on whether price later accepts or rejects that zone.
Example: Ask volume of 900 at 4,512.25 versus bid volume of 250 at 4,512.00 gives a 3.6:1 diagonal ratio; the platform highlights a buy imbalance at that level.
Citation: Sierra Chart — Numbers Bars (Display Ask Bid Imbalance; Diagonal Comparison of Bid Volume and Ask Volume) — https://sierrachart.com/index.php?page=doc/NumbersBars.php (Diagonal Comparison of Bid Volume and Ask Volume)
Citation: FuturesIndicators — Trading With Market Profile: Practical Setups (imbalance defined as one side overwhelming the other by 3:1 or more) — https://futuresindicators.com/learn/trading-with-market-profile (Combining Market Profile With Footprint)
Status: Reviewed

0799. Stacked imbalance
Domain: Volume and order flow
Definition: A cluster of bid/ask imbalances occurring at several adjacent price levels within the same bar — typically three or more consecutive levels exceeding the imbalance ratio on the same side. It indicates sustained one-sided aggression across a price zone rather than at a single level.
Intuition: One lopsided level can be chance; a whole staircase of lopsided levels shows a determined initiative push through a zone.
Mechanics: Platforms scan each bar's diagonal bid/ask comparisons and highlight groups where the imbalance condition holds over a configurable number of consecutive levels; stacked buy imbalances near lows are often read as initiative buying, stacked sell imbalances near highs as initiative selling.
Relationships: Imbalance footprint, Bid-ask footprint, Initiative buying, Initiative selling, Footprint chart
Failure modes: Thresholds (ratio, number of levels) are arbitrary platform settings; stacked imbalances occur frequently in fast directional moves and many are immediately retraced, so they mark zones of interest rather than trade signals.
Misconceptions: Stacked imbalances are often treated as automatic support/resistance, but they only record where aggression was one-sided; if that aggression is absorbed and price closes through the zone, the levels fail like any other.
Example: During a drive off the low, a bar prints buy imbalances at four consecutive ticks; the platform marks a stacked buy imbalance, and the trader watches that zone as a potential pullback reference.
Citation: ATAS — Trading Indicators (Stacked Imbalance indicator) — https://atas.net/features/indicators/ (Assess the Market Imbalance)
Citation: Sierra Chart — Numbers Bars (Highlight Multiple Adjacent Bid or Ask Dominant Prices — Stacked Imbalance) — https://sierrachart.com/index.php?page=doc/NumbersBars.php (Input Settings for Numbers Bars)
Status: Reviewed

0800. Absorption
Domain: Volume and order flow
Definition: A market condition in which sustained aggressive market orders hit a price level but fail to move it, because resting limit orders repeatedly fill the incoming flow. Heavy traded volume with little or no price progress is the footprint signature of a large passive participant absorbing the aggressive side.
Intuition: It is like waves breaking against a seawall: the market orders keep arriving, but a wall of limit orders soaks them up and price refuses to budge.
Mechanics: Detected on footprint/tape as high bid- or ask-side volume at a level combined with stalled price (e.g., bearish candles with positive delta, or iceberg-style reloading of the displayed quote); iceberg orders are a formal special case in which a hidden-size limit order absorbs flow while displaying only a tip.
Relationships: Iceberg detection, Delta divergence, Selling climax, Exhaustion, Volume delta
Failure modes: Absorption is identifiable only after the fact at the level, and the absorbing side can pull its liquidity at any moment; apparent absorption can also be ordinary two-sided interest with no single large participant behind it.
Misconceptions: Absorption does not guarantee reversal — if the absorbing limit orders are eventually consumed, price breaks violently through the level; absorption marks a battle, not its outcome.
Example: Sellers hit the bid at 4,500 with 12,000 contracts over ten minutes yet price never trades below 4,499.75; the stalling on heavy sell-side volume marks absorption by passive buyers.
Citation: ATAS — How to read the order flow (absorption: limit orders absorb market orders, price doesn't move) — https://atas.net/blog/how-to-read-the-order-flow/ (What price movements are seen better on the order flow than on the candle chart?)
Citation: Bookmap Knowledge Base — Iceberg Orders Tracker (Iceberg orders vs Absorption) — https://bookmap.com/knowledgebase/docs/KB-Bookmap-Wiki-Iceberg-Orders-Tracker (Iceberg orders vs Absorption)
Status: Reviewed

0801. Exhaustion
Domain: Volume and order flow
Definition: The fading of aggressive order flow near the end of a move: successive pushes in the trend direction are made on shrinking market-order volume, showing that the initiating side is running out of participants willing to chase the price. On a footprint it appears as very small traded volume at the bar extreme compared with earlier bars in the move.
Intuition: The auction runs out of bidders: price may still tick to a new extreme, but almost nobody is left willing to trade there.
Mechanics: Read by comparing traded volume (or delta) at successive price extremes within a move — e.g., a new high made on a fraction of the market-buy volume of prior highs — often combined with delta divergence and a stalling of price progress.
Relationships: Absorption, Delta divergence, Climax volume, Dry-up volume, Volume divergence
Failure modes: Exhaustion readings are invisible without quality tick data and are confounded by time-of-day liquidity cycles; a paused initiative side can reload at any time, so exhaustion marks vulnerability, not a guaranteed turn.
Misconceptions: Exhaustion is not the same as a reversal signal — a move can end by drifting sideways for hours after exhaustion, and fading the first sign of weak volume at an extreme is a common way to get run over by trend days.
Example: ES makes a new session high, but only 48 market buy orders print at the top of the bar versus 600–900 at prior highs; the buyers are read as exhausted and price rotates back down.
Citation: ATAS — How to read the order flow (buyers 'exhausted' — insignificant buy volume at the high) — https://atas.net/blog/how-to-read-the-order-flow/ (Footprint examples)
Status: Reviewed

0802. Iceberg detection
Domain: Volume and order flow
Definition: The inference of iceberg orders — limit orders whose exchange-visible displayed size is only a small tip of a much larger hidden total — from market data. Because exchanges do not report the hidden size, detection algorithms watch for a displayed quote that keeps replenishing after executions, or trade volume at a price exceeding the displayed size.
Intuition: If the same 50-lot offer keeps reappearing after being hit and thousands of contracts trade through it, something much bigger is sitting below the waterline.
Mechanics: Track market-data dynamics rather than snapshots: with market-by-order data, new limit orders appearing instantly on the opposite side of executions at the same price reveal the reload; with lower-quality data, heuristics (trade size exceeding displayed size, repeated same-size refills) estimate it, always as an approximation.
Relationships: Absorption, Time and sales, Large-lot trade, Footprint chart
Failure modes: Detection is provably limited: hidden size and placement/cancellation moments cannot be observed, and data-vendor aggregation or channel splitting destroys the event sequence the algorithms depend on; high-frequency traders can also mimic icebergs with ordinary limit orders.
Misconceptions: A detected iceberg is not a guaranteed support/resistance wall — the owner can cancel instantly, and some large traders deliberately display iceberg-like behavior to mislead.
Example: The offer at 4,505 displays 100 lots; 2,400 contracts trade there while the display keeps refreshing at 100 — an iceberg tracker marks probable hidden selling, and the level holds as resistance.
Citation: Bookmap Knowledge Base — Iceberg Orders Tracker — https://bookmap.com/knowledgebase/docs/KB-Bookmap-Wiki-Iceberg-Orders-Tracker (Detection Methods and Algorithms)
Status: Reviewed

0803. Large-lot trade
Domain: Volume and order flow
Definition: A single executed trade (or an exchange-fragmented series of prints from one large order) whose size is far above the typical trade size for that instrument, taken in order-flow practice as a sign of institutional participation. Platforms surface them with filters that flag prints above absolute or adaptive size thresholds.
Intuition: Retail trades in ones and tens; when a 2,000-lot print hits the tape, someone with serious size is doing business.
Mechanics: Detected by scanning the time-and-sales stream for trades exceeding a fixed or adaptive threshold (platforms such as ATAS re-aggregate the fragmented prints exchange matching algorithms produce and mark the consolidated size on the chart).
Relationships: Block trade, Time and sales, Tape reading, Iceberg detection, Absorption
Failure modes: Large prints include spread rolls, block reporting, and opening/closing auction volume, which carry different information than directional institutional aggression; size thresholds that work in one volatility regime mislead in another.
Misconceptions: A large print is not automatically 'smart money' to follow — the initiator may be liquidating, hedging, or rolling, and the print says nothing about their remaining intent.
Example: On a day when the median ES trade is 3 contracts, the tape prints a single 1,800-lot at the offer near a session high; the platform flags it and the trader watches whether price accepts above that level.
Citation: ATAS — Trading Indicators (Big Trades: high-volume market trades, aggregated vs fragmented prints) — https://atas.net/features/indicators/ (Never Miss a Big Trade)
Status: Reviewed

0804. Block trade
Domain: Volume and order flow
Definition: A privately negotiated futures, options, or combination transaction that is permitted to be executed apart from the public auction market (the central limit order book) and is then submitted to the exchange for clearing. On CME Group venues, participation is restricted to Eligible Contract Participants as defined in the Commodity Exchange Act, and each product has a minimum quantity threshold (CME Rule 526 regime).
Intuition: Two institutions agree a big price privately, then hand the trade to the exchange to clear — letting size change hands without tipping off or sweeping the public order book.
Mechanics: Counterparties negotiate bilaterally (often via a broker), agree price and quantity at or above the product's block minimum, and report the trade to the exchange within prescribed time windows; the trade must be at a fair and reasonable price and is disseminated to market data after reporting.
Relationships: Large-lot trade, Time and sales, Absorption
Failure modes: Block prints hit the tape delayed and off-book, so they cannot be read as real-time aggressive flow; their price may diverge from the prevailing market because it reflects a negotiated package, not screen liquidity.
Misconceptions: A block trade is not an ordinary large market order sweeping the book, and its direction (buy or sell) is not publicly determinable from the print alone — it is a bilateral transfer.
Example: Two eligible counterparties privately negotiate a 500-lot Treasury futures block at a fair price and submit it to CME for clearing; the print appears in time and sales flagged as a block, away from the lit order book.
Citation: CME Group Client Systems Wiki — Trade Types (Block trade definition) — https://cmegroupclientsite.atlassian.net/wiki/display/EPICSANDBOX/Trade%2BTypes (OTC Products Cleared as Futures — Block)
Status: Reviewed

0805. Time and sales
Domain: Volume and order flow
Definition: A real-time, trade-by-trade record of executions in an instrument, showing for each trade its time, price, and volume (and typically direction relative to the bid/ask). It is the modern digital descendant of the ticker tape and the raw feed from which footprint and delta statistics are built.
Intuition: Time and sales is the market's transaction ledger: every fill, in sequence, with its size and price.
Mechanics: Exchanges disseminate each executed trade in market-data feeds; platforms render it as a scrolling table, often color-coded by whether the trade occurred at, inside, or outside the bid/ask, with filters by size or price to isolate large prints.
Relationships: Tape reading, Large-lot trade, Footprint chart, Bid volume, Ask volume
Failure modes: The raw stream is extremely fast in liquid markets and includes block reports, spreads, and auction prints that distort the apparent flow; aggregated feeds bundle multiple executions into one print, hiding sequence.
Misconceptions: Watching the tape does not reveal 'who' is trading — it shows anonymous executions; attribution to institutions or intent is inference, not data.
Example: A T&S window shows 100 XYZ at $65.84 at 12:31:54, upticked and colored at the ask, followed by three 2,500-share prints at the same price — the trader notes unusual size hitting the offer.
Citation: Investopedia — Understanding Time and Sales for Advanced Trading Strategies — https://www.investopedia.com/terms/t/time-and-sales.asp (What Are Time and Sales?)
Status: Reviewed

0806. Tape reading
Domain: Volume and order flow
Definition: The practice of inferring short-term buying and selling pressure by watching the stream of executed trades — originally the ticker tape, today the time-and-sales window — focusing on trade size, speed, and whether prints occur at the bid or the ask. It is one of the oldest forms of order-flow analysis, descending from the era of Wyckoff and Livermore.
Intuition: Instead of studying charts after the fact, the tape reader watches each transaction as it happens, sensing urgency from the rhythm and size of the prints.
Mechanics: The trader monitors the T&S stream for accelerating print rates, repeated large prints at the offer or bid, stalling price on heavy prints (absorption), and uptick/downtick sequences, forming an intraday read that complements or replaces chart analysis.
Relationships: Time and sales, Large-lot trade, Absorption, Footprint chart, Volume analysis
