Definition: A large, decisive version of a spring occurring at the end of an accumulation trading range, in which price breaks sharply below support and rapidly recovers, forcing the final transfer of shares from weak holders to large operators. The tutorial describes it as 'a spring on steroids'.
Intuition: The last violent flush that scares out everyone still holding, right before the real move up begins.
Mechanics: Like a spring, a terminal shakeout takes price below the range low late in the range, but with a deeper or more dramatic break and a fast, forceful recovery; a subsequent low-volume test of the shakeout low confirms that supply has been exhausted and the stock is ready to be marked up.
Relationships: Spring, Test of spring, Sign of strength, Wyckoff Phase C, Wyckoff accumulation
Failure modes: A deep break that fails to recover quickly is a genuine breakdown, not a shakeout; the label is only validated by the speed of recovery and a successful low-volume test afterward.
Misconceptions: Terminal shakeouts are not required for accumulation and are not identifiable in real time with certainty; many apparent shakeouts turn out to be the start of further declines.
Example: Near the end of a four-month base, a stock plunges 12% under the range low in two days on heavy volume, then reclaims the range within a week; a quiet retest on shrinking volume completes the terminal shakeout.
Citation: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett) — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/market-analysis/wyckoff-analysis-articles/the-wyckoff-method-a-tutorial (Accumulation: Wyckoff Events (note on springs and shakeouts))
Status: Reviewed

0848. Test of spring
Domain: Wyckoff
Definition: The Wyckoff event in which price revisits the low of a spring or shakeout to verify that supply is exhausted. A successful test makes a higher low (or holds near the spring low) on clearly lower volume, indicating the stock is ready for markup.
Intuition: After the fake breakdown, the market dips once more to double-check that no sellers remain; a quiet, low-volume dip passes the check.
Mechanics: Large operators repeatedly test the market for supply; after a spring, one or more tests revisit the spring low. The analyst compares volume and spread with the spring: a successful test shows significantly less volume and holds at or above the spring low, and is treated as a confirmation to initiate or add to long positions.
Relationships: Spring, Terminal shakeout, Secondary test, Sign of strength, No supply, Wyckoff Phase C
Failure modes: A test on volume that is not meaningfully lower, or one that undercuts the spring low decisively, negates the bullish reading; tests can also be repeated many times, delaying or preventing markup.
Misconceptions: The test does not need to exactly match the spring low, and a single successful test is not an absolute guarantee; it is one piece of evidence weighed with the sign of strength that should follow.
Example: After a spring to 87, a stock drifts back to 89 on the lightest volume in months and closes unchanged; the trader buys a partial position, treating it as a successful test of the spring.
Citation: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett) — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/market-analysis/wyckoff-analysis-articles/the-wyckoff-method-a-tutorial (Accumulation: Wyckoff Events (Test); A Five-Step Approach to the Market (Step 4))
Status: Reviewed

0849. Sign of strength
Domain: Wyckoff
Definition: The Wyckoff event (SOS) in which price advances on widening spread and relatively higher volume, showing demand in control; after accumulation, it often validates the preceding spring or test and typically carries price to or through the top of the trading range.
Intuition: The first rally with real conviction behind it, proving buyers have taken the wheel.
Mechanics: The analyst looks for rallies whose price bars widen in spread with expanding volume, in contrast to the narrowing, low-volume reactions of the range. An SOS following a spring confirms the bullish reading; a decisive SOS that crosses the range's resistance is called a 'jump across the creek'.
Relationships: Spring, Last point of support, Jump across the creek, Sign of weakness, Wyckoff Phase D, Law of effort versus result
Failure modes: A single strong bar can be an upthrust or a news-driven spike rather than genuine demand; an SOS that fails to hold its gains and falls back into the range negates the confirmation.
Misconceptions: An SOS is not simply 'a big green bar'; its meaning comes from context — appearing after accumulation events and being followed by shallow, low-volume reactions (LPSs).
Example: Following a spring at 87, a stock rallies from 91 to 104 on expanding volume and wide daily ranges, punching through the range top; the analyst labels the move an SOS and looks for a low-volume pullback to enter.
Citation: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett) — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/market-analysis/wyckoff-analysis-articles/the-wyckoff-method-a-tutorial (Accumulation: Wyckoff Events (SOS))
Status: Reviewed

0850. Last point of support
Domain: Wyckoff
Definition: The Wyckoff event (LPS) marking the low of a reaction or pullback after a sign of strength, typically a retreat to former resistance-turned-support on diminished spread and volume. It is regarded as a low-risk area to initiate or add to long positions before markup.
Intuition: After the breakout rally, the market takes one last quiet step back to the old ceiling, now a floor — the final boarding call for longs.
Mechanics: Once an SOS demonstrates demand, subsequent pullbacks are monitored: an LPS holds at or above prior resistance with narrowing spread and shrinking volume, indicating supply is exhausted. Despite the singular name, several LPSs can occur; Wyckoff's point-and-figure counts are conventionally anchored at the LPS level.
Relationships: Sign of strength, Backup to the edge of the creek, Jump across the creek, Last point of supply, Wyckoff Phase D, Point-and-figure count
Failure modes: A pullback labeled LPS can fail and re-enter the trading range, invalidating the markup scenario; distinguishing a healthy LPS from the start of a reversal is only possible as subsequent action unfolds.
Misconceptions: The LPS is not necessarily the last pullback ever, nor must it touch the exact old resistance; it is a zone defined by diminished volume and spread, not a precise price.
Example: After jumping above its 102 range top, a stock pulls back to 103 on half the breakout volume; the trader buys there with a stop below the old range, treating the dip as the LPS.
Citation: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett) — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/market-analysis/wyckoff-analysis-articles/the-wyckoff-method-a-tutorial (Accumulation: Wyckoff Events (LPS); Wyckoff Point and Figure (P&F) Count Guide)
Status: Reviewed

0851. Backup to the edge of the creek
Domain: Wyckoff
Definition: The Wyckoff event (BU) in which price pulls back toward the resistance it just crossed with a sign of strength, combining profit-taking with a test for remaining supply around the old resistance area. The term comes from Robert Evans's creek metaphor and precedes a more substantial markup.
Intuition: After leaping over the creek of resistance, the market walks back to the water's edge to make sure the far bank is solid before marching on.
Mechanics: Following a jump across the creek (SOS through resistance), price retreats on narrowing spread and lower volume toward the breakout area; a successful back-up holds above or near the old resistance and is treated as an entry or add-on point. A back-up can take several forms, from a simple pullback to a small new trading range at a higher level.
Relationships: Jump across the creek, Creek, Last point of support, Sign of strength, Wyckoff Phase D
Failure modes: A back-up that sinks decisively back into the trading range on expanding volume shows the breakout lacked sponsorship and often precedes a return to the range or a breakdown.
Misconceptions: A back-up is not merely any dip after a breakout; the Wyckoff reading depends on diminished volume and spread during the retreat and on the creek level acting as support.
Example: A stock jumps from 100 to 110 through range resistance, then drifts back to 104 on drying volume over five sessions; the analyst treats the drift as a back-up and adds to the long.
Citation: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett) — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/market-analysis/wyckoff-analysis-articles/the-wyckoff-method-a-tutorial (Accumulation: Wyckoff Events (BU))
Status: Reviewed

0852. Preliminary supply
Domain: Wyckoff
Definition: The Wyckoff event (PSY) in which large interests begin unloading shares in quantity after a pronounced advance, marked by expanding volume and widening price spread that signal a change of trend may be approaching. It mirrors preliminary support at market tops.
Intuition: The first time in a long climb that heavy selling shows up and noticeably slows the rise.
Mechanics: During an uptrend, the analyst watches for bars where volume and spread expand but upward progress stalls; that selling interest is labeled preliminary supply. PSY typically precedes the buying climax and begins Phase A of a distribution trading range.
Relationships: Wyckoff distribution, Wyckoff Phase A, Automatic reaction, Upthrust, Preliminary support
Failure modes: A single heavy-volume stall day can be absorbed and the advance can continue; PSY warns of possible topping but gives no information about how much further the rally may extend.
Misconceptions: Preliminary supply is not the top and does not warrant shorting by itself; confirmation requires the buying climax, automatic reaction, and secondary tests that follow.
Example: After doubling in a year, a stock posts record volume on a wide-range day that closes near unchanged; the analyst marks it as preliminary supply and watches for climactic buying.
Citation: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett) — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/market-analysis/wyckoff-analysis-articles/the-wyckoff-method-a-tutorial (Distribution: Wyckoff Events)
Status: Reviewed

0853. Automatic reaction
Domain: Wyckoff
Definition: The Wyckoff event (AR) in distribution in which price falls sharply after a buying climax because intense buying has been exhausted while heavy supply continues. Its low helps define the lower boundary of the distribution trading range.
Intuition: Once the euphoric buyers are spent, the price drops on its own weight — no extra selling pressure needed.
Mechanics: After the buying climax fills urgent public demand, the withdrawal of bids lets price decline quickly; the AR low, together with the climax high and subsequent secondary tests, sets the boundaries of the distribution range that the analyst uses for later labeling.
Relationships: Wyckoff distribution, Wyckoff Phase A, Upthrust, Sign of weakness, Automatic rally, Ice
Failure modes: The reaction is 'automatic' and can be brief; in a continuing bull market the dip is bought and the advance resumes, so an AR alone does not establish a top.
Misconceptions: The automatic reaction is not yet proof of distribution; it reflects exhausted buyers more than committed sellers, and its significance comes only from the range that develops around it.
Example: After a climax spike to 150 on record volume, a stock sinks to 136 within days on much lighter buying; the analyst draws the bottom of the developing distribution range near 136.
Citation: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett) — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/market-analysis/wyckoff-analysis-articles/the-wyckoff-method-a-tutorial (Distribution: Wyckoff Events)
Status: Reviewed

0854. Upthrust
Domain: Wyckoff
Definition: The Wyckoff event (UT) in which price moves above the resistance of a trading range and then quickly reverses to close back inside the range, acting as a test of remaining demand and a trap for uninformed breakout buyers. It is the mirror image of a spring.
Intuition: A fake breakout: price pops above resistance just long enough to hook breakout traders, then falls back into the range.
Mechanics: Price pushes above the resistance established by a buying climax or prior secondary tests, then reverses and closes below resistance. In Wyckoff analysis this shows large interests selling to breakout buyers; after an upthrust, price often tests the lower boundary of the range, and an upthrust occurring in Phase C of a distribution range is a candidate short area.
Relationships: Upthrust after distribution, Spring, Secondary test, Wyckoff distribution, Sign of weakness, No demand
Failure modes: Not every poke above resistance is an upthrust; if demand is genuine the breakout holds and becomes a jump to a higher range. Upthrusts also occur repeatedly in Phase B of ranges without any bearish resolution.
Misconceptions: An upthrust is not confirmed at its high; the bearish reading depends on the failure back into the range and subsequent weakness, and aggressive shorting at the first upthrust is repeatedly stopped out, as Wyckoff literature itself warns.
Example: A stock ranging between 136 and 150 spikes to 153 intraday but closes at 148; two weeks later it slides to the range bottom, completing the upthrust pattern.
Citation: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett) — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/market-analysis/wyckoff-analysis-articles/the-wyckoff-method-a-tutorial (Distribution: Wyckoff Events (ST/UT); Distribution: Wyckoff Phases (Phase C))
Status: Reviewed

0855. Upthrust after distribution
Domain: Wyckoff
Definition: The Wyckoff event (UTAD) occurring in the latter stages of a distribution trading range, in which price breaks above range resistance and then fails, providing a definitive test of new demand before markdown. It is the distributional counterpart of the spring and terminal shakeout in accumulation.
Intuition: One last fake breakout at the top of a topping range, engineered to squeeze shorts and unload remaining stock onto breakout buyers before the decline.
Mechanics: Late in distribution (Phase C), price breaks above the range high, then reverses back into the range. The UTAD tests whether sufficient demand remains to support higher prices; its failure confirms supply dominance and often precedes the sign of weakness and markdown. Like springs, a UTAD is not a required element of distribution.
Relationships: Upthrust, Wyckoff distribution, Wyckoff Phase C, Sign of weakness, Last point of supply, Terminal shakeout
Failure modes: A UTAD that holds above the range and is followed by strength invalidates the distribution reading; because it looks identical to a genuine breakout at first, shorting it early carries real squeeze risk.
Misconceptions: Distribution does not require a UTAD — the canonical schematics include distribution ranges with and without one — and a UTAD is not necessarily the range's absolute high.
Example: After five months of distribution between 136 and 150, a stock breaks to 155 for two days, then collapses back to 145 on heavy volume; the failed breakout is labeled a UTAD before the markdown begins.
Citation: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett) — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/market-analysis/wyckoff-analysis-articles/the-wyckoff-method-a-tutorial (Distribution: Wyckoff Events (UTAD))
Status: Reviewed

0856. Sign of weakness
Domain: Wyckoff
Definition: The Wyckoff event (SOW) in which price declines to or slightly below the lower boundary of a trading range on increased spread and volume, showing supply in control. Together with the automatic reaction, initial SOWs mark the change of character that precedes markdown.
Intuition: The first selloff with real conviction, proving sellers have taken control.
Mechanics: The analyst looks for down-moves whose bars widen in spread with expanding volume, breaking toward or through range support. A major SOW that decisively breaks the ice is often retested by a feeble rally that fails at or near the old support, offering a short entry before markdown resumes.
Relationships: Sign of strength, Fall through the ice, Last point of supply, Upthrust after distribution, Wyckoff Phase D, Wyckoff distribution
Failure modes: A single wide-range down bar can be a shakeout or news shock rather than genuine supply; an SOW that is quickly recovered on strength negates the bearish confirmation.
Misconceptions: An SOW is not merely 'a big red bar'; its meaning comes from context — appearing after distribution events and being followed by feeble, low-volume rallies (LPSYs).
Example: After a UTAD fails, a stock drops from 148 to 134 through its range floor on the heaviest volume in months; a weak bounce to 138 fails, confirming the SOW before markdown.
Citation: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett) — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/market-analysis/wyckoff-analysis-articles/the-wyckoff-method-a-tutorial (Distribution: Wyckoff Events (SOW))
Status: Reviewed

0857. Last point of supply
Domain: Wyckoff
Definition: The Wyckoff event (LPSY) in which a feeble rally on narrow spread follows a sign of weakness, showing the market's inability to advance because of weak demand, substantial supply, or both. LPSYs represent the final waves of large operators' distribution and preferred areas for short entries before markdown.
Intuition: After support breaks, the market stages one last tired bounce — the final chance to get out or get short before the drop.
Mechanics: Following a SOW, rallies are monitored for narrow spread and low volume, indicating exhausted demand; such rallies that fail at or below the broken support (ice) are labeled LPSYs. Despite the singular name, multiple LPSYs can occur during Phase D of distribution.
Relationships: Sign of weakness, Upthrust after distribution, Fall through the ice, Last point of support, Wyckoff Phase D, No demand
Failure modes: A rally labeled LPSY can regain strength and climb back into or above the range, invalidating the markdown scenario; the label is confirmed only by subsequent weakness.
Misconceptions: The LPSY is not necessarily the last rally ever, nor a precise price; it is a zone identified by narrow spread and poor volume on the rally, not by an exact level.
Example: After breaking support at 136, a stock bounces to 138 over four days on shrinking volume and small ranges; the trader shorts there with a stop above the ice, treating the bounce as an LPSY.
Citation: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett) — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/market-analysis/wyckoff-analysis-articles/the-wyckoff-method-a-tutorial (Distribution: Wyckoff Events (LPSY))
Status: Reviewed

0858. Wyckoff Phase A
Domain: Wyckoff
Definition: The first phase of a Wyckoff trading range, marking the stopping of the prior trend. In accumulation it contains preliminary support, the selling climax, the automatic rally, and secondary tests; in distribution it contains preliminary supply, the buying climax, the automatic reaction, and secondary tests.
Intuition: The moment the old trend finally runs out of gas — panic at bottoms, euphoria at tops — and the sideways battle begins.
Mechanics: Phase A transfers large volumes of shares between the public and professional interests through climactic price and volume action. The highs and lows formed during Phase A (climax and automatic move) set the boundaries of the trading range used in all subsequent analysis.
Relationships: Wyckoff Phase B, Preliminary support, Preliminary supply, Automatic rally, Automatic reaction, Secondary test
Failure modes: Trends can stop without climactic action, making Phase A hard to recognize; and climactic action can be followed by trend continuation rather than a range, so Phase A labeling is provisional until a range develops.
Misconceptions: Phase A does not require a dramatic climax — Wyckoff notes trends can end quietly with decreasing spread and volume — and a climax alone does not guarantee a reversal.
Example: A year-long slide ends with a high-volume support day (PS), a panic flush (SC), a sharp bounce (AR), and a quiet retest (ST); the analyst marks these four events as Phase A and draws range boundaries at the AR high and SC low.
Citation: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett) — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/market-analysis/wyckoff-analysis-articles/the-wyckoff-method-a-tutorial (Accumulation: Wyckoff Phases (Phase A); Distribution: Wyckoff Phases (Phase A))
Status: Reviewed

0859. Wyckoff Phase B
Domain: Wyckoff
Definition: The second phase of a Wyckoff trading range, in which institutions build a 'cause' for the next trend by accumulating (or distributing) inventory over an extended period, sometimes a year or more. Its characteristic back-and-forth price action reflects large operators buying low and checking rallies (or the reverse in distribution).
Intuition: The long, boring middle of the range where the big players quietly load or unload the truck, one oscillation at a time.
Mechanics: Within the Phase A boundaries, price swings repeatedly between support and resistance. Early swings are wide with high volume; as professionals absorb supply (accumulation) or demand (distribution), volume on counter-swings diminishes. Multiple secondary tests and upthrust-type actions occur, and the aggregate horizontal extent of Phase B largely determines the point-and-figure count and hence the price objective.
Relationships: Wyckoff Phase A, Wyckoff Phase C, Law of cause and effect, Point-and-figure count, Secondary test, Wyckoff accumulation
Failure modes: Phase B can extend far longer than expected, exhausting the analyst's patience and capital; the range can also resolve opposite to the presumed accumulation or distribution reading.
Misconceptions: Phase B is not dead time to be traded aggressively in both directions; its function is cause-building, and the balance of volume on rallies versus reactions — not the day-to-day noise — carries the analytical information.
Example: For nine months a stock oscillates between 90 and 102; volume on declines shrinks steadily while rallies hold their gains, and the analyst reads Phase B accumulation and measures a 20-column P&F count.
Citation: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett) — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/market-analysis/wyckoff-analysis-articles/the-wyckoff-method-a-tutorial (Accumulation: Wyckoff Phases (Phase B); Distribution: Wyckoff Phases (Phase B))
Status: Reviewed

0860. Wyckoff Phase C
Domain: Wyckoff
Definition: The third phase of a Wyckoff trading range, in which price undergoes a decisive test of remaining supply (accumulation) or demand (distribution), allowing large operators to judge whether the market is ready to leave the range. Springs, shakeouts, upthrusts, and UTADs are the characteristic Phase C events.
Intuition: The final exam: one engineered fake move probes whether any sellers (at bottoms) or buyers (at tops) are still out there.
Mechanics: In accumulation, a spring or shakeout below range support tests supply; a low-volume break that quickly recovers indicates readiness for markup and offers a high-probability long entry. In distribution, an upthrust or UTAD above range resistance tests demand; its failure indicates readiness for markdown. When testing occurs higher in the range without a spring, Phase C identification is more difficult.
Relationships: Spring, Terminal shakeout, Upthrust, Upthrust after distribution, Wyckoff Phase B, Wyckoff Phase D, Test of spring
Failure modes: The Phase C test can fail — a spring that keeps falling or an upthrust that keeps rising invalidates the range reading — and ranges without a clear test make Phase C easy to mislabel in real time.
Misconceptions: Phase C does not require a spring or UTAD; these are optional, and forcing the label onto every minor penetration of range boundaries is a common misreading.
Example: A stock dips under its six-month base on the lightest volume of the range and closes back inside it the same day (spring); the analyst declares Phase C and buys a starter position.
Citation: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett) — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/market-analysis/wyckoff-analysis-articles/the-wyckoff-method-a-tutorial (Accumulation: Wyckoff Phases (Phase C); Distribution: Wyckoff Phases (Phase C))
Status: Reviewed

0861. Wyckoff Phase D
Domain: Wyckoff
Definition: The fourth phase of a Wyckoff trading range, in which demand (accumulation) or supply (distribution) becomes consistently dominant: advances widen in spread and volume while reactions shrink, carrying price at least to the range boundary. LPSs and LPSYs in this phase are the framework's preferred position-entry areas.
Intuition: The tug-of-war ends and one side visibly wins — rallies get stronger and pullbacks weaker (or vice versa) as price presses toward the range edge.
Mechanics: The analyst verifies the Phase C conclusion by observing the character of subsequent swings: in accumulation, signs of strength on widening spread and volume alternate with shallow, low-volume reactions (LPSs) as price moves to or through the top of the range; in distribution, signs of weakness alternate with feeble rallies (LPSYs) as price moves to or through support.
Relationships: Sign of strength, Sign of weakness, Last point of support, Last point of supply, Wyckoff Phase C, Wyckoff Phase E
Failure modes: The expected dominance can fail to materialize — price returns to mid-range and the phase labels must be revised; entering on an LPS/LPSY assumes Phase D is underway, which is only confirmed by later action.
Misconceptions: Phase D is not the same as the trend itself; the decisive exit from the range belongs to Phase E, and treating every approach to the range edge as a breakout invites losses on failed moves.
Example: After a spring, a stock makes two widening-spread rallies to the top of its range, each followed by shallow low-volume dips; the analyst buys the second dip (LPS) anticipating Phase E markup.
Citation: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett) — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/market-analysis/wyckoff-analysis-articles/the-wyckoff-method-a-tutorial (Accumulation: Wyckoff Phases (Phase D); Distribution: Wyckoff Phases (Phase D))
Status: Reviewed

0862. Wyckoff Phase E
Domain: Wyckoff
Definition: The final phase of a Wyckoff trading range, in which price departs the range and the new trend (markup or markdown) unfolds in the open, with demand or supply in full control. Setbacks are typically short-lived, and new higher- or lower-level ranges (reaccumulation or redistribution 'stepping stones') may form along the way.
Intuition: The range is over and the real move begins — the trend is now obvious to everyone.
Mechanics: Price breaks out of the trading range and trends; pullbacks after markup begins are brief and shallow, and broken support in markdown is often retested by failing rallies. Traders trail stops and may add positions at stepping-stone consolidations, whose point-and-figure counts can confirm the original range's price target.
Relationships: Wyckoff Phase D, Wyckoff reaccumulation, Wyckoff redistribution, Jump across the creek, Fall through the ice, Point-and-figure count
Failure modes: Breakouts into Phase E can fail, returning price to the range; as the trend matures toward the P&F objective, the risk of a new accumulation or distribution range (i.e., a reversal) increases.
Misconceptions: Phase E does not mean risk-free trending; Wyckoff treats P&F targets as places to 'stop, look and listen', not guaranteed endpoints, and stepping-stone ranges can turn into reversal structures.
Example: A stock leaves its 90-102 base and trends to 130 with only two brief pauses; the holder trails stops and watches a small mid-trend range whose count confirms the original 130 target.
Citation: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett) — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/market-analysis/wyckoff-analysis-articles/the-wyckoff-method-a-tutorial (Accumulation: Wyckoff Phases (Phase E); Distribution: Wyckoff Phases (Phase E))
Status: Reviewed

0863. Law of supply and demand
Domain: Wyckoff
Definition: Wyckoff's first law: when demand exceeds supply, prices rise; when supply exceeds demand, prices fall; and the balance is judged by comparing price and volume bars on a chart. It is the foundational heuristic of the method, a framework for reading charts rather than a measurable law of nature.
Intuition: More buyers than sellers pushes price up, more sellers than buyers pushes it down — and the tape tells you which side is winning.
Mechanics: The analyst compares consecutive bars' spread, close location, and volume: wide-spread bars closing near highs on rising volume indicate demand, while wide-spread bars closing near lows on rising volume indicate supply. This bar-by-bar reading underlies the labeling of all Wyckoff events and phases.
Relationships: Law of cause and effect, Law of effort versus result, Wyckoff method, No demand, No supply
Failure modes: The principle is tautological at the margin — price always moves to equilibrate orders — and reading which side is 'really' in control from bar data is subjective and error-prone, especially in news-driven or illiquid markets.
Misconceptions: It is called a law but is an analytical guideline; volume and spread do not reveal institutional intent mechanically, and accurate supply/demand reading takes substantial practice, as Wyckoff teaching itself concedes.
Example: During a pullback, each successive down-bar has narrower spread and lower volume, while the following rally expands in both; the analyst concludes demand dominates supply and the uptrend should resume.
Citation: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett) — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/market-analysis/wyckoff-analysis-articles/the-wyckoff-method-a-tutorial (The Basic Principles: Three Wyckoff Laws (Law 1); Supply and Demand Analysis)
Status: Reviewed

0864. Law of cause and effect
Domain: Wyckoff
Definition: Wyckoff's second law: the horizontal extent of accumulation or distribution within a trading range (the 'cause') is related to the distance of the subsequent trend out of that range (the 'effect'), allowing price objectives to be projected from point-and-figure counts. It is a heuristic projection technique, not a deterministic relationship.
Intuition: The longer and harder you compress the spring inside a range, the further price travels when it's released.
Mechanics: The cause is measured by counting columns horizontally across a point-and-figure chart of the trading range (anchored at the LPS or count line); multiplying the column count by the box size and reversal criterion yields the projected effect, added to the count line, the range low, and their midpoint to produce a target zone.
Formula: Effect ≈ n x B x R, where n = number of P&F columns at the count line, B = box size, R = reversal criterion (e.g. 3); price target zone = count-line level, range low, and their midpoint, each plus (for markup) or minus (for markdown) the effect.
Relationships: Law of supply and demand, Law of effort versus result, Point-and-figure count, Wyckoff Phase B, Wyckoff Phase E
Failure modes: Column counts are sensitive to box size and to subjective choices of where the range and count line begin and end; some moves fall well short of or far exceed their projections, so targets are zones of caution, not certainties.
Misconceptions: The projected target is not a promised destination; Wyckoff teaching explicitly says counts should be treated as 'stop, look and listen' points rather than exact turning levels.
Example: A 20-column count on a 1-point, 3-box-reversal P&F chart of a base gives a 60-point effect; added to the count line at 100, the analyst watches the 160 area for the trend to pause or end.
Citation: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett) — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/market-analysis/wyckoff-analysis-articles/the-wyckoff-method-a-tutorial (The Basic Principles: Three Wyckoff Laws (Law 2); Wyckoff Point and Figure (P&F) Count Guide)
Status: Reviewed

0865. Law of effort versus result
Domain: Wyckoff
Definition: Wyckoff's third law: divergences between volume (effort) and price movement (result) provide early warning of a possible change of trend. Harmony between effort and result suggests trend continuation; large effort with little result suggests absorption by large interests and a potential turn.
Intuition: If the market is pushing hard but going nowhere, someone big is standing in the way — and the direction of travel is about to change.
Mechanics: The analyst compares volume with the price progress it produces: several high-volume, narrow-range bars after a long rally that fail to make new highs indicate unloading into demand (bearish divergence); heavy volume on a decline that produces little downward progress at support indicates absorption (bullish). Rising volume with expanding price progress confirms trend harmony.
Relationships: Law of supply and demand, Law of cause and effect, Sign of strength, Sign of weakness, Wyckoff method
Failure modes: Effort/result judgments are relative and subjective; high-volume churn can also reflect genuine two-sided disagreement, index rebalancing, or news, and divergences can persist for long periods before any turn materializes.
Misconceptions: A single effort-result divergence is not a reversal signal by itself; Wyckoff applies it as an early warning weighed alongside the position within the price cycle and the nine buying or selling tests.
Example: After a long advance, a stock prints three consecutive near-record volume days that close nearly unchanged; the analyst reads large effort with no result as distribution and tightens stops.
Citation: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett) — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/market-analysis/wyckoff-analysis-articles/the-wyckoff-method-a-tutorial (The Basic Principles: Three Wyckoff Laws (Law 3); Supply and Demand Analysis)
Status: Reviewed

0866. Point-and-figure count
Domain: Wyckoff
Definition: Wyckoff's method of projecting price targets by counting the horizontal width of a trading range on a point-and-figure chart, embodying the law of cause and effect. The count measures the 'cause' built in the range and converts it into a projected 'effect' — a target zone rather than an exact destination.
Intuition: Measure how wide the base is, and that width tells you roughly how far the breakout should travel.
Mechanics: On a P&F chart of the range, the analyst selects a count line (typically at the LPS level after an SOS), counts columns from right to left phase by phase, multiplies the column tally by the box size and reversal criterion, and adds the product to the count line (maximum objective), the range low (minimum objective), and their midpoint. Stepping-stone consolidations later in the trend can produce confirming counts with smaller box sizes.
Formula: Target zone = anchor level +/- (n x B x R), where n = number of columns at the count line, B = box size (e.g. 0.5-1 point for low-priced stocks, ~100 for the DJIA), R = reversal criterion (typically 3); anchors are the count line, the trading-range low, and their midpoint (+ for markup targets, - for markdown targets).
Relationships: Law of cause and effect, Last point of support, Wyckoff Phase B, Wyckoff Phase E, Wyckoff method
Failure modes: Results are highly sensitive to box size, count-line placement, and phase segmentation, all of which are discretionary; Wyckoff himself cautioned that some counts fall short and others are exceeded, so targets must be confirmed by bar-chart price and volume action.
Misconceptions: P&F targets are not precise reversal points; the count guide explicitly frames them as places to 'stop, look and listen', and P&F 'phases' used for counting are not the same as Phases A-E of range analysis.
Example: On a 100-point-box, 3-box-reversal chart of a DJIA consolidation, a 34-column count projects 34 x 100 x 3 = 10,200 points of effect; added to the range low and count line, this yields a minimum-to-maximum target band for the ensuing rally.
Citation: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett) — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/market-analysis/wyckoff-analysis-articles/the-wyckoff-method-a-tutorial (Wyckoff Point and Figure (P&F) Count Guide)
Citation: Wyckoff Market Analysis (StockCharts.com ChartSchool) — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/market-analysis/wyckoff-analysis-articles/wyckoff-market-analysis (Price Projections)
Status: Reviewed

0867. Creek
Domain: Wyckoff
Definition: A Wyckoff metaphor, coined by teacher Robert Evans, for the zone of resistance at the upper boundary of an accumulation trading range — the 'creek' that price must jump across to begin markup. It is informal terminology for resistance, not a distinct technical pattern.
Intuition: Resistance is pictured as a stream of sellers; the market has to gather enough strength to leap over it.
Mechanics: The creek level is approximated by the highs of rallies within the accumulation range (often the automatic-rally high and later upthrusts). A decisive advance through it on widening spread and volume is a 'jump across the creek' (SOS); a subsequent low-volume pullback to the creek area is a 'back-up to the creek'.
Relationships: Jump across the creek, Backup to the edge of the creek, Ice, Sign of strength, Automatic rally
Failure modes: Because the creek is a zone rather than a precise line, analysts disagree on its placement; failed jumps that fall back into the range show the level was misjudged or demand insufficient.
Misconceptions: The creek is a teaching metaphor, not a Wyckoff event with formal rules; it appears in the Evans/Pruden tradition rather than in Wyckoff's original course terminology.
Example: An analyst marks the 100-102 zone, where three rallies died inside a base, as the creek; when price later clears 103 on heavy volume, she calls it a jump across the creek.
Citation: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett) — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/market-analysis/wyckoff-analysis-articles/the-wyckoff-method-a-tutorial (Accumulation: Wyckoff Events (BU))
Status: Reviewed

0868. Ice
Domain: Wyckoff
Definition: A Wyckoff metaphor for the zone of support at the lower boundary of a distribution trading range, defined by the lows of the reactions within the range. Price that breaks decisively through it has 'fallen through the ice', marking the transition to markdown.
Intuition: Support is pictured as a frozen surface holding the market up; once it cracks, price plunges into the water below.
Mechanics: The ice is drawn at the lows of the reactions in the range (often simplified to the range's support level, though it can sit higher up depending on where reaction lows cluster). A fall through the ice on wide downside spreads and high volume confirms supply dominance; a subsequent feeble rally back toward the ice zone is treated as a prime short-entry area.
Relationships: Fall through the ice, Creek, Sign of weakness, Last point of supply, Wyckoff distribution
Failure modes: Ice is a zone, not a precise line, so penetrations without the characteristic wide spread and volume may be shakeouts rather than genuine breaks; a quick recovery back above the ice negates the breakdown reading.
Misconceptions: The ice is not always identical to the range's lowest support line — it is defined by the cluster of reaction lows — and the term is metaphorical shorthand rather than a formally defined event.
Example: A distribution range's reaction lows cluster at 136-138, which the analyst marks as the ice; a high-volume drop to 130 is a fall through the ice, and the weak bounce to 137 is shorted.
Citation: Primary Selling Opportunity - Rally Back to the Ice (Last Point of Supply) (Wyckoff Stock Market Institute) — https://wyckoffsmi.com/rally-back-to-the-ice/ (entire article)
Status: Reviewed

0869. Jump across the creek
Domain: Wyckoff
Definition: The Wyckoff metaphor for a sign of strength that decisively carries price above the resistance ('creek') of an accumulation trading range, signaling that demand has overcome the range's supply. It marks the transition from Phase D toward Phase E markup.
Intuition: The market finally leaps over the stream of sellers that capped every rally in the base.
Mechanics: After accumulation phases A-C, price advances through the range's resistance zone on widening spread and relatively high volume. The jump is conventionally confirmed by a subsequent 'back-up to the creek' — a low-volume pullback that holds above the former resistance, now acting as support.
Relationships: Creek, Backup to the edge of the creek, Sign of strength, Last point of support, Wyckoff Phase D, Wyckoff Phase E
Failure modes: A jump that lacks volume or quickly falls back into the range is a failed breakout (potentially an upthrust if the range was actually distribution); confirmation via the back-up is essential.
Misconceptions: Crossing resistance by any amount is not automatically a jump; the Wyckoff reading requires the price-volume character of an SOS, not merely a marginal new high.
Example: After months between 90 and 102, a stock rallies through 103 on triple average volume; a quiet dip to 101 holds, and the analyst treats the move as a confirmed jump across the creek.
Citation: The Wyckoff Method: A Tutorial (StockCharts.com ChartSchool, by Roman Bogomazov and Michael Lipsett) — https://chartschool.stockcharts.com/table-of-contents/market-analysis/wyckoff-analysis-articles/the-wyckoff-method-a-tutorial (Accumulation: Wyckoff Events (BU))
Status: Reviewed

0870. Fall through the ice
Domain: Wyckoff
Definition: The Wyckoff metaphor for a decisive downside break through the support ('ice') of a distribution trading range on wide price spreads and high or increasing volume, constituting a major sign of weakness and the first step of the markdown phase.
Intuition: The frozen floor under the market cracks and price plunges through — the downtrend has begun in earnest.
Mechanics: After distribution is complete, price breaks the ice with wide downside spreads, poor closes, and expanding volume, ideally pushing decisively below the support zone. The subsequent 'rally back to the ice' — a feeble recovery toward the broken support, often retracing about half the fall — is treated as the theoretically best short entry, with stops placed above the ice.
Relationships: Ice, Sign of weakness, Last point of supply, Wyckoff distribution, Wyckoff Phase E, Creek
Failure modes: Penetrations that lack the characteristic spread and volume, or that do not decisively clear the ice, can be shakeouts and even buying opportunities; a strong rally back through the ice zone invalidates the breakdown.
Misconceptions: Any tick below support is not a fall through the ice; the pattern requires a decisive break with confirming price-volume behavior, and its short-side edge depends on the character of the rally back.
Example: A stock's distribution range holds 136 support three times; it then drops to 128 in two sessions on heavy volume — a fall through the ice — and the analyst shorts the weak bounce to 133 with a stop above 137.
Citation: Primary Selling Opportunity - Rally Back to the Ice (Last Point of Supply) (Wyckoff Stock Market Institute) — https://wyckoffsmi.com/rally-back-to-the-ice/ (entire article)
Status: Reviewed

0871. No demand
Domain: Wyckoff
Definition: A price-volume indication, formalized in Tom Williams's Wyckoff-derived Volume Spread Analysis, of a deficit of buyers: typically an up-bar on narrow spread closing mid-range or lower on volume below that of the previous two bars. It signals that professional money is not interested in higher prices at that moment and warns of possible weakness ahead.
Intuition: The price ticks up but almost nobody is buying — a rally running on fumes.
Mechanics: The analyst flags narrow-spread up-bars (or down-bars making a higher high) with volume clearly below the prior two bars, then weighs the market background: near old tops or after signs of weakness, no-demand bars suggest shorts and exits from longs; after signs of strength, they may merely mark a pause. Confirmation comes from a subsequent down-bar on rising volume.
Relationships: No supply, Law of supply and demand, Law of effort versus result, Upthrust, Last point of supply, Sign of weakness
Failure modes: Isolated low-volume up-bars are common in quiet sessions, holidays, and strong uptrends (where supply, not demand, is what is absent); acting on a single bar without background context is a known trap of the pattern.
Misconceptions: No demand does not mean price must fall immediately — in a strong background it often precedes only a brief rest — and the pattern is a process that can unfold over several bars, not a single-bar mechanical signal.
Example: Bitcoin grinds to 9,500 on volume half its average and closes mid-bar; the next day a high-volume down-bar begins a multi-week decline, validating the no-demand reading.
Citation: VSA and cluster analysis. No Demand and No Supply (ATAS blog, describing Tom Williams's Volume Spread Analysis) — https://atas.net/blog/vsa-and-cluster-analysis-no-demand-and-no-supply/ (No Demand)
Status: Reviewed

0872. No supply
Domain: Wyckoff
Definition: A price-volume indication, formalized in Tom Williams's Wyckoff-derived Volume Spread Analysis, of a deficit of sellers: typically a down-bar on narrow spread closing off its low on volume below that of the previous two bars. It indicates that selling pressure has dried up and, in the right context, that higher prices are likely; Williams also called it a 'test of supply' and favored it for long entries.
Intuition: The price dips but almost nobody is selling — the path of least resistance is back up.
Mechanics: The analyst flags narrow-spread down-bars with volume clearly below the prior two bars, then weighs the background: after a spring or during a low-volume reaction in accumulation, no-supply bars confirm supply exhaustion and support long entries. A successful test of supply is conventionally followed by an up-bar or sign of strength.
Relationships: No demand, Test of spring, Secondary test, Law of supply and demand, Law of effort versus result, Sign of strength
Failure modes: Low-volume dips occur constantly in quiet markets and can precede renewed selling; without a bullish background (accumulation, prior spring or test), a no-supply bar has little predictive content.
Misconceptions: No supply does not guarantee a rally — it only shows sellers stepped back at that moment — and it is not simply any low-volume red bar; spread, close location, and context all matter.
Example: After a spring low, a stock drifts down on two narrow-range bars with volume at a month low and closes off the lows; the next session's wide-spread rally confirms the no-supply test and the trader buys.
Citation: VSA and cluster analysis. No Demand and No Supply (ATAS blog, describing Tom Williams's Volume Spread Analysis) — https://atas.net/blog/vsa-and-cluster-analysis-no-demand-and-no-supply/ (No Supply (Test of Supply))
Status: Reviewed

0873. Moneyness
Domain: Options
Definition: Moneyness is the position of an underlying asset's price relative to an option's strike price, classifying the option as in-the-money (positive intrinsic value if exercised now), at-the-money (strike equals the current price), or out-of-the-money (zero intrinsic value). It can be measured against spot or against the forward price, and quantified numerically, e.g., by log-moneyness or by the option's delta.
Intuition: Moneyness tells you whether an option would be worth anything if it expired right now, and roughly how much 'cushion' it has.
Mechanics: Simple moneyness is S/K (or its reciprocal); log-moneyness is ln(F/K); standardized moneyness divides ln(F/K) by sigma*sqrt(T) to express moneyness in standard deviations. Calls are ITM when S > K, puts when S < K. Delta is a common practical proxy for percent moneyness.
Formula: Simple moneyness M = F/K (or S/K); standardized moneyness m = ln(F/K) / (sigma*sqrt(T)), where F is the forward price, K the strike, sigma implied volatility, T time to expiry.
Relationships: In-the-money option, At-the-money option, Out-of-the-money option, Intrinsic value, Delta, Volatility surface
Failure modes: Spot-based moneyness misclassifies options when carry is large (high rates or dividends); forward-based (ATMF) classification is then more meaningful. Delta-as-moneyness breaks down for long-dated or high-volatility options where delta diverges from the risk-neutral probability of finishing ITM.
Misconceptions: Moneyness is not a statement about profitability of the position — an ITM long option can still be a losing trade if the premium paid exceeds the intrinsic value realized. 'At-the-money' in practice usually means nearest strike, not exact equality.
Example: With stock at $100, the $95 call is in-the-money by $5, the $100 call is at-the-money, and the $105 call is out-of-the-money; for puts the relationship is reversed.
Citation: Moneyness — Wikipedia — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moneyness (Definition and measures of moneyness)
Status: Reviewed

0874. In-the-money option
Domain: Options
Definition: An in-the-money (ITM) option is an option with positive intrinsic value: a call whose strike is below the current underlying price, or a put whose strike is above it. Its premium equals intrinsic value plus any remaining time value.
Intuition: An ITM option is already 'winning' — exercising it immediately would capture real value, so most of its price moves one-for-one with the underlying.
Mechanics: Intrinsic value = max(S - K, 0) for calls and max(K - S, 0) for puts. ITM options have deltas approaching +1 (calls) or -1 (puts) and are the ones exercised (or automatically exercised) at expiration.
Formula: Intrinsic value: call = max(S - K, 0); put = max(K - S, 0). Total premium = intrinsic value + time value.
Relationships: Moneyness, At-the-money option, Out-of-the-money option, Deep in-the-money option, Exercise-by-exception, Delta
Failure modes: Deep ITM options are illiquid and wide bid-ask spreads can erode the apparent value; holders of ITM American options also carry early-assignment and dividend considerations. Time value can be negative for deep ITM European puts under discounting.
Misconceptions: Being ITM does not mean the trade is profitable — an option bought for $8 that is now $5 ITM is still a losing position. ITM short options can be assigned at any time (American style), not only at expiration.
Example: With stock at $55, the $50 call is $5 in-the-money; if it trades at $6.20, then $5 is intrinsic value and $1.20 is time value.
Citation: Moneyness — Wikipedia — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moneyness (In the money)
Citation: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Intrinsic Value)
Status: Reviewed

0875. At-the-money option
Domain: Options
Definition: An at-the-money (ATM) option is an option whose strike price equals (or is nearest to) the current price of the underlying; in forward terms (ATMF) the strike equals the forward price. An ATM option has no intrinsic value — its entire premium is time value.
Intuition: The ATM option is the coin-flip strike: it sits exactly at the boundary between finishing valuable and finishing worthless, which makes it the most sensitive to volatility and time.
Mechanics: ATM options have delta near +0.5 (calls) or -0.5 (puts), the highest gamma and theta of the chain, and vega near its maximum. ATM implied volatility is the standard quoting benchmark from which skew/smile adjustments are measured.
Relationships: Moneyness, In-the-money option, Out-of-the-money option, Long straddle, Gamma, Theta
Failure modes: Because gamma and theta peak ATM, hedging errors and time-decay estimates are largest here, especially into expiration when tiny price moves flip the option between ITM and OTM (pin risk).
Misconceptions: ATM does not mean a 50/50 real-world probability of profit — the buyer must overcome the premium, so the breakeven lies beyond the strike; also, 'ATM spot' and 'ATM forward' strikes differ when rates or dividends are material.
Example: With stock at $100.10, the $100 strike is treated as at-the-money; its call might trade at $2.50, entirely time value.
Citation: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (At-the-Money)
Citation: Moneyness — Wikipedia — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moneyness (At the money)
Status: Reviewed

0876. Out-of-the-money option
Domain: Options
Definition: An out-of-the-money (OTM) option is an option with no intrinsic value: a call whose strike is above the current underlying price, or a put whose strike is below it. Its premium consists entirely of time value, and it expires worthless if still OTM at expiration.
Intuition: An OTM option is a lottery-like claim: cheap, but it only pays if the underlying moves far enough before time runs out.
Mechanics: OTM options have small absolute deltas, lower premiums, and percentage-wise high sensitivity to volatility. The CFTC glossary example: a call with a $400 strike on gold trading at $390 is $10 out-of-the-money.
Formula: Intrinsic value = 0; premium = time value only.
Relationships: Moneyness, In-the-money option, Deep out-of-the-money option, Volatility smile, Delta
Failure modes: Most OTM options expire worthless, so repeated buying of cheap OTM options bleeds capital; conversely, OTM sellers face gap risk — a sudden large move can convert small premium income into large losses. Skew means OTM equity puts are often relatively expensive.
Misconceptions: 'Cheap' OTM options are not necessarily good value: their price already embeds the market's implied probability of the required move, and the probability-weighted expected payoff is typically less than the premium after costs.
Example: With stock at $100, the $110 call is OTM and might trade at $0.40; unless the stock exceeds $110 at expiration it expires worthless and the buyer loses the $40 per contract.
Citation: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Out-Of-The-Money)
Citation: Moneyness — Wikipedia — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moneyness (Out of the money)
Status: Reviewed

0877. Deep in-the-money option
Domain: Options
Definition: A deep in-the-money option is an option whose strike is far enough inside the money that its time value is negligible and its price moves almost one-for-one with the underlying (delta near +1 for calls, -1 for puts). 'Deep' is an informal descriptor with no fixed regulatory threshold.
Intuition: A deep ITM option behaves almost like a leveraged surrogate for the stock itself, with most of its value being intrinsic.
Mechanics: Premium approximates intrinsic value plus minimal time value; gamma, vega, and theta are near zero. Deep ITM American calls on dividend stocks and deep ITM puts are the prime early-exercise candidates because remaining time value can fall below the value of capturing the dividend or strike interest.
Relationships: In-the-money option, Moneyness, Delta, Early exercise, Dividend risk
Failure modes: Deep ITM strikes are often illiquid with wide bid-ask spreads, so entry/exit costs can exceed the residual time value. Deep ITM European options can trade below intrinsic value due to discounting.
Misconceptions: Deep ITM calls are not identical to owning stock: they receive no dividends, and holders must still act (sell or exercise) before expiration; brokers may also auto-exercise them, creating an unintended stock position.
Example: With stock at $150, the $100 call is deep ITM and might trade at $50.30 — $50 intrinsic value plus $0.30 time value, with delta near 1.0.
Citation: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Delta Margining (deep out-of-the-money / futures-equivalent usage))
Citation: Moneyness — Wikipedia — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moneyness (Intrinsic value and time value)
Status: Reviewed

0878. Deep out-of-the-money option
Domain: Options
Definition: A deep out-of-the-money option is an option whose strike is far from the current underlying price, so it has no intrinsic value, a very small delta, and a premium close to zero that consists only of time value. 'Deep' is informal; no fixed threshold defines it.
Intuition: A deep OTM option is a cheap tail-risk ticket: it almost always expires worthless but can multiply in value during extreme moves.
Mechanics: Price is dominated by the implied probability of a large move (fat tails and skew make these options systematically pricier than lognormal models suggest). Delta-based margin systems treat, e.g., ten deep OTM options with delta 0.20 as two futures-equivalent contracts.
Relationships: Out-of-the-money option, Moneyness, Volatility smile, Delta, Backspread
Failure modes: Black-Scholes-style models underprice deep OTM options when return distributions have fat tails — a key lesson of the 1987 crash. Deep OTM quotes are wide and stale, so mark-to-model and end-of-day pricing can be unreliable.
Misconceptions: A near-zero price does not mean 'free optionality': the tiny premium reflects a tiny probability-weighted payoff, and repeatedly selling deep OTM options concentrates exposure to rare, severe losses (picking up pennies in front of a steamroller).
Example: With the S&P 500 at 5,000, a 30-day 4,000-strike put is deep OTM and may trade for a few cents, yet it is exactly the instrument that pays off in a crash.
Citation: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Delta Margining (deep out-of-the-money example))
Citation: Black–Scholes model — Wikipedia — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black%E2%80%93Scholes_model (Black–Scholes in practice (deep OTM underpricing))
Status: Reviewed

0879. Option chain
Domain: Options
Definition: An option chain is a quotation display listing all available option series for a given underlying — typically every strike and expiration for both calls and puts — together with bids, asks, last prices, volume, open interest, and often implied volatility and Greeks.
Intuition: The option chain is the menu of every option available on a stock or index, laid out so you can compare strikes and expirations at a glance.
Mechanics: Chains are organized by expiration date and strike, with calls and puts shown side by side. Traders read chains to select strikes for strategies, gauge liquidity via volume/open interest and bid-ask width, and compute implied volatilities across the surface.
Relationships: Option series, Option class, Moneyness, Implied volatility, Open interest
Failure modes: Displayed quotes can be stale or wide on illiquid series, and last-trade prices may be hours old; using last price instead of current bid/ask misstates fair value and strategy P&L.
Misconceptions: High volume on a chain line is not proof of 'smart money' direction — it cannot distinguish opening from closing or buying from selling without trade-level data.
Example: Pulling up the SPY option chain for the monthly expiry shows strikes from 400 to 600 in $5 steps, with the at-the-money calls quoted at $3.10 bid / $3.20 ask and open interest of 85,000 contracts.
Source authority: Authoritative domain source / exact citation pending
Status: Provisional

0880. Option series
Domain: Options
Definition: An option series is the set of option contracts of the same type (all calls or all puts) on the same underlying instrument that share the same expiration date and the same strike (exercise) price — i.e., a single line of an option chain, such as 'XYZ January 100 calls'.
Intuition: If the option chain is the menu, a series is one specific dish: one underlying, one expiry, one strike, one side (call or put).
Mechanics: All contracts within a series are fungible: any long contract in the series can be offset by selling any contract in the same series. Exchanges list new series as the underlying price moves and as new expiration cycles approach; open interest and volume are reported per series.
Relationships: Option class, Option chain, Open interest, Strike price, Calendar spread
Failure modes: Off-the-run series (far dated, deep ITM/OTM) can have zero open interest and no active market maker quotes, making them practically untradable at fair prices.
Misconceptions: A 'series' is not a spread or a sequence of trades — it is simply the identifier for all contracts sharing underlying, type, strike, and expiration.
Example: The 'AAPL Dec 2026 200 call' series groups every AAPL December 2026 call contract struck at $200; buying and later selling that same series closes the position.
Citation: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Series (of Options))
Status: Reviewed

0881. Option class
Domain: Options
Definition: An option class is the set of all option contracts of the same type (calls or puts, but not both) covering the same underlying instrument — for example, all listed calls on XYZ stock across every strike and expiration.
Intuition: A class is the whole family of calls (or puts) on one underlying; series are the individual family members.
Mechanics: Classes are the unit at which exchanges organize listing, and they aggregate series across strikes and expirations. Position limits, exercise limits, and many spread definitions (e.g., spreads use options 'of the same class') are expressed per class.
Relationships: Option series, Option chain, Calendar spread, Bull call spread
Failure modes: Confusing class with series leads to order-entry errors: a spread requires different series within the same class, while offsetting a position requires the identical series.
Misconceptions: Option 'class' has nothing to do with share classes of stock (Class A/B shares); it groups option contracts by type and underlying.
Example: All listed SPY puts — every strike and every expiration — together form the SPY put class; the Dec 480 put is one series within it.
Citation: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Class (of Options))
Status: Reviewed

0882. Option writer
Domain: Options
Definition: An option writer is the party that originates (sells to open) an option contract, receiving the premium and in return accepting the obligation to sell the underlying (call) or buy it (put) if the holder exercises. The CFTC glossary also lists 'option grantor' as a synonym.
Intuition: The writer is like an insurance company: it collects the premium up front and must pay out if the insured event (exercise) happens.
Mechanics: Writers post margin because their obligations can exceed the premium received. When a holder exercises, the clearing organization assigns the obligation to a writer of that series; writers can close by buying back the same series (offsetting).
Relationships: Call option, Put option, Assignment risk, Covered call, Naked call, Exercise-by-exception
Failure modes: Writing naked options exposes the seller to losses many times the premium (unlimited for naked calls); even covered writers face assignment at inconvenient times, e.g., short ITM calls before ex-dividend dates.
Misconceptions: Writing an option is not the same as shorting the underlying, and 'most options expire worthless' does not make writing free money — the tail losses on the minority that finish ITM are what the premium compensates.
Example: A trader writes one XYZ $50 put and collects $1.50 ($150). If XYZ falls to $45 and the holder exercises, the writer is assigned and must buy 100 shares at $50 — a $350 loss net of premium.
Citation: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Option Writer)
Status: Reviewed

0883. Covered call
Domain: Options
Definition: A covered call is a position long the underlying asset and short a call option on it; the long asset 'covers' the writer's obligation to deliver if the call is exercised. It converts some upside potential into immediate premium income.
Intuition: You already own the stock and rent out the upside above the strike: you keep the premium, but if the stock rallies past the strike your shares get called away.
Mechanics: For each 100 shares held, the investor sells one call and collects the premium. By put-call parity, a covered call has the same payoff shape as a cash-secured short put at the same strike. Upside is capped at strike + premium; downside is the full stock decline less the premium.
Formula: Profit at expiration = (S_T - S_0) + premium - max(S_T - K, 0), per share, where S_0 is the stock purchase price and K the call strike. Max profit = (K - S_0) + premium.
Relationships: Call option, Option writer, Cash-secured put, Put-call parity, Collar, Assignment risk
Failure modes: The premium cushions only small declines — a large drop in the stock produces nearly the full stock loss, so it is not downside protection. Repeatedly capping winners while keeping losers can degrade long-run returns (opportunity cost in strong bull markets).
Misconceptions: A covered call is not a 'safe income' or low-risk strategy: its payoff is identical to a naked cash-secured short put, which regulators treat as a higher-risk position. Selling a call against stock does not lock in a gain.
Example: Own 100 shares of XYZ bought at $48; sell the $50 call for $1.50. If XYZ finishes at $55, shares are called away at $50 for a total profit of ($2.00 + $1.50) x 100 = $350; if XYZ falls to $40, the loss is ($8.00 - $1.50) x 100 = $650.
Citation: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Covered Option)
Citation: Option (finance) — Wikipedia — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Option_(finance) (Options strategies (covered call))
Status: Reviewed

0884. Naked call
Domain: Options
Definition: A naked (uncovered) call is a short call option position where the writer does not hold the underlying asset or an offsetting position to cover the obligation; the CFTC defines a naked option as the sale of a call or put without holding an equal and opposite position in the underlying instrument.
Intuition: You have sold someone the right to buy stock from you at a fixed price without owning the stock — if it soars, you must buy it at the market price to deliver, and there is no ceiling on that price.
Mechanics: The writer collects the premium and posts substantial margin. If assigned, the writer must buy the underlying in the open market and deliver it at the strike. Because the underlying price is unbounded, potential loss is theoretically unlimited; brokers restrict naked call writing to high approval levels.
Formula: Profit at expiration = premium - max(S_T - K, 0), per share; maximum gain = premium; maximum loss is unbounded.
Relationships: Option writer, Call option, Covered call, Assignment risk, Margin, Short straddle
Failure modes: Gap moves and short squeezes can produce losses far exceeding posted margin before the writer can react; buy-ins after assignment can compound losses. This is the classic structure behind blow-ups from unlimited-risk premium selling.
Misconceptions: High win rate does not imply positive expectancy: naked call sellers win the premium often but occasionally lose many multiples of all premiums collected. 'The odds are against exercise' is not a risk control.
Example: Write one XYZ $60 call for $2. If XYZ gaps to $90 on takeover news, the writer is assigned and loses ($30 - $2) x 100 = $2,800 on a $200 premium.
Citation: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Naked Option)
Citation: Option (finance) — Wikipedia — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Option_(finance) (Basic trades (American style): Short call)
Status: Reviewed

0885. Cash-secured put
Domain: Options
Definition: A cash-secured put is a short put option position backed by enough cash in the account to buy the underlying at the strike price if assigned. The writer collects the premium and accepts the obligation to purchase the shares at the strike.
Intuition: You get paid a premium to place a limit-buy order: if the stock drops to the strike you buy it (at an effective discount of the premium), and if it doesn't you keep the premium.
Mechanics: Sell one put and set aside K x 100 in cash as security. By put-call parity, its payoff equals a covered call at the same strike. Maximum gain is the premium; maximum loss is (K - premium) x 100 if the stock goes to zero. The CBOE S&P 500 PutWrite Index (PUT) benchmarks this strategy systematically.
Formula: Profit at expiration = premium - max(K - S_T, 0), per share; breakeven = K - premium.
Relationships: Put option, Option writer, Covered call, Put-call parity, Assignment risk, Bull put spread
Failure modes: The 'discount entry' framing fails when the stock falls far below the strike — the writer owns shares well above market. Assignment is likeliest exactly when the stock is collapsing, concentrating losses in bad states.
Misconceptions: It is not lower-risk than a covered call — put-call parity makes the two economically identical at the same strike. The cash security covers the purchase obligation, not the market loss on the resulting stock position.
Example: Sell one XYZ $45 put for $1.20, securing $4,500 in cash. If XYZ finishes at $47, keep the $120 premium; if assigned at $40, the effective cost basis is $43.80 and the position is already down $380.
Citation: Put–call parity — Wikipedia — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Put%E2%80%93call_parity (Statement (cash-secured put / covered call equivalence))
Citation: Option (finance) — Wikipedia — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Option_(finance) (Basic trades (American style): Short put)
Status: Reviewed

0886. Protective put
Domain: Options
Definition: A protective put is a position long the underlying asset plus a long put option on it, which sets a floor on the position's value: losses below the put strike are offset by gains in the put. It is the options-market analogue of buying insurance on a holding.
Intuition: You keep all the upside of owning the stock but pay a premium so that, no matter how far it falls, you can always sell at the strike price.
Mechanics: Hold (or buy) 100 shares and buy one put, typically at or below the current price. Maximum loss is limited to (S_0 - K) + premium per share; upside remains open, reduced by the premium. By put-call parity, long stock + long put equals a long call plus cash (a fiduciary call).
Formula: Profit at expiration = max(S_T, K) - S_0 - premium, per share; maximum loss = (S_0 - K) + premium.
Relationships: Put option, Married put, Collar, Put-call parity, Call option
Failure modes: Chronic put buying is expensive — downside implied volatility (skew) makes protective puts costly, so persistent hedging can erode returns more than the occasional crash would. Hedging only works to expiration; gaps after expiry are unprotected.
Misconceptions: A protective put does not eliminate losses — it caps them at a level that already embeds the premium cost. It is also not 'free insurance' financed by anything; the cost is paid explicitly in premium.
Example: Own 100 shares of XYZ at $50 and buy the $48 put for $1. If XYZ collapses to $30, the total loss is capped at ($2 + $1) x 100 = $300 instead of $2,000.
Citation: Option (finance) — Wikipedia — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Option_(finance) (Options strategies (protective put))
Status: Reviewed

0887. Married put
Domain: Options
Definition: A married put is a protective put in which the underlying shares and the put option are purchased simultaneously as a single package, rather than the put being added to a pre-existing stock holding. The put guarantees a minimum sale price for the shares until expiration.
Intuition: It is buying a stock and its insurance policy on the same ticket — you know your maximum possible loss on the combined position from day one.
Mechanics: Buy 100 shares and one put at the same time. The payoff is identical to a protective put; the distinction is transactional (simultaneous purchase, which also matters for tax-lot identification in some jurisdictions). By put-call parity the position is equivalent to a long call plus discounted strike cash.
Formula: Maximum loss = (S_0 - K) + premium, per share; profit = max(S_T, K) - S_0 - premium.
Relationships: Protective put, Put option, Put-call parity, Call option
Failure modes: Same as protective puts: the recurring premium drag compounds over time, and protection ends at expiration. Choosing strikes too far OTM leaves a large deductible; too far ITM makes the 'insurance' cost prohibitive.
Misconceptions: A married put is not a distinct payoff from a protective put — many texts use the terms interchangeably; the only real difference is the timing of the stock and put purchases. It does not make a falling-stock position safe, only loss-limited.
Example: Buy 100 shares of XYZ at $50 and simultaneously buy the $50 put for $2.50. Worst case at expiration is a $250 loss; if XYZ rises to $60 the net gain is ($10 - $2.50) x 100 = $750.
Citation: Option (finance) — Wikipedia — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Option_(finance) (Options strategies (protective put / married put))
Citation: Put–call parity — Wikipedia — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Put%E2%80%93call_parity (Statement (married put / fiduciary call))
Status: Reviewed

0888. Collar
Domain: Options
Definition: A collar is a position long the underlying asset, long an out-of-the-money put (the floor), and short an out-of-the-money call (the cap) on the same underlying and expiration; the call premium finances part or all of the put. It brackets the position's value between the two strikes.
Intuition: You give up the big upside above the call strike to pay for protection against the big downside below the put strike — outcome is 'collared' into a band.
Mechanics: Hold 100 shares, buy a put at K1 below the price, sell a call at K2 above it. A 'zero-cost collar' chooses strikes so the call premium equals the put premium. Value at expiration is bounded between K1 and K2 (plus net premium effects).
Formula: Value at expiration per share = min(max(S_T, K1), K2) plus/minus net premium; K1 = put strike (floor), K2 = call strike (cap).
Relationships: Protective put, Covered call, Risk reversal, Put option, Call option
Failure modes: The short cap creates regret and assignment risk in strong rallies, and the floor still leaves the band between strikes exposed. Zero-cost construction often forces an uncomfortably tight cap or a distant floor.
Misconceptions: A collar is not a free hedge: the put is paid for by surrendered upside, which is a real economic cost. Nor does a zero-cost collar lock in current value — it only bounds the range of outcomes.
Example: Own XYZ at $100; buy the $90 put for $2 and sell the $110 call for $2 (zero cost). At expiration the position is worth between $90 and $110 per share no matter where XYZ trades.
Citation: Options strategy — Wikipedia — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Options_strategies (Neutral or non-directional strategies (collar))
Status: Reviewed

0889. Bull call spread
Domain: Options
Definition: A bull call spread is a vertical spread consisting of a long call at a lower strike and a short call at a higher strike, same underlying and expiration, entered for a net debit. It profits from a moderate rise in the underlying, with both maximum gain and maximum loss fixed at entry.
Intuition: You buy upside participation but sell away the part above the higher strike to reduce the cost — a cheaper, capped way to be bullish.
Mechanics: Net debit = premium paid - premium received. Maximum loss is the debit (below the lower strike); maximum gain is (strike width - debit) at or above the higher strike. The CFTC describes the call bull spread as buying the lower-strike (higher-delta) call and selling the higher-strike call.
Formula: Max loss = net debit; max gain = (K2 - K1) - net debit; breakeven = K1 + net debit, where K1 < K2 are the call strikes.
Relationships: Call debit spread, Bear call spread, Bull put spread, Call option, Moneyness
Failure modes: The capped upside badly lags outright call or stock ownership in large rallies; early assignment on the short ITM leg (especially before ex-dividend) can disrupt the spread and create an unintended stock position.
Misconceptions: It is not 'free leverage': the reduced cost comes from selling the tail upside, and the probability-weighted expectancy still reflects the market's implied distribution. Limited risk does not mean likely profit.
Example: Buy the XYZ $100 call for $4, sell the $105 call for $1.50: debit $2.50. Above $105 the spread is worth $5, a $2.50 gain; below $100 the $250 debit is lost.
Citation: CFTC Glossary — A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Bull Spread)
Citation: Options strategy — Wikipedia — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Options_strategies (Bullish options strategies (bull spreads))
Status: Reviewed

0890. Bear call spread
Domain: Options
Definition: A bear call spread is a vertical spread consisting of a short call at a lower strike and a long call at a higher strike, same underlying and expiration, entered for a net credit. It profits if the underlying stays below the short strike, with fixed maximum gain (the credit) and maximum loss.
