Mechanics: Under direct quotation the home currency is the price (quote) currency and the foreign currency is the unit (base). If the home currency appreciates, the quoted number falls (fewer home units per foreign unit); if the home currency depreciates, the number rises.
Formula: Direct rate = home-currency units per 1 foreign-currency unit = 1 / (indirect rate).
Relationships: Indirect quotation, Base currency, Quote currency
Failure modes: Whether a quote is 'direct' depends entirely on the observer's home currency, so the label is meaningless in cross-border communication unless the perspective is stated; mixing conventions flips the interpretation of rate moves.
Misconceptions: A rising number under direct quotation is often misread as the home currency strengthening; it actually means the home currency is weakening (more home units are needed per foreign unit).
Example: For a US-based observer, USD 1.11 = EUR 1.00 would be an indirect quote, whereas EUR 0.90 = USD 1.00 is the direct quote used from a euro-area perspective.
Citation: Wikipedia — Exchange rate — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exchange_rate (Quotations)
Status: Reviewed

0992. Indirect quotation
Domain: Foreign exchange
Definition: An exchange rate quotation expressed from the home country's perspective as the number of units of foreign currency per one unit of home currency. For example, from the euro area's perspective, USD 1.11 = EUR 1.00 is an indirect quotation; the convention is common in the United Kingdom, Australia, New Zealand and the euro area.
Intuition: Indirect quotation states how much foreign money one unit of your own currency buys.
Mechanics: Under indirect quotation the home currency is the unit (base) currency and the foreign currency is the price (quote) currency. It is the reciprocal of the direct quotation, so a rising number under indirect quotation means the home currency is appreciating.
Formula: Indirect rate = foreign-currency units per 1 home-currency unit = 1 / (direct rate).
Relationships: Direct quotation, Base currency, Quote currency
Failure modes: Because the same numerical rate can be 'direct' for one party and 'indirect' for the other, reports that omit the perspective invite sign errors in appreciation/depreciation statements.
Misconceptions: Traders sometimes believe one convention is the global standard; in practice both coexist, and only market pair conventions (e.g. EUR/USD, USD/JPY) are standardized, not the direct/indirect label.
Example: British newspapers quote cable as USD per GBP (e.g. GBP 1 = USD 1.27); for a UK resident that is an indirect quotation, and a rise to 1.30 means sterling has strengthened.
Citation: Wikipedia — Exchange rate — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exchange_rate (Quotations)
Status: Reviewed

0993. Pip
Domain: Foreign exchange
Definition: The conventional smallest whole-unit increment of an FX exchange rate quote. For most major currency pairs (priced to four decimal places) one pip is one unit of the fourth decimal place (0.0001); for yen pairs one pip is one unit of the second decimal place (0.01).
Intuition: A pip is the FX market's standard 'cent' for talking about exchange-rate moves and spreads.
Mechanics: Price changes, bid-ask spreads and forward points are quoted in pips. The monetary value of a pip in quote-currency terms equals the pip size multiplied by the position size in base-currency units; a pip is distinct from the tick size, which in a given market may be a fraction (e.g. 1/2 pip) or multiple of a pip.
Formula: Pip value (quote currency) = pip size x position size (base units); pip size = 0.0001 for most pairs, 0.01 for JPY pairs.
Relationships: Pipette, Forward points, Base currency, Quote currency
Failure modes: The four-decimal convention breaks down for pairs quoted with more or fewer decimals (e.g. JPY pairs at 0.01, or pairs priced to five decimals), so 'pip' must be re-anchored per pair; confusing pips with basis points or ticks misstates spread and P&L figures.
Misconceptions: A pip is not a universal 0.01% move in the exchange rate — its percentage value varies with the level of the rate and the pair's decimal convention.
Example: If EUR/USD moves from 1.3000 to 1.3010, the pair has risen 10 pips; on a 500,000 EUR position that move is worth 500,000 x 0.0010 = USD 500.
Citation: Wikipedia — Percentage in point — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percentage_in_point (lead and 'Example')
Status: Reviewed

0994. Pipette
Domain: Foreign exchange
Definition: One tenth of a pip, i.e. the additional decimal place (the fifth decimal for most pairs, the third for yen pairs) that electronic FX platforms added to quotes. Pipettes allow finer pricing than the traditional four-decimal convention.
Intuition: A pipette is the extra digit beyond the pip that lets platforms quote spreads in tenths of a pip.
Mechanics: Electronic trading platforms extended quote precision by one decimal place, displaying rates in 1/10-pip increments. In a five-decimal EUR/USD quote such as 1.30105, the last digit (5) counts pipettes; tighter spreads from electronic price competition made this finer granularity necessary.
Formula: 1 pipette = 0.1 pip = 0.00001 for most pairs (0.001 for JPY pairs).
Relationships: Pip, FX spot
Failure modes: Platforms differ in how many decimals they display, so 'points' on one platform may be pips on another; comparing spreads across venues without checking decimal conventions misstates trading costs.
Misconceptions: A pipette is not a new minimum tick imposed by any authority — it emerged from platform pricing practice and is not uniformly adopted.
Example: If EUR/USD is quoted 1.30105/1.30115, the spread is 1 pipette (0.1 pip), one tenth of the traditional 1-pip minimum increment.
Citation: Wikipedia — Percentage in point — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Percentage_in_point (Fractional pips)
Status: Reviewed

0995. FX spot
Domain: Foreign exchange
Definition: A transaction for the exchange of two currencies at a rate agreed on the trade date for settlement on the standard spot value date, normally two business days later (T+2). Spot is one of the core OTC FX instrument categories in the BIS Triennial Survey and accounted for 28% of the $7.5 trillion average daily global FX turnover in April 2022.
Intuition: A spot FX deal is 'buy currency now at today's rate', with the actual exchange of funds settling a couple of business days later.
Mechanics: Counterparties agree a rate and amounts on the trade date; the two currency legs are delivered on the spot value date (T+2 for most major pairs, T+1 for some such as USD/CAD). Spot transactions settle delivery-versus-payment through systems like CLS for eligible currencies and form the price base from which forwards and swaps are derived.
Relationships: Value date, FX forward, FX swap, Tom-next swap
Failure modes: Spot quotes embed the T+2 settlement convention, so around holidays the actual value date shifts; settlement (Herstatt) risk exists for non-CLS-settled currencies, and spot prices can gap over weekends when the OTC market is closed.
Misconceptions: 'Spot' does not mean immediate same-day settlement — the standard is T+2 — and spot FX is overwhelmingly an OTC interbank/dealer market, not an exchange-traded one.
Example: On Monday a corporate treasurer buys EUR 1 million against USD at 1.0850; the euros and dollars are exchanged on Wednesday, the T+2 spot value date.
Citation: BIS — OTC foreign exchange turnover in April 2022 (Triennial Central Bank Survey) — https://www.bis.org/statistics/rpfx22_fx.htm (Turnover by instrument)
Citation: Wikipedia — Value date — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Value_date (lead)
Status: Reviewed

0996. FX forward
Domain: Foreign exchange
Definition: An over-the-counter contract to exchange one currency for another at a rate fixed today for settlement on a specific future date beyond the spot value date. Outright forwards are used mainly to hedge future currency payments and receipts, and accounted for 15% of global OTC FX turnover in April 2022.
Intuition: An FX forward locks in today the exchange rate for a currency trade you will make weeks or months from now.
Mechanics: The forward rate equals the spot rate adjusted by forward points reflecting the interest rate differential between the two currencies over the contract tenor (covered interest parity). A single outright forward involves one exchange of principals at maturity; non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) settle only the net value difference in a convertible currency. Unlike futures, forwards are bilateral OTC contracts and carry counterparty risk.
Formula: F = S x (1 + r_q x T) / (1 + r_b x T), where F = forward rate, S = spot rate (quote per base), r_q = quote-currency interest rate, r_b = base-currency interest rate, T = tenor in years under the applicable day-count convention.
Relationships: FX spot, FX swap, Forward points, Covered interest parity, Forward premium
Failure modes: Forward rates are a no-arbitrage pricing output, not forecasts of future spot rates; since 2008 persistent cross-currency basis deviations mean forward pricing also embeds balance-sheet costs. Bilateral forwards carry counterparty credit risk absent in centrally cleared instruments.
Misconceptions: A forward rate is not the market's expected future exchange rate; it is mechanically derived from the spot rate and money-market rates.
Example: A US importer owing EUR 10 million in six months buys a 6-month EUR/USD forward at 1.0920; whatever the spot rate is at maturity, the euros cost exactly USD 10.92 million.
Citation: BIS Quarterly Review, December 2022 — Dollar debt in FX swaps and forwards: huge, missing and growing — https://www.bis.org/publ/qtrpdf/r_qt2212h.htm (FX swaps/forwards and currency swaps: some stylised facts)
Citation: BIS — OTC foreign exchange turnover in April 2022 (Triennial Central Bank Survey) — https://www.bis.org/statistics/rpfx22_fx.htm (Turnover by instrument)
Status: Reviewed

0997. FX swap
Domain: Foreign exchange
Definition: A contract combining a spot purchase (sale) of one currency against another with a simultaneous offsetting forward sale (purchase) of the same amounts. In the spot leg one party lends one currency and borrows the other at the spot rate; in the forward leg the exchange is reversed at a pre-agreed forward rate, making the instrument economically similar to collateralized borrowing and lending. FX swaps were the most traded FX instrument, at $3.8 trillion per day (51% of global turnover) in April 2022.
Intuition: An FX swap is like a repo with a currency instead of a security: you swap currencies today and swap them back later at a pre-set rate.
Mechanics: Because the two legs offset, an FX swap creates no net open currency position; its price is the difference between the forward and spot legs, quoted in forward (swap) points that reflect the interest rate differential plus any cross-currency basis. Typical maturities are very short — instruments maturing within a week accounted for about 70% of FX swap turnover in April 2022 — and the instrument is used for funding liquidity management, hedging and rolling forward positions.
Formula: Swap cost is quoted as forward points = F - S, with F = S x (1 + r_q x T) / (1 + r_b x T) under covered interest parity; S = spot, F = forward rate, r_q and r_b = quote- and base-currency interest rates, T = tenor.
Relationships: FX spot, FX forward, Forward points, Covered interest parity, Tom-next swap
Failure modes: FX swap markets are vulnerable to funding squeezes — during the 2008 crisis and March 2020 dollar borrowers faced sharply higher rates when lenders stepped back. Persistent deviations from covered interest parity (the cross-currency basis) mean swap-implied funding costs can differ materially from cash-market rates.
Misconceptions: An FX swap is not a bet on the exchange rate (the legs offset, so there is no open FX position), and it differs from a cross-currency swap, a longer-term instrument that also exchanges periodic interest payments.
Example: A Dutch pension fund borrows dollars and lends euros in the spot leg of a 3-month FX swap, then repays the dollars and receives back euros in the forward leg at the pre-agreed rate, hedging its dollar assets without an open currency position.
Citation: BIS Quarterly Review, December 2022 — Dollar debt in FX swaps and forwards: huge, missing and growing — https://www.bis.org/publ/qtrpdf/r_qt2212h.htm (introduction and stylised facts)
Citation: BIS — OTC foreign exchange turnover in April 2022 (Triennial Central Bank Survey) — https://www.bis.org/statistics/rpfx22_fx.htm (Turnover by instrument)
Status: Reviewed

0998. Currency carry trade
Domain: Foreign exchange
Definition: A strategy of borrowing (funding) in a low-interest-rate currency and investing in a high-interest-rate currency without hedging the exchange-rate exposure, aiming to earn the interest rate differential. Its profitability violates uncovered interest parity, and research documents that carry-trade returns are negatively skewed — subject to sudden crash risk when funding liquidity falls and positions unwind en masse.
Intuition: Collect the interest-rate gap between two currencies and hope the exchange rate doesn't move against you before you exit.
Mechanics: The trader shorts the funding currency (e.g. a low-yielder) and goes long the investment currency, earning the rate differential as 'carry' plus or minus any exchange-rate change. Because UIP predicts the high-rate currency should depreciate by the differential, persistent carry profits are a pricing anomaly; unwind episodes cluster when risk appetite and funding liquidity decline, producing negatively skewed, crash-prone returns and excess co-movement among currencies with similar interest rates.
Formula: Approximate carry-trade return = (r_invest - r_funding) + percentage change in the exchange rate (investment currency vs funding currency) over the holding period.
Relationships: Uncovered interest parity, Interest rate parity, FX spot
Failure modes: Carry trades crash during liquidity squeezes and risk-off episodes: sudden unwinding produces large depreciations of high-yield currencies (negative skewness), e.g. 2008. Losses can exceed years of accumulated carry, and funding-liquidity constraints force deleveraging exactly when prices gap.
Misconceptions: The interest differential is not a free lunch: it is compensation for crash risk, not a market inefficiency that can be harvested risklessly; carry strategies are not reliably profitable on a risk-adjusted basis.
Example: Borrowing Japanese yen at a near-zero rate to buy Australian dollars yielding several percent more earns the differential while AUD/JPY is stable, but a sharp yen rally during a global risk-off episode can wipe out the position.
Citation: NBER Working Paper 14473 — Carry Trades and Currency Crashes (Brunnermeier, Nagel, Pedersen) — https://www.nber.org/papers/w14473 (abstract)
Status: Reviewed

0999. Forward points
Domain: Foreign exchange
Definition: The difference between the forward exchange rate and the spot exchange rate for a given tenor, i.e. the adjustment added to or subtracted from the spot rate to obtain the outright forward rate. FX swaps are typically quoted in forward points rather than outright rates.
Intuition: Forward points are the 'time value' of a currency pair — how much the forward rate differs from spot because of the interest-rate gap.
Mechanics: Under covered interest parity, forward points are approximately proportional to the interest rate differential between the two currencies times the tenor; when the quote-currency interest rate exceeds the base-currency rate, points are positive (forward above spot), and vice versa. Deviations from the parity-implied level appear as the cross-currency basis. Points are expressed in pips of the exchange rate.
Formula: Forward points = F - S = S x [(1 + r_q x T)/(1 + r_b x T) - 1] ~= S x (r_q - r_b) x T for small r_b x T; S = spot, F = forward, r_q and r_b = quote- and base-currency rates, T = tenor in years.
Relationships: FX forward, FX swap, Covered interest parity, Forward premium, Forward discount, Pip
Failure modes: Forward points reflect relative funding costs, not expected currency moves; since the 2008 crisis, balance-sheet constraints and hedging demand have driven persistent non-zero bases, so realized points can diverge from the simple interest-differential formula.
Misconceptions: Positive forward points do not mean the market expects the base currency to appreciate; they mainly encode the interest differential between the two currencies.
Example: With NZD/USD spot at 0.8325 and 1-year forward points quoted at -270 pips, the outright 1-year forward rate is 0.8055 (= 0.8325 - 0.0270).
Citation: BIS Quarterly Review, September 2016 — Covered interest parity lost: understanding the cross-currency basis (Borio, McCauley, McGuire, Sushko) — https://www.bis.org/publ/qtrpdf/r_qt1609e.htm (Box A: CIP, FX swaps, cross-currency swaps and the factors that move the basis)
Citation: Wikipedia — Foreign exchange swap — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_exchange_swap (Pricing)
Status: Reviewed

1000. Forward premium
Domain: Foreign exchange
Definition: The situation in which a currency's forward exchange rate is above its spot rate, i.e. the currency trades at a premium for future delivery (equivalently, positive forward points). Under covered interest parity, a currency trades at a forward premium when its interest rate is below that of the other currency in the pair.
Intuition: A currency at a forward premium costs more in the forward market than in the spot market — the mirror image of its lower interest rate.
Mechanics: With the exchange rate quoted as quote currency per base currency, positive forward points (F > S) mean the base currency is at a forward premium and the quote currency at a forward discount. The size of the premium, annualized as (F - S)/S, is tied by covered interest parity to the interest differential, plus any cross-currency basis.
Formula: Annualized forward premium = (F - S) / S x (360 / days to maturity); F = forward rate, S = spot rate.
Relationships: Forward discount, Forward points, Covered interest parity, FX forward
Failure modes: The premium is an arithmetic consequence of interest differentials and carries no information about expected appreciation; treating it as a bullish signal is an error. Basis deviations can also make the observed premium differ from the parity-implied value.
Misconceptions: A forward premium does not indicate that the market expects the currency to strengthen — under CIP it simply compensates for the currency's lower interest rate.
Example: If the yen's interest rate is below the dollar's and USD/JPY spot is 150.00 with a 1-year forward of 146.50, the dollar is at a forward discount and the yen at a forward premium of roughly 2.3% annualized.
Citation: BIS Quarterly Review, September 2016 — Covered interest parity lost: understanding the cross-currency basis (Borio, McCauley, McGuire, Sushko) — https://www.bis.org/publ/qtrpdf/r_qt1609e.htm (Box A)
Citation: Wikipedia — Exchange rate — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exchange_rate (Uncovered interest rate parity model (premium/discount usage))
Status: Reviewed

1001. Forward discount
Domain: Foreign exchange
Definition: The situation in which a currency's forward exchange rate is below its spot rate, i.e. the currency trades at a discount for future delivery (equivalently, negative forward points for that currency). Under covered interest parity, a currency trades at a forward discount when its interest rate is above that of the other currency in the pair.
Intuition: A currency at a forward discount costs less forward than spot — the arithmetic counterpart of its higher interest rate.
Mechanics: With the rate quoted as quote currency per base currency, negative forward points (F < S) mean the base currency is at a forward discount and the quote currency at a forward premium. The annualized discount (F - S)/S is tied by covered interest parity to the interest differential, plus any cross-currency basis. High-yielding (carry target) currencies normally trade at a forward discount.
Formula: Annualized forward discount = (F - S) / S x (360 / days to maturity) < 0; F = forward rate, S = spot rate.
Relationships: Forward premium, Forward points, Covered interest parity, Currency carry trade
Failure modes: The discount is not a forecast of depreciation; uncovered interest parity — which would turn the discount into an expected spot change — fails empirically, and high-rate currencies often appreciate instead, which is the basis of the carry trade.
Misconceptions: Selling a currency 'because it is at a forward discount' double-counts the interest differential: hedging a high-yielder via forwards surrenders exactly the carry that the discount reflects.
Example: If USD/MXN spot is 18.00 and Mexican rates exceed US rates, the 1-year forward might be 19.10: the peso is at a forward discount (it buys fewer dollars forward than spot).
Citation: BIS Quarterly Review, September 2016 — Covered interest parity lost: understanding the cross-currency basis (Borio, McCauley, McGuire, Sushko) — https://www.bis.org/publ/qtrpdf/r_qt1609e.htm (Box A)
Citation: Wikipedia — Exchange rate — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exchange_rate (Uncovered interest rate parity model (premium/discount usage))
Status: Reviewed

1002. Interest rate parity
Domain: Foreign exchange
Definition: The family of equilibrium conditions linking spot and forward exchange rates to interest rate differentials between two currencies. It comprises covered interest parity — a no-arbitrage condition tying the forward premium to the interest differential — and uncovered interest parity, which relates the interest differential to the expected change in the spot rate.
Intuition: Money should earn the same total return wherever it is parked once currency effects are accounted for; IRP is the statement of that idea, hedged (covered) or unhedged (uncovered).
Mechanics: In its covered form, borrowing in one currency, converting at spot, investing in the other, and locking in the conversion back with a forward must yield no riskless profit, forcing F/S to equal the ratio of gross interest returns. The uncovered form replaces the forward rate with the expected future spot rate and is a hypothesis about expectations rather than a pure arbitrage condition. Spot/forward pricing of FX swaps is read off these parity relations.
Formula: Covered: F/S = (1 + r_q x T)/(1 + r_b x T). Uncovered: E[S_T]/S = (1 + r_q x T)/(1 + r_b x T), with S and F in quote currency per base currency, r_q and r_b the two interest rates, T the tenor.
Relationships: Covered interest parity, Uncovered interest parity, Forward points, FX swap, Currency carry trade
Failure modes: CIP has been systematically violated since 2008 (persistent cross-currency basis) because of hedging demand and limits to arbitrage from bank balance-sheet constraints. UIP fails empirically as well: high-interest-rate currencies tend to appreciate rather than depreciate, the 'forward premium puzzle'.
Misconceptions: IRP is not a law that markets obey at all times; only the covered version is arbitrage-enforced, and even it has broken down persistently since the financial crisis.
Example: If 1-year rates are 5% in USD and 1% in JPY, CIP requires the 1-year USD/JPY forward to trade roughly 4% below spot; a materially different forward would open a covered arbitrage.
Citation: BIS Quarterly Review, September 2016 — Covered interest parity lost: understanding the cross-currency basis (Borio, McCauley, McGuire, Sushko) — https://www.bis.org/publ/qtrpdf/r_qt1609e.htm (Box A)
Citation: Wikipedia — Exchange rate — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exchange_rate (Uncovered interest rate parity model)
Status: Reviewed

1003. Covered interest parity
Domain: Foreign exchange
Definition: The no-arbitrage condition that interest rates on two otherwise identical assets in different currencies must be equal once the foreign currency risk is hedged in the forward market: the interest rate differential should equal the differential between the forward and spot exchange rates. Often described as the closest thing to a physical law in international finance, it has been systematically violated since the 2008 financial crisis, visible in a persistent cross-currency basis.
Intuition: If you fully hedge the currency risk, borrowing dollars to invest in yen (or vice versa) should earn nothing extra — CIP is what makes that true.
Mechanics: If CIP fails, an arbitrageur can borrow the cheaper currency in the cash market, swap it via an FX swap (sell spot, repurchase forward), and lock in a riskless profit; such trades should close the gap. Post-crisis, CIP deviations persist because FX hedging demand (from banks, institutional investors and bond issuers) meets limits to arbitrage: arbitrageurs' balance-sheet space is costly, so the basis is not competed away. The deviation is measured by the cross-currency basis — the amount by which swap-implied funding costs differ from cash-market rates.
Formula: (1 + r) = (F/S) x (1 + r*), where S = spot and F = forward in US dollars per foreign currency, r = USD interest rate, r* = foreign interest rate (BIS Box A convention).
Relationships: Interest rate parity, Uncovered interest parity, Forward points, FX swap, FX forward
Failure modes: CIP breaks down when arbitrage is balance-sheet-constrained: during the GFC, the euro-area crisis, and persistently since 2014, the cross-currency basis has stayed non-zero, with quarter-end spikes reflecting regulatory reporting constraints. Deviations mean synthetic dollar funding via FX swaps can be costlier (or cheaper) than direct funding.
Misconceptions: CIP is not enforced by nature — it requires arbitrageurs with free balance-sheet capacity, so 'riskless' CIP arbitrage in practice consumes capital, carries counterparty and liquidity risk, and may not be executable at scale.
Example: If borrowing dollars via a USD/JPY FX swap costs 25 bp more than borrowing dollars directly in the cash market, the dollar is said to command a premium in swaps — a CIP violation measured by the negative cross-currency basis.
Citation: BIS Quarterly Review, September 2016 — Covered interest parity lost: understanding the cross-currency basis (Borio, McCauley, McGuire, Sushko) — https://www.bis.org/publ/qtrpdf/r_qt1609e.htm (whole feature, esp. Box A)
Status: Reviewed

1004. Uncovered interest parity
Domain: Foreign exchange
Definition: The hypothesis that the interest rate differential between two currencies equals the expected change in their exchange rate, so that the higher-yielding currency is expected to depreciate just enough to offset its yield advantage for an unhedged investor. Empirically UIP fails: high-interest-rate currencies tend to appreciate rather than depreciate, a puzzle that underlies carry-trade profitability.
Intuition: UIP says there's no free lunch from chasing higher foreign interest rates — the exchange rate should move to cancel the extra yield. In practice it often doesn't.
Mechanics: Unlike covered parity, UIP cannot be enforced by arbitrage because the future spot rate is unknown; it is a joint hypothesis about expectations and risk neutrality. Research links its failure to funding-liquidity constraints on carry traders: exchange-rate moves between high- and low-rate currencies are negatively skewed, and controlling for liquidity helps explain the uncovered interest-rate puzzle.
Formula: E[S_T] / S = (1 + r_q x T) / (1 + r_b x T), equivalently the expected percentage change in the spot rate ~= r_b - r_q over the tenor; S = spot in quote per base currency.
Relationships: Interest rate parity, Covered interest parity, Currency carry trade, Forward discount
Failure modes: UIP fails systematically (the forward premium puzzle): since the 1990s high-rate currencies characteristically appreciated, so unhedged carry positions earned excess returns punctuated by crash episodes when funding liquidity dried up.
Misconceptions: UIP is not an arbitrage condition that 'must' hold — it is a falsifiable expectations hypothesis, and treating the forward rate as an unbiased forecast of the future spot rate is empirically wrong.
Example: If Australian rates exceed Japanese rates by 4%, UIP predicts the AUD should depreciate about 4% against the JPY over the year; historically AUD/JPY instead appreciated for long stretches, rewarding carry traders until sharp reversals.
Citation: NBER Working Paper 14473 — Carry Trades and Currency Crashes (Brunnermeier, Nagel, Pedersen) — https://www.nber.org/papers/w14473 (abstract)
Citation: Wikipedia — Exchange rate — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exchange_rate (Uncovered interest rate parity model)
Status: Reviewed

1005. Cross rate
Domain: Foreign exchange
Definition: An exchange rate between two currencies that does not directly involve the home reference currency — in market practice, a pair not involving the US dollar (e.g. EUR/GBP, GBP/JPY). Because most currencies are quoted primarily against the dollar, cross rates are typically derived by multiplying or dividing the two currencies' dollar rates.
Intuition: A cross rate is the exchange rate between two 'non-anchor' currencies, usually computed through their rates against the dollar.
Mechanics: The derived (implicit) cross rate is obtained as S(a/b) = S(a/$) x S($/b) using the quoted dollar pairs. Dealers quote liquid crosses directly, but the bid-ask of the implicit cross disciplines market makers: if a directly quoted cross diverges from the implicit value, triangular arbitrage becomes possible. The dollar's vehicle-currency role (on one side of 88% of all FX trades in 2022) is why crosses route through it.
Formula: S(a/b) = S(a/$) x S($/b); for quotes sharing the same base, divide: EUR/GBP = EUR/USD / GBP/USD.
Relationships: Base currency, Quote currency, FX triangular arbitrage, FX spot
Failure modes: Derived crosses inherit the spreads and stale prices of both dollar legs, so in fast or illiquid markets the implicit cross can be wrong; thin crosses have wide spreads and limited depth compared with dollar pairs.
Misconceptions: Cross rates are not independent prices: arbitrage keeps them aligned with the constituent dollar pairs, so a 'mispriced cross' is usually just a fleeting inconsistency, not a distinct market view.
Example: With EUR/USD at 1.0850 and USD/JPY at 150.00, the implicit EUR/JPY cross is 1.0850 x 150.00 = 162.75.
Citation: Wikipedia — Currency pair — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Currency_pair (Syntax and quotation (currency crosses))
Citation: BIS — OTC foreign exchange turnover in April 2022 (Triennial Central Bank Survey) — https://www.bis.org/statistics/rpfx22_fx.htm (Turnover by currency and currency pairs (US dollar on one side of 88% of trades))
Status: Reviewed

1006. FX triangular arbitrage
Domain: Foreign exchange
Definition: The practice of exploiting a pricing discrepancy among three currencies by executing three trades — exchanging an initial currency for a second, the second for a third, and the third back into the initial — when the quoted cross exchange rate diverges from the implicit cross rate derived from the other two pairs. High-frequency studies find such opportunities are rare, small (often ~1 basis point) and fleeting (mostly lasting seconds or less).
Intuition: If EUR/USD and USD/JPY imply one EUR/JPY rate but a bank quotes another, you can cycle through the three pairs and end up with more than you started.
Mechanics: The arbitrageur computes the implicit cross rate S(a/b) = S(a/$) x S($/b) from quoted rates and compares it with the market cross quote, accounting for bid and ask on each leg. A profitable cycle exists only if the discrepancy exceeds transaction costs; electronic trading systems detect and exhaust such gaps in milliseconds, which is why opportunity incidence fell as algorithmic trading spread.
Formula: Implicit cross rate S(a/b) = S(a/$) x S($/b); a no-arbitrage condition requires the quoted cross to equal the implicit cross (within bid-ask bounds).
Relationships: Cross rate, FX spot, Covered interest parity
Failure modes: Execution risk dominates: even millisecond delays between identifying the gap and filling all three legs mean one leg can re-price, leaving the arbitrageur with an unwanted position and a close-out cost equal to the price move that killed the gap. Fees, latency and competition from faster systems erode the thin margins.
Misconceptions: Triangular arbitrage is not an easy retail strategy: executable opportunities at sizes above a basis point or two are essentially competed away by professional low-latency systems before slower participants can act.
Example: If dealers quote EUR/USD 0.8171 (euros per dollar) and GBP/USD 1.4650, the implicit EUR/GBP is 1.1971; a bank offering pounds at EUR 1.1910 lets an arbitrageur cycle $5m through the three pairs for about $25,400 profit before costs.
Citation: Wikipedia — Triangular arbitrage — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triangular_arbitrage (whole article (mechanics, worked example, Fenn et al. 2009 evidence))
Status: Reviewed

1007. Dollar index
Domain: Foreign exchange
Definition: A proprietary index, designed and published by ICE Data Indices, measuring the value of the US dollar as a weighted geometric mean against a fixed basket of six currencies: euro (57.6%), yen (13.6%), pound sterling (11.9%), Canadian dollar (9.1%), Swedish krona (4.2%) and Swiss franc (3.6%). Set at 100.000 at its March 1973 start, it rises when the dollar strengthens against the basket; futures on the index trade on ICE.
Intuition: DXY is the standard single number summarizing how strong the dollar is overall against other major currencies.
Mechanics: The index is a geometric average with fixed weights applied to the six bilateral rates, with EUR and GBP entering with negative exponents (they are quoted as dollars per unit of currency) and the others with positive exponents. The basket composition has been revised only once, when euro-area currencies were subsumed by the euro in 1999; the Federal Reserve's broader trade-weighted dollar index is a separate measure.
Formula: USDX = 50.14348112 x EURUSD^(-0.576) x USDJPY^0.136 x GBPUSD^(-0.119) x USDCAD^0.091 x USDSEK^0.042 x USDCHF^0.036.
Relationships: Nominal effective exchange rate, Real effective exchange rate, Base currency
Failure modes: The 1970s-era basket omits major current US trade partners (China, Mexico, Korea, Brazil) while retaining Sweden and Switzerland, and the euro dominates with a 57.6% weight, so DXY moves often reflect EUR/USD more than broad dollar strength; it is not a trade-representative effective exchange rate.
Misconceptions: DXY is not an official or trade-weighted measure of the dollar — it is a commercial futures-underlying index — and a rising DXY says little about the dollar against emerging-market currencies.
Example: A sharp EUR/USD sell-off from 1.10 to 1.05 lifts DXY mechanically because of the euro's 57.6% weight, even if the dollar is flat against most Asian and Latin American currencies.
Citation: ICE Futures U.S. — U.S. Dollar Index Futures (product page) — https://www.theice.com/products/194/US-Dollar-Index-Futures (product page (ICE ownership/trademark of the index))
Citation: Wikipedia — U.S. Dollar Index — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/U.S._Dollar_Index (lead, weights and calculation formula)
Status: Reviewed

1008. Real effective exchange rate
Domain: Foreign exchange
Definition: A trade-weighted index of a currency's value against a basket of partner currencies, adjusted for relative price levels — in the BIS methodology, derived by adjusting the nominal effective exchange rate by relative consumer prices. An increase in the REER indicates a real appreciation of the currency, interpreted as a loss of price competitiveness.
Intuition: The REER tells you whether your currency is really getting more expensive abroad, after accounting for inflation differences — not just what the nominal rate says.
Mechanics: The BIS computes NEER as a geometric trade-weighted average of bilateral rates and then adjusts by relative consumer price indices to obtain the REER. Weights derive from manufacturing trade flows, double-weighted to capture both direct bilateral trade and third-market competition, and are time-varying on a three-year basis; BIS broad indices cover 64 economies. REER changes thus reflect both nominal exchange-rate moves and the inflation differential against trading partners.
Formula: REER = NEER adjusted by relative consumer prices: REER_t ~ Product over i of [S_i,t x (P_t / P_i,t*)]^(w_i), where S_i are bilateral rates, w_i trade weights (sum to 1), P home and P_i* partner consumer price indices.
Relationships: Nominal effective exchange rate, Dollar index, FX spot
Failure modes: REER indices are sensitive to the choice of price deflator (CPI vs unit labour costs vs GDP deflator), weighting scheme and base period, so different providers' REERs can give different competitiveness readings; they are indices relative to a base year and carry no absolute 'fair value'.
Misconceptions: A rising REER does not by itself prove overvaluation or predict depreciation — it is a competitiveness statistic relative to a chosen base period, not an equilibrium benchmark.
Example: If a country's nominal effective rate is flat but its inflation runs well above its trading partners', its BIS REER appreciates, signalling eroding export price competitiveness.
Citation: BIS — Effective exchange rate indices (about/methodology) — https://www.bis.org/statistics/eer.htm (About (NEER/REER definitions) and Methodology)
Status: Reviewed

1009. Nominal effective exchange rate
Domain: Foreign exchange
Definition: A trade-weighted index of a currency's nominal value against a basket of trading-partner currencies — in the BIS methodology, calculated as a geometric trade-weighted average of bilateral exchange rates. An increase in the NEER indicates a nominal appreciation of the currency; it is the building block from which the real effective exchange rate is derived by adjusting for relative prices.
Intuition: The NEER collapses a currency's many bilateral exchange rates into one number weighted by how much you trade with each partner.
Mechanics: Bilateral rates are combined as a weighted geometric mean using weights derived from manufacturing trade flows, double-weighted to capture direct bilateral trade and third-market competition; weights are time-varying on a three-year basis. BIS broad NEER indices cover 64 economies (narrow indices 26) and use published US dollar exchange rates as inputs where possible.
Formula: NEER_t = Product over i of S_i,t^(w_i), where S_i,t is the bilateral exchange-rate index against partner i and w_i are trade weights summing to 1 (geometric trade-weighted average).
Relationships: Real effective exchange rate, Dollar index, Cross rate
Failure modes: NEER ignores inflation differentials, so a country with high inflation can show a stable NEER while losing real competitiveness; results also depend on the weighting scheme and base period, limiting cross-provider comparability.
Misconceptions: The NEER is not a forecast or an equilibrium measure — it is a descriptive weighted average, and its level is meaningful only relative to the index base year.
Example: If the euro appreciates against the dollar and yen but weakens against sterling, the BIS euro NEER moves by the trade-weighted net of those changes rather than by any single pair.
Citation: BIS — Effective exchange rate indices (about/methodology) — https://www.bis.org/statistics/eer.htm (About (NEER/REER definitions) and Methodology)
Status: Reviewed

1010. Value date
Domain: Foreign exchange
Definition: The date on which the counterparties to a foreign exchange trade actually exchange the funds, i.e. when the traded amounts become effective (delivered). For a spot FX transaction the value date is normally two business days after the trade is agreed (T+2); for forwards and swaps it is the agreed future delivery date of each leg.
Intuition: The trade date is when you agree the deal; the value date is when the money actually changes hands.
Mechanics: The value date determines when interest accrues and when currency deliveries occur; it rolls forward over weekends and currency holidays under modified-following conventions. Interest rate differentials between the two currencies are earned or paid for each day a position's value date is shifted, which is what tom-next and other short-dated swaps price. Forward rates are derived by adjusting the spot rate for the interest carry between the spot value date and the forward value date.
Relationships: FX spot, Tom-next swap, FX forward, FX swap
Failure modes: Holidays in either currency's center push the value date and change the number of interest days, so quotes around month-ends, year-ends and holidays embed extra carry; assuming a fixed 'T+2 = 2 days of interest' misprices rollovers (e.g. Wednesday spot rolls three days).
Misconceptions: The value date is not the trade date and not necessarily two calendar days later — it is counted in good business days for both currency centers.
Example: A EUR/USD spot trade agreed on Thursday 3 August has a T+2 value date of Monday 7 August (skipping the weekend), so the interest carry covers three calendar days.
Citation: Wikipedia — Value date — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Value_date (lead (spot FX settles normally two days after the transaction is agreed))
Status: Reviewed

1011. Tom-next swap
Domain: Foreign exchange
Definition: A short-dated FX swap used to roll a currency position forward by one day: the holder buys (or sells) a foreign currency amount settling tomorrow and simultaneously does the opposite transaction settling the day after (the spot value date). Institutions use tom-next swaps at the end of each day to close out and re-institute foreign balances, thereby collecting or paying the overnight interest differential (cost of carry) without holding an open FX position.
Intuition: Tom-next is the daily 'roll' that keeps a spot FX position from ever settling, in exchange for paying or receiving one day of the interest-rate gap.
Mechanics: The near leg settles on the tomorrow date (T+1) and the far leg on the spot date (T+2), shifting the position's value date by one day. The price, in swap points, reflects the one-day interest rate differential between the two currencies (with extra days priced over weekends and holidays); retail platforms implement the same economics as the daily rollover or swap charge on open positions.
Formula: Tom-next swap points ~ S x (r_q - r_b) x (days / 360 or 365 by convention), where S = spot rate and r_q, r_b = quote- and base-currency overnight rates.
Relationships: FX swap, Value date, FX spot, Currency carry trade, Forward points
Failure modes: Tom-next pricing turns on overnight rates and day counts, so costs jump over weekends (three days) and quarter/ year-ends when funding rates spike; traders ignoring the roll can see carry economics dominate returns on long-held leveraged positions.
Misconceptions: A tom-next roll is not a new directional trade and not a fee set arbitrarily by the broker — it is the market-priced interest differential for deferring settlement by one day.
Example: A desk long EUR/USD over value date Tuesday executes a tom-next swap: it sells EUR settling Wednesday and buys it back settling Thursday, paying or earning one day of the EUR-USD rate differential.
Citation: Wikipedia — Foreign exchange swap — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foreign_exchange_swap (Uses (tom-next rolls and cost of carry) and Pricing)
Status: Reviewed

1012. Fixing
Domain: Foreign exchange
Definition: A reference exchange rate determined at a set time each trading day from market transactions and orders around a fixing window, used to value portfolios, settle contracts and execute customer 'fix orders' at a common published price. The most prominent is the London WM/Reuters 4 p.m. fixing in the interbank forex market.
Intuition: A fixing is the market's agreed 'official' exchange rate for a given moment each day, so that funds and contracts everywhere can be valued on the same number.
Mechanics: A benchmark administrator computes the rate from trades and order-book data captured during a short window around the fixing time (the WM/Reuters 4 p.m. window was widened from one to five minutes in the 2015 reform). Banks accept customer orders guaranteed to execute at the fix price, which concentrates volume into the window; investigations found banks had colluded around the window, leading to penalties and the 2015 reform of the London fixing.
Relationships: London 4 p.m. fix, FX spot
Failure modes: Fixings create manipulation incentives: dealers holding guaranteed fix orders profit by moving the window price, and the 2013-15 FX scandal showed collusive behavior around the London fix. Post-reform, price anomalies around the window and passive execution strategies still generate predictable price patterns.
Misconceptions: The fix is not a transaction price anyone can always trade at — it is a computed reference from a short window, and large fix orders are typically executed by dealers over time rather than all at the fix print.
Example: An index fund rebalancing at month-end instructs its bank to execute a large currency conversion 'at the 4 p.m. fix'; the bank's execution and hedging flows concentrate into the fixing window.
Citation: NBER Working Paper 23327 — Did the Reform Fix the London Fix Problem? (Ito and Yamada) — https://www.nber.org/papers/w23327 (abstract)
Status: Reviewed

1013. London 4 p.m. fix
Domain: Foreign exchange
Definition: The daily reference exchange rate computed from market activity in a window around 4:00 p.m. London time, historically administered as the WM/Reuters benchmark. It is the most widely used FX fixing for valuing funds, settling derivatives and executing customer orders, and was the focus of the 2013-15 benchmark-manipulation investigations and the subsequent 2015 reform that widened the fixing window.
Intuition: The 4 p.m. London fix is the FX market's global 'closing price' — the single rate the world's asset managers use to value and convert currencies.
Mechanics: The rate is computed from actual trades and order data over a window centred on 4 p.m. London time; the window was lengthened from one minute to five minutes in the 2015 reform to reduce manipulability. Banks accepting client fix orders guarantee execution at the fix price and hedge the resulting exposure, which produces volume spikes and characteristic price dynamics in the window — patterns that persisted in altered form after the reform, as banks shifted to passive execution strategies.
Relationships: Fixing, FX spot, FX forward
Failure modes: The pre-2015 one-minute window was manipulable: traders at major banks colluded to push the fix, resulting in multi-billion-dollar fines. Post-reform, the fix still exhibits anomalous price dynamics and heavy month-end volume, so execution quality at the fix can differ systematically from prevailing market prices.
Misconceptions: The fix is not set in London by a committee of quotes (like old LIBOR) — it is computed from actual market transaction data in the window — and trading 'at the fix' does not guarantee the mid-market price.
Example: A global equity fund's NAV converts its foreign holdings to dollars each day using the WM/Reuters 4 p.m. rates, so its reported performance is tied to those fix prints.
Citation: NBER Working Paper 23327 — Did the Reform Fix the London Fix Problem? (Ito and Yamada) — https://www.nber.org/papers/w23327 (abstract)
Status: Reviewed

1014. Yield curve
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: A curve that plots the yields of bonds of the same credit quality (typically government securities) against their times to maturity at a given point in time. The U.S. Treasury's official version is a par yield curve relating the par yield on a Treasury security to its time to maturity, derived daily from market price quotations.
Intuition: It is a snapshot of what it costs to borrow money for different lengths of time, showing how the market prices time, risk, and expectations about future rates.
Mechanics: Market prices of on-the-run securities are converted to yields, and a curve-fitting method (Treasury uses bootstrapping of forward rates plus monotone convex interpolation) produces a continuous curve from which constant-maturity yields are read.
Relationships: Normal yield curve, Inverted yield curve, Flat yield curve, Spot rate curve, Par yield, Yield spread
Failure modes: Curve shapes mix expected future rates, term premia, and supply/demand effects, so the curve alone cannot identify which driver dominates. Fitted curves are also model-dependent: different fitting methods produce slightly different yields at the same maturities.
Misconceptions: A common mistake is treating the yield curve as a forecast of future rates; Treasury itself states that the curve indicates what rates were and are, not what they will be.
Example: On a day when the 2-year Treasury yields 4.0% and the 10-year yields 4.3%, the 2s10s segment of the curve is upward sloping by 30 basis points.
Citation: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Interest Rate Statistics (Daily Treasury Par Yield Curve Rates) — https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics (Daily Treasury PAR Yield Curve Rates)
Status: Reviewed

1015. Normal yield curve
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: A yield curve configuration in which longer-maturity yields are higher than shorter-maturity yields, giving the curve an upward slope. It is the historically most common configuration, reflecting term premia and typical expectations that rates will not fall sharply.
Intuition: Lenders usually demand more compensation for tying up money longer, so longer loans carry higher rates — that is the 'normal' state of the curve.
Mechanics: The slope is measured as a spread between constant-maturity yields, e.g. the 10-year minus the 2-year Treasury yield; a positive value corresponds to a normal (upward-sloping) curve.
Formula: Slope ≈ y(long maturity) − y(short maturity) > 0, e.g. 10-year CMT minus 2-year CMT.
Relationships: Yield curve, Inverted yield curve, Flat yield curve, Term premium, Yield spread
Failure modes: An upward slope does not prove rates will rise; the slope conflates term premium, rate expectations, and issuance/demand effects, so reading it as a pure forecast is unreliable.
Misconceptions: It is wrong to assume 'normal' means guaranteed or stable; curves can steepen or flatten quickly, and a normal curve is simply the modal historical shape, not a law.
Example: If 3-month bills yield 3.5%, the 2-year note yields 4.0%, and the 10-year yields 4.5%, the curve is normal (upward sloping).
Citation: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Interest Rate Statistics (Daily Treasury Par Yield Curve Rates) — https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics (Daily Treasury PAR Yield Curve Rates)
Status: Reviewed

1016. Inverted yield curve
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: A yield curve configuration in which shorter-maturity yields exceed longer-maturity yields, giving the curve a downward slope. The U.S. Treasury notes that short-term rates can exceed longer-term rates when market expectations about future rates and monetary policy shift; inversions have historically preceded U.S. recessions, though the relationship is a statistical regularity, not a causal law.
Intuition: Investors accept lower yields on long bonds because they expect rates to fall in the future — often because they expect the central bank to cut rates in a slowdown.
Mechanics: Measured as a negative term spread, e.g. the 10-year Treasury constant maturity yield minus the 2-year (FRED series T10Y2Y) falling below zero. Inversions often arise when policy tightening pushes short rates up while long yields stay anchored by weak growth expectations.
Formula: Inversion when y(short) − y(long) > 0, e.g. 2-year CMT − 10-year CMT > 0.
Relationships: Yield curve, Normal yield curve, Flat yield curve, Yield spread, Policy rate, Term premium
Failure modes: Inversions have produced false or very early recession signals, and post-2008 term premium compression (e.g. from quantitative easing) can invert curves without implying a downturn; timing between inversion and recession varies widely.
Misconceptions: Inversion does not cause recessions, nor does it guarantee one; it is an indicator of market expectations and term premia, not a mechanical trigger.
Example: In 2022–2023 the 2-year Treasury yield rose above the 10-year yield, leaving the 2s10s spread negative for an extended period.
Citation: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Interest Rates — Frequently Asked Questions — https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics/interest-rates-frequently-asked-questions (Why do longer CMT maturities sometimes have yields lower than the shorter maturities (i.e., "inverted yield curve rates")?)
Citation: FRED, 10-Year Treasury Constant Maturity Minus 2-Year Treasury Constant Maturity [T10Y2Y] — https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/T10Y2Y (Notes)
Status: Reviewed

1017. Flat yield curve
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: A yield curve configuration in which yields are approximately equal across maturities, so the term spread is near zero. It typically appears as a transitional state between an upward-sloping (normal) curve and an inverted curve, or vice versa.
Intuition: The market is charging roughly the same rate to borrow for one year as for ten years — a sign that expectations about the future are unusually uncertain or in transition.
Mechanics: Identified when the spread between long- and short-maturity constant-maturity yields (e.g. 10-year minus 2-year Treasury) is close to zero; flattening occurs when short rates rise toward long rates (bear flattener) or long rates fall toward short rates (bull flattener).
Formula: Flat when |y(long) − y(short)| ≈ 0.
Relationships: Yield curve, Normal yield curve, Inverted yield curve, Yield spread
Failure modes: A flat curve carries little standalone signal: it can precede steepening or inversion, and 'flatness' has no precise threshold, so classification is judgment-dependent.
Misconceptions: A flat curve is not a neutral or 'no information' state in a predictive sense, and it is not a distinct market regime with proven consequences — it is simply a descriptive shape.
Example: If the 2-year Treasury yields 4.20% and the 10-year yields 4.25%, the 2s10s segment is essentially flat at 5 basis points.
Citation: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Interest Rates — Frequently Asked Questions — https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics/interest-rates-frequently-asked-questions (Par yield curve and CMT rates discussion)
Citation: FRED, 10-Year Treasury Constant Maturity Minus 2-Year Treasury Constant Maturity [T10Y2Y] — https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/T10Y2Y (Notes)
Status: Reviewed

1018. Spot rate curve
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: The curve of yields on zero-coupon instruments across maturities — the set of rates at which a single future cash flow is discounted to today. It is built by bootstrapping coupon-bearing bond prices so that each instrument is repriced without error, and it is the curve used for present-value calculations.
Intuition: Instead of one blended yield per bond, the spot curve gives a separate 'pure' interest rate for every single future date, like a price tag for money delivered at each point in time.
Mechanics: Starting from the shortest maturity, each bond's price is decomposed into its cash flows; the discount rate that prices each successive maturity's cash flow exactly (given already-solved shorter rates) is the spot rate for that maturity. The U.S. Treasury bootstraps instantaneous forward rates from on-the-run prices, which equivalently determines the spot curve; Treasury does not publish a daily zero-coupon curve itself.
Formula: P = sum over t of CF_t / (1 + z_t)^t, where z_t is the t-year spot (zero-coupon) rate, CF_t the cash flow at time t, and P the bond's price.
Relationships: Yield curve, Zero-coupon rate, Discount factor, Forward rate curve, Par yield
Failure modes: The bootstrapped curve depends on the fitting/interpolation method and the input securities chosen, so different constructions give different spot rates, especially between quoted maturities and at the long end.
Misconceptions: Spot rates are not directly observable in coupon-bond markets and are not the same as par yields; the par yield curve and the spot curve differ whenever the curve is not flat.
Example: If the 2-year spot rate is 4.2%, a single $100 payment due in exactly 2 years is worth 100 / (1.042)^2 ≈ $92.10 today.
Citation: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Treasury Yield Curve Methodology — https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics/treasury-yield-curve-methodology (Bootstrapping and monotone convex interpolation description)
Citation: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Interest Rates — Frequently Asked Questions — https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics/interest-rates-frequently-asked-questions (Does the par yield curve assume semiannual interest payments or is it a zero-coupon curve?)
Status: Reviewed

1019. Forward rate curve
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: The curve of interest rates implied today for borrowing or lending over future periods, derived from the spot (zero-coupon) curve so that investing to a long horizon equals rolling over at the shorter rate plus the forward rate. The U.S. Treasury's curve construction bootstraps instantaneous forward rates at input maturities as an intermediate step.
Intuition: If you know the 1-year rate and the 2-year rate, the market is implicitly quoting a rate for year two alone — the forward curve is the set of all such implied future-period rates.
Mechanics: Forward rates are extracted from spot rates by no-arbitrage: chaining the short spot rate with the forward rate over the remaining period must reproduce the long spot rate. Treasury derives instantaneous forward rates so that input securities are sequentially priced without error.
Formula: (1 + z_T)^T = (1 + z_t)^t × (1 + f(t,T))^(T−t), so f(t,T) = [ (1 + z_T)^T / (1 + z_t)^t ]^(1/(T−t)) − 1, where z_t, z_T are spot rates and f(t,T) is the forward rate from t to T.
Relationships: Spot rate curve, Zero-coupon rate, Discount factor, Yield curve
Failure modes: Forward rates embed term and risk premia, so they are biased predictors of realized future rates; empirically the expectations hypothesis performs poorly, especially at longer horizons.
Misconceptions: An implied forward rate is not a market forecast agreed by participants; it is an arithmetic consequence of today's spot curve plus premia, not a prediction.
Example: If the 1-year spot rate is 4.0% and the 2-year spot rate is 4.5%, the implied 1-year forward rate one year ahead is (1.045^2 / 1.04) − 1 ≈ 5.0%.
Citation: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Treasury Yield Curve Methodology — https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics/treasury-yield-curve-methodology (Bootstrapping of instantaneous forward rates)
Status: Reviewed

1020. Discount factor
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: The present value of one unit of currency received at a specified future date, equivalently the price today of a risk-free zero-coupon payment of 1 at that date. The full set of discount factors across dates is the discount function, which is derived from the spot rate curve.
Intuition: A discount factor answers: how much is a dollar delivered on a given future date worth right now?
Mechanics: Each cash flow of an instrument is multiplied by the discount factor for its payment date and summed to get the instrument's present value. Discount factors are obtained from spot rates (or, equivalently, from the bootstrapped forward-rate curve used in curve construction such as Treasury's).
Formula: DF(t) = 1 / (1 + z_t)^t with annual compounding (DF(t) = e^(−z_t × t) under continuous compounding), where z_t is the t-year spot rate; PV = Σ CF_t × DF(t).
Relationships: Spot rate curve, Zero-coupon rate, Forward rate curve
Failure modes: Because discount factors inherit the chosen curve-fitting method and day-count/compounding conventions, they can differ across vendors even for the same date; using a single yield for all maturities instead of term-specific factors misprices non-standard cash flows.
Misconceptions: A discount factor is not a 'discount' in the retail sense and is not the same as a coupon rate; it is a present-value weight between 0 and 1 for a specific date.
Example: With a 2-year spot rate of 4%, the 2-year discount factor is 1 / 1.04^2 ≈ 0.9246, so $1,000 due in 2 years is worth about $924.60 today.
Citation: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Treasury Yield Curve Methodology — https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics/treasury-yield-curve-methodology (Bootstrapping and curve construction description)
Status: Reviewed

1021. Zero-coupon rate
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: The yield earned on an investment that makes a single payment at maturity with no intermediate coupons, for a specific maturity. It is the building block of the spot (zero-coupon) curve used to discount individual future cash flows.
Intuition: It is the pure interest rate for money delivered at one exact future date, with nothing paid in between — like the rate on a Treasury bill or a STRIP.
Mechanics: For a zero-coupon instrument the rate follows directly from price and face value; for coupon-bearing markets the zero-coupon rates are bootstrapped from bond prices so all input securities price without error. The U.S. Treasury notes its published par yield curve is a semiannual bond-equivalent curve and that it does not publish daily zero-coupon curve rates.
Formula: z_t = (F / P)^(1/t) − 1, where P is the price today, F the single payment at maturity, and t the time in years.
Relationships: Spot rate curve, Discount factor, Forward rate curve, Par yield
Failure modes: Zero-coupon rates are model-derived rather than directly quoted for most maturities, so they inherit bootstrapping and interpolation assumptions; liquidity differences between coupon bonds and STRIPS can also create small inconsistencies.
Misconceptions: The zero-coupon rate for maturity t is not the yield of the t-year coupon bond; confusing par yields with spot rates produces systematic valuation errors when the curve is sloped.
Example: A 2-year zero-coupon bond priced at 92.10 per 100 face implies a 2-year zero rate of (100/92.10)^(1/2) − 1 ≈ 4.2%.
Citation: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Interest Rates — Frequently Asked Questions — https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics/interest-rates-frequently-asked-questions (Does the par yield curve assume semiannual interest payments or is it a zero-coupon curve?)
Status: Reviewed

1022. Par yield
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: The coupon rate at which a hypothetical bond of a given maturity would price exactly at par (100% of face value), given the current discount function. The U.S. Treasury's official daily yield curve is a par yield curve, and its constant-maturity (CMT) rates are par yields read from that curve.
Intuition: It is the coupon a brand-new bond of a given maturity would have to pay today for investors to accept it at full face value.
Mechanics: Treasury converts indicative bid-side price quotations on the most recently auctioned securities to yields, bootstraps forward rates, and applies monotone convex interpolation to construct a curve of true par rates; CMT yields are then read at fixed maturities and quoted as semiannual bond-equivalent yields.
Formula: Par coupon c solves 100 = Σ_t (c/2) × DF(t) + 100 × DF(T), where DF(t) are discount factors and T is maturity (semiannual coupons).
Relationships: Yield curve, Spot rate curve, Zero-coupon rate, Discount factor
Failure modes: CMT par yields are read from a fitted curve and may not match the actual yield of any specific traded security; the curve also depends on the fitting methodology, which Treasury has changed over time.
Misconceptions: A par yield is not the same as the spot rate for that maturity, and a CMT rate is not the yield on an actual outstanding bond of exactly that maturity.
Example: If the fitted 10-year par yield is 4.30%, a new theoretical 10-year bond with a 4.30% coupon would be worth exactly 100.
Citation: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Treasury Yield Curve Methodology — https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics/treasury-yield-curve-methodology (Full methodology description)
Citation: U.S. Department of the Treasury, Interest Rates — Frequently Asked Questions — https://home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics/interest-rates-frequently-asked-questions (What is the difference between the Daily Treasury Long-Term Rates and the Daily Treasury Par Yield Curve Rates?)
Status: Reviewed

1023. Yield spread
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: The difference between two yields, typically expressed in basis points. Depending on context it may compare maturities on the same curve (term spread, e.g. 10-year minus 2-year Treasury), or securities of different credit quality at the same maturity (credit spread).
Intuition: It is the extra (or lesser) yield one instrument offers relative to another, summarizing how the market prices the difference in time, risk, or liquidity between them.
Mechanics: Computed as a simple subtraction of yields at matched or specified maturities; e.g. FRED's T10Y2Y is the 10-year Treasury constant maturity yield minus the 2-year, and term or credit spreads widen or narrow as relative yields move.
Formula: s = y_A − y_B, quoted in basis points (1 bp = 0.01 percentage point).
Relationships: Credit spread, Option-adjusted spread, Z-spread, Swap spread, Yield curve, Basis point
Failure modes: A raw yield spread ignores differences in maturity, coupon, embedded options, and compounding conventions, so comparing spreads across unlike instruments can mislead; spreads also mix risk, liquidity, and tax effects.
Misconceptions: A wider spread does not automatically mean a bond is 'cheap'; it may simply reflect genuinely higher expected losses or worse liquidity.
Example: If a 10-year corporate bond yields 5.6% and the 10-year Treasury yields 4.3%, the yield spread is 130 basis points.
Citation: FRED, 10-Year Treasury Constant Maturity Minus 2-Year Treasury Constant Maturity [T10Y2Y] — https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/T10Y2Y (Notes)
Status: Reviewed

1024. Credit spread
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: The difference between the yield on the debt securities of a particular corporate or sovereign borrower (or a rating class of borrowers) and the yield on similar-maturity Treasury securities. It compensates investors for bearing default and credit-migration risk, plus a liquidity component.
Intuition: It is the extra interest a risky borrower must pay over the government to persuade investors to lend to it.
Mechanics: Measured as corporate (or other non-Treasury) yield minus the matched-maturity Treasury yield, or at index level as an option-adjusted spread over the Treasury spot curve, e.g. the ICE BofA US Corporate Index OAS published on FRED.
Formula: Credit spread = y(corporate bond) − y(matched-maturity Treasury), in basis points.
Relationships: Yield spread, Option-adjusted spread, Z-spread, Swap spread
Failure modes: Spreads conflate expected default losses, risk premia, and illiquidity, so they overstate pure default compensation; in crises, liquidity-driven widening can look like surging default risk. Maturity or option mismatches also distort simple yield differences.
Misconceptions: The credit spread is not a direct estimate of default probability, and a high spread does not by itself imply a mispricing or an attractive trade.
Example: If BBB-rated 10-year corporate bonds yield 5.5% while the 10-year Treasury yields 4.3%, the credit spread is 120 basis points.
Citation: CFTC Glossary (A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry) — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Credit Spread)
Citation: FRED, ICE BofA US Corporate Index Option-Adjusted Spread [BAMLC0A0CM] — https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/BAMLC0A0CM (Notes)
Status: Reviewed

1025. Option-adjusted spread
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: The constant spread added to a benchmark spot curve that makes the model value of a security's cash flows — adjusted for the value of embedded options such as calls or prepayment rights — equal to its market price. It is the standard spread measure for callable bonds and mortgage-backed securities.
Intuition: It is the yield premium a bond pays over Treasuries after stripping out the value of any options hidden in the bond, leaving a cleaner measure of credit and liquidity compensation.
Mechanics: An interest-rate model generates many rate paths; cash flows on each path reflect option exercise (e.g. calls or prepayments). The spread over the benchmark curve that equates the average present value across paths to the market price is the OAS. ICE BofA computes index OAS as the market-cap-weighted average of constituent bond OAS versus a spot Treasury curve.
Formula: Price = (1/N) Σ_paths Σ_t CF_t(path) × DF_t(path; benchmark + OAS); OAS is solved numerically.
Relationships: Z-spread, Credit spread, Yield spread, Negative convexity
Failure modes: OAS is model-dependent: results vary with the volatility assumptions and interest-rate/prepayment model used, so OAS values from different models are not strictly comparable. It is also an average over scenarios, not a guaranteed earned spread.
Misconceptions: OAS is not the spread an investor will actually realize; realized excess return depends on path, default, and prepayment outcomes, not just the option adjustment.
Example: The ICE BofA US Corporate Index OAS (FRED series BAMLC0A0CM) stood around 0.8–1.0% in calm periods and spiked above 4% in March 2020, reflecting the market-wide corporate spread adjustment over the Treasury spot curve.
Citation: FRED, ICE BofA US Corporate Index Option-Adjusted Spread [BAMLC0A0CM] (source: ICE Data Indices) — https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/BAMLC0A0CM (Notes)
Status: Reviewed

1026. Z-spread
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: The constant spread that, when added to each point of the Treasury (or benchmark) spot rate curve, makes the present value of a bond's cash flows equal to its market price. Unlike a nominal spread measured at a single maturity, it accounts for the entire term structure; unlike OAS, it does not adjust for embedded options.
Intuition: It is the single number of extra yield the bond must offer at every point along the curve for its promised cash flows to be worth today's price.
Mechanics: Each cash flow is discounted at the benchmark spot rate for its maturity plus the spread Z; Z is solved numerically so the discounted cash flows sum to the full (dirty) price. For option-free bonds the Z-spread and OAS coincide; for bonds with embedded options the Z-spread includes compensation for option risk.
Formula: P = Σ_t CF_t / (1 + (z_t + Z)/2)^(2t), where P is the full price, CF_t the cash flow at time t, z_t the spot rate at t, and Z the Z-spread (semiannual convention).
Relationships: Option-adjusted spread, Credit spread, Yield spread, Spot rate curve
Failure modes: For callable or prepayable bonds the Z-spread misattributes option value to credit/liquidity, overstating the option-free spread; it also assumes cash flows are certain, so it is misleading for credit-risky securities near distress.
Misconceptions: The 'zero-volatility' name does not mean the bond is riskless; it means the spread is constant and no interest-rate volatility model (option adjustment) is applied.
Example: A 3-year bond priced at 104.90 with cash flows of 5, 5, and 105 against spot rates of 2.5%, 2.7%, and 3.0% has a Z-spread of about 0.29% (29 bp).
Citation: Investopedia, Zero-Volatility Spread (Z-Spread) — https://www.investopedia.com/terms/z/zspread.asp (Understanding the Zero-Volatility Spread Formula and Calculation)
Status: Reviewed

1027. Asset swap spread
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: The spread over the floating benchmark in an asset swap — a package in which an investor buys a fixed-rate bond and simultaneously enters an interest rate swap, paying the bond's fixed coupons and receiving a floating rate plus a spread. It expresses the bond's yield relative to the swap curve rather than to government bonds.
Intuition: It measures how much extra return a bond offers once its interest-rate exposure has been swapped away, isolating the credit and liquidity premium versus the derivatives market's benchmark.
Mechanics: In a par asset swap, the investor pays the bond's fixed coupon into the swap and receives floating (e.g. SOFR) plus or minus a fixed spread; the package is priced at par, and the spread solves for the floating-leg margin. The asset swap spread is thus the difference between the bond's economics and the matched-maturity swap rate, expressed in basis points.
Formula: ASW spread ≈ bond's spread over the swap curve such that (bond price + swap value) = par at inception; roughly ASW ≈ (bond yield − swap rate) adjusted for any premium/discount to par amortized over the swap.
Relationships: Swap spread, Z-spread, Credit spread, Option-adjusted spread
Failure modes: The spread depends on the swap benchmark and the assumed funding of the position; benchmark transitions (LIBOR to SOFR) changed its level and comparability. Unlike a CDS, an asset swap does not terminate on default, so it embeds recovery-risk differences.
Misconceptions: A high asset swap spread does not mean the position is protected against default — the investor keeps the bond's credit risk, since the swap typically continues even if the issuer defaults.
Example: An investor buys a bond yielding 6% when the matched swap rate is 5%; after accounting for the price premium, the asset swap spread might be quoted as SOFR + 50 bp.
Citation: Investopedia, Asset Swap — https://www.investopedia.com/terms/a/assetswap.asp (Exploring Asset Swap Spreads)
Status: Reviewed

1028. Swap spread
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: The difference between the fixed rate on a plain-vanilla interest rate swap of a given maturity and the yield on a government bond of the same maturity. It reflects the relative pricing of the derivatives and government bond markets, including intermediation and funding costs.
Intuition: It compares the cost of exchanging fixed-for-floating payments in the swap market with the government's borrowing cost — a gauge of how dealers price balance-sheet usage and of relative supply and demand in the two markets.
Mechanics: Swap rate minus same-maturity government bond yield, in basis points. Arbitrage links the two markets (hold the bond funded via repo, pay fixed on the swap), but dealer balance-sheet costs, repo funding rates, bond supply, and demand to receive fixed can push spreads away from zero; long-maturity USD spreads have been persistently negative in recent years, and the shift from LIBOR to risk-free rates such as SOFR mechanically lowered swap spreads.
Formula: Swap spread = swap rate(maturity T) − government bond yield(maturity T), in basis points.
Relationships: Asset swap spread, Yield spread, Credit spread, Repo rate, Secured Overnight Financing Rate
Failure modes: Spreads are not a pure credit measure: they move with repo funding costs, dealer constraints, Treasury supply, and benchmark conventions, so treating them as a simple risk gauge misleads. Negative spreads are not exploitable arbitrage profits — they compensate intermediaries for real balance-sheet costs.
Misconceptions: A negative swap spread is not a 'free lunch' arbitrage left on the table; capturing it requires repo-funded bond holdings whose financing and balance-sheet costs consume the apparent profit.
Example: If the 10-year SOFR swap rate is 3.60% and the 10-year Treasury yields 4.05%, the 10-year swap spread is −45 basis points.
Citation: BIS Quarterly Review, December 2024 — 'Negative interest rate swap spreads signal pressure in government debt absorption' — https://www.bis.org/publ/qtrpdf/r_qt2412y.htm (Special feature box)
Status: Reviewed

1029. DV01
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: The change in a bond's (or portfolio's) value, in currency units, for a one-basis-point (0.01%) change in yield. In the U.S. it is also called the dollar value of an 01; it is essentially the price value of a basis point (PVBP), often written PV01.
Intuition: It answers the trader's core question: how many dollars do I make or lose if yields move by one basis point?
Mechanics: Computed either analytically as modified duration times full price times 0.0001, or numerically by repricing the position with yields shifted up and down one basis point and halving the difference. Because it is additive across positions, it is the standard unit for sizing and hedging interest-rate risk.
Formula: DV01 = ModDur × P × 0.0001, where ModDur is modified duration and P the full price; equivalently DV01 = (PV(−1bp) − PV(+1bp)) / 2.
Relationships: PV01, Macaulay duration, Effective duration, Key rate duration, Basis point
Failure modes: DV01 is a linear (first-order) sensitivity: for large yield moves it ignores convexity, so realized P&L deviates from the DV01 estimate. For option-embedded bonds it shifts with the level of rates.
Misconceptions: DV01 is not a percentage and not a probability; and a DV01-hedged book is only hedged against small parallel yield moves, not against curve reshaping or volatility changes.
Example: A bond with modified duration 8.5 and full price 101 has DV01 ≈ 8.5 × 101 × 0.0001 ≈ $0.0859 per $100 face — about $859 per $1 million face per basis point.
Citation: AnalystPrep, CFA Level 1 Fixed Income — Modified Duration, Money Duration, and Price Value of a Basis Point (PVBP) — https://analystprep.com/cfa-level-1-exam/fixed-income/modified-duration-money-duration-and-price-value-of-a-basis-point-pvbp/ (Price Value of a Basis Point (PVBP))
Status: Reviewed

1030. PV01
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: The change in the present value (full price) of a bond or swap for a one-basis-point change in yield. It is the same quantity as PVBP and the U.S. market term DV01; in swap markets PV01 is the standard sensitivity measure per basis point of the swap rate.
Intuition: It is the cash value gained or lost when the relevant rate ticks up or down by a single basis point.
Mechanics: Estimated numerically by repricing with yields one basis point lower and one basis point higher and taking half the difference, which works even when cash flows are uncertain (e.g. callable bonds); analytically it equals modified duration times price times 0.0001.
Formula: PV01 = (PV(−1bp) − PV(+1bp)) / 2 ≈ ModDur × P × 0.0001.
Relationships: DV01, Effective duration, Macaulay duration, Key rate duration, Basis point
