Failure modes: Like all first-order sensitivities it ignores convexity and is valid only locally; PV01 quoted on swaps depends on curve-construction and discounting conventions, so cross-vendor values can differ slightly.
Misconceptions: PV01 and DV01 are sometimes claimed to be fundamentally different measures; in practice both denote the present-value change per basis point, with naming differences by market segment rather than by concept.
Example: If a swap's present value rises by $4,600 when its rate falls 1 bp and falls by $4,400 when the rate rises 1 bp, its PV01 ≈ (4,600 + 4,400)/2 = $4,500 per bp on the position.
Citation: AnalystPrep, CFA Level 1 Fixed Income — Modified Duration, Money Duration, and Price Value of a Basis Point (PVBP) — https://analystprep.com/cfa-level-1-exam/fixed-income/modified-duration-money-duration-and-price-value-of-a-basis-point-pvbp/ (Price Value of a Basis Point (PVBP))
Status: Reviewed

1031. Key rate duration
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: A measure of a bond's or portfolio's price sensitivity to a change in yield at one specific maturity point on the curve, holding other points fixed. The set of key rate durations across maturities decomposes total interest-rate sensitivity, and they sum (approximately) to the effective duration.
Intuition: Instead of asking 'what if all rates move?', it asks 'what if only the 5-year rate moves?' — locating where along the curve a portfolio's risk actually sits.
Mechanics: The yield at a chosen key maturity (e.g. 2, 5, 10, 30 years) is shifted by a small amount (with the shift tapered to neighboring points), the security is repriced both ways, and duration is computed from the price changes; repeating across 11 standard maturities gives a sensitivity profile used for non-parallel curve hedging.
Formula: KRD_i = (P(−) − P(+)) / (2 × Δy × P_0), where P(−), P(+) are prices after a 1% down/up shift of the key rate at maturity i, and P_0 the original price.
Relationships: Effective duration, DV01, Yield curve, Macaulay duration
Failure modes: Real yield curves rarely move one point at a time, so isolated key rate shifts are artificial; results also depend on how the shift is tapered to adjacent maturities, making values convention-dependent.
Misconceptions: A high total duration does not reveal curve exposure: two portfolios with the same effective duration can have very different key rate profiles and behave oppositely when the curve twists.
Example: A portfolio with a 10-year key rate duration of 4.0 loses roughly 4% of value if the 10-year rate alone rises 100 bp, regardless of what other maturities do.
Citation: Investopedia, Key Rate Duration — https://www.investopedia.com/terms/k/keyrateduration.asp (What Is Key Rate Duration?)
Status: Reviewed

1032. Effective duration
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: A bond's price sensitivity to a parallel shift in the benchmark yield curve, computed numerically by repricing the bond at higher and lower yields while allowing cash flows to change (e.g. via call or prepayment options). It is the appropriate duration measure for bonds with embedded options, where cash flows are not fixed.
Intuition: It measures how much a bond's price actually moves when rates move, recognizing that for callable or mortgage bonds the payments themselves change when rates change.
Mechanics: The bond is valued under a small downward and upward parallel shift of the curve (using a model that adjusts cash flows for embedded options), and duration is approximated from the three prices; it equals the percentage price change for a 1% parallel rate move.
Formula: EffDur = (P(−) − P(+)) / (2 × Δy × P_0), where P(−), P(+) are prices after a parallel curve shift down/up of Δy, and P_0 the current price.
Relationships: Macaulay duration, Key rate duration, DV01, Negative convexity, Option-adjusted spread
Failure modes: It assumes parallel curve shifts, so it misses reshaping risk; it is also model-dependent for option-embedded bonds, since the prepayment or option model determines the shifted prices.
Misconceptions: Duration is not the bond's maturity and not a fixed property of the security — effective duration changes as rates, volatility, and time move, especially for callable bonds.
Example: If a callable bond priced at 100 would be worth 103.5 at rates 50 bp lower and 96.8 at rates 50 bp higher, its effective duration is (103.5 − 96.8)/(2 × 0.005 × 100) = 6.7.
Citation: AnalystPrep, CFA Level 1 Fixed Income — Modified Duration, Money Duration, and Price Value of a Basis Point (PVBP) — https://analystprep.com/cfa-level-1-exam/fixed-income/modified-duration-money-duration-and-price-value-of-a-basis-point-pvbp/ (Approximating Modified Duration)
Citation: Fidelity, Duration: Understanding the Relationship Between Bond Prices and Interest Rates — https://www.fidelity.com/learning-center/investment-products/fixed-income-bonds/duration (Using a bond's duration to gauge interest rate risk)
Status: Reviewed

1033. Macaulay duration
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: The weighted-average time until a bond's cash flows are received, with each cash flow weighted by its share of the bond's present value. Expressed in years, it equals maturity for a zero-coupon bond and is always shorter than maturity for a coupon bond; it is the foundation from which modified and effective duration are derived.
Intuition: It is the 'center of gravity' of a bond's payments — the single point in time at which the average dollar of the bond's value arrives.
Mechanics: Each cash flow's present value is divided by the bond's full price to get a weight; the weights are multiplied by the time to receipt and summed. Dividing Macaulay duration by (1 + yield per period) gives modified duration, the direct price-sensitivity measure.
Formula: MacDur = Σ_t [ t × PV(CF_t) ] / P, where PV(CF_t) is the present value of the cash flow at time t and P the full price; ModDur = MacDur / (1 + r), with r the yield per period.
Relationships: Effective duration, Key rate duration, DV01, Zero-coupon rate
Failure modes: As a time measure it applies cleanly only to fixed cash flows; for callable or floating-rate instruments the cash-flow weights are not fixed, so Macaulay duration is undefined or misleading without an options model.
Misconceptions: Duration in years is often mistaken for the bond's remaining life; a 10-year coupon bond's Macaulay duration is well below 10 years, and duration (not maturity) is what governs rate sensitivity.
Example: A 4-year, 4% semiannual-pay bond at a 6% yield has an annualized Macaulay duration of about 3.72 years — less than its 4-year maturity because coupons arrive earlier.
Citation: AnalystPrep, CFA Level 1 Fixed Income — Modified Duration, Money Duration, and Price Value of a Basis Point (PVBP) — https://analystprep.com/cfa-level-1-exam/fixed-income/modified-duration-money-duration-and-price-value-of-a-basis-point-pvbp/ (Relation to Macaulay Duration and worked example)
Status: Reviewed

1034. Negative convexity
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: A property of a bond whose price-yield relationship is concave: prices rise less when yields fall and fall more when yields rise than duration alone predicts. It is typical of callable bonds and mortgage-backed securities, whose cash flows shorten when rates decline (calls/prepayments) and lengthen when rates rise.
Intuition: The bond works against you both ways: it stops appreciating just when rates fall (because it gets called or prepaid) and keeps falling when rates rise.
Mechanics: Convexity is the second derivative of price with respect to yield, approximated as (P(−) + P(+) − 2P_0) / (P_0 × Δy²); when this quantity is negative, duration rises as yields rise (extension risk) and falls as yields fall (contraction risk), making duration-only hedges systematically wrong in the adverse direction.
Formula: Convexity ≈ (P(−) + P(+) − 2 × P_0) / (P_0 × Δy²); negative when P(−) + P(+) < 2 × P_0.
Relationships: Positive convexity, Effective duration, Option-adjusted spread, DV01
Failure modes: Duration-based estimates fail precisely when they are most needed (large rate moves) for negatively convex securities; hedging MBS or callable books with duration alone creates pro-cyclical hedging flows that can amplify rate swings.
Misconceptions: Negative convexity does not mean the bond must lose money; it means the price response is asymmetric, and investors are compensated for bearing it through higher yield (option-adjusted spread).
Example: A callable bond priced at 100 might gain only 3 points if yields fall 100 bp (its price is capped near the call price) but lose 6 points if yields rise 100 bp.
Citation: Investopedia, Negative Convexity — https://www.investopedia.com/terms/n/negative_convexity.asp (What Is Negative Convexity?)
Status: Reviewed

1035. Positive convexity
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: A property of a bond whose price-yield relationship is convex: prices rise more when yields fall and fall less when yields rise than duration alone predicts. All standard non-callable fixed-rate bonds exhibit positive convexity; the effect grows with longer maturity and lower coupons.
Intuition: The bond's price accelerates in your favor: you gain a bit extra when rates fall and lose a bit less when rates rise, compared with the straight-line duration estimate.
Mechanics: Convexity is the curvature (second derivative) of the price-yield function; with positive convexity, duration falls as yields rise and rises as yields fall. The effect is most pronounced in long-duration, low-coupon bonds, and the price impact is captured by adding a convexity adjustment to the duration estimate.
Formula: Convexity ≈ (P(−) + P(+) − 2 × P_0) / (P_0 × Δy²) > 0; price change ≈ −ModDur × Δy × P_0 + ½ × Convexity × (Δy)² × P_0.
Relationships: Negative convexity, Macaulay duration, Effective duration, DV01
Failure modes: Convexity benefits are already priced in (higher-convexity bonds trade at lower yields), so it is not a free advantage; for small rate moves the convexity term is negligible and adds little to the duration estimate.
Misconceptions: Positive convexity is not a guarantee of outperformance and does not mean prices cannot fall; it only describes the curvature of the price-yield relationship.
Example: A 30-year zero-coupon bond has very high positive convexity: a 100 bp yield decline lifts its price by more than duration suggests, while a 100 bp rise costs it less.
Citation: Fidelity, Duration: Understanding the Relationship Between Bond Prices and Interest Rates — https://www.fidelity.com/learning-center/investment-products/fixed-income-bonds/duration (Using a bond's convexity to gauge interest rate risk)
Status: Reviewed

1036. Basis point
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: A unit of measure for interest rates and yields equal to one one-hundredth of a percentage point (0.01%). It is the standard unit for quoting yield changes, spreads, and rate moves.
Intuition: It is the 'cent' of interest rates: saying 'up 25 basis points' unambiguously means up 0.25 percentage points.
Mechanics: Yields, spreads, and rate changes are multiplied by 100 to convert percentage points to basis points; e.g. the Federal Reserve describes changes in the federal funds target in basis points, and DV01 measures value change per one basis point.
Formula: 1 bp = 0.01% = 0.0001 in decimal; value in bp = value in percent × 100.
Relationships: DV01, PV01, Yield spread, Policy rate
Failure modes: Confusion between basis points and percent (or between relative percent change and percentage-point change) causes order-of-magnitude errors in P&L and risk calculations.
Misconceptions: A '1% rise in rates' is ambiguous; professional usage distinguishes a 100 bp (one percentage point) rise from a 1 percent relative increase, which are very different.
Example: If the 10-year Treasury yield moves from 4.25% to 4.50%, it has risen 25 basis points.
Citation: Investor.gov Glossary (U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission) — https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/glossary (Basis Point)
Citation: CFTC Glossary (A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry) — https://www.cftc.gov/LearnAndProtect/AdvisoriesAndArticles/CFTCGlossary/index.htm (Basis Point)
Status: Reviewed

1037. Policy rate
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: The short-term interest rate that a central bank sets (or targets) to implement monetary policy. In the United States it is the Federal Open Market Committee's target range for the federal funds rate, which the New York Fed's trading desk defends through open market operations and administered rates.
Intuition: It is the central bank's main dial: raising it tightens financial conditions to cool the economy, lowering it loosens conditions to stimulate activity.
Mechanics: The FOMC announces a target range for the federal funds rate; the Desk conducts repo, reverse repo, and other operations, and sets administered rates (interest on reserve balances, ON RRP offering rate, standing repo rate) to keep the effective market rate within the range.
Relationships: Federal funds rate, Overnight rate, Repo rate, Basis point, Yield curve
Failure modes: The policy rate directly anchors only very short-term rates; long-term yields are driven by expectations and term premia, so policy moves can fail to transmit (e.g. the 2000s 'conundrum' when long yields fell as the Fed hiked). At the zero lower bound, the rate loses room as a tool.
Misconceptions: The central bank does not 'set all interest rates'; it targets one overnight rate and influences the rest of the curve only indirectly through expectations and operations.
Example: In 2022–2023 the FOMC raised its target range for the federal funds rate from 0–0.25% to 5.25–5.50% in a series of moves of 25 to 75 basis points.
Citation: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Open Market Operations — https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/openmarket.htm (Open market operations and FOMC target federal funds rate table)
Status: Reviewed

1038. Overnight rate
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: The interest rate on loans or deposits with a maturity of one business day, typically traded between financial institutions to manage daily reserve or cash positions. Key U.S. overnight rates include the effective federal funds rate (unsecured) and SOFR (secured by Treasury collateral).
Intuition: It is the price of borrowing money until tomorrow — the shortest-maturity interest rate in the financial system and the anchor for all longer rates.
Mechanics: Institutions lend and borrow cash for one day in money markets; transaction-level data are aggregated into published benchmarks (the New York Fed computes EFFR and SOFR as volume-weighted medians of overnight transactions). Central banks steer overnight rates to implement policy.
Relationships: Federal funds rate, Secured Overnight Financing Rate, Policy rate, Repo rate
Failure modes: Overnight rates can spike under collateral or reserve scarcity (e.g. the September 2019 repo spike), breaking the link with the policy target; month- and quarter-end reporting effects also distort measured rates.
Misconceptions: There is no single 'overnight rate': secured (repo/SOFR) and unsecured (fed funds) overnight rates coexist and can diverge because they price different risks and counterparties.
Example: On a typical day, a bank lending reserves to another bank overnight earns the federal funds rate, while a money market fund lending cash against Treasury collateral earns a rate near SOFR.
Citation: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Effective Federal Funds Rate (EFFR) — https://www.newyorkfed.org/markets/reference-rates/effr (EFFR calculation and publication)
Status: Reviewed

1039. Secured Overnight Financing Rate
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: A broad measure of the cost of borrowing cash overnight collateralized by U.S. Treasury securities, published each business day by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. It is the principal U.S. dollar benchmark that replaced LIBOR for derivatives and loans.
Intuition: It is the going rate for a one-day loan backed by Treasuries — essentially a near-risk-free overnight borrowing cost built from actual repo market transactions.
Mechanics: SOFR is calculated as a volume-weighted median of transaction-level tri-party repo data, GCF Repo data, and bilateral Treasury repo cleared through FICC's DVP service (filtered to remove specials), and is published at approximately 8:00 a.m. ET each business day.
Relationships: Repo rate, Overnight rate, Federal funds rate, Swap spread
Failure modes: Because it is secured and transaction-based, SOFR can spike when repo funding is scarce (e.g. September 2019) and reflects collateral market conditions rather than bank credit risk; unlike LIBOR it has no term or credit component, complicating its use in loan pricing.
Misconceptions: SOFR is not set by the Federal Reserve as a policy rate, nor is it a forecast — it is a backward-looking measure of realized overnight repo transactions.
Example: A floating-rate note might pay 'SOFR + 80 bp', resetting its coupon off the daily-published SOFR benchmark.
Citation: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR) — https://www.newyorkfed.org/markets/reference-rates/sofr (SOFR definition and calculation)
Status: Reviewed

1040. Federal funds rate
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: The interest rate at which depository institutions lend reserve balances to other depository institutions overnight, uncollateralized. The FOMC sets a target rate or range for it, and the New York Fed publishes the effective federal funds rate (EFFR) as the volume-weighted median of actual transactions.
Intuition: It is the rate banks charge each other for overnight loans of their reserve balances at the Fed — the rate U.S. monetary policy directly targets.
Mechanics: The federal funds market consists of domestic unsecured overnight borrowings in U.S. dollars by depository institutions from other institutions, primarily GSEs. The EFFR is computed as a volume-weighted median of transactions reported on the FR 2420 report and published for the prior business day at about 9:00 a.m.; the Desk's operations keep it within the FOMC's target range.
Relationships: Policy rate, Overnight rate, Secured Overnight Financing Rate, Repo rate
Failure modes: The fed funds market is thin and dominated by specific players (GSEs lending to banks), so the EFFR can be unrepresentative of marginal funding costs; the rate also lost its role as the sole steering variable once abundant reserves made administered rates the main control tools.
Misconceptions: The Fed does not directly set the market fed funds rate by decree — it sets a target range and uses operations and administered rates to steer the traded rate into it.
Example: With an FOMC target range of 3.50–3.75%, the EFFR typically prints near the middle of the range, e.g. 3.62%.
Citation: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Effective Federal Funds Rate (EFFR) — https://www.newyorkfed.org/markets/reference-rates/effr (Federal funds market and EFFR calculation)
Citation: Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, Open Market Operations — https://www.federalreserve.gov/monetarypolicy/openmarket.htm (Implementation of monetary policy)
Status: Reviewed

1041. Repo rate
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: The implicit interest rate on a repurchase agreement, a transaction in which one party sells securities and agrees to repurchase them later at a slightly higher price — economically a loan collateralized by securities. The rate is set by the difference between the sale and repurchase prices relative to the term.
Intuition: It is the cost of borrowing cash against bonds: you hand over the securities, get cash, and pay back a bit more later — that bit more, annualized, is the repo rate.
Mechanics: In a repo the cash borrower sells securities and commits to repurchase them at a predetermined higher price; the price gap implies the repo interest. General collateral (GC) rates apply to non-specific securities, while repos on particular issues in high demand ('specials') trade at lower rates. The New York Fed uses repo and reverse repo operations to help keep the fed funds rate in its target range.
Formula: Repo rate = ((repurchase price − sale price) / sale price) × (360 or 365 / term in days), per the market's day-count convention.
Relationships: Haircut, Secured Overnight Financing Rate, Overnight rate, Swap spread, Federal funds rate
Failure modes: Repo rates can spike abruptly when collateral or dealer balance-sheet capacity is scarce (September 2019, March 2020), transmitting stress across funding markets; specialness can also drive individual-issue repo rates far below GC, distorting funding-cost readings.
Misconceptions: A repo is not an outright sale of the bond for risk-transfer purposes — the seller retains the economic exposure and the obligation to repurchase, so it functions as secured borrowing.
Example: A dealer sells $100 million of Treasuries overnight and agrees to repurchase them for $100.015 million; the implied overnight repo rate is about 5.4% annualized (0.015/100 × 360).
Citation: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Repo and Reverse Repo Agreements — https://www.newyorkfed.org/markets/domestic-market-operations/monetary-policy-implementation/repo-reverse-repo-agreements (Overview of repo and reverse repo operations)
Citation: Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Secured Overnight Financing Rate (SOFR) — https://www.newyorkfed.org/markets/reference-rates/sofr (General collateral vs. specials)
Status: Reviewed

1042. Haircut
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: The percentage reduction applied to the market value of collateral when determining how much cash can be borrowed against it. In a repo, the haircut is the gap between the collateral's value and the cash lent, protecting the lender against a fall in collateral value before it could be sold.
Intuition: If you pledge $1 million of bonds with a 5% haircut, the lender only gives you $950,000 — the haircut is the lender's safety cushion.
Mechanics: Cash lent = collateral market value × (1 − haircut). Haircuts are set per asset class based on price volatility, liquidity, credit quality, and borrower risk; riskier or less liquid collateral receives larger haircuts.
Formula: Loan amount = collateral value × (1 − h), where h is the haircut (e.g. h = 0.05 for 5%).
Relationships: Repo rate, Secured Overnight Financing Rate, Overnight rate
Failure modes: Haircuts set in calm times can prove inadequate in stressed markets when collateral gaps down in value; conversely, abrupt haircut increases force deleveraging and can propagate fire sales, as seen in 2008.
Misconceptions: A haircut is not a fee or interest charge — it reduces the amount lent, not the price of the loan, and the full collateral value (less the loan) is returned when the repo unwinds.
Example: Pledging $1,000,000 of Treasury bonds at a 2% haircut lets the borrower draw $980,000 in cash; the extra $20,000 of collateral covers the lender if bond prices fall.
Citation: Investopedia, Haircut — https://www.investopedia.com/terms/h/haircut.asp (How a Haircut Works)
Status: Reviewed

1043. Term premium
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: The extra yield investors demand for holding a longer-term bond instead of rolling over a series of short-term instruments — compensation for the risk that future rates and inflation differ from expectations. It is the difference between a long-term yield and the expected average of future short rates, and it is not directly observable.
Intuition: Locking your money up for ten years is riskier than renewing a one-year loan ten times; the term premium is the extra pay for bearing that risk.
Mechanics: Estimated with term-structure models: a model (e.g. the Fed's Kim–Wright three-factor arbitrage-free model, published on FRED as THREEFYTP10) decomposes observed yields into expected short-rate paths plus a residual term premium. Estimates are model-dependent and can be negative.
Formula: y(T) ≈ (1/T) × Σ E[short rate_t] + TP(T), where y(T) is the T-year yield and TP(T) the term premium.
Relationships: Yield curve, Forward rate curve, Breakeven inflation, Policy rate
Failure modes: Term premium estimates vary substantially across models and can flip sign with specification changes; using any single estimate as ground truth for 'rich/cheap' bonds is fragile.
Misconceptions: The term premium is not a measured quantity like a yield — it is a model-implied residual, and a rising long yield does not tell you whether expectations or the premium moved without a model.
Example: If the 10-year Treasury yields 4.5% while the expected average short rate over the decade is 4.0%, the model-implied 10-year term premium is about 0.5%.
Citation: FRED, Term Premium on a 10 Year Zero Coupon Bond [THREEFYTP10] (source: Board of Governors, Kim and Wright 2005) — https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/THREEFYTP10 (Notes)
Status: Reviewed

1044. Breakeven inflation
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: The inflation rate that would make an investor indifferent between holding a nominal Treasury and a same-maturity Treasury Inflation-Protected Security (TIPS), computed as the nominal yield minus the real (TIPS) yield. It is a market-based measure of expected average inflation over the horizon, though it also embeds inflation risk and liquidity premia.
Intuition: If nominal bonds pay 4.5% and inflation-protected bonds pay 2.0%, the market is pricing roughly 2.5% average inflation — that gap is the breakeven.
Mechanics: Computed from constant-maturity series, e.g. FRED's T10YIE = 10-Year Treasury Constant Maturity (DGS10) minus 10-Year Treasury Inflation-Indexed Constant Maturity (DFII10); the latest value implies what market participants expect inflation to average over the next 10 years.
Formula: Breakeven inflation ≈ y(nominal, T) − y(real TIPS, T); exactly, (1 + y_nom)/(1 + y_real) − 1 under compounding.
Relationships: Inflation swap, Term premium, Par yield, Yield spread
Failure modes: Breakevens mix inflation expectations with inflation risk premia and the liquidity disadvantage of TIPS, so they can diverge from true expectations — e.g. they collapsed in 2008 partly because TIPS became deeply illiquid, not because deflation was genuinely expected.
Misconceptions: Breakeven inflation is not a pure forecast of CPI; it is the rate that equates two bond prices, so reading it as the market's literal inflation expectation ignores embedded premia.
Example: With the 10-year nominal Treasury at 4.3% and the 10-year TIPS real yield at 2.0%, the 10-year breakeven inflation rate is about 2.3%.
Citation: FRED, 10-Year Breakeven Inflation Rate [T10YIE] (source: Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis) — https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/T10YIE (Notes)
Status: Reviewed

1045. Inflation swap
Domain: Fixed income and rates
Definition: A derivative in which one party pays a fixed rate and the other pays the realized change in an inflation index (e.g. U.S. CPI-U) on a notional amount, transferring inflation risk. In the standard zero-coupon form, both legs are compounded and exchanged as a single payment at maturity.
Intuition: It is a bet or hedge on inflation itself: one side pays a pre-agreed inflation rate, the other pays whatever inflation actually turns out to be.
Mechanics: The fixed leg compounds at the agreed fixed rate; the floating leg accrues the realized growth of the reference inflation index (USD uses CPI-U), typically with a publication lag of a few months. In a zero-coupon inflation swap the two compounded amounts are netted and paid once at maturity; the quoted fixed rate is the market's swap-implied inflation level.
Formula: Fixed leg payment = N × [(1 + k)^n − 1]; inflation leg payment = N × [I(T)/I(0) − 1], where N is notional, k the fixed swap rate, n the tenor in years, and I the inflation index level.
Relationships: Breakeven inflation, Secured Overnight Financing Rate, Swap spread
Failure modes: Index publication lags, revisions, and seasonal patterns complicate pricing and hedging; the market is also less liquid than nominal swaps, and quoted rates embed inflation risk premia just like TIPS breakevens.
Misconceptions: The fixed rate on an inflation swap is not a pure inflation forecast; like breakevens, it includes risk and liquidity premia, so it overstates or understates true expected inflation.
Example: A pension fund enters a 10-year zero-coupon inflation swap paying a fixed 2.6% and receiving realized CPI-U growth on $50 million notional, hedging its inflation-linked liabilities.
Citation: ICE (Intercontinental Exchange) SDX Interest Rates Help — Zero Coupon Inflation Swap — https://idd.ice.com/IRHelp/Content/FM/Zero_Coupon_Inflation_Sw.htm (Zero Coupon Inflation Swap)
Status: Reviewed

1046. Gross domestic product
Domain: Macro and fundamentals
Definition: The total value of the final goods and services produced within a country during a given period. In the United States it is estimated quarterly by the Bureau of Economic Analysis as the signature measure of the National Income and Product Accounts.
Intuition: GDP is the economy's scoreboard: it tells you how much the country actually produced in a quarter or year, and its growth rate is the standard gauge of whether the economy is expanding or contracting.
Mechanics: BEA sums spending on final goods and services (consumption, investment, government spending, and net exports), counting only final output to avoid double-counting intermediates. Each quarter is estimated three times (advance, second, third) as more source data arrive, and figures are seasonally adjusted and reported at annual rates.
Formula: GDP = C + I + G + (X - M), where C = personal consumption expenditures, I = gross private domestic investment, G = government consumption and investment, X = exports, M = imports (expenditure approach).
Relationships: Real GDP, Nominal GDP, Industrial production, Retail sales, Unemployment rate, Monetary policy
Failure modes: GDP is revised repeatedly, so the first estimate traders react to can change materially; it is also backward-looking, ignores non-market activity and income distribution, and annualized quarterly rates can exaggerate one-off swings.
Misconceptions: GDP does not measure well-being or total wealth, and a high GDP level does not imply strong growth; what markets trade on is the growth rate relative to expectations, not the level.
Example: When BEA reported Q1 2020 GDP falling at a 5.0% annual rate, it confirmed the pandemic contraction; traders compared each release against consensus to reprice Fed policy expectations.
Citation: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis — Gross Domestic Product (Learning Center) — https://www.bea.gov/resources/learning-center/what-to-know-gdp (What is GDP?)
Status: Reviewed

1047. Real GDP
Domain: Macro and fundamentals
Definition: Gross domestic product adjusted to remove the effects of price changes, so that output in different periods can be compared in constant purchasing-power terms. When media report 'GDP growth' they almost always mean the percent change in real GDP.
Intuition: Real GDP answers: did the country actually produce more stuff, or did prices just go up? It strips out inflation so growth reflects volume, not price changes.
Mechanics: BEA deflates each component of nominal spending using detailed price indexes (producing chained-dollar estimates), so real GDP changes reflect changes in quantities produced. Growth rates are computed from these chained series, seasonally adjusted at annual rates.
Formula: Real GDP = Nominal GDP / GDP price index x 100 (conceptually); in practice BEA uses chained (Fisher) quantity indexes rather than a single deflator.
Relationships: Gross domestic product, Nominal GDP, Inflation, Consumer price index
Failure modes: Deflation choices and base-year/index updates can revise history; real GDP can rise while living standards for typical households stagnate if gains accrue narrowly or population grows faster.
Misconceptions: Real GDP is not 'GDP with inflation subtracted at the CPI'; BEA uses its own chain-type price indexes, so the implied GDP deflator differs from CPI inflation.
Example: If nominal GDP rises 5% but prices rise 3%, real GDP rises roughly 2% — the growth that economists and the Fed treat as actual output growth.
Citation: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis — Gross Domestic Product (Learning Center) — https://www.bea.gov/resources/learning-center/what-to-know-gdp (More to know ('Real' or 'chained' GDP))
Status: Reviewed

1048. Nominal GDP
Domain: Macro and fundamentals
Definition: Gross domestic product measured at the market prices prevailing during the period being measured, without adjustment for inflation. It moves with both the quantity of output and the price level.
Intuition: Nominal GDP is the raw dollar size of the economy; it grows even if the country produces the same amount, simply because everything costs more.
Mechanics: BEA values current-period final output at current-period prices (current-dollar estimates). Comparing nominal GDP across periods mixes volume and price changes, so analysts deflate it to obtain real GDP.
Formula: Nominal GDP = sum over goods i of (P_i,t x Q_i,t), where P_i,t and Q_i,t are current-period prices and quantities of final goods and services.
Relationships: Gross domestic product, Real GDP, Inflation
Failure modes: In high-inflation episodes nominal GDP can look strong while real output stagnates; cross-period or cross-country comparisons in nominal terms conflate price-level differences with size differences.
Misconceptions: Nominal GDP is not 'wrong' or useless — it is the right denominator for debt-to-GDP and tax-revenue ratios, since debts and revenues are nominal; it is only misleading when used to infer real growth.
Example: U.S. nominal GDP grew briskly in 2021-2022, but a large share of that increase was price inflation, which is why real GDP grew much more slowly over the same period.
Citation: U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis — Gross Domestic Product (Learning Center) — https://www.bea.gov/resources/learning-center/what-to-know-gdp (More to know ('Current-dollar' or 'nominal' GDP))
Status: Reviewed

1049. Inflation
Domain: Macro and fundamentals
Definition: A sustained increase in the general level of prices for goods and services over time, equivalently a decline in the purchasing power of money. In the U.S. it is most commonly measured by the 12-month percent change in the Consumer Price Index or the PCE price index.
Intuition: Inflation means your dollar buys less this year than last year; central banks target a low, stable rate (the Fed aims for 2%) because both very high inflation and deflation damage the economy.
Mechanics: Statistical agencies track a fixed basket of consumer goods and services and compute the average price change over time; the 12-month percent change of the index is the headline inflation rate. Persistent inflation is ultimately associated with money supply growing faster than output, though shocks (energy, supply chains) drive short-run swings.
Formula: Inflation rate (12-month) = (CPI_t / CPI_{t-12} - 1) x 100, where CPI_t is the consumer price index in month t.
Relationships: Consumer price index, Core inflation, Producer price index, Deflation, Disinflation, Monetary policy, Stagflation
Failure modes: Headline rates are dominated by volatile food and energy swings; substitution, quality change, and housing measurement make any single index an approximation, and base effects can make year-over-year rates jump mechanically.
Misconceptions: A fall in the inflation rate does not mean prices are falling (that is deflation) — it means prices are rising more slowly; also, one expensive item is not inflation, which refers to the general price level.
Example: U.S. CPI inflation peaked at 9.1% year-over-year in June 2022, prompting the Federal Reserve's 2022-2023 rate-hiking cycle.
Citation: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — Consumer Price Index (CPI Home) — https://www.bls.gov/cpi/ (CPI Home / 12-month percentage change tables)
Status: Reviewed

1050. Consumer price index
Domain: Macro and fundamentals
Definition: A measure of the average change over time in the prices paid by urban consumers for a market basket of consumer goods and services, published monthly by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics. The headline series is the CPI for All Urban Consumers (CPI-U).
Intuition: The CPI is a giant shopping basket whose total cost is tracked every month; how fast that basket's cost rises is the most-watched U.S. inflation reading.
Mechanics: BLS collects prices for thousands of items across urban areas, weights them by consumer spending patterns from the Consumer Expenditure Surveys, and aggregates them into an index (reference base 1982-84=100). Monthly releases report seasonally adjusted month-over-month and unadjusted 12-month changes, including the 'all items less food and energy' core series.
Formula: Percent change = (Index_t / Index_{t-1} - 1) x 100; the index itself is a weighted average of item-level price relatives with expenditure weights.
Relationships: Inflation, Core inflation, Producer price index, Real GDP, Monetary policy
Failure modes: CPI covers only urban consumers' out-of-pocket spending, uses owners' equivalent rent for housing, and embeds substitution and quality-adjustment assumptions, so it can diverge from any household's lived inflation and from the Fed's preferred PCE measure.
Misconceptions: The CPI is not a cost-of-living index in the strict sense and does not measure price levels across cities; a higher index in one period means prices rose, not that every item did.
Example: In June 2026, BLS reported CPI-U fell 0.4% month over month (seasonally adjusted) while rising 3.5% over 12 months — the 12-month figure is the headline inflation rate.
Citation: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — Consumer Price Index (CPI Home) — https://www.bls.gov/cpi/ (CPI Home)
Status: Reviewed

1051. Producer price index
Domain: Macro and fundamentals
Definition: A family of indexes published monthly by the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics measuring the average change over time in selling prices received by domestic producers of goods and services. It measures price change from the seller's perspective, in contrast to the CPI's purchaser perspective.
Intuition: PPI tracks what producers charge at the factory gate or for their services; because it captures price pressure before the retail level, traders watch it as a possible early signal of consumer inflation.
Mechanics: BLS surveys over 16,000 establishments for roughly 64,000 price quotes per month and publishes indexes by industry, by commodity, and by the Final Demand-Intermediate Demand (FD-ID) system, which groups goods, services, and construction by buyer type and processing stage. Weights come from value-of-shipments data in the economic censuses.
Formula: PPI percent change = (PPI_t / PPI_{t-1} - 1) x 100 for a given index; indexes are weighted averages of establishment price relatives.
Relationships: Consumer price index, Inflation, Core inflation, Industrial production
Failure modes: PPI excludes most imports and part of the service sector, margins between producer and consumer prices vary, and pass-through to CPI is incomplete and lagged, so PPI spikes do not map one-for-one into consumer inflation.
Misconceptions: PPI is not a direct predictor of next month's CPI; sellers' and purchasers' prices differ due to taxes, subsidies, and distribution costs, and many services in CPI have no PPI counterpart.
Example: When the PPI for final demand jumped in early 2021-2022 amid supply bottlenecks, analysts read it as pipeline pressure that preceded the broader CPI surge.
Citation: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — Producer Price Indexes Overview — https://www.bls.gov/ppi/overview.htm (Data / Coverage)
Status: Reviewed

1052. Core inflation
Domain: Macro and fundamentals
Definition: An inflation measure that excludes the volatile food and energy components, intended to reveal the underlying, persistent trend in prices. In the U.S. the standard readings are 'all items less food and energy' in the CPI and the core PCE price index.
Intuition: Gasoline and grocery prices whipsaw month to month; stripping them out gives a cleaner read on whether inflation is really embedded in the economy, which is what central banks care about.
Mechanics: Statistical agencies compute the same price index over the basket minus food and energy items and report its monthly and 12-month changes alongside headline figures. The concept of excluding food and energy originated in the 1970s when oil shocks made headline inflation noisy; the Fed's 2% target is defined on PCE, with core PCE watched as the trend gauge.
Formula: Core inflation rate = (CoreIndex_t / CoreIndex_{t-12} - 1) x 100, where the core index is the CPI (or PCE index) excluding food and energy components.
Relationships: Inflation, Consumer price index, Producer price index, Monetary policy
Failure modes: Food and energy shocks can persist and pass through into core (second-round effects), so core can understate true inflation pressure for long stretches; shelter measurement lags also distort core readings.
Misconceptions: Core inflation is not a claim that food and energy 'don't matter' to households — it is a signal-extraction device for policy, not a measure of the cost of living.
Example: In June 2026, headline CPI rose 3.5% over 12 months while the index for all items less food and energy rose 2.6%, showing energy drove much of the headline overshoot.
Citation: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics — Consumer Price Index (CPI Home) — https://www.bls.gov/cpi/ (12-month percentage change table ('All items less food and energy'))
Status: Reviewed

1053. Deflation
Domain: Macro and fundamentals
Definition: A sustained general decline in the prices of goods and services, equivalently an increase in the purchasing power of money. It is typically associated with contracting money and credit or collapsing aggregate demand and is considered more dangerous than moderate inflation because it raises the real burden of debt and encourages delayed spending.
Intuition: When prices fall broadly, cash gains value just by sitting still, so consumers postpone purchases and borrowers must repay debts with more valuable money — a self-reinforcing drag on the economy.
Mechanics: Deflation shows up as a negative 12-month change in a price index (e.g., CPI below zero). Causes include falls in aggregate demand, contractions in money and credit (as in the 1930s U.S. bank failures), or strong productivity gains; policymakers counter it with rate cuts, asset purchases, and fiscal stimulus.
Formula: Deflation occurs when (CPI_t / CPI_{t-12} - 1) < 0, i.e., a negative inflation rate.
Relationships: Inflation, Disinflation, Consumer price index, Monetary policy, Quantitative easing
Failure modes: As a concept it can mislead when driven by productivity or technology (good deflation) rather than demand collapse; debt-deflation dynamics described by Fisher apply mainly when falling prices coincide with high leverage.
Misconceptions: Cheaper prices are not always good: economy-wide deflation raises real debt burdens and real interest rates even at zero nominal rates, which is why central banks fight it as hard as inflation.
Example: The U.S. last experienced significant deflation in the early 1930s after widespread bank failures shrank the money supply; Japan suffered prolonged deflation in the 1990s.
Citation: Investopedia — Deflation: Definition, Causes, and Impact — https://www.investopedia.com/terms/d/deflation.asp (What Is Deflation?)
Status: Reviewed

1054. Disinflation
Domain: Macro and fundamentals
Definition: A decrease in the rate of inflation — prices are still rising, but at a slower pace. It is distinct from deflation, which is an actual decline in the price level.
Intuition: Disinflation is easing off the accelerator, not going in reverse: inflation falling from 9% to 3% is disinflation even though everything still costs more than before.
Mechanics: Measured as a decline in the 12-month percent change of a price index while it remains positive. It typically follows tighter monetary policy (higher interest rates) or the fading of supply shocks; the 1980s Volcker disinflation and the 2023 cooldown from the June 2022 CPI peak of 9.1% are canonical episodes.
Formula: Disinflation: inflation_t < inflation_{t-1} with inflation_t > 0, e.g., CPI 12-month change falling from 3% to 2%.
Relationships: Inflation, Deflation, Core inflation, Rate hike, Monetary policy
Failure modes: Disinflation driven by collapsing demand can precede recession or slide into deflation; base effects can also make the inflation rate fall mechanically even as monthly price gains stay firm.
Misconceptions: Disinflation does not mean prices are coming down — confusing it with deflation leads to wrong expectations about purchasing power and policy.
Example: After CPI inflation peaked at 9.1% in June 2022, the U.S. experienced disinflation through 2023 as the Fed's rate hikes slowed price increases without prices falling.
Citation: Investopedia — Disinflation: Definition, Causes, and Examples — https://www.investopedia.com/terms/d/disinflation.asp (What Is Disinflation?)
Status: Reviewed

1055. Stagflation
Domain: Macro and fundamentals
Definition: The simultaneous occurrence of high or rising inflation with stagnant output and elevated unemployment — a combination that contradicts the simple Phillips-curve trade-off. The term is identified with the 1970s U.S. experience, when inflation and unemployment rose together after the oil shocks.
Intuition: Stagflation is the worst of both worlds: the economy stops growing and jobs disappear while prices keep climbing, leaving policymakers with no painless option.
Mechanics: It typically arises when adverse supply shocks (e.g., the 1973 and 1979 oil crises) raise costs and prices while reducing output, and monetary accommodation of those shocks entrenches inflation expectations. Fighting unemployment with stimulus worsens inflation; fighting inflation with tightening worsens unemployment — the 1970s dilemma that ended only with the Volcker tightening of 1979-82.
Relationships: Inflation, Unemployment rate, Monetary policy, Gross domestic product, Rate hike
Failure modes: The label is often misapplied to any period of above-target inflation with mediocre growth; true stagflation requires sustained inflation together with economic stagnation, and the 1970s lesson (unstable Phillips trade-off) may not generalize to anchored-expectation regimes.
Misconceptions: Stagflation is not simply 'high inflation' or 'a recession'; its defining feature is the coexistence of both, which standard demand-management policy cannot fix from one side.
Example: By summer 1980, U.S. inflation was near 14.5% while unemployment exceeded 7.5% — the textbook stagflation that followed a decade of oil shocks and accommodative policy.
Citation: Federal Reserve History — The Great Inflation — https://www.federalreservehistory.org/essays/great-inflation (From High Inflation to Inflation Targeting ('This, then, became the era of stagflation'))
Status: Reviewed

1195. Scalping
Domain: Trading systems
Definition: An ultra-short-horizon trading style in which a trader opens and closes positions within seconds to minutes to capture very small price movements, often exploiting the bid-ask spread or momentary micro-imbalances in highly liquid instruments. It is the shortest-horizon form of day trading and relies on high trade frequency, tight risk limits, and low per-trade costs.
Intuition: Instead of trying to catch a big move, the scalper skims many tiny moves, accepting a few ticks of profit per trade and repeating this dozens or hundreds of times a day.
Mechanics: Positions are established and liquidated within minutes or seconds, using direct-access execution, level-2/order-book data, and strict stop discipline. Profit per trade is typically a fraction of a percent, so commissions, fees, and slippage must be minimized; small losses are cut immediately because a single large loss can erase dozens of wins.
Relationships: Day trading, Market making, Latency arbitrage, Bid-ask spread
Failure modes: Transaction costs and slippage can exceed the small gross edge; during volatility spikes or thin liquidity, stops are jumped and small losses become large ones.
Misconceptions: That scalping is easy money because each trade is small and quick; in practice most retail scalpers lose after costs, and the SEC warns that day traders typically suffer severe financial losses. Scalping is also confused with the illegal practice of 'scalping' by advisers who tout a stock after secretly buying it.
Example: A trader buys 2,000 shares of a liquid large-cap stock at $50.01 and sells them seconds later at $50.04, capturing about $60 gross before fees, repeating the process many times per session.
Citation: Wikipedia: Day trading (section: Scalping) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day_trading (Techniques - Scalping)
Citation: SEC, Day Trading: Your Dollars at Risk — https://www.sec.gov/investor/pubs/daytips.htm (Investor Publications)
Status: Reviewed

1196. Day trading
Domain: Trading systems
Definition: A speculative trading approach in which a trader buys and sells (or sells and buys) the same financial instrument within the same trading day, closing all positions before the session ends to avoid overnight gap risk. Under FINRA rules, a 'day trade' is the purchase and sale of the same security on the same day in a margin account, and customers executing four or more day trades in five business days are designated pattern day traders subject to special margin requirements.
Intuition: Day traders try to profit from intraday price swings, riding a stock's momentum for seconds to hours, and never hold positions overnight.
Mechanics: Positions are opened and closed during a single session, often on margin and with direct-access platforms; true day traders hold nothing overnight. In U.S. margin accounts, pattern day traders must maintain at least $25,000 in equity and are subject to day-trading buying-power limits.
Relationships: Scalping, Swing trading, Momentum trading, News trading, Pattern day trader rule
Failure modes: High leverage, commissions, and spread costs cause most retail day traders to lose money; academic studies of day traders find that the large majority are unprofitable after fees.
Misconceptions: That day trading is a form of investing or a reliable income source; the SEC states that day traders do not 'invest', typically suffer severe losses in their first months, and should never risk money needed for living expenses or retirement.
Example: A trader buys 500 shares of XYZ at $41.20 at 10:00 a.m. after a breakout, sells them at $41.75 by 11:30 a.m., and holds no position into the close.
Citation: SEC, Day Trading: Your Dollars at Risk — https://www.sec.gov/investor/pubs/daytips.htm (Investor Publications)
Citation: Investor.gov Glossary (Day Trade; Day Trading entries) — https://www.investor.gov/introduction-investing/investing-basics/glossary (Glossary D)
Status: Reviewed

1197. Swing trading
Domain: Trading systems
Definition: A speculative trading style in which positions are held for one or more days up to several weeks to profit from short- to medium-term price 'swings'. Holding periods sit between day trading (closed intraday) and position trading or buy-and-hold (months to years), and entries/exits are typically driven by technical analysis, sometimes combined with fundamentals.
Intuition: The swing trader tries to catch the middle chunk of a move that plays out over days, without needing to buy the exact bottom or sell the exact top.
Mechanics: Traders identify setups (trend continuation, pullbacks to support, breakouts) on daily or intraday charts, enter with predefined stops and targets, and hold overnight, accepting gap risk in exchange for capturing multi-day moves. Rule-based swing systems encode entry/exit as objective technical rules.
Relationships: Day trading, Position trading, Trend following, Momentum trading, Technical analysis
Failure modes: Overnight and weekend gaps can blow through stops; in choppy, trendless markets swing signals whipsaw and repeated small losses accumulate.
Misconceptions: That swing trading reliably times tops and bottoms, or that widely followed rule-based setups keep their edge; competition and regime change erode simple swing rules.
Example: A trader buys a stock pulling back to its rising 20-day average at $88, places a stop at $85 and a target at $96, and exits eight trading days later.
Citation: Wikipedia: Swing trading — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swing_trading (Lead and Swing trading methods)
Status: Reviewed

1198. Position trading
Domain: Trading systems
Definition: A trading style in which positions are held for weeks to months (or longer) to capture major price trends, with decisions driven mainly by macro trends, fundamentals, or long-horizon technical analysis. The term is sometimes used interchangeably with buy and hold, though position traders may actively exit when the underlying thesis or long-term trend ends.
Intuition: Position traders ignore daily noise and try to own an asset for the big part of a long move, reviewing the thesis periodically rather than watching the tape.
Mechanics: Entries are based on long-term trend signals (e.g., weekly charts, macro or fundamental theses); stops are wide and positions are reviewed weekly or monthly rather than intraday. Transaction costs are low because turnover is low, but capital is exposed to drawdowns over long holding periods.
Relationships: Buy and hold, Swing trading, Trend following, Global macro trading
Failure modes: Wide stops mean large per-trade losses when a long-term thesis is wrong; secular reversals or value traps can hold capital in losing positions for years.
Misconceptions: That position trading is identical to passive buy-and-hold indexing; position traders actively select securities and exit when trends or theses fail, whereas buy and hold implies no market timing at all.
Example: A trader goes long an equity index ETF after a weekly golden cross, holds for nine months through interim corrections, and exits when the weekly trend breaks.
Citation: Wikipedia: Buy and hold — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buy_and_hold (Lead (position trading as synonym))
Status: Reviewed

1199. Trend following
Domain: Trading systems
Definition: A systematic trading approach that takes long positions in instruments whose own recent returns have been positive and short positions in those whose recent returns have been negative, on the hypothesis that price trends persist. It is an empirical strategy family, not a proven predictive law; academic work documents that a security's own past returns positively predict its near-term future returns across many futures markets, with partial reversal at longer horizons.
Intuition: Rather than predicting turning points, trend followers assume a market that has been going up will keep going up for a while, and they ride it until the trend reverses.
Mechanics: Signals are computed from past returns or price series (e.g., sign of the trailing 12-month excess return, moving-average filters, channel breakouts); positions are often scaled by inverse volatility and diversified across equity index, bond, currency, and commodity futures. Positions are exited or flipped when the trend signal reverses.
Formula: Position sign s_t = sign(r_{t-12,t}), where r_{t-12,t} is the instrument's excess return over the past 12 months (Moskowitz, Ooi, Pedersen 2012); position size is commonly scaled as s_t / sigma_t with sigma_t an ex-ante volatility estimate.
Relationships: Time-series momentum, Cross-sectional momentum, Donchian breakout strategy, Turtle trading, Moving-average crossover strategy
Failure modes: In range-bound or mean-reverting markets trend signals whipsaw, producing strings of small losses; trend strategies also suffer sharp drawdowns at abrupt trend reversals (e.g., V-shaped recoveries).
Misconceptions: That trend following predicts where prices will go; it is purely reactive to what prices have done and its documented edge is a statistical regularity that can weaken as it is crowded, not a guarantee.
Example: A CTA goes long S&P 500 futures because the 12-month return is positive, sizes the position to 10% annualized volatility, and flips short a year later after the trailing return turns negative.
Citation: AQR: Time Series Momentum (Moskowitz, Ooi, Pedersen, Journal of Financial Economics 2012) — https://www.aqr.com/Insights/Research/Journal-Article/Time-Series-Momentum (Abstract)
Status: Reviewed

1200. Mean reversion
Domain: Trading systems
Definition: The hypothesis, and the family of strategies built on it, that asset prices or returns contain a transitory component that tends to revert toward a long-run mean, so that extreme moves are at least partially undone. Empirically, stock returns show positive serial correlation at short horizons and negative autocorrelation at long horizons, consistent with a slowly decaying transitory price component, though the effect is statistical and contested, not a law.
Intuition: What stretches too far from its usual level tends to snap back; mean-reversion traders buy what has fallen too far and sell what has risen too far.
Mechanics: Traders measure deviation from an estimated mean (moving average, fair-value model, or historical spread) and take positions expecting reversion, exiting when the series returns toward its mean. Statistically, mean reversion is tested with variance-ratio tests or modeled with mean-reverting processes such as Ornstein-Uhlenbeck.
Formula: Ornstein-Uhlenbeck model: dX_t = theta * (mu - X_t) dt + sigma dW_t, where mu is the long-run mean, theta the speed of reversion, and sigma the volatility; variance-ratio test: VR(q) = Var(r_t^q) / (q * Var(r_t)), with VR < 1 indicating mean reversion (Poterba and Summers 1988).
Relationships: Pairs trading, Statistical arbitrage, Range trading, Fade strategy, Momentum trading
Failure modes: When the underlying equilibrium shifts (structural breaks, bankruptcies, regime change), 'cheap' assets keep getting cheaper; betting against strong trends produces large losses, and estimated reversion speeds are unstable out of sample.
Misconceptions: That prices must revert to a historical mean on a predictable schedule, or that mean reversion contradicts momentum; empirically both coexist at different horizons, and apparent reversion can reflect time-varying required returns rather than mispricing.
Example: A stock drops 12% in two weeks on no fundamental news while its sector is flat; a mean-reversion trader buys, expecting the gap versus its 60-day average to close, and exits after an 8% rebound.
Citation: NBER Working Paper 2343: Mean Reversion in Stock Prices: Evidence and Implications (Poterba and Summers) — https://www.nber.org/papers/w2343 (Abstract)
Status: Reviewed

1201. Momentum trading
Domain: Trading systems
Definition: A family of strategies that buy assets with strong recent performance and sell or short assets with weak recent performance, based on the empirically documented pattern that securities outperforming their peers over the past 3 to 12 months tend to keep outperforming over the following month. Momentum is a well-studied cross-sectional anomaly, not a guaranteed law, and is distinct from time-series momentum, which uses an asset's own past return rather than its rank versus peers.
Intuition: Winners tend to keep winning for a while, so the momentum trader buys what is already strong and avoids or shorts what is weak.
Mechanics: Universe securities are ranked on trailing (typically 3- to 12-month) returns, skipping the most recent month to avoid short-term reversal; the portfolio goes long the top decile/quintile and short the bottom, rebalanced periodically. Retail implementations simply buy instruments breaking to new highs or showing high relative strength.
Formula: Momentum score M_i = R_i(t-12, t-1), the cumulative return of asset i from 12 months to 1 month before formation; portfolios are formed by sorting on M (Jegadeesh and Titman 1993).
Relationships: Cross-sectional momentum, Time-series momentum, Trend following, Relative strength rotation, Breakout trading
Failure modes: Momentum crashes occur at sharp market reversals (e.g., 2009), when past losers rebound violently and the short leg surges; crowding and transaction costs also erode the gross anomaly.
Misconceptions: That momentum means simply chasing whatever is up; systematic momentum is a ranked, hedged, periodically rebalanced portfolio construction, and its long-run returns come with occasional severe crashes.
Example: Each month a quant ranks 500 stocks on their trailing 6-month return, buys the top 30, shorts the bottom 30, and rebalances monthly.
Citation: AQR: Time Series Momentum (Moskowitz, Ooi, Pedersen 2012), discussion of the cross-sectional momentum literature — https://www.aqr.com/Insights/Research/Journal-Article/Time-Series-Momentum (Abstract)
Status: Reviewed

1202. Breakout trading
Domain: Trading systems
Definition: A technical-analysis trading style that enters a position when price passes through and holds beyond a defined support or resistance level, on the hypothesis that such breakouts mark the early stage of a new trend. It is an analytical framework, not a proven predictive law; broken resistance is often treated as new support and vice versa.
Intuition: When price finally escapes the ceiling or floor where it has been stuck, breakout traders jump in, betting the escape is the start of a real move.
Mechanics: Traders mark horizontal support/resistance from prior swing highs and lows, then place buy stops above resistance or sell stops below support, often confirming with volume. Stops are placed back inside the broken level (a breakout that immediately re-enters the range is treated as failed).
Formula: Typical long trigger: enter if P_t > R, where R = max(High_{t-N}, ..., High_{t-1}) over a chosen lookback N; stop placed at or below R after entry.
Relationships: Channel breakout strategy, Donchian breakout strategy, Opening-range breakout, Trend following, Range trading
Failure modes: False breakouts are common, especially in low-volume or range-bound conditions: price pokes through the level, triggers entries, then reverses back into the range, stopping out breakout traders repeatedly.
Misconceptions: That a breakout predicts continued movement with high probability; support/resistance levels are heuristic constructs, and the frequency of failed breakouts means risk control, not prediction, drives any edge.
Example: A stock has failed three times near $60; a trader places a buy stop at $60.25 with volume confirmation and a protective stop at $58.50 when filled.
Citation: Wikipedia: Breakout (technical analysis) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breakout_(technical_analysis) (Lead)
Status: Reviewed

1203. Range trading
Domain: Trading systems
Definition: A trading style applied to non-trending markets in which price repeatedly rises off a support level and falls off a resistance level; the trader buys near support and sells or shorts near resistance, expecting the oscillation to persist. It is a technical-analysis heuristic whose validity ends when the range breaks.
Intuition: If a stock keeps bouncing between the same floor and ceiling, trade the bounce: buy low in the band, sell high in the band.
Mechanics: Support and resistance are identified from repeated reaction highs/lows; entries are taken near the boundaries with stops just outside the range and targets near the opposite boundary. Oscillators (e.g., stochastic, RSI) are often used to time entries within the range.
Relationships: Mean reversion, Breakout trading, Support and resistance, Grid trading
Failure modes: The strategy is destroyed by range breakouts: a position entered at the 'wrong' boundary just before a genuine breakout loses continuously, and repeated range profits can be erased by one failed range.
Misconceptions: That ranges are stable structures; what looks like a range is often just a pause in a trend, and the edges are fuzzy zones rather than precise prices.
Example: EUR/USD oscillates between 1.0800 and 1.1000 for two months; a range trader buys near 1.0820 with a stop at 1.0770 and a target at 1.0970.
Citation: Wikipedia: Day trading (section: Range trading) — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Day_trading (Techniques - Range trading)
Status: Reviewed

1204. Pairs trading
Domain: Trading systems
Definition: A market-neutral strategy that matches two securities whose prices historically move together, then goes long the underperformer and short the outperformer when their prices diverge, profiting if the spread between them reconverges. Gatev, Goetzmann, and Rouwenhorst (2006) formalized the canonical version: stocks are paired by minimum distance between normalized historical prices and traded with a simple divergence/convergence rule.
Intuition: If two similar companies' prices drift apart, bet they will come back together: buy the laggard, short the leader, and you profit on the gap closing regardless of market direction.
Mechanics: Pairs are formed from a historical estimation window (e.g., 12 months of normalized prices or a cointegration/hedge-ratio regression); a trade opens when the spread widens beyond a threshold (e.g., two standard deviations) and closes on convergence or at the end of a fixed horizon. Dollar-neutral sizing makes the position roughly insensitive to market moves.
Formula: Spread S_t = ln P_A,t - beta * ln P_B,t, where beta is the hedge ratio from regressing A's log price on B's; trade when z_t = (S_t - mu_S) / sigma_S exceeds an entry band (commonly +/-2), exit when z_t crosses 0.
Relationships: Statistical arbitrage, Mean reversion, Pairs spread z-score strategy, Pairs convergence trade, Pairs divergence trade
Failure modes: When the historical co-movement breaks for fundamental reasons (e.g., one firm is deteriorating), the spread widens instead of converging; pairs profits also decayed after the strategy became crowded in the 2000s.
Misconceptions: That a diverging pair must reconverge because it always did before; co-movement is a statistical association that can break permanently, so divergence can signal a real relative-value change rather than a temporary mispricing.
Example: Coca-Cola and PepsiCo normalized prices diverge by 2.5 standard deviations; the trader shorts the outperformer and buys the underperformer in equal dollar amounts, exiting when the spread returns to its mean.
Citation: Gatev, Goetzmann, Rouwenhorst, Pairs Trading: Performance of a Relative Value Arbitrage Rule (SSRN, Yale ICF Working Paper 08-03) — https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=141615 (Abstract)
Status: Reviewed

1205. Statistical arbitrage
Domain: Trading systems
Definition: A family of quantitative, typically market-neutral strategies that exploit statistical mispricings among large portfolios of related securities, using short-horizon mean reversion and factor models rather than the strict riskless mispricing of classical arbitrage. Pairs trading is the canonical example; profits are expected values over many small trades, not risk-free arbitrage.
Intuition: Instead of one guaranteed mispricing, stat arb places hundreds of small, hedged bets that each have a slight statistical edge, so the law of large numbers does the work.
Mechanics: Models estimate expected short-horizon returns from residuals after removing factor exposures; portfolios are built long undervalued and short overvalued securities, neutralized to market and common factors, and turned over quickly. Gatev et al. (2006) link pairs-trading profits to temporary mispricing of close substitutes with a common return factor.
Relationships: Pairs trading, Mean reversion, Volatility arbitrage, Index arbitrage
Failure modes: Model risk and regime shifts: estimated relationships degrade exactly when correlations spike in crises, and deleveraging events (e.g., August 2007 quant unwind) cause many stat-arb books to lose simultaneously.
Misconceptions: That 'arbitrage' here means riskless profit; statistical arbitrage is a set of probabilistic bets that can and do produce extended losses.
Example: A fund residuals-neutralizes 2,000 U.S. stocks against sector and style factors, shorts stocks 2 sigma above their model price, buys those 2 sigma below, and rebalances daily.
Citation: Gatev, Goetzmann, Rouwenhorst, Pairs Trading: Performance of a Relative Value Arbitrage Rule (SSRN) — https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=141615 (Abstract)
Status: Reviewed

1206. Convertible arbitrage
Domain: Trading systems
Definition: A market-neutral hedge-fund strategy involving the simultaneous purchase of a convertible security (usually a convertible bond) and the short sale of the same issuer's common stock, designed to exploit inefficient pricing of the convertible relative to the underlying equity. The short stock position is sized to the convertible's equity sensitivity (delta), and the position is dynamically re-hedged.
Intuition: Buy the convertible bond, short the stock against it: if the bond is cheap relative to the stock-plus-option it embeds, you harvest the difference while staying roughly immune to small stock moves.
Mechanics: The arbitrageur buys the convertible and shorts a delta-neutral ratio of the underlying shares, capturing the bond's coupon plus the cheapness of the embedded equity option; as the stock moves, the hedge ratio is rebalanced (dynamic delta hedging), and this re-hedging of a long-gamma position adds to returns.
Formula: Shares shorted = delta_cv x conversion ratio x number of bonds, where delta_cv is the sensitivity of the convertible's price to the underlying stock price.
Relationships: Delta-neutral trading, Gamma scalping, Volatility arbitrage, Fixed-income arbitrage
Failure modes: Credit events hurt both legs at once (e.g., the 2005 GM downgrade: long convertibles lost on credit while short equity rallied); liquidity gaps can also make convertible prices fall faster than the stock hedge gains, as in 1987.
Misconceptions: That the trade is riskless because it is hedged; it carries credit risk, liquidity risk, and model risk in the delta estimate, and returns depend heavily on cheap financing and borrow availability for the short leg.
Example: A fund buys $10 million face of a convertible trading below theoretical value and shorts 60,000 shares of the issuer (the delta hedge), earning the coupon and gamma P&L as it re-hedges.
Citation: Wikipedia: Convertible arbitrage — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convertible_arbitrage (Lead and Risks)
Status: Reviewed

1207. Fixed-income arbitrage
Domain: Trading systems
Definition: A group of market-neutral strategies that exploit pricing differences between related fixed-income securities or contracts, such as swap-spread, yield-curve, mortgage, and cash-futures basis trades. Positions pair long and short exposures in economically similar instruments and bet on the convergence of small yield or price discrepancies, usually with substantial leverage.
Intuition: Two bonds or rates that should be priced almost identically sometimes are not; fixed-income arbs buy the cheap one, short the rich one, and wait for the tiny gap to close.
Mechanics: Traders identify rich/cheap points using yield-curve models, financing via repo; typical trades include long Treasury/short swap (swap-spread), butterfly structures on the curve, long MBS hedged with Treasuries or swaps, and long cash bond/short futures (basis). Returns per trade are small, so leverage is high.
Formula: Swap spread = yield to maturity of the Treasury bond minus the fixed rate of the matched-maturity interest-rate swap (sign conventions vary by market).
Relationships: Basis trade, Cash-futures basis trade, Convertible arbitrage, Statistical arbitrage, Volatility arbitrage
Failure modes: High leverage on small spreads means liquidity and financing shocks force losses: the LTCM collapse (1998) and the March 2020 Treasury basis unwind show convergence trades diverging further before converging, triggering margin spirals.
Misconceptions: That convergence is guaranteed within a tolerable horizon; 'riskless' relative-value trades can stay mispriced longer than a levered trader can stay solvent.
Example: A desk buys the cheapest-to-deliver 10-year Treasury, shorts the matched futures contract, finances the bond in repo, and plans to hold the position as the basis converges toward delivery.
Citation: Wikipedia: Fixed income arbitrage — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fixed_income_arbitrage (Lead and strategy sections)
Citation: OFR Brief 20-01: Basis Trades and Treasury Market Illiquidity — https://www.financialresearch.gov/briefs/2020/07/16/basis-trades-and-treasury-market-illiquidity/ (Brief summary)
Status: Reviewed

1208. Volatility arbitrage
Domain: Trading systems
Definition: A class of option-based relative-value strategies that trade the difference between an option's implied volatility and a forecast of the underlying's future realized volatility, implemented through a delta-neutral portfolio of options and the underlying. The trader treats volatility, rather than price, as the unit of relative value: buying options delta-hedged is a bet that realized volatility will exceed implied, and selling them is the opposite bet.
Intuition: If the market is pricing options as if the stock will move 10% but you think it will move 20%, you can buy the options, hedge out the direction, and profit from the extra movement itself.
Mechanics: Forecast realized volatility (e.g., from historical or high-frequency returns), compare with implied volatility backed out of market option prices, then buy underpriced or sell overpriced options and keep the book delta-neutral by trading the underlying. Profit is realized through the continuous re-hedging (gamma scalping) of the position over the option's life.
Formula: Option value C = f(S, sigma, ...); implied volatility sigma_imp solves C_market = f(S, sigma_imp, ...). Trade long vol if sigma_imp < sigma_forecast, short vol if sigma_imp > sigma_forecast.
Relationships: Delta-neutral trading, Gamma scalping, Dispersion trading, Statistical arbitrage, Implied volatility
Failure modes: It is not true arbitrage: the forecast can be wrong, and volatility spikes correlated across markets (black-swan events) cause losses across a whole book, as with LTCM's short-volatility positions.
Misconceptions: That delta-hedging removes all risk; a delta-neutral book still carries gamma, vega, theta, and jump risk, and 'buying vol cheap' loses steadily through theta if the realized move never comes.
Example: A trader buys S&P 500 straddles at 12% implied volatility while forecasting 18% realized, delta-hedging daily; if realized vol comes in near 18%, the re-hedging gains exceed the theta paid.
Citation: Wikipedia: Volatility arbitrage — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Volatility_arbitrage (Overview, Market (implied) volatility, Mechanism)
Status: Reviewed

1345. Trading psychology
Domain: Psychology and process
Definition: The study of how emotions, cognitive biases, and mental processes affect trading decisions and performance, and the applied discipline of managing those factors. It is a core topic of behavioral finance, which documents systematic, predictable departures from the rational-agent model of traditional finance.
Intuition: Two traders with the same strategy get different results because fear, greed, and bias change what they actually do. Trading psychology is about understanding and managing that human layer.
Mechanics: Draws on behavioral finance and decision science to catalog biases (loss aversion, overconfidence, herding) and emotional states (fear, euphoria, tilt) that distort trade selection, sizing, and exit timing; practitioners counter them with plans, checklists, journals, and review routines.
Relationships: Loss aversion, Prospect theory, Overconfidence bias, Herding, Trading discipline, Process orientation
Failure modes: Awareness of psychological pitfalls does not by itself eliminate them; under real-time stress, knowledge of biases often fails to change behavior. It also cannot compensate for a strategy with no genuine edge.
Misconceptions: The belief that mastering psychology alone makes trading profitable; psychology governs execution quality, not whether the underlying method has positive expectancy. Another misconception is that emotions should be eliminated rather than recognized and managed.
Example: A trader who knows her edge but repeatedly exits winners early out of fear studies her journal, finds the pattern, and adopts pre-committed exit rules to close the gap between plan and action.
Citation: Behavioral Patterns and Pitfalls of U.S. Investors (Library of Congress, Federal Research Division, prepared for the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission, August 2010) — https://www.sec.gov/investor/locinvestorbehaviorreport.pdf (Overview and The Role of Behavioral Finance, pp. 1-4)
Citation: Brett N. Steenbarger, The Psychology of Trading: Tools and Techniques for Minding the Markets (Wiley, 2003) - publisher page — https://www.wiley.com/en-us/The+Psychology+of+Trading%3A+Tools+and+Techniques+for+Minding+the+Markets-p-9780471267614 (Book description)
Status: Reviewed

1346. Loss aversion
Domain: Psychology and process
Definition: The empirically documented tendency for losses to be psychologically weighted more heavily than equivalent gains relative to a reference point; in Kahneman and Tversky's prospect theory the value function is steeper for losses than for gains. It is a component of prospect theory and is distinct from rational risk aversion.
Intuition: Losing $100 hurts roughly twice as much as winning $100 feels good, so people go to disproportionate lengths to avoid realizing losses.
Mechanics: Prospect theory's value function v(x) is concave for gains, convex for losses, and kinked at the reference point, with the loss limb about twice as steep as the gain limb (loss-aversion coefficient lambda near 2 in many estimates), producing risk aversion over gains and risk seeking over losses.
Formula: v(x) = x^alpha for x >= 0; v(x) = -lambda * (-x)^beta for x < 0, with 0 < alpha, beta < 1 and lambda > 1 (empirically lambda is often estimated near 2); x is the gain or loss relative to a reference point.
Relationships: Prospect theory, Disposition effect, Endowment effect, Status quo bias, Sunk-cost fallacy
Failure modes: Its magnitude and even existence at small stakes are debated in the replication literature, and 'loss attention' accounts argue losses attract attention without extra subjective weight. The reference point shifts with framing and expectations, so predictions can move.
Misconceptions: Loss aversion is not the same as risk aversion: it is a gain/loss asymmetry around a reference point, not a general preference for certainty. It is also not uniform across stake sizes, individuals, or domains.
Example: An investor refuses to sell a stock down 20% because realizing the loss feels far worse than the equivalent gain felt good, yet sells a stock up 20% quickly to lock in the win.
