Example: A trading-knowledge assistant abstains — 'no verified source available' — when asked for a contract specification absent from its knowledge library, instead of guessing a plausible tick value.
Citation: Geifman & El-Yaniv, 'Selective Classification for Deep Neural Networks' (NeurIPS 2017) — https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.08500 (Abstract)
Status: Reviewed

1429. Trading-agent guardrail
Domain: AI and knowledge engineering
Definition: A deterministic control that bounds what an automated trading agent may do, enforced outside the model: order-size and price limits, credit/capital thresholds, duplicate-order rejection, restricted-instrument lists, and kill switches. The regulatory archetype is SEC Rule 15c3-5, which requires broker-dealers with market access to maintain automated, systematically applied financial and regulatory risk management controls that prevent the entry of erroneous or excessive orders.
Intuition: The agent proposes; hard code disposes. Whatever the model decides, orders must pass through non-negotiable software checks before they can reach the market.
Mechanics: Guardrails sit in the execution path as pre-trade checks: each proposed order is validated against pre-set credit or capital thresholds, price and size parameters, duplicative-order detection, and restricted-security lists, and is rejected on violation; post-trade execution reports flow to surveillance. Because they are enforced in code — not in the model's prompt — they cannot be talked around by prompt injection.
Relationships: Execution-enabled trading agent, Read-only trading agent, Approval gate, Audit log, Prompt injection
Failure modes: Guardrails only bound what they measure: mis-set thresholds, stale restricted lists, or unchecked order types leave holes, and controls allocated to or dependent on third parties weaken accountability. They bound order flow, not reasoning quality — a guardrail-compliant stream of bad trades is still possible.
Misconceptions: Guardrails in the prompt ('do not exceed X') are not guardrails — model behavior is stochastic and injectable; effective controls are external, deterministic, and under the direct control of the responsible party, as Rule 15c3-5 requires of broker-dealers.
Example: An execution agent proposes selling 50 ES contracts; the pre-trade layer rejects it because it exceeds the 10-contract per-order size cap and the account's daily loss threshold was already breached that session.
Citation: 17 CFR § 240.15c3-5, Risk management controls for brokers or dealers with market access (SEC Market Access Rule) — https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/17/240.15c3-5 (Paragraphs (b)-(c): required financial and regulatory risk management controls)
Status: Reviewed

1430. Read-only trading agent
Domain: AI and knowledge engineering
Definition: A trading agent whose tool permissions are restricted to data retrieval and computation — market data, knowledge bases, analytics — with no capability to submit, modify, or cancel orders. It operationalizes the least-privilege principle: the system's action space is limited to the minimum necessary for its function, so even malfunction or prompt injection cannot move money.
Intuition: An analyst with a terminal and no trading button: it can look everything up and tell you what it thinks, but it physically cannot place a trade.
Mechanics: The agent's declared tool set contains only query/compute functions; the broker or exchange connection either has no API credentials for order entry or routes through an account with trading disabled. Because enforcement is in credentials and infrastructure rather than instructions, no prompt — user or injected — can escalate its privileges.
Relationships: Execution-enabled trading agent, Trading-agent guardrail, Tool use, Prompt injection, Approval gate
Failure modes: The safety property fails if the 'read-only' boundary is implemented in the prompt or application layer rather than in credentials, or if read access itself leaks sensitive data (positions, strategies) to injected instructions. Read-only agents can still cause harm through wrong analysis that a human acts on.
Misconceptions: Read-only does not mean harmless — outputs still influence decisions, and data access still needs scoping. It also is not a compromise on usefulness for many roles: research, review, and coaching agents need no order capability at all.
Example: A knowledge agent answers 'walk me through the margin math on this spread' using market-data and library lookups; its API token has trading disabled at the broker, so no prompt it receives can result in an order.
Citation: OWASP, 'LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection' (OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications) — https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/ (Prevention and Mitigation Strategies, item 4 (privilege control and least-privilege access))
Status: Reviewed

1431. Execution-enabled trading agent
Domain: AI and knowledge engineering
Definition: A trading agent with the technical capability to submit, modify, or cancel orders on a market — the category of automation that pre-trade risk controls exist to govern. Under SEC Rule 15c3-5, any broker-dealer providing such market access must maintain automated financial and regulatory risk management controls — credit/capital thresholds, erroneous-order prevention, restricted-security checks — under its direct and exclusive control.
Intuition: The moment an agent can touch the order book, it stops being software and starts being market access — with the same regulatory obligations and blow-up potential as any automated trading system.
Mechanics: The agent holds order-routing credentials; every order it generates passes through mandatory pre-trade risk checks (size, price, credit, duplicates, restricted lists) before reaching the exchange or ATS, and executions are reported to surveillance in real time. The control layer must be documented, tested annually, and certified by the CEO under 15c3-5(e).
Relationships: Trading-agent guardrail, Approval gate, Read-only trading agent, Audit log, Tool use
Failure modes: Failure modes compound the model's and the market's: hallucinated or injected instructions become real orders at machine speed, and feedback loops between an errant agent and a moving market can amplify losses before humans react. Kill switches and throttles bound the blast radius but cannot prevent the first bad orders.
Misconceptions: A paper-trading track record does not certify an execution-enabled agent — live order flow faces slippage, partial fills, and market impact the simulation may omit. 'The strategy is good' is not an argument against mandatory pre-trade controls; the controls exist for when the agent is wrong or compromised.
Example: An execution agent managing a futures portfolio can submit orders only through a gateway enforcing 15c3-5-style checks: per-order size caps, daily loss limits, fat-finger price bands, and a restricted list excluding illiquid contracts.
Citation: 17 CFR § 240.15c3-5, Risk management controls for brokers or dealers with market access (SEC Market Access Rule) — https://www.law.cornell.edu/cfr/text/17/240.15c3-5 (Paragraphs (b)-(e): controls, direct and exclusive control, annual review and CEO certification)
Status: Reviewed

1432. Approval gate
Domain: AI and knowledge engineering
Definition: A control point in an agentic workflow where a designated human must explicitly authorize a proposed action before the system executes it. OWASP lists requiring human approval for high-risk actions — human-in-the-loop controls for privileged operations — as a core mitigation against unauthorized actions by LLM-integrated applications.
Intuition: The agent can prepare the trade, fill in the ticket, and explain the reasoning — but a person has to click 'confirm' before anything happens.
Mechanics: The workflow pauses at the gate: the proposed action, its parameters, and supporting evidence are presented to an authorized approver; execution proceeds only on an affirmative decision, and the decision (who, what, when) is written to the audit log. Gates are typically risk-tiered, so routine low-risk actions proceed automatically while consequential ones block.
Relationships: Human-in-the-loop review, Trading-agent guardrail, Execution-enabled trading agent, Audit log, Abstention
Failure modes: Approval fatigue turns the gate into a rubber stamp: too many requests, or too little context per request, and approvers stop reading. Gates also fail if the approver lacks authority or expertise, or if the same action can be reached by an ungated path.
Misconceptions: An approval gate is not the same as notifying a human — notification after execution provides no control. Nor does a gate transfer accountability to the model: the approver and the system owner remain responsible for what is approved.
Example: A trading agent proposes rolling a futures position three days before expiry; the order ticket appears in a review queue and is sent to the broker only after the portfolio owner clicks approve, with the approval recorded in the audit log.
Citation: OWASP, 'LLM01:2025 Prompt Injection' (OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications) — https://genai.owasp.org/llmrisk/llm01-prompt-injection/ (Prevention and Mitigation Strategies, item 5 (require human approval for high-risk actions))
Status: Reviewed

1433. Audit log
Domain: AI and knowledge engineering
Definition: A tamper-evident, time-ordered record of significant system events — actions taken, by whom or what, when, and with what inputs and outcomes — maintained for security, accountability, and forensics. NIST SP 800-92 provides guidance on establishing log management infrastructures and processes, covering log generation, protection, storage, analysis, and disposal across an organization.
Intuition: The black-box recorder of the system: when something goes wrong (or right), you can reconstruct exactly what happened, in order, and prove it wasn't rewritten afterward.
Mechanics: Components emit structured log records at defined events (authentication, tool calls, orders, approvals, overrides); records are transmitted to protected centralized storage with synchronized timestamps, integrity protection, access controls, and retention policies, and are analyzed for anomalies and compliance reporting.
Relationships: Source provenance, Citation traceability, Approval gate, Trading-agent guardrail, Reproducible analysis
Failure modes: Logs fail when they are incomplete (the decisive event was never logged), writable by the entity they monitor (the agent or attacker edits history), or too voluminous to analyze. Poor time synchronization across components destroys ordering, which is often the crucial evidence.
Misconceptions: Logging is not the same as monitoring: an unreviewed log only helps after the fact. Application-level 'history' features (chat transcripts) are not audit logs — they lack integrity protection and completeness guarantees.
Example: For every order an execution agent submits, the audit log records the model's proposal, the guardrail checks applied, the approver's decision, the broker's acknowledgment, and the fill — enabling reconstruction of any trading day.
Citation: NIST Special Publication 800-92, 'Guide to Computer Security Log Management' — https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/92/final (Publication abstract (NIST CSRC))
Status: Reviewed

1434. Reproducible analysis
Domain: AI and knowledge engineering
Definition: An analysis whose results can be independently regenerated from the same data, code, and documented procedure. The U.S. National Academies (2019) distinguish reproducibility — obtaining consistent results using the same input data, computational steps, methods, and code — from replicability, obtaining consistent results across studies aimed at the same question with new data.
Intuition: Someone else (or you, six months later) should be able to rerun the pipeline from the recorded inputs and get the same numbers — otherwise the result is a story, not a finding.
Mechanics: Reproducibility is engineered by pinning data versions, code, parameters, random seeds, and environments; recording provenance of every artifact; and automating the pipeline so re-execution is one command. Reports declare assumptions, costs, and evaluation splits so results can be checked rather than trusted.
Relationships: Source provenance, Audit log, Model evaluation, Golden dataset, Trust status
Failure modes: Silent dependencies break reproduction: unpinned library or data versions, hidden manual steps, nondeterministic components (including LLM calls at nonzero temperature), and lookahead-prone data handling that cannot be reconstructed later. Vendor data that is revised retroactively (e.g., restated fundamentals) makes past inputs unrecoverable unless snapshotted.
Misconceptions: Reproducibility is not a claim that the result is correct — a wrong analysis can be perfectly reproducible, and a true finding can be irreproducibly presented. 'The code is available' is not enough if the data and environment are not.
Example: A backtest report ships with the exact data snapshot, commit hash, parameter file, and seed; a reviewer reruns it and regenerates the identical equity curve and drawdown statistics before the strategy is discussed further.
Citation: National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 'Reproducibility and Replicability in Science' (2019) — https://nap.nationalacademies.org/catalog/25303/reproducibility-and-replicability-in-science (Study description (definitions of reproducibility and replicability))
Status: Reviewed

1435. Model drift
Domain: AI and knowledge engineering
Definition: The decay of a deployed model's predictive performance over time as the world departs from the conditions captured in its training data. It is the observable symptom of underlying data drift or concept drift: the model stays the same, but the mapping it learned fits reality less and less.
Intuition: The model is a snapshot of how the world worked at training time; as the world moves on, the snapshot yellows — predictions get stale even though nothing in the model changed.
Mechanics: Production monitoring tracks performance proxies (error rate, calibration, business metrics) and input/output statistics against validation baselines; sustained degradation beyond tolerance triggers investigation into data drift or concept drift and, where warranted, retraining or recalibration. In markets, regime change, crowding of known effects, and structural breaks are the dominant drivers.
Relationships: Data drift, Concept drift, Model evaluation, Confidence calibration
Failure modes: Drift is hard to detect quickly when ground-truth labels arrive late (e.g., long-horizon trade outcomes), so degradation is discovered only after losses accumulate. Retraining on recent data can overfit the newest regime and discard still-valid older structure.
Misconceptions: Model drift does not mean the model's weights changed — deployed models are usually static; the environment moved. Monitoring aggregate accuracy alone misses drift concentrated in specific segments or regimes.
Example: A classifier that ranked momentum signals well through a trending year silently degrades after a volatility-regime shift; weekly monitoring shows its precision falling from 0.62 to 0.51 before anyone re-examines the strategy.
Citation: Lu et al., 'Learning under Concept Drift: A Review' (IEEE TKDE, 2018) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.05785 (Abstract)
Status: Reviewed

1436. Data drift
Domain: AI and knowledge engineering
Definition: A change over time in the distribution of a model's input data, P(X), while the relationship between inputs and labels may remain unchanged. In the concept-drift literature it is distinguished from 'real' concept drift: the world looks different, but the rule mapping features to outcomes has not (yet) changed.
Intuition: The questions arriving at the model change, even if the correct answers to each question would still be computed the same way — like an exam suddenly full of topics the course barely covered.
Mechanics: Detected by comparing the distribution of live inputs against training/validation baselines using per-feature statistics, population stability indices, or multivariate tests; sustained shift flags inputs the model may handle poorly because they are sparse in training data. Mitigations include retraining on current data, importance weighting, and input validation gates.
Formula: Data drift at time t: P_t(X) ≠ P_{t0}(X), possibly with P_t(y|X) = P_{t0}(y|X) unchanged, where t0 is the training-distribution reference time.
Relationships: Concept drift, Model drift, Model evaluation, Adversarial test
Failure modes: Distribution-shift detectors fire on benign seasonal or cyclical variation (alert fatigue) while missing slow multivariate drift no single feature reveals. Purely statistical detection cannot tell harmless shift from shift that actually hurts predictions.
Misconceptions: Data drift is not necessarily a data-quality bug — legitimate market evolution (new participants, new instruments) shifts inputs without any pipeline error. And passing input validation does not mean the model remains accurate on the shifted data.
Example: After a volatility regime change, the input feature '20-day realized vol' for an index-forex model shifts from a 8-15% range to a 25-40% range; the model now operates mostly on inputs near the edge of its training data.
Citation: Lu et al., 'Learning under Concept Drift: A Review' (IEEE TKDE, 2018) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.05785 (Abstract; taxonomy of drift types)
Status: Reviewed

1437. Concept drift
Domain: AI and knowledge engineering
Definition: An unforeseeable change over time in the underlying relationship between inputs and outputs — formally, a change in P(y|X) — so that the mapping a model learned no longer holds even for identical inputs. The concept-drift literature (e.g., Lu et al., IEEE TKDE) organizes the field into drift detection, drift understanding, and drift adaptation.
Intuition: The rules of the game changed: the same setup that used to mean 'buy' now means nothing — the model's knowledge itself is outdated, not just its inputs.
Mechanics: Drift may be sudden (structural breaks, rule changes), gradual, incremental, or recurring (regimes). Detection uses error-rate monitoring and statistical change tests; adaptation uses incremental learning, sliding windows, or ensemble reweighting. In trading, crowding out of an anomaly, a central-bank regime shift, or a market-structure rule change are canonical causes.
Formula: Concept drift between times t0 and t1: P_{t1}(y|X) ≠ P_{t0}(y|X) — the conditional distribution of the label given the features changes, with or without a change in P(X).
Relationships: Data drift, Model drift, Model evaluation, Confidence calibration
Failure modes: Concept drift can be invisible in input statistics (P(X) unchanged), so input-only monitoring misses it while errors accumulate. Adaptation mechanisms risk chasing noise: retraining on every apparent drift whipsaws the model and destroys stability.
Misconceptions: Concept drift is not the model 'forgetting' or a bug to be patched once — in non-stationary environments like markets it is a permanent operating condition requiring continuous detection and adaptation. Retraining on more old data does not help when the old relationship itself is obsolete.
Example: A carry-trade signal learned when central banks moved in sync stops working after policy divergence: identical interest-rate inputs now map to different outcomes, and only error-rate monitoring reveals the shift.
Citation: Lu et al., 'Learning under Concept Drift: A Review' (IEEE TKDE, 2018) — https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.05785 (Abstract)
Citation: Google for Developers, 'Machine Learning Glossary' — https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/glossary (Glossary entry: concept drift)
Status: Reviewed

1438. 2-period simple return
Domain: Parameterized analytics
Definition: The simple (holding-period) return of an asset between the current observation and the observation 2 periods earlier, expressed as the fractional change in price over that span. It is the standard discrete, non-compounded return measure applied to a 2-period lookback on any bar frequency (minutes, days, weeks, etc.).
Intuition: It answers: 'how much did the price move, in percentage terms, over the last 2 bars?' A 2-period simple return of 0.05 means the price is 5% higher than it was 2 periods ago.
Mechanics: Divide the current closing price by the closing price 2 periods earlier and subtract 1; the result is a fraction (multiply by 100 for a percentage). Standard implementation convention: pandas Series.pct_change(periods=2), which leaves the first 2 values undefined (NaN) because 2 prior observations are required; the span covers 2 sampling intervals and therefore uses 3 prices. Use split- and dividend-adjusted prices for a total-return measure; raw closes yield a price return only.
Formula: R_t(2) = P_t / P_(t-2) - 1 = (P_t - P_(t-2)) / P_(t-2), where P_t is the (adjusted) closing price at observation t and 2 is the lookback in periods. Multiply by 100 to express the result as a percentage.
Relationships: Simple return, Holding period return, Log return, Rate of change (ROC), Momentum, Total return
Failure modes: The measure depends only on the two endpoint prices, so a single outlier, stale quote, or illiquid print at either end distorts it, and it ignores the path taken in between. Overlapping 2-period windows also induce strong serial correlation in the resulting series, which invalidates naive statistical tests.
Misconceptions: A 2-period simple return is not 2 times the average one-period return (multi-period gains compound: R = product of (1 + r_i) - 1), and a +x% move is not cancelled by a later -x% move. It also excludes dividends unless adjusted prices are used, so it understates the total return of income-paying assets.
Example: On daily bars, a stock closed at $42.00 2 trading days ago and closes at $43.26 today; the 2-period simple return is 43.26/42.00 - 1 = +3.00%.
Citation: Business Finance (Mishra, Deakin University, 2023, CAUL OER Collective) — Topic 2: Risk and Return Part I, Concept 1: Measures of return (holding period return, percentage returns) — https://oer.uinsyahada.ac.id/files/original/05c3f1413aa8e4d238fed45431db5239.pdf (Topic 2, pp. 14-16 (holding period return; capital gains yield = (ending price - beginning price)/beginning price))
Citation: pandas.DataFrame.pct_change — pandas 3.0.5 documentation — https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.pct_change.html (Parameters: periods (int, default 1) — periods to shift for forming percent change)
Status: Reviewed

1442. 6-period simple return
Domain: Parameterized analytics
Definition: The simple (holding-period) return of an asset between the current observation and the observation 6 periods earlier, expressed as the fractional change in price over that span. It is the standard discrete, non-compounded return measure applied to a 6-period lookback on any bar frequency (minutes, days, weeks, etc.).
Intuition: It answers: 'how much did the price move, in percentage terms, over the last 6 bars?' A 6-period simple return of 0.05 means the price is 5% higher than it was 6 periods ago.
Mechanics: Divide the current closing price by the closing price 6 periods earlier and subtract 1; the result is a fraction (multiply by 100 for a percentage). Standard implementation convention: pandas Series.pct_change(periods=6), which leaves the first 6 values undefined (NaN) because 6 prior observations are required; the span covers 6 sampling intervals and therefore uses 7 prices. Use split- and dividend-adjusted prices for a total-return measure; raw closes yield a price return only.
Formula: R_t(6) = P_t / P_(t-6) - 1 = (P_t - P_(t-6)) / P_(t-6), where P_t is the (adjusted) closing price at observation t and 6 is the lookback in periods. Multiply by 100 to express the result as a percentage.
Relationships: Simple return, Holding period return, Log return, Rate of change (ROC), Momentum, Total return
Failure modes: The measure depends only on the two endpoint prices, so a single outlier, stale quote, or illiquid print at either end distorts it, and it ignores the path taken in between. Overlapping 6-period windows also induce strong serial correlation in the resulting series, which invalidates naive statistical tests.
Misconceptions: A 6-period simple return is not 6 times the average one-period return (multi-period gains compound: R = product of (1 + r_i) - 1), and a +x% move is not cancelled by a later -x% move. It also excludes dividends unless adjusted prices are used, so it understates the total return of income-paying assets.
Example: On daily bars, a stock closed at $46.00 6 trading days ago and closes at $46.92 today; the 6-period simple return is 46.92/46.00 - 1 = +2.00%.
Citation: Business Finance (Mishra, Deakin University, 2023, CAUL OER Collective) — Topic 2: Risk and Return Part I, Concept 1: Measures of return (holding period return, percentage returns) — https://oer.uinsyahada.ac.id/files/original/05c3f1413aa8e4d238fed45431db5239.pdf (Topic 2, pp. 14-16 (holding period return; capital gains yield = (ending price - beginning price)/beginning price))
Citation: pandas.DataFrame.pct_change — pandas 3.0.5 documentation — https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.pct_change.html (Parameters: periods (int, default 1) — periods to shift for forming percent change)

Formula: R_t(16) = P_t / P_(t-16) - 1 = (P_t - P_(t-16)) / P_(t-16), where P_t is the (adjusted) closing price at observation t and 16 is the lookback in periods. Multiply by 100 to express the result as a percentage.
Relationships: Simple return, Holding period return, Log return, Rate of change (ROC), Momentum, Total return
Failure modes: The measure depends only on the two endpoint prices, so a single outlier, stale quote, or illiquid print at either end distorts it, and it ignores the path taken in between. Overlapping 16-period windows also induce strong serial correlation in the resulting series, which invalidates naive statistical tests.
Misconceptions: A 16-period simple return is not 16 times the average one-period return (multi-period gains compound: R = product of (1 + r_i) - 1), and a +x% move is not cancelled by a later -x% move. It also excludes dividends unless adjusted prices are used, so it understates the total return of income-paying assets.
Example: On daily bars, a stock closed at $56.00 16 trading days ago and closes at $57.40 today; the 16-period simple return is 57.40/56.00 - 1 = +2.50%.
Citation: Business Finance (Mishra, Deakin University, 2023, CAUL OER Collective) — Topic 2: Risk and Return Part I, Concept 1: Measures of return (holding period return, percentage returns) — https://oer.uinsyahada.ac.id/files/original/05c3f1413aa8e4d238fed45431db5239.pdf (Topic 2, pp. 14-16 (holding period return; capital gains yield = (ending price - beginning price)/beginning price))
Citation: pandas.DataFrame.pct_change — pandas 3.0.5 documentation — https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.pct_change.html (Parameters: periods (int, default 1) — periods to shift for forming percent change)
Status: Reviewed

1453. 17-period simple return
Domain: Parameterized analytics
Definition: The simple (holding-period) return of an asset between the current observation and the observation 17 periods earlier, expressed as the fractional change in price over that span. It is the standard discrete, non-compounded return measure applied to a 17-period lookback on any bar frequency (minutes, days, weeks, etc.).
Intuition: It answers: 'how much did the price move, in percentage terms, over the last 17 bars?' A 17-period simple return of 0.05 means the price is 5% higher than it was 17 periods ago.
Mechanics: Divide the current closing price by the closing price 17 periods earlier and subtract 1; the result is a fraction (multiply by 100 for a percentage). Standard implementation convention: pandas Series.pct_change(periods=17), which leaves the first 17 values undefined (NaN) because 17 prior observations are required; the span covers 17 sampling intervals and therefore uses 18 prices. Use split- and dividend-adjusted prices for a total-return measure; raw closes yield a price return only.
Formula: R_t(17) = P_t / P_(t-17) - 1 = (P_t - P_(t-17)) / P_(t-17), where P_t is the (adjusted) closing price at observation t and 17 is the lookback in periods. Multiply by 100 to express the result as a percentage.
Relationships: Simple return, Holding period return, Log return, Rate of change (ROC), Momentum, Total return
Failure modes: The measure depends only on the two endpoint prices, so a single outlier, stale quote, or illiquid print at either end distorts it, and it ignores the path taken in between. Overlapping 17-period windows also induce strong serial correlation in the resulting series, which invalidates naive statistical tests.
Misconceptions: A 17-period simple return is not 17 times the average one-period return (multi-period gains compound: R = product of (1 + r_i) - 1), and a +x% move is not cancelled by a later -x% move. It also excludes dividends unless adjusted prices are used, so it understates the total return of income-paying assets.
Example: On daily bars, a stock closed at $57.00 17 trading days ago and closes at $57.68 today; the 17-period simple return is 57.68/57.00 - 1 = +1.19%.

1463. 27-period simple return
Domain: Parameterized analytics
Definition: The simple (holding-period) return of an asset between the current observation and the observation 27 periods earlier, expressed as the fractional change in price over that span. It is the standard discrete, non-compounded return measure applied to a 27-period lookback on any bar frequency (minutes, days, weeks, etc.).
Intuition: It answers: 'how much did the price move, in percentage terms, over the last 27 bars?' A 27-period simple return of 0.05 means the price is 5% higher than it was 27 periods ago.
Mechanics: Divide the current closing price by the closing price 27 periods earlier and subtract 1; the result is a fraction (multiply by 100 for a percentage). Standard implementation convention: pandas Series.pct_change(periods=27), which leaves the first 27 values undefined (NaN) because 27 prior observations are required; the span covers 27 sampling intervals and therefore uses 28 prices. Use split- and dividend-adjusted prices for a total-return measure; raw closes yield a price return only.
Formula: R_t(27) = P_t / P_(t-27) - 1 = (P_t - P_(t-27)) / P_(t-27), where P_t is the (adjusted) closing price at observation t and 27 is the lookback in periods. Multiply by 100 to express the result as a percentage.
Relationships: Simple return, Holding period return, Log return, Rate of change (ROC), Momentum, Total return
Failure modes: The measure depends only on the two endpoint prices, so a single outlier, stale quote, or illiquid print at either end distorts it, and it ignores the path taken in between. Overlapping 27-period windows also induce strong serial correlation in the resulting series, which invalidates naive statistical tests.
Misconceptions: A 27-period simple return is not 27 times the average one-period return (multi-period gains compound: R = product of (1 + r_i) - 1), and a +x% move is not cancelled by a later -x% move. It also excludes dividends unless adjusted prices are used, so it understates the total return of income-paying assets.
Example: On daily bars, a stock closed at $67.00 27 trading days ago and closes at $66.33 today; the 27-period simple return is 66.33/67.00 - 1 = -1.00%.
Citation: Business Finance (Mishra, Deakin University, 2023, CAUL OER Collective) — Topic 2: Risk and Return Part I, Concept 1: Measures of return (holding period return, percentage returns) — https://oer.uinsyahada.ac.id/files/original/05c3f1413aa8e4d238fed45431db5239.pdf (Topic 2, pp. 14-16 (holding period return; capital gains yield = (ending price - beginning price)/beginning price))
Citation: pandas.DataFrame.pct_change — pandas 3.0.5 documentation — https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.pct_change.html (Parameters: periods (int, default 1) — periods to shift for forming percent change)
Status: Reviewed

Example: On daily bars, a stock closed at $77.00 37 trading days ago and closes at $75.84 today; the 37-period simple return is 75.84/77.00 - 1 = -1.51%.
Citation: Business Finance (Mishra, Deakin University, 2023, CAUL OER Collective) — Topic 2: Risk and Return Part I, Concept 1: Measures of return (holding period return, percentage returns) — https://oer.uinsyahada.ac.id/files/original/05c3f1413aa8e4d238fed45431db5239.pdf (Topic 2, pp. 14-16 (holding period return; capital gains yield = (ending price - beginning price)/beginning price))
Citation: pandas.DataFrame.pct_change — pandas 3.0.5 documentation — https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.pct_change.html (Parameters: periods (int, default 1) — periods to shift for forming percent change)
Status: Reviewed

1474. 38-period simple return
Domain: Parameterized analytics
Definition: The simple (holding-period) return of an asset between the current observation and the observation 38 periods earlier, expressed as the fractional change in price over that span. It is the standard discrete, non-compounded return measure applied to a 38-period lookback on any bar frequency (minutes, days, weeks, etc.).
Intuition: It answers: 'how much did the price move, in percentage terms, over the last 38 bars?' A 38-period simple return of 0.05 means the price is 5% higher than it was 38 periods ago.
Mechanics: Divide the current closing price by the closing price 38 periods earlier and subtract 1; the result is a fraction (multiply by 100 for a percentage). Standard implementation convention: pandas Series.pct_change(periods=38), which leaves the first 38 values undefined (NaN) because 38 prior observations are required; the span covers 38 sampling intervals and therefore uses 39 prices. Use split- and dividend-adjusted prices for a total-return measure; raw closes yield a price return only.
Formula: R_t(38) = P_t / P_(t-38) - 1 = (P_t - P_(t-38)) / P_(t-38), where P_t is the (adjusted) closing price at observation t and 38 is the lookback in periods. Multiply by 100 to express the result as a percentage.
Relationships: Simple return, Holding period return, Log return, Rate of change (ROC), Momentum, Total return
Failure modes: The measure depends only on the two endpoint prices, so a single outlier, stale quote, or illiquid print at either end distorts it, and it ignores the path taken in between. Overlapping 38-period windows also induce strong serial correlation in the resulting series, which invalidates naive statistical tests.
Misconceptions: A 38-period simple return is not 38 times the average one-period return (multi-period gains compound: R = product of (1 + r_i) - 1), and a +x% move is not cancelled by a later -x% move. It also excludes dividends unless adjusted prices are used, so it understates the total return of income-paying assets.
Example: On daily bars, a stock closed at $78.00 38 trading days ago and closes at $80.34 today; the 38-period simple return is 80.34/78.00 - 1 = +3.00%.
Citation: Business Finance (Mishra, Deakin University, 2023, CAUL OER Collective) — Topic 2: Risk and Return Part I, Concept 1: Measures of return (holding period return, percentage returns) — https://oer.uinsyahada.ac.id/files/original/05c3f1413aa8e4d238fed45431db5239.pdf (Topic 2, pp. 14-16 (holding period return; capital gains yield = (ending price - beginning price)/beginning price))
Citation: pandas.DataFrame.pct_change — pandas 3.0.5 documentation — https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.pct_change.html (Parameters: periods (int, default 1) — periods to shift for forming percent change)
Status: Reviewed

Formula: R_t(48) = P_t / P_(t-48) - 1 = (P_t - P_(t-48)) / P_(t-48), where P_t is the (adjusted) closing price at observation t and 48 is the lookback in periods. Multiply by 100 to express the result as a percentage.
Relationships: Simple return, Holding period return, Log return, Rate of change (ROC), Momentum, Total return
Failure modes: The measure depends only on the two endpoint prices, so a single outlier, stale quote, or illiquid print at either end distorts it, and it ignores the path taken in between. Overlapping 48-period windows also induce strong serial correlation in the resulting series, which invalidates naive statistical tests.
Misconceptions: A 48-period simple return is not 48 times the average one-period return (multi-period gains compound: R = product of (1 + r_i) - 1), and a +x% move is not cancelled by a later -x% move. It also excludes dividends unless adjusted prices are used, so it understates the total return of income-paying assets.
Example: On daily bars, a stock closed at $88.00 48 trading days ago and closes at $89.76 today; the 48-period simple return is 89.76/88.00 - 1 = +2.00%.
Citation: Business Finance (Mishra, Deakin University, 2023, CAUL OER Collective) — Topic 2: Risk and Return Part I, Concept 1: Measures of return (holding period return, percentage returns) — https://oer.uinsyahada.ac.id/files/original/05c3f1413aa8e4d238fed45431db5239.pdf (Topic 2, pp. 14-16 (holding period return; capital gains yield = (ending price - beginning price)/beginning price))
Citation: pandas.DataFrame.pct_change — pandas 3.0.5 documentation — https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.pct_change.html (Parameters: periods (int, default 1) — periods to shift for forming percent change)
Status: Reviewed

1485. 49-period simple return
Domain: Parameterized analytics
Definition: The simple (holding-period) return of an asset between the current observation and the observation 49 periods earlier, expressed as the fractional change in price over that span. It is the standard discrete, non-compounded return measure applied to a 49-period lookback on any bar frequency (minutes, days, weeks, etc.).
Intuition: It answers: 'how much did the price move, in percentage terms, over the last 49 bars?' A 49-period simple return of 0.05 means the price is 5% higher than it was 49 periods ago.
Mechanics: Divide the current closing price by the closing price 49 periods earlier and subtract 1; the result is a fraction (multiply by 100 for a percentage). Standard implementation convention: pandas Series.pct_change(periods=49), which leaves the first 49 values undefined (NaN) because 49 prior observations are required; the span covers 49 sampling intervals and therefore uses 50 prices. Use split- and dividend-adjusted prices for a total-return measure; raw closes yield a price return only.
Formula: R_t(49) = P_t / P_(t-49) - 1 = (P_t - P_(t-49)) / P_(t-49), where P_t is the (adjusted) closing price at observation t and 49 is the lookback in periods. Multiply by 100 to express the result as a percentage.
Relationships: Simple return, Holding period return, Log return, Rate of change (ROC), Momentum, Total return
Failure modes: The measure depends only on the two endpoint prices, so a single outlier, stale quote, or illiquid print at either end distorts it, and it ignores the path taken in between. Overlapping 49-period windows also induce strong serial correlation in the resulting series, which invalidates naive statistical tests.
Misconceptions: A 49-period simple return is not 49 times the average one-period return (multi-period gains compound: R = product of (1 + r_i) - 1), and a +x% move is not cancelled by a later -x% move. It also excludes dividends unless adjusted prices are used, so it understates the total return of income-paying assets.
Example: On daily bars, a stock closed at $89.00 49 trading days ago and closes at $87.66 today; the 49-period simple return is 87.66/89.00 - 1 = -1.51%.
Citation: Business Finance (Mishra, Deakin University, 2023, CAUL OER Collective) — Topic 2: Risk and Return Part I, Concept 1: Measures of return (holding period return, percentage returns) — https://oer.uinsyahada.ac.id/files/original/05c3f1413aa8e4d238fed45431db5239.pdf (Topic 2, pp. 14-16 (holding period return; capital gains yield = (ending price - beginning price)/beginning price))

1495. 59-period simple return
Domain: Parameterized analytics
Definition: The simple (holding-period) return of an asset between the current observation and the observation 59 periods earlier, expressed as the fractional change in price over that span. It is the standard discrete, non-compounded return measure applied to a 59-period lookback on any bar frequency (minutes, days, weeks, etc.).
Intuition: It answers: 'how much did the price move, in percentage terms, over the last 59 bars?' A 59-period simple return of 0.05 means the price is 5% higher than it was 59 periods ago.
Mechanics: Divide the current closing price by the closing price 59 periods earlier and subtract 1; the result is a fraction (multiply by 100 for a percentage). Standard implementation convention: pandas Series.pct_change(periods=59), which leaves the first 59 values undefined (NaN) because 59 prior observations are required; the span covers 59 sampling intervals and therefore uses 60 prices. Use split- and dividend-adjusted prices for a total-return measure; raw closes yield a price return only.
Formula: R_t(59) = P_t / P_(t-59) - 1 = (P_t - P_(t-59)) / P_(t-59), where P_t is the (adjusted) closing price at observation t and 59 is the lookback in periods. Multiply by 100 to express the result as a percentage.
Relationships: Simple return, Holding period return, Log return, Rate of change (ROC), Momentum, Total return
Failure modes: The measure depends only on the two endpoint prices, so a single outlier, stale quote, or illiquid print at either end distorts it, and it ignores the path taken in between. Overlapping 59-period windows also induce strong serial correlation in the resulting series, which invalidates naive statistical tests.
Misconceptions: A 59-period simple return is not 59 times the average one-period return (multi-period gains compound: R = product of (1 + r_i) - 1), and a +x% move is not cancelled by a later -x% move. It also excludes dividends unless adjusted prices are used, so it understates the total return of income-paying assets.
Example: On daily bars, a stock closed at $99.00 59 trading days ago and closes at $100.19 today; the 59-period simple return is 100.19/99.00 - 1 = +1.20%.
Citation: Business Finance (Mishra, Deakin University, 2023, CAUL OER Collective) — Topic 2: Risk and Return Part I, Concept 1: Measures of return (holding period return, percentage returns) — https://oer.uinsyahada.ac.id/files/original/05c3f1413aa8e4d238fed45431db5239.pdf (Topic 2, pp. 14-16 (holding period return; capital gains yield = (ending price - beginning price)/beginning price))
Citation: pandas.DataFrame.pct_change — pandas 3.0.5 documentation — https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.DataFrame.pct_change.html (Parameters: periods (int, default 1) — periods to shift for forming percent change)
Status: Reviewed
